sourceNotes.summary: Specifications were checked live on aqa.org.uk during the build of this scheme (30 August 2026). NONE of the six specifications used here has been reformed for summer 2028 examinations: all remain the 2015-2017 first-teaching specifications. practicalRisksForAPrivateCandidate: DESIGN AND TECHNOLOGY 8552 is the highest risk: the NEA is 50% of the grade, takes 30-35 supervised hours, requires workshop facilities, and must be marked and authenticated by the centre. Contextual challenges are released 1 June 2027 (end of Year 10), so the centre relationship must be in place from the start of Year 10. Many centres that accept private candidates will not accept D&T.

GEOGRAPHY 8035 requires two fieldwork enquiries and a signed written statement from the centre giving dates, locations, questions investigated and specification links. Failure to provide it constitutes malpractice. Plan the fieldwork in Year 10 with the centre's agreement.

ENGLISH LANGUAGE 8700 requires the Spoken Language endorsement to be delivered and recorded by a centre. The candidate can be entered without it, but the certificate will then show 'Not Classified' for spoken language. Confirm early whether the chosen centre offers it.

MATHEMATICS 8300, ENGLISH LITERATURE 8702 and BUSINESS 8132 are 100% examined with no centre-assessed component and are straightforward for a private candidate at any centre accepting external entries.

Tier decision for Mathematics (Foundation or Higher) is normally confirmed in spring of Year 11. This scheme assumes Higher and deliberately secures the whole Foundation crossover during Year 10 so that either decision remains open.

subjects.name: GCSE Mathematics
subjects.notes: AQA GCSE Mathematics 8300, Higher tier. AQA is the largest maths board in England and 8300 has NOT been reformed for 2028 exams; the subject content is the DfE 2015 content, coded N1-N16 (number), A1-A25 (algebra), R1-R16 (ratio, proportion and rates of change), G1-G25 (geometry and measures), P1-P9 (probability) and S1-S6 (statistics). Assessment is three 1h30 papers of 80 marks each (Paper 1 non-calculator, Papers 2 and 3 calculator), sat summer 2028. Following Ofqual's decision (published 2024), from the 2028 series onwards exam boards must publish the formulae sheet by 1 September of the preceding year and supply a clean copy in the exam, and cannot set questions answerable purely by copying from the sheet - so this candidate WILL have a formulae sheet, but must still know when each formula applies. Higher tier is assumed (grades 4-9); the tier decision is normally confirmed in the spring of Year 11, so Year 10 deliberately secures the whole Foundation crossover before layering Higher-only content. Topic weighting at Higher: Number 15%, Algebra 30%, Ratio 20%, Geometry 20%, Probability and Statistics 15% - which is why Autumn is algebra-heavy.
deferredToYear11: Completing the square, and the turning point of a quadratic from completed-square form (A11, A18 Higher) - conventionally Year 11 because it depends on secure quadratic factorisation and surd fluency built in Year 10.
Simultaneous equations where one equation is quadratic (A19 Higher) - needs both quadratic solving and straight-line/circle graphs, all of which land across Year 10.
Iterative methods for approximate solutions (A20) - a short Year 11 topic that depends on calculator fluency and on interpreting graphs of cubics.
Functions: function notation, composite and inverse functions (A7 Higher) - taught in Year 11 in almost all schemes as it abstracts over algebra already secure.
Full graph transformation work including transformations of trigonometric graphs (A13) - Year 10 covers the basic four transformations only.
Adding and subtracting algebraic fractions, and solving equations containing algebraic fractions (A4 Higher) - Year 11, after quadratic factorisation is automatic.
Quadratic inequalities and regions bounded by curves (A22 Higher) - Year 11.
Circle theorems and their proofs (G10 Higher) - the single largest deferred block. Conventionally Year 11 because it requires the whole angle-reasoning toolkit of Year 10 plus proof discipline.
The sine rule, the cosine rule and Area = 1/2 ab sin C (G22, G23 Higher) - Year 11, immediately after right-angled trigonometry has become automatic.
3D trigonometry in non-right-angled figures (G20 Higher) - Year 11.
Vector geometry: constructing geometric arguments and proofs with vectors (G25 Higher) - Year 11.
Histograms with unequal class widths and frequency density (S3 Higher) - Year 11.
Full upper and lower bounds problem solving in compound-measure contexts (N16 Higher) - introduced in Year 10, extended in Year 11.
Gradient of a curve as instantaneous rate of change in modelling contexts (R15 Higher) - introduced in Year 10 Summer 1, developed fully in Year 11.
Frustums, and similar-solid problems combining area and volume scale factors with mensuration (G17, G19 Higher) - Year 11.

weeks.unit: Number: integers, place value and the four operations

lessons.title: Place value, ordering and rounding integers and decimals
objectives: I can order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions using <, > and =
I can round any number to a given number of decimal places or significant figures
misconceptions: Thinking -8 is larger than -3 because 8 > 3
Counting the leading zeros in 0.00456 as significant figures
Rounding 2.999 to 1 d.p. as 2.9 instead of 3.0

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: The four operations with integers and decimals (written methods)
objectives: I can use column methods for addition and subtraction of decimals
I can use long multiplication and short/long division with decimals
I can use the order of operations correctly
misconceptions: Applying BIDMAS left-to-right so 3 + 4 x 2 = 14
Misaligning decimal points when adding decimals
Believing division is commutative, so 12 divided by 4 equals 4 divided by 12

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Negative numbers and directed number arithmetic
objectives: I can add, subtract, multiply and divide directed numbers
I can apply directed number rules within substitution and context problems
misconceptions: Treating - - as negative rather than positive
Thinking the product of two negatives is negative
Losing the sign when squaring, e.g. (-3)^2 = -9

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: The order of operations is brackets, indices, division/multiplication (left to right), addition/subtraction (left to right).
On a number line, a number further left is always smaller.
To round to n significant figures, count from the first non-zero digit.
Rounding a 5 rounds up by convention.
A number written to 2 d.p. has exactly two digits after the decimal point.
To multiply decimals, ignore the points, multiply as integers, then place the point so the total number of decimal places matches the question.
To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by a power of 10 until the divisor is an integer.
Multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive number smaller.
Subtracting a negative is the same as adding the positive.
A negative times a negative gives a positive; a negative times a positive gives a negative.
(-a)^2 is positive for any non-zero a; -a^2 is negative.
Zero is neither positive nor negative.

weeks.unit: Number: factors, multiples, primes and systematic listing

lessons.title: Factors, multiples and prime numbers
objectives: I can list the factors and multiples of a number
I can identify prime numbers and explain why 1 is not prime
misconceptions: Believing 1 is prime
Believing 2 is not prime because it is even
Confusing factors (which divide into) with multiples (which are built from)

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Prime factor decomposition and index form
objectives: I can express any integer as a product of its prime factors using a factor tree
I can write the product of primes in index form
misconceptions: Leaving a composite number such as 4 in the final answer
Writing the answer as a sum rather than a product
Assuming a different factor tree gives a different final answer

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: HCF and LCM using prime factors and Venn diagrams
objectives: I can find the HCF and LCM of two or more numbers using prime factorisation
I can solve worded problems that require deciding between HCF and LCM
misconceptions: Choosing the LCM when the context needs the HCF (e.g. cutting into equal pieces)
Multiplying the two numbers and calling it the LCM without dividing by the HCF
Reading the HCF as everything in the Venn diagram rather than only the intersection

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

knowledgeComponents.statement: A prime number has exactly two distinct factors: 1 and itself.
1 is not prime because it has only one factor.
2 is the only even prime number.
Every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation.
To build a factor tree, split repeatedly until every branch end is prime.
The HCF is the product of the primes common to both factorisations, using the lower power of each.
The LCM is the product of all primes appearing in either factorisation, using the higher power of each.
HCF(a,b) x LCM(a,b) = a x b.
In a Venn diagram of prime factors, the intersection gives the HCF and the whole union gives the LCM.
A number is divisible by 3 if its digit sum is divisible by 3.
A square number has an odd number of factors.
The product rule for counting: if there are m ways of doing one thing and n ways of doing another, there are m x n combined outcomes.

weeks.unit: Number: indices, roots and standard form

lessons.title: Laws of indices with integer powers
objectives: I can apply the multiplication, division and power laws of indices
I can interpret zero and negative indices
misconceptions: Adding the bases as well as the indices when multiplying
Thinking a negative index makes the answer negative rather than a reciprocal
Thinking x^0 = 0 rather than 1

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Fractional indices and roots (Higher)
objectives: I can evaluate expressions with fractional indices
I can convert between root notation and index notation
misconceptions: Reading 8^(2/3) as 8 x 2/3
Applying the power before the root without checking which is easier
Thinking a negative fractional index means a negative answer

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Standard form: calculating and interpreting
objectives: I can write large and small numbers in standard form
I can multiply and divide numbers in standard form without a calculator
I can enter and interpret standard form on a calculator
misconceptions: Leaving an answer such as 34 x 10^5 in non-standard form
Getting the sign of the index wrong for small numbers
Adding the indices when adding numbers in standard form

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: give your answer in standard form

knowledgeComponents.statement: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n).
a^m / a^n = a^(m-n).
(a^m)^n = a^(mn).
a^0 = 1 for any non-zero a.
a^(1/n) is the nth root of a.
a^(m/n) = (nth root of a) raised to the power m.
A number in standard form is written A x 10^n where 1 <= A < 10 and n is an integer.
To multiply numbers in standard form, multiply the A values and add the indices.
To divide numbers in standard form, divide the A values and subtract the indices.
A negative index in standard form indicates a number less than 1.
To add or subtract in standard form, convert to ordinary numbers or make the indices equal first.

weeks.unit: Number: fractions

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting fractions and mixed numbers
objectives: I can add and subtract fractions using a common denominator
I can convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators separately
Forgetting to deal with the integer parts of mixed numbers
Choosing a common denominator but failing to scale the numerator

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
objectives: I can multiply fractions and mixed numbers
I can divide by a fraction by multiplying by its reciprocal
misconceptions: Finding a common denominator before multiplying
Inverting the first fraction rather than the second when dividing
Believing multiplication always makes numbers bigger

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question
commandWords: give your answer in its simplest form

lessons.title: Fractions as operators and fractions of amounts
objectives: I can find a fraction of a quantity and reverse the process
I can solve problems where fractions act on other fractions
misconceptions: Multiplying by the reciprocal when reversing is not required
Treating 'two thirds of the remainder' as two thirds of the original
Adding fractions of different wholes

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

knowledgeComponents.statement: To add or subtract fractions, rewrite them with a common denominator, then add or subtract only the numerators.
A mixed number a b/c equals (a x c + b)/c as an improper fraction.
Two fractions are equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by multiplying numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number.
To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators.
The reciprocal of a/b is b/a.
Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.
Cancelling common factors before multiplying keeps numbers small and gives the answer in simplest form.
Multiplying by a proper fraction reduces a positive quantity.
To find a fraction of an amount, divide by the denominator and multiply by the numerator.
To reverse 'x is 3/5 of y', divide x by 3 and multiply by 5.
The word 'of' between a fraction and a quantity means multiply.
A fraction is in its simplest form when the HCF of numerator and denominator is 1.

weeks.unit: Number: decimals, estimation and limits of accuracy

lessons.title: Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages, including recurring decimals
objectives: I can convert terminating decimals to fractions and back
I can convert a recurring decimal to a fraction using an algebraic method
misconceptions: Multiplying by the wrong power of 10 for the recurring block length
Thinking every fraction gives a recurring decimal

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Estimation and checking calculations
objectives: I can round numbers to 1 significant figure to estimate a calculation
I can state whether an estimate is an over- or under-estimate and justify it
misconceptions: Rounding to 1 s.f. only some of the numbers
Estimating then giving an exact answer
Not explaining the direction of the error when asked

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Error intervals and truncation
objectives: I can write the error interval for a rounded or truncated value
I can use inequality notation for upper and lower bounds
misconceptions: Using a strict inequality on the lower bound
Giving the upper bound as 4.49 rather than 4.5 for a value rounded to 1 d.p.
Treating truncation the same as rounding

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: A fraction gives a terminating decimal exactly when its denominator, in simplest form, has only 2s and 5s as prime factors.
To convert a recurring decimal to a fraction, set x equal to the decimal, multiply by 10^n where n is the length of the recurring block, and subtract.
0.1 recurring = 1/9, 0.01 recurring = 1/99.
To convert a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100.
To estimate, round every number in the calculation to 1 significant figure.
Rounding the divisor down makes the estimated quotient larger than the true value.
The symbol for 'approximately equal to' is a wavy equals sign.
A value x rounded to the nearest 10 has error interval 'lower bound <= x < upper bound', where the bounds are 5 either side.
The upper bound is never included in the error interval when rounding.
Truncation always cuts digits off, so the truncated value is the lower bound of the interval.
For a length given as 8.6 cm to 1 d.p., the error interval is 8.55 <= L < 8.65.
Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit reading left to right.

weeks.unit: Number: surds and exact calculation

lessons.title: Simplifying surds
objectives: I can simplify a surd by extracting square factors
I can add and subtract like surds
misconceptions: Believing root(a) + root(b) equals root(a+b)
Failing to extract the largest square factor
Adding unlike surds such as root2 + root3

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question
commandWords: write in the form a root b

lessons.title: Multiplying and expanding brackets with surds
objectives: I can multiply surds and simplify the result
I can expand double brackets containing surds
misconceptions: Thinking root(a) x root(a) is still a surd
Forgetting the cross terms when expanding
Assuming the product of two surds is always irrational

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Rationalising the denominator
objectives: I can rationalise a denominator of the form root(a)
I can rationalise a denominator of the form a + root(b) using the conjugate
misconceptions: Multiplying only the denominator by the surd
Using the same sign rather than the conjugate
Failing to simplify the resulting fraction

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question
commandWords: give your answer in the form

knowledgeComponents.statement: A surd is an irrational root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction.
root(a) x root(b) = root(ab).
root(a) / root(b) = root(a/b).
root(a) + root(b) does not equal root(a+b).
To simplify a surd, write the number as a product with the largest possible square factor.
root(50) = 5 root(2).
Only like surds can be collected, in the same way as like algebraic terms.
root(a) x root(a) = a.
Expanding (a + root b)(c + root d) needs all four products.
To rationalise 1/root(a), multiply numerator and denominator by root(a).
The conjugate of a + root(b) is a - root(b).
(a + root b)(a - root b) = a^2 - b, which is rational.

weeks.unit: Algebra: notation, collecting terms and expanding

lessons.title: Algebraic notation, terms and substitution
objectives: I can use correct algebraic notation for products, powers and division
I can substitute positive and negative values into expressions and formulae
misconceptions: Reading 3x^2 as (3x)^2
Losing brackets when substituting a negative value
Treating ab as a + b

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Collecting like terms and simplifying
objectives: I can simplify expressions by collecting like terms
I can simplify products and quotients involving indices
misconceptions: Collecting x and x^2 as like terms
Dropping the sign attached to a term when reordering
Adding indices when adding terms rather than multiplying

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Expanding single and double brackets
objectives: I can expand and simplify expressions with one or more sets of brackets
I can expand two binomials and collect like terms
misconceptions: Only multiplying the first term inside the bracket
Sign errors when the bracket is preceded by a minus
Forgetting the middle term when squaring a binomial

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: A term is a single number, variable, or product of these; terms are separated by + or - signs.
The coefficient is the number multiplying the variable part of a term.
3x^2 means 3 multiplied by x squared, not (3x) squared.
An expression has no equals sign; an equation does; an identity is true for all values.
When substituting a negative value, always write it in brackets first.
Like terms have exactly the same variable part including powers.
x + x + x = 3x, but x times x times x = x^3.
To simplify a(b) x c(b), multiply the coefficients and add the indices of matching variables.
a(b + c) = ab + ac.
(x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a+b)x + ab.
(x + a)^2 = x^2 + 2ax + a^2, so the middle term must not be omitted.
(x + a)(x - a) = x^2 - a^2 (the difference of two squares).

weeks.unit: Algebra: factorising and linear equations (Autumn 1 assessment)

lessons.title: Factorising into a single bracket
objectives: I can take out the highest common factor of an algebraic expression
I can factorise expressions involving powers of a variable
misconceptions: Taking out only part of the common factor
Losing a term when the HCF equals a whole term (leaving nothing rather than 1)
Confusing factorising with expanding

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Solving linear equations, including unknowns on both sides and with brackets
objectives: I can solve linear equations with brackets and fractions
I can solve equations with the unknown on both sides
misconceptions: Only applying an operation to one side of the equation
Dividing before expanding a bracket incorrectly
Sign errors when moving negative terms across the equals sign

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Autumn 1 assessment: number and algebraic manipulation
objectives: I can apply number and algebra skills to unfamiliar multi-step problems
I can present my working clearly enough for method marks
misconceptions: Writing only a final answer and losing method marks
Rounding partway through a multi-step calculation
Ignoring instructions such as 'give your answer in its simplest form'

assessment.type: Mixed non-calculator and calculator assessment paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: To factorise, write the HCF outside the bracket and what remains inside.
Factorising fully means the terms inside the bracket share no further common factor.
6x^2 + 9x factorises to 3x(2x + 3).
If the HCF equals a whole term, a 1 must be left inside the bracket.
Expanding a factorised expression should return the original expression - this is the check.
An equation stays balanced when the same operation is applied to both sides.
To solve, undo operations in reverse order of BIDMAS.
To clear a fraction in an equation, multiply every term on both sides by the denominator.
Collect the unknowns on the side where the coefficient will stay positive.
A linear equation in one unknown has exactly one solution unless it simplifies to a contradiction or an identity.
Substituting the solution back into the original equation checks the answer.
Method marks are awarded for correct process even when the final answer is wrong.

weeks.unit: Algebra: quadratic expressions

lessons.title: Expanding products of two and three binomials
objectives: I can expand and simplify the product of two binomials
I can expand the product of three binomials (Higher)
misconceptions: Missing the cross terms in a triple expansion
Sign errors when both brackets contain negatives
Failing to simplify after expanding

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Factorising quadratics of the form x^2 + bx + c
objectives: I can factorise a quadratic where the coefficient of x^2 is 1
I can recognise and factorise the difference of two squares
misconceptions: Choosing factors that add rather than multiply to give c
Getting the signs the wrong way round when c is negative
Trying to factorise x^2 + a^2 as a difference of two squares

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Factorising quadratics of the form ax^2 + bx + c (Higher)
objectives: I can factorise a quadratic with a leading coefficient greater than 1
I can use the splitting-the-middle-term method reliably
misconceptions: Forgetting to multiply a by c when finding the factor pair
Losing a sign when grouping
Not checking by re-expanding

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: (x + a)(x + b) expands to x^2 + (a+b)x + ab.
To expand three brackets, expand two first and then multiply the result by the third term by term.
A quadratic expression has degree 2; a cubic has degree 3.
To factorise x^2 + bx + c, find two numbers with product c and sum b.
x^2 + a^2 does not factorise over the real numbers.
If c is negative, the two factors have opposite signs.
If c is positive and b is negative, both factors are negative.
To factorise ax^2 + bx + c, find two numbers with product ac and sum b, split the middle term, then factorise by grouping.
6x^2 + 11x + 3 factorises to (3x + 1)(2x + 3).
Expanding the factorised form is the standard check for a factorisation.
Always take out a numerical common factor before attempting to factorise a quadratic.

weeks.unit: Algebra: solving quadratic equations

lessons.title: Solving quadratics by factorising
objectives: I can rearrange a quadratic equation into the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0
I can solve a quadratic equation by factorising and applying the zero product property
misconceptions: Dividing both sides by x and losing the root x = 0
Giving the factors rather than the solutions
Sign errors when reading solutions from brackets

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Solving quadratics using the quadratic formula (Higher)
objectives: I can use the quadratic formula to solve any quadratic equation
I can give solutions to a stated degree of accuracy or in surd form
misconceptions: Getting the sign of b wrong when b is negative
Only finding the + root and forgetting the - root
Failing to bracket -b^2 correctly on the calculator

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: give your answers to 2 decimal places

lessons.title: Setting up and solving quadratic equations from context
objectives: I can form a quadratic equation from a geometric or worded context
I can reject solutions that are not valid in the context
misconceptions: Accepting a negative length or a negative number of objects
Forgetting to set the equation equal to zero before solving
Not defining the variable at the start

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

knowledgeComponents.statement: If a product equals zero, at least one of its factors must be zero.
A quadratic equation must be rearranged to equal zero before factorising to solve.
A quadratic equation has at most two real solutions.
If (x - 3)(x + 5) = 0 then x = 3 or x = -5.
Dividing a quadratic equation through by x loses the root x = 0.
The quadratic formula is x = (-b +/- root(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a.
The quadratic formula is provided on the AQA formulae sheet from 2028.
The discriminant is b^2 - 4ac; if it is negative there are no real roots.
When b is negative, -b in the formula becomes positive.
If the discriminant is a perfect square, the quadratic factorises over the integers.
Define the unknown explicitly before forming an equation from a context.
A solution that gives a negative length, negative time or negative count must be rejected with a reason.
The area of a rectangle with sides x and x + 3 is x^2 + 3x.

weeks.unit: Algebra: formulae and algebraic fractions

lessons.title: Changing the subject of a formula
objectives: I can rearrange a formula to make a different variable the subject
I can rearrange formulae involving powers, roots and fractions
misconceptions: Taking the square root of only one term
Dividing by a term instead of subtracting it
Not applying an operation to the whole of both sides

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Changing the subject when the variable appears twice (Higher)
objectives: I can collect terms in the required subject on one side and factorise to isolate it
I can present the answer clearly as a single fraction
misconceptions: Failing to factorise after collecting terms
Cancelling terms rather than factors
Leaving the subject on both sides

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Simplifying algebraic fractions
objectives: I can simplify algebraic fractions by factorising numerator and denominator
I can multiply and divide algebraic fractions
misconceptions: Cancelling individual terms rather than whole factors
Cancelling across an addition sign
Forgetting to factorise before cancelling

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: The subject of a formula is the variable that stands alone on one side.
To change the subject, apply inverse operations to both sides in reverse BIDMAS order.
Squaring both sides is the inverse of taking a square root, and vice versa.
Multiplying every term by a denominator clears fractions from a formula.
When the required subject appears in two terms, collect those terms on one side.
After collecting, factorise out the required subject and divide by the bracket.
The result of making x the subject may legitimately be a fraction with a bracket in the denominator.
An algebraic fraction can only be simplified by cancelling a factor common to the whole numerator and the whole denominator.
(x^2 - 9)/(x + 3) simplifies to x - 3.
To divide algebraic fractions, multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction.
To add algebraic fractions, use a common denominator formed from the product or LCM of the denominators.
Cancelling across a + or - sign is invalid.

weeks.unit: Algebra: inequalities

lessons.title: Solving linear inequalities and representing solutions
objectives: I can solve linear inequalities algebraically
I can show a solution set on a number line and in set notation
misconceptions: Reversing the inequality sign when it is not required
Not reversing the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative
Using a closed circle for a strict inequality

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Inequalities in two variables and graphical regions (Higher)
objectives: I can represent a linear inequality in two variables as a region on a graph
I can identify a region satisfying several inequalities
misconceptions: Using a solid line for a strict inequality
Shading the wrong side of the boundary
Forgetting to test a point to decide which side to shade

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Error intervals, inequalities and bounds in context
objectives: I can use inequality notation to express limits of accuracy
I can solve simple problems using upper and lower bounds
misconceptions: Using the upper bound of the divisor to maximise a quotient
Adding bounds when subtracting quantities
Rounding bounds to the same accuracy as the data

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: An inequality is solved using the same balancing operations as an equation.
Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
An open circle on a number line means the endpoint is not included (< or >).
A closed (filled) circle means the endpoint is included (<= or >=).
-3 <= x < 4 has integer solutions -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3.
A double inequality is solved by performing the same operation on all three parts.
A dashed boundary line indicates the line itself is not part of the region.
To decide which side of a boundary to shade, substitute a test point such as the origin.
The region satisfying several inequalities is the overlap of all the individual regions.
To maximise a quotient a/b, use the upper bound of a and the lower bound of b.
To find the lower bound of a difference a - b, use the lower bound of a and the upper bound of b.
Bounds should not be rounded before the final answer is calculated.

weeks.unit: Algebra: sequences

lessons.title: Sequences, term-to-term and position-to-term rules
objectives: I can continue a sequence and describe its term-to-term rule
I can generate terms from a position-to-term rule
misconceptions: Confusing the term-to-term rule with the nth term
Assuming every sequence is linear
Starting the position count at 0

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: The nth term of a linear sequence
objectives: I can find the nth term rule of an arithmetic sequence
I can use the nth term to decide whether a number is in a sequence
misconceptions: Writing the nth term as the common difference plus n rather than times n
Using the first term as the constant instead of the zeroth term
Answering 'is 100 in the sequence?' without solving an equation

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Special sequences: triangular, square, cube, Fibonacci and geometric
objectives: I can recognise and continue triangular, square, cube, Fibonacci and geometric sequences
I can find missing terms in a Fibonacci-style sequence
lessons.specRef: A24 (Higher for geometric and other sequences)
misconceptions: Assuming any sequence that grows quickly is geometric
Using addition when the rule is multiplicative
Confusing the common ratio with the common difference

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: A term-to-term rule tells you how to get from one term to the next.
A position-to-term (nth term) rule gives any term directly from its position number.
In a linear (arithmetic) sequence, the difference between consecutive terms is constant.
The nth term of a linear sequence is dn + (first term - d), where d is the common difference.
For 5, 8, 11, 14 the nth term is 3n + 2.
To test whether a number is a term, set the nth term equal to it and check n is a positive integer.
A decreasing linear sequence has a negative coefficient of n.
The triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21.
The square numbers are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36.
The cube numbers are 1, 8, 27, 64, 125.
In a Fibonacci-type sequence each term is the sum of the two preceding terms.
In a geometric sequence each term is found by multiplying the previous term by a constant common ratio.
The nth term of a geometric sequence is a r^(n-1).

weeks.unit: Algebra: quadratic sequences and consolidation

lessons.title: The nth term of a quadratic sequence (Higher)
objectives: I can identify a quadratic sequence from its second differences
I can find the nth term of a quadratic sequence
misconceptions: Halving the second difference incorrectly, or forgetting to halve it
Stopping after finding the an^2 term
Confusing first and second differences

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question
commandWords: find an expression for the nth term

lessons.title: Algebraic proof and reasoning with number properties
objectives: I can write general expressions for odd, even and consecutive numbers
I can construct a simple algebraic proof
misconceptions: Testing a few cases and calling it a proof
Using the same letter for two different unknowns
Not stating the conclusion in words at the end

assessment.type: Reasoning and proof question (AO2)

lessons.title: Autumn 2 assessment: algebra
objectives: I can select and apply the right algebraic technique to unfamiliar problems
I can lay out working so that method marks are secured
misconceptions: Rushing to a numerical answer without algebra
Mixing up expanding and factorising instructions
Not answering the actual question asked (e.g. giving x when asked for the area)

assessment.type: Mixed algebra assessment paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: A quadratic sequence has constant second differences.
The coefficient of n^2 is half the second difference.
To find a quadratic nth term, subtract an^2 from each term and find the linear nth term of what remains.
The sequence of square numbers has nth term n^2 and second difference 2.
A cubic sequence has constant third differences.
Any even number can be written as 2n.
Any odd number can be written as 2n + 1.
Consecutive integers can be written n, n+1, n+2.
A multiple of 3 can be written as 3n for integer n.
A proof must hold for all cases, so it must use general algebra, not examples.
Showing an expression factorises as 2 x (something integer) proves it is even.
An identity uses the triple-bar symbol and is true for every value of the variable.

weeks.unit: Number and algebra: review, feedback and problem-solving

lessons.title: Assessment feedback and targeted correction
objectives: I can identify the specific error type in each question I lost marks on
I can redo each lost mark correctly and record the corrected method
misconceptions: Copying the answer without understanding the method
Attributing errors to carelessness rather than a knowledge gap
Not re-attempting a similar unseen question

assessment.type: Directed improvement and reflection task

lessons.title: Multi-step problem solving across number and algebra
objectives: I can break an unfamiliar problem into steps
I can decide which topic areas a problem is testing
misconceptions: Starting to calculate before reading the whole question
Not writing units or context in the final answer
Using a calculator method on a non-calculator paper

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

lessons.title: Calculator fluency and efficient methods
objectives: I can use the fraction, power, root and memory functions accurately
I can use the ANS key to avoid rounding errors mid-calculation
misconceptions: Rounding intermediate values and losing accuracy
Leaving the calculator in radians mode
Retyping a long decimal rather than using ANS

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: give your answer to 3 significant figures

knowledgeComponents.statement: An accuracy error is a slip in a correct method; a method error means the wrong process was chosen.
Retesting on a fresh similar question is the only reliable check that a misconception has been fixed.
Reading the whole question first identifies what the final answer must look like.
Underlining the command word tells you what type of response is required.
'You must show your working' means marks are unavailable for an unsupported answer.
Units must be included in a contextual answer when the question does not supply them.
Intermediate values should be kept to full calculator accuracy and rounded only at the end.
The ANS key recalls the full unrounded previous answer.
The calculator must be in degrees mode for GCSE trigonometry.
A calculator's fraction key gives exact values that a decimal would lose.
'Give your answer to 3 significant figures' overrides any earlier rounding instruction in the question.
Estimating the answer first flags calculator keying errors.

weeks.unit: Ratio: notation, sharing and comparison

lessons.title: Ratio notation, simplifying and equivalent ratios
objectives: I can write and simplify a ratio, including with units
I can write a ratio in the form 1 : n
misconceptions: Simplifying without converting to the same units first
Writing the ratio in the wrong order
Confusing a ratio with a fraction of the whole

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question
commandWords: give your answer in the form 1 : n

lessons.title: Dividing a quantity in a given ratio
objectives: I can share an amount in a given ratio
I can solve problems where one share or the difference between shares is known
misconceptions: Dividing by the largest number in the ratio rather than the total parts
Treating the given amount as the total when it is one share
Forgetting to check the shares add back to the total

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

lessons.title: Ratio and fractions, and combining ratios
objectives: I can convert between ratios and fractions of a whole
I can combine two ratios that share a common element
misconceptions: Reading a : b as the fraction a/b of the whole
Failing to scale both ratios so the shared element matches
Adding ratios term by term

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

knowledgeComponents.statement: A ratio a : b compares parts, not a part to the whole.
To simplify a ratio, divide all parts by their HCF.
Both quantities must be in the same units before a ratio is simplified.
To write a : b in the form 1 : n, divide both parts by a.
The order of a ratio matters: 3 : 5 is not the same as 5 : 3.
To share in a ratio, add the parts, divide the total by the number of parts, then multiply.
If the difference between two shares is given, divide that difference by the difference in parts.
A check for a sharing problem is that the shares sum to the original total.
In the ratio a : b, the first quantity is the fraction a/(a+b) of the whole.
To combine a : b and b : c, scale each ratio so the b terms are equal.
Ratios are unchanged when every part is multiplied by the same non-zero number.
A ratio in the form 1 : n is useful for direct comparison and for map scales.

weeks.unit: Proportion: direct and inverse

lessons.title: Direct proportion and the unitary method
objectives: I can solve direct proportion problems using the unitary method
I can recognise direct proportion from a table or graph
misconceptions: Assuming any increasing relationship is direct proportion
Adding rather than scaling multiplicatively
Forgetting that a direct proportion graph passes through the origin

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Inverse proportion
objectives: I can solve inverse proportion problems
I can recognise inverse proportion from a table or context
misconceptions: Treating 'more workers, less time' as direct proportion
Dividing rather than multiplying to find the constant
Assuming halving one quantity halves the other

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Proportion formulae and graphs (Higher)
objectives: I can write and use an equation of the form y = kx or y = k/x
I can find k from given values and use it to make predictions
misconceptions: Not finding k before substituting other values
Confusing y proportional to x^2 with y proportional to x
Sketching a reciprocal graph as a straight line

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Two quantities are in direct proportion if their ratio is constant.
A direct proportion graph is a straight line through the origin.
The unitary method finds the value of one unit first, then scales.
Best-buy problems compare cost per unit or units per pound.
Two quantities are in inverse proportion if their product is constant.
If x doubles and y halves, x and y are inversely proportional.
An inverse proportion graph is a hyperbola that never touches the axes.
The symbol for 'is proportional to' is a stylised alpha.
If y is proportional to x, then y = kx for some constant k.
If y is inversely proportional to x, then y = k/x.
If y is proportional to x squared, doubling x multiplies y by 4.
Always substitute the given pair of values to find k before answering the rest of the question.

weeks.unit: Percentages and percentage change

lessons.title: Percentages of amounts and percentage change using multipliers
objectives: I can find a percentage of an amount with and without a calculator
I can use a single multiplier to increase or decrease a quantity
misconceptions: Using 1.15 as the multiplier for a 15% decrease
Adding percentages of different totals
Confusing percentage change with percentage of

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Reverse percentages
objectives: I can find the original amount before a percentage change
I can decide when a problem requires a reverse percentage
misconceptions: Taking the same percentage off the new amount to get back
Multiplying by the multiplier rather than dividing
Not recognising the phrase 'after a 20% increase the price is...' as reverse

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Percentage change and expressing one quantity as a percentage of another
objectives: I can calculate percentage increase, decrease and profit or loss
I can express one quantity as a percentage of another
misconceptions: Dividing by the new value rather than the original
Giving the new value as the percentage change
Ignoring the direction (increase or decrease)

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Per cent means 'out of 100'.
The multiplier for a p% increase is 1 + p/100.
The multiplier for a p% decrease is 1 - p/100.
To find 10% divide by 10; to find 1% divide by 100; other percentages are built from these.
Successive percentage changes are found by multiplying the multipliers, not adding the percentages.
To reverse a percentage change, divide the new amount by the multiplier.
If a price of 60 pounds includes a 20% increase, the original is 60 / 1.2 = 50 pounds.
A reverse percentage question always gives the value after the change.
Percentage change = (change / original) x 100.
Percentage profit uses the cost price as the denominator.
A 50% increase followed by a 50% decrease does not return to the original value.
VAT in the UK is charged at 20%, giving a multiplier of 1.2.

weeks.unit: Growth, decay and repeated percentage change

lessons.title: Compound interest and depreciation
objectives: I can calculate compound interest using repeated multipliers
I can calculate depreciation over several years
misconceptions: Calculating simple interest when compound is required
Multiplying the interest by the number of years instead of using powers
Rounding partway through a multi-year calculation

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Growth and decay problems, including finding the number of periods
objectives: I can use the general formula amount = P x multiplier^n
I can find the number of years needed to reach a target by trial or iteration
misconceptions: Assuming exponential growth is linear
Rounding n down when the target has not yet been reached
Using the wrong multiplier for a decreasing quantity

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Simple interest, repeated change and comparison problems
objectives: I can compare simple and compound interest outcomes
I can compare financial options and justify a choice
misconceptions: Comparing without calculating both options fully
Not stating the actual difference when asked to compare
Ignoring the time period specified in the question

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Compound interest is calculated on the new balance each period, not on the original.
Compound amount = P x (multiplier)^n where n is the number of periods.
Depreciation uses a multiplier less than 1.
A 5% annual increase over 3 years uses the multiplier 1.05^3.
Simple interest = P x r x t / 100 and stays the same each year.
Compound interest always exceeds simple interest at the same rate over more than one period.
To find the number of periods, increase n step by step until the target is passed.
Exponential decay approaches but never reaches zero.
Half-life is the time for a decaying quantity to reduce to half its value.
Population growth and radioactive decay are both modelled by repeated multipliers.
A comparison answer must state both computed values and an explicit conclusion.
Rounding to the nearest penny should be done only at the final step.

weeks.unit: Compound measures and rates of change

lessons.title: Speed, distance and time
objectives: I can calculate speed, distance or time using the correct rearrangement
I can convert between compound units such as m/s and km/h
misconceptions: Averaging two speeds by adding and halving
Mixing minutes and decimals of an hour (e.g. 1 h 30 min as 1.30)
Getting the conversion factor between m/s and km/h the wrong way

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Density, mass and volume; pressure, force and area (Higher)
objectives: I can calculate density, mass or volume using the correct formula
I can calculate pressure, force or area and use appropriate units
misconceptions: Confusing mass with weight
Failing to convert cm^3 to m^3 correctly
Using the wrong rearrangement of the formula triangle

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: give the units of your answer

lessons.title: Converting units of area, volume and compound measures
objectives: I can convert between units of area and volume using squared and cubed scale factors
I can convert compound units systematically
misconceptions: Using 100 rather than 10 000 to convert m^2 to cm^2
Using 1000 rather than 1 000 000 to convert m^3 to cm^3
Converting only one part of a compound unit

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Speed = distance / time.
Average speed = total distance / total time, which is not the mean of the speeds.
1 hour 30 minutes is 1.5 hours, not 1.30 hours.
To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 3.6.
Density = mass / volume.
Pressure = force / area.
The SI unit of pressure is the pascal, which is one newton per square metre.
Density is commonly measured in g/cm^3 or kg/m^3.
1 litre = 1000 cm^3.
Area conversions square the linear conversion factor; volume conversions cube it.

weeks.unit: Ratio and proportion in geometry and finance (Spring 1 assessment)

lessons.title: Scale drawings, maps and scale factors
objectives: I can use a map scale to convert between map and real distances
I can construct and interpret a scale drawing
misconceptions: Multiplying when you should divide when converting real to map distance
Not converting to consistent units before applying the scale
Ignoring the units in a scale such as 1 cm to 2 km

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Similar shapes and ratio in geometry
objectives: I can find missing lengths in similar shapes using a scale factor
I can identify corresponding sides in similar figures
misconceptions: Pairing non-corresponding sides
Assuming similar shapes have equal areas
Using the additive difference instead of the multiplicative scale factor

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: show that the triangles are similar

lessons.title: Spring 1 assessment: ratio, proportion and rates of change
objectives: I can select the correct proportional reasoning method under exam conditions
I can show working clearly for multi-step proportion problems
misconceptions: Reaching for a formula before checking whether the relationship is direct or inverse
Using percentages of the wrong base
Omitting units in compound-measure answers

assessment.type: Mixed calculator and non-calculator assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: A scale of 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm on the map is 50 000 cm (0.5 km) in real life.
To go from map distance to real distance, multiply by the scale.
To go from real distance to map distance, divide by the scale.
A bearing is a three-figure angle measured clockwise from north.
Similar shapes have equal corresponding angles and sides in a constant ratio.
The linear scale factor is the ratio of any pair of corresponding sides.
Corresponding sides are identified by the corresponding angles they lie between.
Congruent shapes are similar with scale factor 1.
If the linear scale factor is k, the area scale factor is k^2.
If the linear scale factor is k, the volume scale factor is k^3.
Proportional reasoning questions should be checked by asking whether the answer should be larger or smaller.
Compound-measure answers require units unless the question supplies them.

weeks.unit: Geometry: angles, parallel lines and polygons

lessons.title: Angle facts and angles in parallel lines
objectives: I can use angle facts at a point, on a line and in a triangle
I can find and justify angles in parallel lines using correct reasoning language
misconceptions: Naming the correct angle relationship but the wrong pair of lines
Assuming lines are parallel when not marked as such
Giving an answer without the required reason

assessment.type: Reasoning and proof question (AO2)
commandWords: give a reason for your answer

lessons.title: Angles in polygons
objectives: I can calculate interior and exterior angles of regular and irregular polygons
I can solve problems involving polygon angle sums
misconceptions: Using 360 divided by n for the interior angle of a regular polygon
Confusing the sum of exterior angles (360) with the sum of interior angles
Assuming all polygons are regular

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Angle reasoning problems and geometric proof
objectives: I can chain several angle facts together to reach a required result
I can write a structured geometric argument
misconceptions: Assuming a triangle is isosceles from the diagram
Skipping steps in a chain of reasoning
Using 'because it looks like it' as a reason

assessment.type: Reasoning and proof question (AO2)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees.
Angles around a point sum to 360 degrees.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Alternate angles on parallel lines are equal (Z shape).
Corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal (F shape).
Co-interior (allied) angles on parallel lines sum to 180 degrees (C shape).
The angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees.
The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
The sum of interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n - 2) x 180 degrees.
The exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360 degrees.
Each exterior angle of a regular n-gon is 360/n degrees.
An interior angle and its adjacent exterior angle sum to 180 degrees.
Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
A geometric reason must name the fact used, e.g. 'alternate angles are equal'.

Not stating the condition used at the end of the proof
Matching vertices in the wrong order

assessment.type: Reasoning and proof question (AO2)

lessons.title: Similar shapes: lengths, areas and volumes

I can use area and volume scale factors (Higher)
misconceptions: Using the linear scale factor for area
Cubing when the question asks for area
Failing to identify which shape is the enlargement

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Standard constructions and loci
objectives: I can construct perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors and perpendiculars from a point
I can identify and shade regions satisfying loci conditions
misconceptions: Rubbing out construction arcs
Confusing the perpendicular bisector with the angle bisector
Shading the wrong side of a locus boundary

assessment.type: Construction and loci question with accuracy tolerance

knowledgeComponents.statement: Two shapes are congruent if they are identical in size and shape (reflections and rotations allowed).
SSS, SAS, ASA (or AAS) and RHS are the four valid congruence conditions.
SSA is not a valid congruence condition.
In SAS, the angle must be between the two given sides.
A congruence proof must state the three matching elements and name the condition.
If the linear scale factor is k, corresponding areas are in the ratio k^2 : 1.
If the linear scale factor is k, corresponding volumes are in the ratio k^3 : 1.
To find the linear scale factor from an area ratio, take the square root.
To find the linear scale factor from a volume ratio, take the cube root.
The perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus of points equidistant from A and B.
The bisector of an angle is the locus of points equidistant from the two lines.
The locus of points a fixed distance from a point is a circle.
Construction arcs must be left visible to earn method marks.

weeks.unit: Geometry: Pythagoras' theorem

lessons.title: Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled triangles
objectives: I can find the hypotenuse and a shorter side using Pythagoras' theorem
I can decide whether a triangle is right-angled
misconceptions: Adding the squares when finding a shorter side
Forgetting to square root at the end
Assuming the longest side in the diagram is always labelled c

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Pythagoras in context and on coordinate axes
objectives: I can apply Pythagoras to ladders, diagonals and journeys
I can find the distance between two points on a coordinate grid
misconceptions: Not drawing a right-angled triangle to model the situation
Subtracting coordinates in inconsistent order
Giving a rounded answer when an exact answer is required

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question
commandWords: give your answer in surd form

lessons.title: Pythagoras in 3D (Higher)
objectives: I can find the length of a space diagonal in a cuboid
I can identify and use the right-angled triangle inside a 3D solid
misconceptions: Using only two of the three dimensions
Not identifying the correct right-angled triangle within the solid
Rounding the intermediate diagonal before the second application

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Pythagoras' theorem states a^2 + b^2 = c^2 where c is the hypotenuse.
The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle and is the longest side.
To find a shorter side, subtract the square of the known shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse.
A triangle is right-angled if and only if the squares of the two shorter sides sum to the square of the longest.
3-4-5 and 5-12-13 are common Pythagorean triples.
Pythagoras applies only to right-angled triangles.
The distance between (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) is root((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2).
Sketching and labelling a right-angled triangle is the first step in a contextual Pythagoras problem.
An exact answer for a Pythagoras problem is often left as a simplified surd.
The space diagonal of a cuboid with sides a, b, c is root(a^2 + b^2 + c^2).
A 3D Pythagoras problem is solved by applying the theorem twice, first in the base plane.
Intermediate lengths in 3D problems should be stored unrounded.

weeks.unit: Geometry: trigonometry in right-angled triangles

lessons.title: Sine, cosine and tangent ratios: finding sides
objectives: I can label a right-angled triangle with opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse
I can choose and apply the correct trigonometric ratio to find a missing side
misconceptions: Labelling opposite and adjacent relative to the right angle rather than the given angle
Multiplying when division is required
Leaving the calculator in radian mode

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: give your answer to 3 significant figures

lessons.title: Finding missing angles using inverse trigonometric functions
objectives: I can use inverse sine, cosine and tangent to find an angle
I can solve angle-of-elevation and depression problems
misconceptions: Using sin rather than inverse sin
Confusing angle of elevation with angle of depression
Not converting a bearing into an angle inside the triangle

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: work out the size of angle

lessons.title: Exact trigonometric values and non-calculator trigonometry
objectives: I can recall the exact values of sin, cos and tan for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees
I can use exact values in non-calculator problems
misconceptions: Mixing up sin 30 and cos 30
Writing tan 60 as root(3)/3
Believing tan 90 has a finite value

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; the opposite side faces the given angle; the adjacent side is next to it.
sin(theta) = opposite / hypotenuse.
cos(theta) = adjacent / hypotenuse.
tan(theta) = opposite / adjacent.
Trigonometric ratios apply only to right-angled triangles at Foundation and to any triangle only via the sine and cosine rules.
To find an angle from a ratio, apply the inverse function.
The angle of elevation is measured upwards from the horizontal.
The angle of depression is measured downwards from the horizontal and equals the corresponding angle of elevation.
sin 30 = 1/2 and cos 60 = 1/2.
cos 30 = root(3)/2 and sin 60 = root(3)/2.
sin 45 = cos 45 = root(2)/2.
tan 30 = 1/root(3), tan 45 = 1, tan 60 = root(3).
tan 90 is undefined.

weeks.unit: Geometry: bearings, applications and Spring 2 assessment

lessons.title: Bearings with trigonometry
objectives: I can measure and calculate three-figure bearings
I can combine bearings with Pythagoras and trigonometry
misconceptions: Giving a two-figure bearing such as 65 rather than 065
Measuring anticlockwise
Forgetting to add 180 for a back bearing

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Mixed geometry problem solving
objectives: I can combine angle facts, Pythagoras and trigonometry in a single problem
I can decide which geometric technique a problem requires
misconceptions: Not annotating the diagram with known values
Using trigonometry where a simple angle fact would do
Rounding intermediate values

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment: geometry and measures
objectives: I can apply geometric reasoning accurately under timed conditions
I can supply reasons where a question demands them
misconceptions: Omitting reasons in 'give a reason' questions
Measuring rather than calculating when calculation is required
Using a rounded value from an earlier part of the question

assessment.type: Mixed geometry assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: A bearing is measured clockwise from north and always written with three figures.
The bearing of B from A is measured at A, from the north line at A.
A back bearing differs from the forward bearing by 180 degrees.
Bearings between 000 and 090 are north-east of the starting point.
North lines on a bearings diagram are parallel, so alternate and co-interior angle facts apply.
Annotating a diagram with all known lengths and angles is the first step in geometric problem solving.
Check whether a problem needs Pythagoras (three sides, no angles) or trigonometry (an angle involved).
An answer should be checked for plausibility against the diagram's scale.
A 'give a reason' instruction requires a named geometric fact, not a calculation.
Diagrams in GCSE papers are not accurately drawn unless stated.
Angles must be given in degrees with the degree symbol.
Working must be shown when a question says 'you must show your working', or no marks are available for the answer alone.

weeks.unit: Graphs: coordinates and straight lines

lessons.title: Coordinates, midpoints and plotting straight lines
objectives: I can plot points in all four quadrants and find a midpoint
I can plot a straight line from a table of values
misconceptions: Reversing x and y when plotting
Adding rather than averaging when finding a midpoint
Plotting only positive values and missing the negative branch

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Gradient and the equation y = mx + c
objectives: I can find the gradient and y-intercept of a line from its graph or equation
I can write the equation of a line given its gradient and intercept
misconceptions: Reading the gradient as the y-intercept
Getting the sign of a negative gradient wrong
Not rearranging into y = mx + c before reading off m

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: find the equation of the line

lessons.title: Finding the equation of a line through two points
objectives: I can calculate a gradient from two points
I can find the full equation of a line through two given points
misconceptions: Subtracting coordinates in inconsistent order
Stopping after finding the gradient
Confusing the change in y with the change in x

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: find the equation of the line

knowledgeComponents.statement: Coordinates are written (x, y) with x measured horizontally first.
The midpoint of (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) is ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2).
The four quadrants are numbered anticlockwise from the top right.
Gradient = change in y / change in x.
In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept.
A positive gradient rises left to right; a negative gradient falls.
A horizontal line has equation y = k; a vertical line has equation x = k.
A vertical line has an undefined gradient.
To find the equation through two points, compute the gradient then substitute one point to find c.
The gradient between (1,3) and (4,12) is 3.
An equation such as 2y = 6x + 8 must be divided through by 2 before reading the gradient.
A point lies on a line if its coordinates satisfy the line's equation.

weeks.unit: Graphs: parallel and perpendicular lines

lessons.title: Parallel and perpendicular gradients (Higher)
objectives: I can identify parallel lines from their gradients
I can find the gradient of a line perpendicular to a given line
misconceptions: Taking the reciprocal but forgetting the negative
Believing perpendicular gradients multiply to give 1
Not rearranging into y = mx + c before comparing gradients

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: find the equation of the line perpendicular to
show that the lines are parallel

lessons.title: Equations of lines through given points, including perpendiculars
objectives: I can find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line through a given point
I can find the point of intersection of two lines
misconceptions: Using the original line's gradient for the perpendicular
Not substituting the given point to find c
Confusing intersection with the midpoint

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: work out the coordinates of the point of intersection

lessons.title: The equation of a circle centred at the origin (Higher)
objectives: I can recognise and use x^2 + y^2 = r^2
I can determine whether a point lies inside, on or outside a circle
misconceptions: Using r rather than r^2 on the right-hand side
Confusing the circle equation with a straight line
Forgetting to square root to find the radius

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: show that the point lies on the circle

knowledgeComponents.statement: Parallel lines have equal gradients.
The gradients of perpendicular lines multiply to give -1.
The gradient perpendicular to m is -1/m, the negative reciprocal.
Lines with the same gradient but different intercepts never meet.
A line perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient -1/2.
To find the equation of a line through a point with a known gradient, substitute the point into y = mx + c.
The intersection of two lines is found by solving their equations simultaneously.
The perpendicular bisector of a segment passes through its midpoint at right angles.
The equation of a circle of radius r centred at the origin is x^2 + y^2 = r^2.
x^2 + y^2 = 25 is a circle of radius 5.
A point (a,b) lies inside the circle if a^2 + b^2 < r^2.
A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

weeks.unit: Simultaneous equations

lessons.title: Solving linear simultaneous equations by elimination
objectives: I can solve a pair of linear simultaneous equations by elimination
I can check my solution in both original equations
misconceptions: Adding when the matching coefficients have the same sign
Multiplying only one term of an equation when scaling
Giving only one of the two unknowns

assessment.type: Non-calculator (Paper 1) structured question

lessons.title: Solving linear simultaneous equations by substitution and graphically
objectives: I can solve simultaneous equations by substitution
I can find a solution graphically as the point of intersection
misconceptions: Substituting into the same equation it came from
Reading the intersection coordinates the wrong way round
Not stating both coordinates as the solution

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Forming and solving simultaneous equations from context
objectives: I can translate a worded situation into a pair of simultaneous equations
I can interpret my solution in the original context
misconceptions: Not defining what each letter represents
Mixing units within an equation
Failing to answer the actual contextual question

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Simultaneous equations are solved by finding values that satisfy both equations at once.
To eliminate a variable, make its coefficients equal in size in both equations.
Subtract the equations when the matching coefficients have the same sign; add when they have opposite signs.
Every term in an equation must be multiplied when scaling it.
A solution should be checked by substituting into the equation not used to find the second variable.
In the substitution method, rearrange one equation for one variable and put that expression into the other.
The graphical solution of two linear equations is the coordinates of their intersection.
Parallel lines give simultaneous equations with no solution.
Identical lines give infinitely many solutions.
Defining variables clearly (let x be the cost of one pen) is worth a mark in forming questions.
Both equations must be written before solving in a 'form and solve' question.
The final answer to a contextual problem must be given in context with units.

weeks.unit: Quadratic graphs

lessons.title: Plotting and interpreting quadratic graphs
objectives: I can complete a table of values and plot a quadratic curve
I can read roots, the y-intercept and the turning point from a graph
misconceptions: Joining plotted points with straight line segments
Squaring a negative x value incorrectly in the table
Confusing the roots with the turning point

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Solving equations graphically using quadratic curves
objectives: I can use a quadratic graph to solve an associated equation
I can add a straight line to a curve to solve a new equation
misconceptions: Reading solutions from the y-axis rather than the x-axis
Not rearranging the given equation to match the plotted curve
Giving only one of two solutions

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Turning points and the line of symmetry
objectives: I can find the line of symmetry of a quadratic from its roots
I can identify a maximum or minimum point from the shape of the curve
misconceptions: Assuming every parabola opens upwards
Giving the turning point as a single number rather than coordinates
Confusing the line of symmetry with the y-axis

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: write down the coordinates of the turning point

knowledgeComponents.statement: The graph of a quadratic function is a smooth parabola.
If the coefficient of x^2 is positive the parabola opens upwards and has a minimum.
If the coefficient of x^2 is negative the parabola opens downwards and has a maximum.
The roots of a quadratic are the x values where the curve crosses the x-axis.
The y-intercept of y = ax^2 + bx + c is c.
A quadratic curve must be drawn as a single smooth curve, not straight segments.
(-3)^2 = 9, so negative x values give positive x^2 values.
The line of symmetry passes midway between the two roots.
The turning point lies on the line of symmetry and is written as a coordinate pair.
To solve f(x) = k graphically, draw the line y = k and read the x values at the intersections.
To solve a rearranged equation, subtract the plotted function to find which line to draw.
A quadratic can have two, one or no real roots depending on where the curve meets the x-axis.

weeks.unit: Other graphs: cubic, reciprocal, exponential and trigonometric

lessons.title: Cubic and reciprocal graphs (Higher)
objectives: I can recognise and sketch the shape of cubic and reciprocal graphs
I can plot a cubic or reciprocal function from a table of values
misconceptions: Drawing a reciprocal graph crossing the axes
Joining the two branches of a reciprocal graph
Confusing a cubic with a quadratic shape

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: match the graph to the equation

lessons.title: Exponential graphs and growth (Higher)
objectives: I can recognise and sketch exponential growth and decay graphs
I can interpret an exponential model in context
misconceptions: Treating exponential growth as linear
Believing an exponential decay graph reaches zero
Confusing y = 2^x with y = x^2

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Trigonometric graphs (Higher)
objectives: I can recognise the graphs of y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x
I can read solutions to trigonometric equations from a graph
misconceptions: Confusing the sine and cosine graphs
Giving only the first solution in a given range
Forgetting the asymptotes of the tangent graph

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: write down all the solutions in the range

knowledgeComponents.statement: A cubic graph has an S shape and can cross the x-axis up to three times.
A reciprocal graph y = k/x has two separate branches and never touches either axis.
An asymptote is a line the curve approaches but never reaches.
y = 1/x is undefined at x = 0.
An exponential graph y = a^x passes through (0, 1) when a is positive.
Exponential growth has a > 1; exponential decay has 0 < a < 1.
An exponential model P x (multiplier)^t has initial value P.
y = sin x and y = cos x both have amplitude 1 and period 360 degrees.
y = sin x passes through the origin; y = cos x passes through (0, 1).
y = tan x has period 180 degrees and asymptotes at 90 and 270 degrees.
sin x = sin(180 - x), which generates the second solution in a range.
Recognising the shape of a graph from its equation is a common 1-mark matching question.

weeks.unit: Real-life graphs and rates of change

lessons.title: Distance-time and velocity-time graphs
objectives: I can interpret gradient on a distance-time graph as speed
I can interpret gradient and area on a velocity-time graph
misconceptions: Reading a horizontal section of a distance-time graph as 'moving at constant speed'
Confusing distance-time with velocity-time graphs
Not including units for speed or acceleration

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Estimating the gradient of a curve and area under a curve (Higher)
objectives: I can draw a tangent to estimate the rate of change at a point
I can estimate the area under a curve using trapezia and say whether it is an over- or under-estimate
misconceptions: Using two points on the curve rather than on the tangent
Not stating whether the estimate is over or under
Forgetting the area represents a physical quantity such as distance

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: explain whether your answer is an over-estimate

lessons.title: Conversion graphs and other real-life graphs
objectives: I can read values from conversion, capacity and depth graphs
I can interpret the meaning of gradient and intercept in context
misconceptions: Extrapolating beyond the plotted data without comment
Reading the wrong axis scale
Giving a gradient without contextual units

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: On a distance-time graph, gradient represents speed.
A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is stationary.
On a velocity-time graph, gradient represents acceleration.
On a velocity-time graph, the area under the graph represents distance travelled.
A steeper section of a distance-time graph means a faster speed.
To estimate the rate of change at a point on a curve, draw a tangent and find its gradient.
Estimating area under a curve with trapezia under-estimates when the curve is concave and over-estimates when convex.
The units of a gradient are the y-axis units divided by the x-axis units.
Interpolation reads within the plotted data; extrapolation goes beyond it and is less reliable.
A conversion graph is a straight line through the origin because the quantities are in direct proportion.
Area under a rate-of-flow graph gives total volume.
Speed is a scalar; velocity includes direction.

weeks.unit: Graphs review and Summer 1 assessment

lessons.title: Graph transformations: translations and reflections
objectives: I can describe the effect of f(x) + a and f(x + a) on a graph
I can describe the effect of -f(x) and f(-x)
misconceptions: Translating f(x + a) in the positive x direction
Confusing -f(x) with f(-x)
Describing a translation without a vector

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Mixed graph problem solving
objectives: I can select the right graphical technique for an unfamiliar problem
I can move fluently between an equation, a table and a graph
misconceptions: Working only algebraically when a graph would be quicker
Not labelling axes or curves
Misreading scales that are not one unit per square

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

lessons.title: Summer 1 assessment: graphs and equations
objectives: I can answer graph questions accurately within a time limit
I can draw curves and lines to the required accuracy
misconceptions: Plotting points inaccurately on a scaled axis
Failing to extend a line across the required domain
Reading solutions to insufficient accuracy

assessment.type: Mixed graphs and algebra assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: y = f(x) + a translates the graph a units in the positive y direction.
y = f(x + a) translates the graph a units in the negative x direction.
y = -f(x) reflects the graph in the x-axis.
y = f(-x) reflects the graph in the y-axis.
A translation must be described using a column vector or both directions.
Transformations inside the bracket affect x and behave in the opposite way to expectation.
A graph and an equation are two representations of the same relationship.
Axes must be labelled with the variable and the scale checked before reading values.
Curves must be drawn freehand and smooth, passing through all plotted points.
Points should be plotted with a sharp pencil to within half a small square.
A line drawn to solve an equation graphically must be labelled with its equation.
Where a scale is 2 units per square, each small square is 0.4 units on a 5-square block.

weeks.unit: Mensuration: perimeter, area and circles

lessons.title: Area and perimeter of 2D shapes and compound shapes
objectives: I can find the area and perimeter of triangles, parallelograms, trapezia and compound shapes
I can work backwards from an area to find a missing length
misconceptions: Using the slant side rather than the perpendicular height
Adding all sides of a compound shape including internal edges
Confusing area and perimeter units

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Circumference and area of circles
objectives: I can calculate the circumference and area of a circle
I can give answers in terms of pi or to a stated accuracy
misconceptions: Using the diameter in the area formula instead of the radius
Confusing the circumference and area formulae
Forgetting the straight edge when finding the perimeter of a semicircle

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: give your answer in terms of pi

lessons.title: Arc length, sector area and segments
