objectives: I can calculate arc length and sector area using the angle fraction
I can find the perimeter of a sector
misconceptions: Forgetting the two radii when finding a sector's perimeter
Using the angle out of 180 rather than 360
Confusing a sector with a segment

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: work out the area of the sector

knowledgeComponents.statement: Area of a triangle = 1/2 x base x perpendicular height.
Area of a parallelogram = base x perpendicular height.
Area of a trapezium = 1/2 (a + b) x h.
Perimeter is a length measured in cm; area is measured in cm squared.
A compound area is found by splitting into known shapes or subtracting from a larger one.
Circumference = pi x diameter = 2 pi r.
Area of a circle = pi r^2.
The diameter is twice the radius.
'In terms of pi' means leaving pi as a symbol in the answer.
Arc length = (angle/360) x circumference.
Sector area = (angle/360) x pi r^2.
The perimeter of a sector is the arc length plus two radii.
A segment is the region between a chord and an arc.

weeks.unit: Mensuration: volume and surface area

lessons.title: Volume and surface area of prisms and cylinders
objectives: I can calculate the volume of any prism using cross-sectional area x length
I can calculate the surface area of a prism and a cylinder
misconceptions: Using the slant length rather than the perpendicular height for a triangular prism
Forgetting the two circular ends of a cylinder's surface area
Confusing volume and surface area units

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Volume and surface area of spheres, cones and pyramids (Higher)
objectives: I can use the formulae for the volume and surface area of spheres, cones and pyramids
I can calculate the slant height of a cone using Pythagoras
misconceptions: Using the perpendicular height as the slant height in the curved surface area formula
Forgetting to halve for a hemisphere
Omitting the base of a cone when total surface area is required

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: give your answer in terms of pi

lessons.title: Composite solids and reverse mensuration problems
objectives: I can find volumes and surface areas of composite solids
I can work backwards from a volume to find a missing dimension
misconceptions: Counting internal joining faces in surface area
Not rearranging the formula before substituting
Mixing units within a single composite solid

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Volume of a prism = cross-sectional area x length.
Volume of a cylinder = pi r^2 h.
Curved surface area of a cylinder = 2 pi r h.
Total surface area of a closed cylinder = 2 pi r h + 2 pi r^2.
Volume is measured in cubic units; surface area in square units.
Volume of a sphere = 4/3 pi r^3.
Surface area of a sphere = 4 pi r^2.
Volume of a cone = 1/3 pi r^2 h.
Curved surface area of a cone = pi r l where l is the slant height.
Volume of a pyramid = 1/3 x base area x perpendicular height.
The slant height of a cone is found by Pythagoras from the radius and perpendicular height.
Joining faces inside a composite solid are not part of its external surface area.
To find a missing dimension from a given volume, rearrange the volume formula before substituting.

weeks.unit: Transformations

lessons.title: Translation, reflection and rotation
objectives: I can carry out and describe translations, reflections and rotations
I can give the full description required for each transformation
misconceptions: Describing a rotation without stating the centre
Reflecting in the wrong line, e.g. y = x versus y = -x
Giving a translation as words rather than a column vector

assessment.type: Transformation description question

lessons.title: Enlargement, including fractional and negative scale factors (Higher)
objectives: I can enlarge a shape by a positive, fractional or negative scale factor about a centre
I can describe an enlargement fully, giving the scale factor and centre
misconceptions: Enlarging without using the centre, so the image is in the wrong position
Treating a fractional scale factor as a reduction that is not an enlargement
Forgetting that a negative scale factor puts the image on the opposite side of the centre

assessment.type: Transformation construction and description

lessons.title: Combined transformations and vectors
objectives: I can carry out combinations of transformations and describe the single equivalent transformation
I can add, subtract and multiply column vectors
misconceptions: Applying transformations in the wrong order
Describing the result as two transformations when one is required
Adding vectors by multiplying components

assessment.type: Combined transformation question

knowledgeComponents.statement: A translation is described by a column vector, with the top number horizontal and the bottom number vertical.
A reflection is described by giving the equation of the mirror line.
A rotation is described by the angle, the direction and the centre of rotation.
Reflection in y = x swaps the x and y coordinates.
Translations, reflections and rotations all preserve size and shape, so the image is congruent.
An enlargement is described by the scale factor and the centre of enlargement.
A scale factor between 0 and 1 makes the image smaller but is still called an enlargement.
A negative scale factor produces an inverted image on the opposite side of the centre.
Enlargement changes size but preserves shape, so the image is similar to the object.
The centre of enlargement is found by drawing lines through corresponding points of object and image.
Column vectors are added by adding corresponding components.
The magnitude of a vector (a, b) is root(a^2 + b^2).
A combination of two reflections in parallel mirror lines is equivalent to a single translation.

weeks.unit: Probability: basics, sample space and tree diagrams

lessons.title: Probability scale, relative frequency and expected outcomes
objectives: I can use the probability scale and calculate relative frequency
I can calculate expected frequency from a probability
misconceptions: Believing a fair coin 'is due' a head after several tails
Writing a probability greater than 1 or as a ratio
Confusing expected frequency with actual outcomes

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Mutually exclusive events, sample space diagrams and probability tables
objectives: I can use the fact that probabilities of exhaustive events sum to 1
I can construct a sample space diagram for two events
misconceptions: Adding probabilities of events that are not mutually exclusive
Missing outcomes when listing systematically
Not using the complement when 'at least one' is required

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Tree diagrams for independent and dependent events (Higher)
objectives: I can draw and complete a probability tree diagram
I can calculate probabilities for events without replacement
misconceptions: Not reducing the denominator on the second set of branches when there is no replacement
Adding along branches instead of multiplying
Forgetting to consider all the successful paths

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: All probabilities lie between 0 and 1 inclusive.
Relative frequency = number of successful trials / total trials.
Relative frequency approaches theoretical probability as the number of trials increases.
Expected frequency = probability x number of trials.
Past outcomes of independent events do not affect future ones.
The probabilities of a set of mutually exclusive and exhaustive events sum to 1.
P(not A) = 1 - P(A).
A sample space diagram lists every possible outcome of two combined events.
Two dice give 36 equally likely outcomes.
Multiply along the branches of a tree diagram (the AND rule).
Add between separate complete paths of a tree diagram (the OR rule).
Without replacement, both the numerator and the denominator change on the second set of branches.
'At least one' is most efficiently found as 1 minus P(none).

weeks.unit: Probability: Venn diagrams and conditional probability

lessons.title: Set notation and Venn diagrams
objectives: I can complete a Venn diagram from given information
I can use set notation for union, intersection and complement
misconceptions: Placing the intersection count in each circle as well as the overlap
Confusing union with intersection
Forgetting elements outside both sets

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Conditional probability from Venn diagrams and two-way tables (Higher)
objectives: I can calculate a conditional probability from a Venn diagram or table
I can interpret the phrase 'given that' in a probability question
misconceptions: Using the whole total as the denominator instead of the restricted group
Reversing the condition
Assuming the events are independent when they are not

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Probability problem solving with algebra (Higher)
objectives: I can form and solve an equation from a probability situation
I can justify whether two events are independent
misconceptions: Assuming independence without checking P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)
Not accounting for the reducing total in an algebraic without-replacement problem
Leaving the answer as an equation rather than solving it

assessment.type: Multi-step problem-solving / AO3 question

knowledgeComponents.statement: The intersection of A and B contains elements in both sets.
The union of A and B contains elements in A, in B, or in both.
The complement of A contains everything in the universal set not in A.
When completing a Venn diagram, fill the intersection first.
The universal set is represented by the rectangle around the circles.
Disjoint sets have an empty intersection and are mutually exclusive.
A conditional probability restricts the sample space to the given condition.
P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B).
In a two-way table, a conditional probability uses a row or column total as the denominator.
Events A and B are independent if P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).
An algebraic without-replacement problem usually generates a quadratic equation.
Negative or non-integer solutions to a counting problem must be rejected.

weeks.unit: Statistics: sampling, averages and representation

lessons.title: Sampling and populations
objectives: I can explain why a sample is used and identify sources of bias
I can describe a random or stratified sampling method
misconceptions: Believing a larger sample is automatically unbiased
Describing 'asking friends' as random
Confusing the population with the sample

assessment.type: Reasoning and proof question (AO2)

lessons.title: Averages and spread from lists, tables and grouped data
objectives: I can find the mean, median, mode and range from a frequency table
I can estimate the mean from grouped data and explain why it is an estimate
misconceptions: Dividing by the number of classes rather than the total frequency
Giving the frequency rather than the data value as the mode
Believing an exact mean can be found from grouped data

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: work out an estimate for the mean

lessons.title: Scatter graphs, correlation and lines of best fit
objectives: I can draw a line of best fit and use it to make predictions
I can describe correlation and explain why correlation does not imply causation
misconceptions: Claiming that correlation proves causation
Forcing the line of best fit through the origin
Extrapolating far beyond the data without noting the unreliability

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question
commandWords: draw a line of best fit

knowledgeComponents.statement: A sample is used when surveying the whole population is impractical.
A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection.
Bias occurs when a sample is not representative of the population.
A larger sample tends to be more reliable but can still be biased.
A stratified sample takes numbers from each group in proportion to the population.
Mean = total of values / number of values.
The median is the middle value when the data is ordered; with n values it is at position (n+1)/2.
The mode is the most frequent value; the modal class is the group with the highest frequency.
To estimate the mean of grouped data, use the midpoint of each class, multiply by frequency, sum and divide by total frequency.
The grouped-data mean is an estimate because the original values are unknown.
Positive correlation means one variable increases as the other increases.
Correlation does not imply causation; a third factor may explain both.
Extrapolation outside the range of the data is unreliable.
An outlier is a data point that does not fit the general trend and should be ignored when drawing a line of best fit.

weeks.unit: Statistics: cumulative frequency, box plots and end-of-year examination

lessons.title: Cumulative frequency graphs and the median from a curve
objectives: I can construct a cumulative frequency graph from a grouped frequency table
I can estimate the median, quartiles and interquartile range from the curve
misconceptions: Plotting against the class midpoint rather than the upper class boundary
Reading the median at half the highest value rather than half the total frequency
Giving the quartile values rather than the interquartile range

assessment.type: Calculator (Paper 2/3) structured question

lessons.title: Box plots and comparing distributions
objectives: I can draw a box plot from a five-number summary or a cumulative frequency curve
I can compare two distributions using a measure of average and a measure of spread
misconceptions: Comparing only the medians and not the spread
Describing the data without referring to the context
Reading the box as showing the full range

assessment.type: Reasoning and proof question (AO2)

lessons.title: Year 10 end-of-year examination
objectives: I can work accurately across the full Year 10 Higher content under exam conditions
I can manage time across a full-length paper
lessons.specRef: All Year 10 content: N, A, R, G, P, S
misconceptions: Spending too long on a low-tariff question
Leaving blank answers rather than attempting a method
Not checking answers against the number of marks available

assessment.type: Full-length Higher tier mock paper set (Papers 1, 2 and 3)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies.
Cumulative frequency is plotted against the upper class boundary of each group.
The median is read at half the total cumulative frequency.
The lower quartile is at 1/4 of the total frequency and the upper quartile at 3/4.
The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile.
The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data and ignores outliers.
A box plot shows minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum.
A comparison of distributions must mention both an average and a measure of spread, in context.
A smaller interquartile range means the data is more consistent.
The number of marks indicates roughly how many distinct steps the examiner expects.
Attempting a method scores method marks even if the final answer is wrong.
Roughly one mark per minute is a reasonable time-allocation guide on a GCSE maths paper.

subjects.name: GCSE English Language
subjects.notes: AQA GCSE English Language 8700. AQA is the dominant board for English Language in England and 8700 has NOT been reformed for 2028; it remains the 2015 specification, first teaching 2015. Assessment is two written papers, each 1 hour 45 minutes and 80 marks (50% each), sat summer 2028, plus a separately reported Spoken Language endorsement (AO7-AO9, graded Pass/Merit/Distinction). Paper 1 'Explorations in creative reading and writing' uses ONE literary fiction extract: Q1 (4 marks, AO1), Q2 language (8 marks, AO2), Q3 structure (8 marks, AO2), Q4 evaluation (20 marks, AO4), Q5 descriptive or narrative writing (40 marks: 24 AO5 + 16 AO6). Paper 2 'Writers' viewpoints and perspectives' uses TWO non-fiction sources, one 19th century and one 20th/21st century: Q1 true statements (4 marks, AO1), Q2 summary of differences (8 marks, AO1), Q3 language in one source (12 marks, AO2), Q4 comparison of viewpoints and methods (16 marks, AO3), Q5 viewpoint writing (40 marks: 24 AO5 + 16 AO6). All sources are UNSEEN, so Year 10 is entirely skills-based: there is no content to 'cover' and defer. The conventional Year 10 split is therefore by paper and by skill - Paper 1 in the autumn, Paper 2 in the spring, the Spoken Language endorsement in the summer - leaving Year 11 free for interleaved practice, past-paper volume and grade refinement. IMPORTANT FOR A HOME-EDUCATED CANDIDATE: the Spoken Language endorsement must be delivered and recorded by a registered exam centre. Not every centre that accepts private candidates offers it. Confirm this with the chosen centre during Year 10, not Year 11. A candidate can be entered for 8700 without the endorsement, but the certificate will then record 'Not Classified' for spoken language.
deferredToYear11: High-volume past-paper practice under full exam conditions (multiple complete papers per half-term) - conventionally Year 11, once every question type has been taught once.
Grade 8-9 refinement of Paper 1 Question 4 (critical evaluation): sustaining a conceptualised argument across the whole 20-mark answer - Year 11, after the basic evaluative structure is automatic.
Grade 8-9 refinement of Paper 2 Question 4 (comparison of viewpoints and methods) at 16 marks, particularly conceptual comparison of perspectives - Year 11.
Sustained speed-writing practice to reliably produce a Level 4 40-mark response in 45 minutes - Year 11.
Systematic vocabulary and technical-accuracy intervention targeted at the individual candidate's error log - Year 11, informed by Year 10 mock data.
Extended breadth of 19th-century non-fiction reading (many more sources, wider range of forms) - continues through Year 11 as background reading.
Final Spoken Language endorsement delivery, if not completed in Year 10 Summer 1 (must be recorded by the centre).
Full mock-examination series and targeted intervention cycles - Year 11 only.

weeks.unit: Induction: the shape of GCSE English Language

lessons.title: What the two papers ask of you: assessment objectives and question types
objectives: I can name the five reading and writing assessment objectives and what each rewards
I can describe the structure and timing of Paper 1 and Paper 2
misconceptions: Believing English Language exams test knowledge of set texts (they use unseen sources)
Assuming the writing section is worth less than the reading section (each is 50% of a paper)
Treating Paper 1 and Paper 2 questions as interchangeable

assessment.type: Diagnostic overview task

lessons.title: Baseline assessment: a full Paper 1 reading section
objectives: I can attempt every Paper 1 reading question under timed conditions
I can identify from my own script which question types I find hardest
misconceptions: Writing at length on the 4-mark question and running out of time
Retelling the story instead of answering the question
Ignoring the specified line references

assessment.type: Full Paper 1 Section A

knowledgeComponents.statement: GCSE English Language 8700 is assessed by two written papers, each 1 hour 45 minutes and worth 80 marks.
Each paper is 50% of the GCSE; there is no coursework component in the grade.
AO1 is identifying and interpreting explicit and implicit information and selecting evidence.
AO2 is explaining and analysing how writers use language and structure, using subject terminology.
AO3 is comparing writers' ideas and perspectives and how these are conveyed, and is tested only on Paper 2.
AO4 is evaluating texts critically and supporting evaluation with references, and is tested only on Paper 1 Question 4.
AO5 is content and organisation in writing, worth 24 marks on each writing question.
AO6 is technical accuracy (vocabulary, sentence structure, spelling, punctuation), worth 16 marks on each writing question.
Paper 1 uses one extract from a piece of literary fiction, usually 20th or 21st century.
Paper 2 uses two non-fiction sources, one from the 19th century and one from the 20th or 21st century.
The recommended split on each paper is 45 minutes on writing and 60 minutes on reading, plus 15 minutes reading time.
The Spoken Language endorsement is reported separately as Pass, Merit or Distinction and does not affect the 9-1 grade.

weeks.unit: Paper 1 Question 1: retrieval and inference

lessons.title: Question 1: listing four things from a specified section
objectives: I can locate information only within the stated lines
I can write four separate, accurate points in short form
misconceptions: Reading outside the given line numbers and losing all four marks
Writing one long point instead of four distinct ones
Adding analysis when only retrieval is required

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 1 (identify and interpret explicit information)

lessons.title: Inference: reading between the lines
objectives: I can distinguish explicit statements from implied meaning
I can support an inference with a short precise quotation
misconceptions: Guessing beyond what the text can support
Quoting a whole sentence when a phrase would be sharper
Confusing an inference with a personal opinion

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 1 (identify and interpret explicit information)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Question 1 on Paper 1 is worth 4 marks and should take about 5 minutes.
Question 1 only credits information found within the lines specified in the question.
Each of the four points must be a separate idea to earn a separate mark.
Points on Question 1 can be quoted or paraphrased; both are accepted.
No analysis or explanation is required or rewarded on Question 1.
Explicit information is stated directly in the text.
Implicit information is suggested but not stated, and must be inferred.
An inference must be anchored to a specific word or phrase in the text.
Connotation is the set of associations a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning.
Denotation is a word's literal dictionary meaning.
Short embedded quotations are more effective than long copied sentences.
Checking the line numbers before reading is the single most reliable way to secure all four marks.

weeks.unit: Paper 1 Question 2: language analysis - words and phrases

lessons.title: Word classes and precise word-level analysis
objectives: I can identify nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs and their effects
I can zoom in on a single word and analyse its connotations
misconceptions: Feature-spotting: naming a technique without explaining its effect
Analysing content rather than the writer's language choices
Using the word 'shows' repeatedly without developing the point

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 2 (language analysis)
commandWords: how does the writer use language to

lessons.title: Imagery, figurative language and sentence forms
objectives: I can analyse similes, metaphors and personification
I can comment on sentence forms as part of a language answer
misconceptions: Confusing a simile with a metaphor
Labelling every image as a metaphor
Writing about structure when the question asks about language

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 2 (language analysis)
commandWords: how does the writer use language
you could include the writer's choice of

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 1 Question 2 is worth 8 marks and should take about 10 minutes.
Question 2 assesses AO2 only: how the writer uses language for effect.
The question prompt offers three areas: words and phrases, language features and techniques, and sentence forms.
A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; an abstract noun names something intangible.
A verb expresses action or state; a dynamic verb conveys movement or energy.
An adjective modifies a noun; an adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.
A semantic field is a group of words in a text that share a common area of meaning.
Level 4 (7-8 marks) responses analyse the effects of language and use subtle, precise subject terminology.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states one thing is another.
Personification gives human qualities to something non-human.
A short simple sentence after longer sentences creates emphasis or abruptness.
A useful structure for each point is: quotation, precise terminology, effect on the reader, alternative reading.
Offering more than one interpretation of a single quotation is a marker of top-band analysis.

weeks.unit: Paper 1 Question 3: structure analysis

lessons.title: What structure means in a fiction extract
objectives: I can describe how a writer sequences an extract from beginning to end
I can explain the effect of shifts in focus, perspective and time
misconceptions: Writing about language features instead of structure
Describing paragraph one, two, three without explaining effect
Assuming structure means only punctuation or paragraph length

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 3 (structure analysis)
commandWords: how has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader

lessons.title: Openings, endings and topic shifts: writing a whole-text structure answer
objectives: I can track structural movement across a whole extract
I can write three developed structural points with linked effects
misconceptions: Only writing about the opening and running out of text to discuss
Confusing juxtaposition with contrast without explaining the placement
Failing to connect a structural feature to the reader's interest

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 3 (structure analysis)
commandWords: how has the writer structured the text

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 1 Question 3 is worth 8 marks and should take about 10 minutes.
Question 3 asks specifically about structure across the WHOLE source, not a section.
The prompt suggests: what the writer focuses on at the beginning, how and why the focus changes, and any other structural features.
Structure includes the order of ideas, shifts in time, place, perspective and focus.
A zoom-in narrows the reader's attention from a wide setting to a small detail.
A zoom-out widens attention from a detail to a broader scene.
A shift in narrative perspective changes whose viewpoint the reader occupies.
Exposition introduces setting and character; the climax is the point of highest tension.
Juxtaposition places two contrasting ideas next to each other for effect.
Foreshadowing plants a hint of something that happens later.
A cyclical structure ends where it began, often suggesting entrapment or return.
A motif is a repeated image or idea that develops a theme across a text.
Every structural point must end by explaining the effect on the reader.

weeks.unit: Paper 1 Question 4: critical evaluation (part 1)

lessons.title: Understanding the evaluation question and the statement
objectives: I can break a critical statement into its component claims
I can decide the extent to which I agree and plan a line of argument
misconceptions: Ignoring the statement and simply analysing language
Agreeing without evidence or exploring alternatives
Treating Question 4 as a longer Question 2

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 4 (evaluation)
commandWords: to what extent do you agree

lessons.title: Writing evaluative paragraphs: methods plus judgement
objectives: I can write a paragraph that evaluates a writer's methods and their success
I can use evaluative vocabulary to express a critical judgement
misconceptions: Describing what happens rather than judging how well it is done
Using 'this makes the reader want to read on' as a default effect
Only agreeing with the statement and never qualifying

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 4 (evaluation)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 1 Question 4 is worth 20 marks and should take about 20 minutes.
Question 4 is the only Paper 1 question that assesses AO4 (critical evaluation).
Question 4 directs students to a specific part of the source, usually from a stated line to the end.
The question always provides a student's statement and asks 'to what extent do you agree'.
A strong response takes a clear position and may partly agree and partly disagree.
Evaluation means judging how successfully the writer achieves an effect, not just naming the effect.
Level 4 (16-20 marks) responses are described as 'perceptive, detailed' evaluation.
The evaluative paragraph structure is: claim about the statement, evidence, analysis of method, judgement of effectiveness.
Useful evaluative verbs include conveys, captures, unsettles, undermines, intensifies, exposes.
Evaluative adverbs such as 'strikingly', 'relentlessly' and 'deliberately' signal judgement.
Three to four developed paragraphs is a realistic target for a 20-mark answer in 20 minutes.
Alternative interpretations strengthen an evaluation because they show critical awareness.

weeks.unit: Paper 1 Question 4: critical evaluation (part 2) and Section A timing

lessons.title: Developing conceptual, whole-text evaluative responses
objectives: I can evaluate the writer's overall intention as well as individual moments
I can sustain an argument across a whole answer
misconceptions: Producing a list of separate points with no overall argument
Repeating the same judgement in every paragraph
Running out of time and leaving the answer unfinished

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 4 (evaluation)
commandWords: to what extent do you agree

lessons.title: Section A under timed conditions: pace and prioritisation
objectives: I can complete all four reading questions in 60 minutes
I can allocate time in proportion to marks
misconceptions: Spending 15 minutes on the 4-mark question
Annotating the source so heavily there is no time to write
Leaving Question 4 unattempted

assessment.type: Full Paper 1 Section A under timed conditions

knowledgeComponents.statement: A conceptualised response treats the extract as a deliberate construct with an authorial purpose.
A thesis statement in the opening sentence signals the position the answer will argue.
Acknowledging a counter-argument and then refuting it demonstrates critical control.
Judgements should be graded, using words such as 'largely', 'only partly', 'entirely'.
Repetition of the same idea in new words does not gain further marks.
Question tariffs on Paper 1 Section A are 4, 8, 8 and 20 marks.
A useful time allocation is roughly one minute per mark plus reading and planning time.
The 15 minutes of reading and annotation at the start pays for itself across all four questions.
Annotation should be selective: mark the shifts, the strongest images and anything odd.
An unfinished 20-mark answer costs more marks than an imperfect complete one.
Questions should be answered in order because each builds familiarity with the source.
The command 'how does the writer' always requires analysis of method, never plot retelling.

weeks.unit: Reading widely: 19th, 20th and 21st century fiction

lessons.title: Reading unseen fiction extracts from different periods
objectives: I can read an unfamiliar extract quickly and grasp its situation and mood
I can adapt to archaic vocabulary and older sentence structures
lessons.specRef: AQA 8700 Paper 1 Section A source selection
misconceptions: Panicking at unfamiliar vocabulary rather than reading around it
Assuming an older text is automatically about the same themes
Judging older texts by modern expectations

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 2 (language analysis)
commandWords: how does the writer use language

lessons.title: Vocabulary for analysis: building a precise critical lexicon
objectives: I can use precise adjectives to describe tone, mood and atmosphere
I can avoid vague terms such as 'interesting' and 'good'
misconceptions: Using 'negative' or 'positive' as the only tonal description
Using ambitious vocabulary inaccurately
Describing the reader's feelings rather than the text's effects

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 2 (language analysis)
commandWords: how does the writer use language

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 1 sources are literary fiction, most often from the 20th or 21st century but sometimes 19th century.
Archaic vocabulary can usually be decoded from surrounding context rather than looked up.
Register is the level of formality a writer adopts.
Syntax is the arrangement of words within sentences.
A first-person narrator uses 'I' and gives limited, subjective access.
A third-person omniscient narrator can access any character's thoughts.
Tone is the writer's attitude; mood is the feeling created in the reader.
Atmosphere is the emotional quality of a described setting.
Precise tonal vocabulary (ominous, wistful, sardonic, elegiac) earns credit over vague description.
Ambitious vocabulary only helps if it is used accurately.
Wide independent reading is the most reliable long-term preparation for the unseen reading papers.
Reading a paragraph aloud in your head helps decode complex 19th-century syntax.

weeks.unit: Autumn 1 assessment: Paper 1 Section A

lessons.title: Autumn 1 assessment: full Paper 1 reading section
objectives: I can complete Paper 1 Section A accurately in 60 minutes
I can apply the question-specific approach for each of the four questions
lessons.specRef: AQA 8700 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2, AO4
misconceptions: Reverting to plot summary under time pressure
Using the same approach for Question 2 and Question 3
Not checking the line references

assessment.type: Full Paper 1 Section A
commandWords: how does the writer use language
to what extent do you agree

lessons.title: Mark scheme decoding and directed improvement
objectives: I can place my own response on the AQA level descriptors
I can rewrite one paragraph to move up a level
misconceptions: Believing more writing automatically means a higher level
Not identifying which specific descriptor is missing
Rewriting without changing the analytical approach

assessment.type: Directed improvement and reflection

knowledgeComponents.statement: AQA reading mark schemes use four levels, moving from simple, to some, to clear, to perceptive and detailed.
Level 2 typically shows 'some understanding' with attempted subject terminology.
Level 3 shows 'clear, relevant' explanation with accurate subject terminology.
Level 4 shows 'perceptive, detailed' analysis with sophisticated terminology.
Level progression comes from the quality of analysis, not the quantity of writing.
Question 1 requires no explanation; Questions 2 and 3 require analysis of method; Question 4 requires judgement.
Question 2 asks about language; Question 3 asks about structure; conflating them loses marks.
The 'to what extent' command requires an explicit degree of agreement.
Line references in a question define the only creditable part of the source.
Redrafting one paragraph against the descriptor is more useful than rewriting a whole answer.
A response can be well written and still be Level 2 if it does not analyse method.
Self-assessment against the descriptors before feedback improves retention of the criteria.

weeks.unit: Creative writing: the demands of Question 5

lessons.title: Understanding Paper 1 Question 5: choices, marks and criteria
objectives: I can explain how the 40 marks split between content/organisation and technical accuracy
I can choose between the descriptive and narrative options for a given prompt
misconceptions: Believing the picture prompt must be described literally
Assuming narrative writing needs a complete plot with a twist
Neglecting technical accuracy, which is 40% of the question's marks

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)
commandWords: you may wish to base your writing on

lessons.title: Planning for effect: structure before sentences
objectives: I can plan a piece of writing with a deliberate structure
I can decide on a controlling image or idea before writing
misconceptions: Starting to write without a plan and losing shape halfway
Planning a plot too large for 45 minutes
Writing one enormous paragraph

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)
commandWords: write the opening part of a story

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 1 Question 5 is worth 40 marks, half the marks on the paper, and should take about 45 minutes.
AO5 (content and organisation) is worth 24 marks; AO6 (technical accuracy) is worth 16 marks.
Question 5 offers a choice, usually between describing an image and writing the opening of a story.
The picture prompt is a starting point, not a description task; candidates may write beyond it.
Level 4 AO5 requires communication that is convincing and compelling, with varied and inventive structure.
AO6 rewards a range of punctuation used with accuracy, varied sentence forms and ambitious vocabulary.
Five minutes spent planning is recommended within the 45 minutes.
A controlling image repeated and developed gives a piece unity.
A cyclical structure returns at the end to the image or moment of the opening.
Deliberate paragraph breaks, including a one-line paragraph, are a structural device.
A narrative opening does not need a resolution; the question asks only for an opening.
Writing about a small moment in depth outperforms trying to cover a large plot.

weeks.unit: Descriptive writing: crafting the sentence

lessons.title: Sensory description and precise noun and verb choice
objectives: I can use all five senses selectively rather than mechanically
I can replace weak verb-plus-adverb pairs with a single precise verb
misconceptions: Listing all five senses in one paragraph as a checklist
Overloading sentences with adjectives
Telling the reader an emotion instead of showing it

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)

lessons.title: Figurative language and originality
objectives: I can create original similes and extended metaphors
I can avoid cliche in my imagery
misconceptions: Using cliches such as 'as quiet as a mouse'
Piling up unrelated images that cancel each other out
Using figurative language that does not fit the mood

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)
commandWords: write a description suggested by this picture

knowledgeComponents.statement: Concrete nouns create sharper images than abstract nouns in descriptive writing.
A single precise verb usually beats a weak verb plus an adverb.
Showing an emotion through physical detail is more effective than naming it.
Two or three well-chosen sensory details beat a checklist of all five senses.
Over-modification (too many adjectives) slows the reader and weakens impact.
An extended metaphor develops a single comparison across several sentences.
Pathetic fallacy uses weather or landscape to mirror emotion.
A cliche is an overused expression that signals unoriginal thinking.
Original imagery is built by comparing something to an unexpected but apt thing.
Imagery should be consistent in tone with the rest of the piece.
Personification of an inanimate object can create menace or tenderness depending on the verb.
Ambitious vocabulary is credited under AO6 only when used accurately and appropriately.

weeks.unit: Narrative writing: openings, voice and shape

lessons.title: Powerful openings and narrative voice
objectives: I can write an opening that establishes voice, place and tension quickly
I can choose and sustain a consistent narrative perspective
misconceptions: Slipping between past and present tense
Switching narrative person mid-piece
Spending the first page on backstory

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)
commandWords: write the opening part of a story

lessons.title: Tension, pace and endings
objectives: I can vary sentence length to control pace
I can end a piece deliberately rather than stopping when time runs out
lessons.specRef: AQA 8700 Paper 1 Q5; AO5, AO6 (sentence forms)
misconceptions: Ending with 'and then I woke up'
Using only long sentences in an action sequence
Introducing a new character in the final line

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)
commandWords: write the opening part of a story

knowledgeComponents.statement: 'In medias res' means beginning in the middle of the action.
Narrative voice must remain consistent in person and tense throughout.
A first-person narrator creates immediacy but limits what can be known.
An effective opening establishes situation, voice and a question in the reader's mind.
Backstory is better woven in later than front-loaded in the opening.
Short sentences accelerate pace; long, subordinate-heavy sentences slow it.
Tension is created by delay, restricted information and a sense of threat.
A deliberate ending mirrors, subverts or resolves something set up in the opening.
'And then I woke up' is a cliched ending that undermines the whole piece.
Paragraph breaks can be used for pacing, not only for topic change.
Reading the final sentence aloud is a quick test of whether an ending lands.
A 45-minute piece should aim for roughly 500-700 words of controlled writing.

weeks.unit: Technical accuracy: sentences and punctuation (AO6)

lessons.title: Sentence forms: simple, compound, complex and minor
objectives: I can identify and use simple, compound and complex sentences deliberately
I can vary sentence openings
misconceptions: Believing a long sentence is automatically complex
Creating comma splices when joining clauses
Starting every sentence with the subject

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)

lessons.title: Punctuation for effect: the full toolkit
objectives: I can use colons, semicolons, dashes, brackets and ellipsis accurately
I can use punctuation to shape meaning and rhythm
misconceptions: Using a comma where a semicolon or full stop is needed (comma splice)
Using an apostrophe for a plural
Sprinkling semicolons without understanding the rule

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A simple sentence has one main clause.
A compound sentence joins two main clauses with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
A complex sentence contains a main clause and at least one subordinate clause.
A subordinate clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.
A fronted adverbial opens a sentence with an adverbial phrase followed by a comma.
A minor sentence lacks a finite verb and is used sparingly for effect.
A comma splice is two main clauses joined by only a comma, and is an error.
A semicolon joins two closely related main clauses.
A colon introduces an explanation, an example or a list.
A pair of dashes or brackets encloses a parenthesis.
An apostrophe shows possession or omission, never a plural.
Singular possession takes 's; plural possession of a word ending in s takes s'.
AO6 is worth 16 marks on each writing question, so accuracy errors are expensive.

weeks.unit: Technical accuracy: spelling, vocabulary and proofreading

lessons.title: Spelling patterns and commonly misspelt words
objectives: I can apply the main English spelling rules and their exceptions
I can spell the words most commonly misspelt at GCSE
misconceptions: Confusing their/there/they're and its/it's
Applying the doubling rule to words not stressed on the final syllable
Assuming a spell-checker habit transfers to handwritten exams

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)

lessons.title: Proofreading under exam conditions
objectives: I can leave time to proofread and correct my writing
I can identify my own recurring error types
misconceptions: Rereading for meaning only and missing surface errors
Crossing out so heavily the work becomes illegible
Not leaving any time for checking

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.
'Its' is possessive; 'it's' is a contraction of 'it is' or 'it has'.
'Their' is possessive, 'there' is place, 'they're' is 'they are'.
The doubling rule doubles a final consonant before a vowel suffix when the final syllable is stressed.
'i before e except after c' applies only when the sound is a long ee.
Words ending in a consonant plus y change the y to i before most suffixes.
Common GCSE misspellings include definitely, separate, necessary, embarrass, occurred, rhythm and conscience.
Proofreading should be a separate pass focused only on surface accuracy.
Reading backwards sentence by sentence helps catch spelling errors that meaning-reading hides.
Keeping a personal error log identifies the small set of recurring mistakes worth drilling.
A single neat line through an error is preferable to heavy crossing out.
Legible handwriting is a practical requirement: an examiner cannot credit what cannot be read.

weeks.unit: Creative writing workshop and redrafting

lessons.title: Writing workshop: extended descriptive piece with redrafting
objectives: I can draft, receive feedback and redraft a descriptive piece
I can make specific improvements at word, sentence and whole-text level
misconceptions: Making only surface changes when redrafting
Adding length instead of improving quality
Ignoring feedback that requires structural change

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)

lessons.title: Modelling excellence: analysing high-level exemplar responses
objectives: I can identify what makes an exemplar response Level 4
I can steal specific techniques from a model and use them in my own writing
misconceptions: Copying the content of a model rather than its technique
Assuming complexity of vocabulary alone raises the level
Not applying the technique immediately in own writing

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 5 (descriptive or narrative writing)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Redrafting should address structure first, then sentences, then words.
Cutting weak material improves a piece more reliably than adding new material.
Feedback is only useful when a specific change is made in response to it.
A strong descriptive piece usually has a clear structural journey, not just accumulated detail.
Reading work aloud exposes rhythm problems and repeated sentence openings.
An exemplar should be annotated for technique, not admired for content.
Top-band descriptive writing uses varied sentence lengths deliberately, not accidentally.
Level 4 AO5 language is 'convincing and compelling'; Level 3 is 'clear and consistent'.
Level 4 AO5 organisation uses 'varied and inventive structural features'.
Copying one specific technique from a model into your own writing is the fastest way to internalise it.
Vocabulary should be chosen for precision and mood, not for difficulty.
A piece can score highly on AO5 and poorly on AO6, and vice versa; both need attention.

weeks.unit: Autumn 2 assessment: full Paper 1

lessons.title: Autumn 2 assessment: complete Paper 1 under exam conditions
objectives: I can complete both sections of Paper 1 in 1 hour 45 minutes
I can leave adequate time for the 40-mark writing question
lessons.specRef: AQA 8700 Paper 1; AO1, AO2, AO4, AO5, AO6
misconceptions: Overrunning on Section A and rushing the writing
Not planning the writing at all under time pressure
Leaving no proofreading time

assessment.type: Full Paper 1

lessons.title: Feedback, targets and the Year 10 English Language reading habit
objectives: I can set three specific targets from my Paper 1 performance
I can plan an independent reading and vocabulary routine
misconceptions: Setting vague targets such as 'do better on Question 4'
Treating reading for pleasure as unrelated to exam performance
Not recording new vocabulary in a usable form

assessment.type: Reflection and target setting

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 1 lasts 1 hour 45 minutes for 80 marks: about 60 minutes on reading and 45 on writing.
Both sections of Paper 1 are worth 40 marks each.
Running out of time on Question 5 costs up to 40 marks, the largest single risk on the paper.
Planning time is part of the 45 minutes, not additional to it.
Answering questions in order builds familiarity with the source and is usually most efficient.
A target must name the question, the specific weakness and the action, to be useful.
Wide reading builds the vocabulary and syntactic range that AO6 rewards.
A vocabulary notebook should record the word, a definition and a sentence of your own.
Reading fiction from the 19th century specifically prepares for archaic syntax on either paper.
Reviewing your own script against the mark scheme is more useful than reading the mark scheme alone.
Three specific targets are more actionable than a long list.
Skills built for Paper 1 reading transfer directly to English Literature extract questions.

weeks.unit: Paper 2: non-fiction reading and Question 1

lessons.title: Introducing Paper 2: two sources, two centuries
objectives: I can describe the structure of Paper 2 and how it differs from Paper 1
I can read a 19th-century non-fiction source with confidence
misconceptions: Approaching Paper 2 sources as if they were fiction
Assuming the 19th-century source is always Source A
Not reading both sources before starting

assessment.type: Paper 2 overview and source annotation

lessons.title: Question 1: shading true statements
objectives: I can identify which statements are true against a specified section of Source A
I can avoid statements that are true in general but not stated in the lines given
misconceptions: Shading more than four statements
Choosing a statement that is plausible but not in the specified lines
Ticking rather than shading

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 1 (true or false statements)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 2 is 1 hour 45 minutes for 80 marks and uses two non-fiction sources.
One Paper 2 source is from the 19th century and one from the 20th or 21st century.
Paper 2 non-fiction includes letters, diaries, articles, speeches, essays and travel writing.
Paper 2 assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 in the reading section.
AO3, comparing writers' ideas and perspectives, is assessed only on Paper 2.
Reading both sources before answering is essential because Questions 2 and 4 use both.
A viewpoint is the writer's opinion; a perspective is the position from which they see the subject.
Paper 2 Question 1 is worth 4 marks and requires shading exactly four true statements.
Question 1 statements must be true according to the specified lines, not according to general knowledge.
Shading more than four statements loses marks.
Question 1 should take about 5 minutes.
Circles must be shaded fully in pencil or pen as instructed on the paper.

weeks.unit: Paper 2 Question 2: summarising differences

lessons.title: Writing an inferential summary of differences
objectives: I can identify differences between two sources on a stated topic
I can support each difference with evidence from both sources
misconceptions: Summarising each source separately rather than comparing
Writing about how the writers write rather than what they say
Giving only similarities when differences are asked for

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 2 (summary of differences)
commandWords: write a summary of the differences between

lessons.title: Developing inference in summary: perceptive difference statements
objectives: I can move from a literal difference to an inferred one
I can use comparative connectives to structure a summary
misconceptions: Quoting at length without interpreting
Making an inference the text cannot support
Repeating one difference in different words

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 2 (summary of differences)
commandWords: write a summary of the differences

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 2 Question 2 is worth 8 marks and should take about 10 minutes.
Question 2 assesses AO1: identifying and interpreting information from both sources.
Question 2 is about WHAT the sources say, not HOW the writers write.
Each point should include evidence from both Source A and Source B.
The question always names the specific topic on which differences must be found.
Level 4 (7-8 marks) on Question 2 requires perceptive summary and perceptive inferences.
A literal difference states what each source says; an inferred difference states what it implies.
Comparative connectives include 'whereas', 'in contrast', 'however' and 'on the other hand'.
Two to three developed differences is a realistic target for 8 marks in 10 minutes.
Short embedded quotations keep a summary tight and leave room for inference.
A summary must not analyse language; that is Question 3's job.
Differences may be about attitude, tone, experience or circumstance, not only facts.

weeks.unit: Paper 2 Question 3: language analysis of one source

lessons.title: Analysing non-fiction language for 12 marks
objectives: I can analyse how a non-fiction writer uses language to convey a viewpoint
I can structure a 12-mark language response with developed points
misconceptions: Listing persuasive devices without analysing effect
Analysing the wrong source
Treating a 12-mark question like an 8-mark one

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 3 (language analysis of one source)
commandWords: how does the writer use language to

lessons.title: Analysing tone and the writer's attitude
objectives: I can identify a writer's tone and trace how it shifts
I can link language choices to the writer's purpose and attitude
misconceptions: Missing irony and taking a statement literally
Describing tone without naming it precisely
Not linking tone to purpose

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 3 (language analysis of one source)
commandWords: how does the writer use language

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 2 Question 3 is worth 12 marks and should take about 15 minutes.
Question 3 asks about ONE named source only.
Question 3 assesses AO2: analysis of language, not structure.
Common non-fiction techniques include rhetorical questions, direct address, emotive language, statistics, anecdote and the rule of three.
A rhetorical question is asked for effect and does not expect an answer.
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect.
Naming a device without explaining its effect on the reader earns little credit.
Three or four developed points suit a 12-mark answer in 15 minutes.
Tone is the writer's attitude to the subject, conveyed through word choice.
Irony says the opposite of what is meant, often to criticise.
Tracking a shift in tone across a source is a mark of a perceptive response.
Non-fiction language analysis should always connect back to the writer's purpose.

weeks.unit: Paper 2 Question 4: comparing viewpoints (part 1)

lessons.title: Identifying and comparing viewpoints across two sources
objectives: I can state each writer's viewpoint in a single clear sentence
I can find genuine points of comparison rather than superficial ones
misconceptions: Writing about the two sources in separate halves with no comparison
Comparing content only and ignoring methods
Assuming a 19th-century writer must hold outdated views

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 4 (comparison of viewpoints and methods)
commandWords: compare how the writers convey their different views
you must refer to both sources

lessons.title: Comparing methods: how viewpoints are conveyed
objectives: I can compare the methods two writers use to convey their attitudes
I can integrate comparison within a paragraph rather than across paragraphs
misconceptions: Comparing methods without saying what viewpoint they convey
Using a comparative connective without a genuine comparison
Spending 15 of 20 minutes on one source

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 4 (comparison of viewpoints and methods)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 2 Question 4 is worth 16 marks and should take about 20 minutes.
Question 4 assesses AO3: comparing writers' ideas and perspectives and how they are conveyed.
Question 4 requires reference to BOTH sources throughout.
A viewpoint statement should capture the writer's attitude in a single sentence.
Comparison of attitudes must come before or alongside comparison of methods.
Integrated comparison discusses both sources within the same paragraph.
Level 4 (13-16 marks) requires comparison of ideas and perspectives that is perceptive, with detailed analysis of methods.
Useful comparative connectives are 'whereas', 'similarly', 'conversely', 'by contrast', 'in the same way'.
Three developed comparative paragraphs is a realistic target for 16 marks.
Method comparison includes tone, structure, imagery, sentence forms and choice of evidence.
A 19th-century writer's context shapes but does not determine their viewpoint.
Question 4 usually specifies a topic, such as attitudes to a particular experience or place.

weeks.unit: Paper 2 Question 4: comparing viewpoints (part 2) and 19th-century context

lessons.title: Reading 19th-century non-fiction with confidence
objectives: I can decode long 19th-century sentences and archaic vocabulary
I can use contextual knowledge to understand a 19th-century writer's assumptions
misconceptions: Assuming an unfamiliar word makes the whole sentence unreadable
Applying modern values without recognising historical context
Skipping the source introduction, which supplies key context

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 3 (language analysis of one source)
commandWords: how does the writer use language

lessons.title: Refining Question 4: perceptive comparison
objectives: I can compare writers' perspectives conceptually, not only their opinions
I can sustain comparison across a full 20-minute answer
misconceptions: Restating the same comparison with different quotations
Losing the comparative thread in the final paragraph
Not commenting on what the differences reveal

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 4 (comparison of viewpoints and methods)
commandWords: compare how the writers convey their different views and experiences

knowledgeComponents.statement: The short italicised introduction above each Paper 2 source supplies essential context.
Nineteenth-century prose often uses long multi-clause sentences that can be broken at the punctuation.
Understanding the gist of an archaic word from context is sufficient; a precise definition is not required.
Victorian non-fiction frequently addresses reform, class, empire, travel and morality.
Historical context explains a writer's assumptions but should not be used to dismiss them.
Sources on Paper 2 are chosen to be linked by theme, which is where the comparison lives.
A conceptual comparison identifies the underlying assumption behind each writer's position.
A perceptive comparison notes what a difference in viewpoint reveals about each writer.
Each comparative paragraph should end with a statement of what the comparison shows.
Comparison must be sustained to the end of the answer; a final one-source paragraph loses AO3 credit.
Quotation from both sources within a single paragraph is the clearest signal of integrated comparison.
Perspective can differ because of era, class, gender, purpose or audience.

weeks.unit: Spring 1 assessment: Paper 2 Section A

lessons.title: Spring 1 assessment: full Paper 2 reading section
objectives: I can complete all four Paper 2 reading questions in 60 minutes
I can distinguish the demands of Questions 2, 3 and 4
lessons.specRef: AQA 8700 Paper 2 Section A; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Analysing language in Question 2
Comparing in Question 3
Summarising in Question 4

assessment.type: Full Paper 2 Section A
commandWords: how does the writer use language

lessons.title: Assessment review and question-discrimination drill
objectives: I can state in one sentence what each Paper 2 reading question requires
I can correct a response that answers the wrong question
misconceptions: Confusing the summary question with the comparison question
Using the same paragraph structure for all four questions
Not adjusting length to the tariff

assessment.type: Directed improvement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 2 Section A tariffs are 4, 8, 12 and 16 marks.
Question 2 is summary of differences in content; Question 4 is comparison of viewpoints and methods.
Question 3 focuses on ONE source; Questions 2 and 4 use BOTH sources.
Time allocation on Paper 2 Section A is roughly 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes.
The most common Paper 2 error is answering Question 2 as though it were Question 4.
Answer length should scale with the tariff, not with familiarity with the topic.
Question 3 does not ask for comparison and gains no credit for it.
Question 4 gains no credit for a paragraph that discusses only one source.
Underlining the command and the focus of each question before writing prevents question drift.
A response can be well written and score in Level 2 if it answers the wrong question.
Both papers reward evidence-led points; unsupported assertion is Level 1.
Rewriting one mis-focused paragraph correctly is the most efficient improvement task.

weeks.unit: Paper 2 Question 5: writing to present a viewpoint

lessons.title: Form, audience and purpose in transactional writing
objectives: I can adapt my writing to a specified form, audience and purpose
I can use the conventions of a letter, article, speech, essay or leaflet
misconceptions: Ignoring the specified form and writing a generic essay
Using an inappropriately informal register for a broadsheet audience
Spending marks-worth of time on decorative layout features

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 5 (writing to present a viewpoint)

lessons.title: Building an argument: structure and line of reasoning
objectives: I can plan an argument with a clear line of reasoning
I can use counter-argument and concession to strengthen my case
misconceptions: Listing unconnected opinions rather than building an argument
Conceding a point without rebutting it
Repeating the introduction as the conclusion

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 5 (writing to present a viewpoint)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 2 Question 5 is worth 40 marks and should take about 45 minutes.
Question 5 always specifies a form, an audience and a purpose in the statement.
A letter needs an appropriate opening and sign-off; addresses are not required.
An article needs a headline and may use a subheading; a speech needs direct address to an audience.
Register must match the stated audience: a broadsheet readership expects formal Standard English.
Marks are for writing quality, not for decorative presentation features.
A thesis states the position the whole piece will argue.
A topic sentence opens a paragraph by stating its single main point.
A concession acknowledges the opposing view; a rebuttal then answers it.
A line of reasoning means each paragraph advances the argument rather than restating it.
A conclusion should reframe the argument, not simply repeat the introduction.
Four to five well-developed paragraphs is a realistic shape for a 45-minute argument.

weeks.unit: Rhetoric and persuasive craft

lessons.title: Classical rhetoric: ethos, pathos and logos
objectives: I can use credibility, emotion and logic to persuade
I can select evidence that suits my audience
misconceptions: Inventing statistics that sound implausible
Relying only on emotion with no reasoning
Using an anecdote that does not support the point

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 5 (writing to present a viewpoint)

lessons.title: Rhetorical devices and sentence-level persuasion
objectives: I can use triplets, anaphora, antithesis and rhetorical questions purposefully
I can vary sentence structure for rhetorical impact
misconceptions: Overloading a piece with devices so none has impact
Using rhetorical questions as a substitute for argument
Applying devices without regard to the specified form

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 5 (writing to present a viewpoint)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Ethos persuades through the credibility of the speaker.
Pathos persuades through emotion.
Logos persuades through logic and evidence.
A plausible invented statistic is acceptable in an exam; an implausible one undermines credibility.
An anecdote persuades by making an abstract point concrete.
The most persuasive writing combines ethos, pathos and logos rather than relying on one.
A triplet (rule of three) groups three items for rhythm and emphasis.
Anaphora repeats the same phrase at the start of successive clauses or sentences.
Antithesis places two contrasting ideas in parallel structure.
Direct address uses 'you' to involve the reader.
An imperative issues a command and is common in calls to action.
Devices used sparingly and purposefully score higher than devices used constantly.

weeks.unit: Vocabulary, tone and control in viewpoint writing

lessons.title: Controlling tone: formal, satirical, impassioned and measured
objectives: I can sustain a chosen tone across a whole piece
I can shift tone deliberately for effect
misconceptions: Beginning formally and drifting into informality
Attempting satire without control and appearing merely rude
Confusing strong feeling with shouting in capitals

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 5 (writing to present a viewpoint)

lessons.title: Ambitious vocabulary and Standard English
objectives: I can use precise, ambitious vocabulary accurately
I can write in Standard English and correct non-standard forms
misconceptions: Using slang or text abbreviations in a formal piece
Subject-verb agreement errors with collective nouns
Using a thesaurus word whose connotation is wrong

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 5 (writing to present a viewpoint)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Tone must be consistent with the stated audience and purpose.
Satire criticises through humour and exaggeration and requires control to work.
Understatement can be more powerful than exaggeration in a measured argument.
Capital letters and multiple exclamation marks weaken rather than strengthen a piece.
A deliberate tonal shift, such as from measured to urgent, can mark a turning point in an argument.
Standard English is the variety expected in formal written GCSE responses.
A double negative is non-standard in written Standard English.
Subject and verb must agree in number.
Colloquialisms and slang are appropriate only when the form and audience invite them.
A word chosen from a thesaurus must be checked for connotation and register.
AO6 rewards vocabulary that is 'extensive and ambitious' AND used with accuracy.
Precision matters more than difficulty when selecting vocabulary.

weeks.unit: Viewpoint writing workshop and redrafting

lessons.title: Extended viewpoint writing with redrafting
objectives: I can draft a full 40-mark viewpoint response
I can redraft to sharpen argument, tone and accuracy
misconceptions: Redrafting only for spelling and missing the structural weakness
Losing the specified form during redrafting
Adding paragraphs rather than strengthening existing ones

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 5 (writing to present a viewpoint)

lessons.title: Cohesion and discourse markers across a whole piece
objectives: I can link paragraphs so the argument flows
I can use discourse markers to signal the direction of my argument
misconceptions: Using 'firstly, secondly, finally' as the only structure
Starting every paragraph with the same connective
Placing an unlinked paragraph in the middle of an argument

assessment.type: Paper 2 Question 5 (writing to present a viewpoint)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Redrafting for argument should precede redrafting for accuracy.
A weak paragraph is usually better rewritten around a sharper topic sentence than expanded.
The specified form must be maintained from first line to last.
Reading a draft against the question statement checks that the piece still answers it.
Cohesion is the sense that a text holds together as a single argument.
Discourse markers signal relationships between ideas: however, moreover, consequently, nevertheless.
Paragraph transitions can echo a word or idea from the end of the previous paragraph.
Signposting tells the reader where the argument is going.
Numbered sequencing (firstly, secondly) is the weakest form of structure at GCSE.
Level 4 AO5 organisation is described as 'varied and inventive use of structural features'.
A one-sentence paragraph used once can create emphasis in an argument.
Every paragraph should be defensible as necessary to the argument.

weeks.unit: Spring 2 assessment: full Paper 2

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment: complete Paper 2 under exam conditions
objectives: I can complete Paper 2 in 1 hour 45 minutes
I can produce a full-length viewpoint piece in 45 minutes
lessons.specRef: AQA 8700 Paper 2; AO1, AO2, AO3, AO5, AO6
misconceptions: Running over on Question 4 and cutting the writing
Abandoning the specified form under pressure
Not planning the argument

assessment.type: Full Paper 2
commandWords: how does the writer use language

lessons.title: Paper 2 review and Year 10 target setting
objectives: I can compare my Paper 1 and Paper 2 performance and identify patterns
I can set specific targets for the summer term
misconceptions: Setting targets by paper rather than by assessment objective
Assuming a weakness in one paper does not affect the other
Not testing whether a target has been met

assessment.type: Reflection and target setting

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 2 is 1 hour 45 minutes for 80 marks, split 40 reading and 40 writing.
The recommended split is 60 minutes on reading and 45 minutes on writing.
Form, audience and purpose are stated in the Question 5 prompt and must all be honoured.
Planning the argument in five minutes protects the AO5 organisation marks.
Overrunning on Question 4 is the most common cause of a weak Paper 2 writing response.
AO5 and AO6 are assessed identically on Paper 1 Q5 and Paper 2 Q5.
Writing skills therefore transfer directly between the two papers.
An AO profile shows which objectives are strong or weak across both papers.
Targets should be phrased as an action, e.g. 'plan a thesis before writing Question 5'.
A target is only met when it has been demonstrated in a new timed response.
Weak AO2 will depress both Paper 1 Q2/Q3 and Paper 2 Q3 performance.
Weak technical accuracy costs up to 32 marks across the two papers.

weeks.unit: Spoken Language endorsement: preparation

lessons.title: The Spoken Language endorsement: requirements and criteria
objectives: I can explain what the endorsement requires and how it is graded
I can choose a suitable topic for a presentation
lessons.specRef: AQA 8700 NEA: Spoken Language endorsement; AO7, AO8, AO9
misconceptions: Believing the endorsement affects the 9-1 grade (it is reported separately)
Choosing a topic too broad to cover in the time
Reading a script verbatim rather than presenting

assessment.type: Spoken Language endorsement (separately reported, AO7-AO9)

lessons.title: Researching and planning a formal presentation
objectives: I can research a topic and select relevant evidence
I can structure a presentation with a clear opening, development and close
misconceptions: Reading dense slides aloud
Using unverified sources
Preparing content but not rehearsing delivery

assessment.type: Spoken Language endorsement (separately reported, AO7-AO9)

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Spoken Language endorsement is assessed against AO7, AO8 and AO9.
AO7 is demonstrating presentation skills in a formal setting.
AO8 is listening and responding appropriately to spoken language, including to questions and feedback.
AO9 is using spoken Standard English effectively in speeches and presentations.
The endorsement is reported as Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified, separately from the 9-1 grade.
The endorsement must be completed in a registered exam centre, which private candidates must arrange in advance.
A presentation must be followed by responding to questions from the audience.
Spoken Standard English means avoiding slang and non-standard grammar while speaking.
A presentation should have a clear opening, two or three developed sections and a conclusion.
Cue cards with prompts are better than a full script read aloud.
Signposting phrases tell the audience where the presentation is going.
Rehearsal aloud, timed, is the single most effective preparation step.

weeks.unit: Spoken Language endorsement: delivery and assessment

lessons.title: Delivery skills: voice, pace, eye contact and body language
objectives: I can vary pace, volume and emphasis to hold an audience
I can maintain eye contact and use purposeful gesture
misconceptions: Speaking too fast when nervous
Filling every pause with 'um' or 'like'
Reading from notes throughout

assessment.type: Spoken Language endorsement (separately reported, AO7-AO9)

lessons.title: Assessed presentation and responding to questions
objectives: I can deliver a formal presentation of the required length
I can listen to and answer unprepared questions in Standard English
lessons.specRef: AQA 8700 Spoken Language; AO7, AO8, AO9
misconceptions: Answering a question that was not asked
Giving one-word answers to questions
Becoming defensive when challenged

assessment.type: Spoken Language endorsement (separately reported, AO7-AO9)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A deliberate pause is more effective than a filler word.
Varying pace and volume signals emphasis and maintains attention.
Eye contact should be spread across the audience, not fixed on one point.
Purposeful gesture supports meaning; repetitive gesture distracts.
Nervousness typically speeds up delivery, so a conscious slowing is needed.
Distinction requires confident, fluent use of spoken Standard English and skilful response to questions.
A good answer to a question restates the question briefly, answers it, then gives evidence.
Asking for clarification is an acceptable and mature response to an unclear question.
AO8 credits listening and responding, so the question-and-answer section is genuinely assessed.
Elaborating an answer with an example demonstrates depth of knowledge.
A presentation is normally expected to last several minutes with a Q and A afterwards.
Presenting to an unfamiliar audience is a more valid rehearsal than presenting to family.

weeks.unit: Consolidating reading: Question 2 and Question 3 mastery

lessons.title: Paper 1 Question 2 mastery: from clear to perceptive analysis
objectives: I can offer more than one reading of a single quotation
I can analyse the effect of word class and sentence form together
misconceptions: Making a point about the whole sentence rather than a single word
Repeating the same point about three different quotations
Using terminology inaccurately in an attempt to sound sophisticated

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 2 (language analysis)
commandWords: how does the writer use language

lessons.title: Paper 1 Question 3 mastery: whole-text structural argument
objectives: I can track structural development across a whole extract with confidence
I can explain why a writer sequenced material as they did
misconceptions: Treating structure as a list of features
Ignoring the ending of the extract
Failing to explain authorial purpose behind a structural choice

assessment.type: Paper 1 Question 3 (structure analysis)
commandWords: how has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader

knowledgeComponents.statement: Perceptive analysis explores nuance, ambiguity and alternative meanings.
Zooming in on one word within a quotation is the most reliable route to Level 4 on Question 2.
Subject terminology is only credited when used accurately.
Three developed points is usually the right length for an 8-mark question in 10 minutes.
Combining word-level and sentence-level comment within one point shows range.
A structural argument should follow the reader's journey through the extract.
The ending of an extract is frequently the richest structural material and is often neglected.
Narrative distance is how close the narration stands to a character's consciousness.
A structural pattern such as repetition, contrast or narrowing focus is worth identifying explicitly.
Explaining WHY the writer sequenced material as they did distinguishes Level 4 from Level 3.

Nineteenth-century narrators often address the reader directly.
Formal diction and elevated register are common features of 19th-century prose.
Irony in 19th-century writing is often signalled by exaggerated formality.
Breaking a long sentence at its punctuation makes it readable.
The Industrial Revolution, urban poverty, empire and social reform recur in 19th-century non-fiction.
Class distinctions shape the assumptions of many 19th-century writers.
