subjects.name: GCSE English Literature
subjects.notes: AQA GCSE English Literature 8702. AQA is the largest Literature board in England and 8702 has NOT been reformed for 2028 exams; it remains the 2015 specification. AQA did refresh its set-text lists with effect from the 2025 series - three new modern texts (Princess & The Hustler by Chinonyerem Odimba, Leave Taking by Winsome Pinnock, My Name is Leon by Kit de Waal) and a new 'Worlds and Lives' poetry cluster were added, and The History Boys, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time and Never Let Me Go had their last exam in 2024. This scheme selects the four most widely taught texts in England, chosen for the density of published support material available to a home-educating family: MACBETH (Paper 1 Section A), A CHRISTMAS CAROL (Paper 1 Section B), AN INSPECTOR CALLS (Paper 2 Section A) and the POWER AND CONFLICT poetry cluster (Paper 2 Section B). Assessment: Paper 1, 1h45, 64 marks, 40% - Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay) and Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay). Paper 2, 2h15, 96 marks, 60% - Section A modern text essay (choice of two), Section B poetry anthology comparison (one poem printed, one from memory), Section C unseen poetry (one 24-mark analysis and one 8-mark comparison of methods). BOTH PAPERS ARE CLOSED BOOK, which is why quotation retrieval is built into this scheme from Week 8 onward. AO4 (spelling, punctuation and grammar) is assessed on one question per paper: the Shakespeare question and the modern text question. The individual section mark tariffs quoted throughout (30 + 4 AO4 for Shakespeare, 30 for the novel, 30 + 4 AO4 for the modern text, 30 for poetry, 24 + 8 for unseen) are from established practice rather than a page verified live during this build; the paper totals of 64 and 96 marks were verified on the AQA specification-at-a-glance page.
deferredToYear11: Seven of the fifteen Power and Conflict poems: Poppies (Weir), Tissue (Dharker), The Emigree (Rumens), Checking Out Me History (Agard), Kamikaze (Garland), and full study of the remaining cluster poems - conventionally Year 11, because schools teach roughly half the anthology in each year and comparison practice needs a critical mass of poems first.
High-volume comparative poetry practice across the full fifteen-poem cluster - Year 11.
Full-length past-paper practice under exam conditions (multiple complete Paper 1 and Paper 2 sittings) - Year 11.
Grade 8-9 refinement: sustained conceptualised argument, critical interpretations used with confidence, and analysis of form and structure at the level the top band requires - Year 11.
Systematic quotation-bank consolidation across all four texts with weekly spaced retrieval - continues and intensifies in Year 11.
Extended unseen poetry practice across a wide range of forms and periods - Year 11.
Comparative work across texts (e.g. linking Macbeth's ambition to Scrooge's greed) used to deepen thematic understanding - Year 11 enrichment.
Wider reading of other 19th-century novels and Shakespeare plays to build critical range - Year 11 enrichment.

weeks.unit: Induction and A Christmas Carol: context and Stave One

lessons.title: The shape of GCSE English Literature: papers, texts and assessment objectives
objectives: I can name the four texts I am studying and which paper each belongs to
I can explain what AO1, AO2, AO3 and AO4 reward
misconceptions: Believing the texts are available in the exam (both papers are closed book)
Assuming context means writing a history essay
Thinking Paper 2 is worth the same as Paper 1

assessment.type: Course overview and diagnostic

lessons.title: Dickens's Victorian London: poverty, the Poor Law and Malthus
objectives: I can describe the social conditions Dickens was responding to in 1843
I can explain how context shapes Dickens's purpose
misconceptions: Writing about context in a separate paragraph rather than integrating it
Confusing the 1834 Poor Law with earlier provision
Treating Dickens as a neutral observer rather than a campaigner

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)

knowledgeComponents.statement: English Literature 8702 is assessed by two closed-book written papers.
Paper 1 is 1 hour 45 minutes, 64 marks, 40% of the GCSE, covering Shakespeare and the 19th-century novel.
Paper 2 is 2 hours 15 minutes, 96 marks, 60% of the GCSE, covering modern texts, poetry anthology and unseen poetry.
AO1 is responding to texts with a critical style and using textual references.
AO2 is analysing language, form and structure using subject terminology.
AO3 is showing understanding of the relationship between texts and the contexts in which they were written.
AO4 is accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, assessed on one question per paper.
Both Paper 1 questions begin from a printed extract but require a response to the whole text.
A Christmas Carol was published in December 1843.
The 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act created the workhouse system Dickens attacks.
Thomas Malthus argued that population growth would outstrip food supply, a view Scrooge echoes with 'decrease the surplus population'.
Utilitarianism judged actions by their usefulness and is satirised through Scrooge's economic logic.
Dickens wrote the novella as a deliberate intervention in the debate about poverty.
An allegory is a narrative whose characters and events stand for moral or political ideas.

weeks.unit: A Christmas Carol: Stave One - Marley's Ghost

lessons.title: Scrooge's introduction: characterisation through language
objectives: I can analyse how Dickens constructs Scrooge in the opening pages
I can select and embed short quotations to support a point
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section B; AO1, AO2

Quoting long passages instead of embedding short phrases

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)

lessons.title: Marley's Ghost: the supernatural and moral warning
objectives: I can analyse the presentation of Marley and the chains motif
I can explain the structural function of Stave One
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Reading the ghosts as horror rather than as moral instruction
Missing that Marley's chains are self-forged
Not linking the supernatural to Dickens's social purpose

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Dickens use the supernatural

knowledgeComponents.statement: A Christmas Carol is divided into five staves, a musical term meaning verses of a carol.
Stave One is titled 'Marley's Ghost'.
Scrooge is described as 'solitary as an oyster' and 'hard and sharp as flint'.
Dickens uses cold imagery throughout to characterise Scrooge's emotional state.
The narrator addresses the reader directly, creating intimacy and moral pressure.
Scrooge answers the charity collectors by asking whether the prisons and workhouses are still in operation.
Scrooge says the poor should die and 'decrease the surplus population'.
Marley's ghost wears a chain 'made link by link, and yard by yard' of cash-boxes, keys, padlocks and ledgers.
Marley's chain is a symbol of the self-imposed consequences of a life of greed.
Marley warns that 'Mankind was my business' - the novella's central moral claim.
The gothic conventions of the novella serve a didactic, not merely sensational, purpose.
Stave One establishes the problem the remaining four staves work to solve.
An embedded quotation is integrated into the grammar of your own sentence.

weeks.unit: A Christmas Carol: Stave Two - the Ghost of Christmas Past

lessons.title: Fezziwig, Fan and the young Scrooge: what made him
objectives: I can analyse how Dickens uses the past to explain Scrooge's character
I can compare Fezziwig and Scrooge as models of employer
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Assuming Scrooge was always cruel
Treating Fezziwig as a minor comic character rather than a moral contrast
Missing that Dickens shows greed as learned, not innate

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)

lessons.title: Belle and the loss of love: structure and regret
objectives: I can analyse the Belle scene and its effect on Scrooge
I can explain the structural function of Stave Two in Scrooge's redemption
misconceptions: Reading Belle's departure as a romance subplot rather than a moral turning point
Not linking Scrooge's emotional response to his eventual change
Forgetting that Scrooge is a witness who cannot intervene

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Stave Two is titled 'The First of the Three Spirits'.
The Ghost of Christmas Past is presented with a bright light on its head, symbolising illuminating truth.
The young Scrooge is shown alone at school, neglected at Christmas.
Fan, Scrooge's sister, is presented as loving and is the mother of Fred.
Fezziwig spends little money but creates great happiness, showing that generosity is not about wealth.
Fezziwig functions as a foil to the adult Scrooge as an employer.
Belle releases Scrooge from their engagement because 'a golden idol' has displaced her.
Belle accuses Scrooge of fearing the world too much and of a 'master-passion, Gain'.
Scrooge's distress at the Belle scene is the first evidence that he can be moved.
A redemption arc traces a character's movement from moral failure to moral recovery.
Scrooge can see but not act in the visions, which intensifies his helpless regret.
Dickens structures the past to show that Scrooge's coldness was chosen, and can therefore be unchosen.

weeks.unit: A Christmas Carol: Stave Three - the Ghost of Christmas Present

lessons.title: The Cratchits: poverty, family and Tiny Tim
objectives: I can analyse Dickens's presentation of the Cratchit family
I can discuss the criticism that Dickens sentimentalises poverty
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Reading the Cratchits as simply happy rather than as an argument
Ignoring that Bob's wage is deliberately specified as fifteen shillings
Missing Mrs Cratchit's anger at Scrooge

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Dickens present the Cratchit family

lessons.title: Ignorance and Want: allegory and Dickens's warning
objectives: I can analyse the allegorical children and their function
I can link the allegory to Dickens's contemporary purpose
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section B; AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Treating Ignorance and Want as real children
Forgetting that Dickens says Ignorance is the more dangerous
Not connecting the allegory to Victorian education debates

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Dickens present ideas about poverty

knowledgeComponents.statement: Stave Three is titled 'The Second of the Three Spirits'.
The Ghost of Christmas Present is presented as a giant surrounded by abundance, evoking generosity.
Bob Cratchit earns fifteen shillings a week, a wage Dickens's readers would recognise as inadequate.
Tiny Tim says 'God bless Us, Every One!'
The Cratchit Christmas dinner is small but celebrated, arguing that joy is not bought.
Mrs Cratchit refuses at first to toast Scrooge, showing the family are not idealised saints.
Some critics argue Dickens sentimentalises poverty; the Cratchits are presented as deserving poor.
The Ghost reveals two children, Ignorance and Want, beneath its robe.
Dickens writes that Ignorance is the more dangerous of the two because 'on his brow I see that written which is Doom'.
The allegory of Ignorance and Want reflects Dickens's belief in education as the remedy for poverty.
The Ghost quotes Scrooge's own words about the surplus population back at him.
Personification presents an abstract idea as a person, as with Ignorance and Want.

weeks.unit: A Christmas Carol: Staves Four and Five

lessons.title: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come: fear, death and the gothic
objectives: I can analyse how Dickens uses silence and darkness in Stave Four
I can explain the structural function of the third spirit
misconceptions: Missing that the third spirit never speaks
Treating the graveyard scene as the climax of horror rather than of moral choice
Not noticing Scrooge is not named by the businessmen

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)

lessons.title: Stave Five: redemption, transformation and the ending
objectives: I can analyse the language of Scrooge's transformation
I can evaluate whether the ending is convincing or too easy
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Describing the change without analysing how the language changes
Assuming a critical view must be negative
Not linking the ending to Dickens's persuasive purpose

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Stave Four is titled 'The Last of the Spirits'.
The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come never speaks and only points.
The businessmen discuss a dead man's funeral with complete indifference.
Old Joe and the charwoman sell the dead man's belongings, including his bed curtains.
Scrooge sees Tiny Tim's death in this stave, giving the warning emotional force.
The unnamed corpse forces Scrooge to recognise himself, delaying the revelation for maximum effect.
Stave Five is titled 'The End of It'.
Scrooge describes himself as 'as light as a feather', 'as happy as an angel', 'as merry as a schoolboy'.
The simile cluster in Stave Five mirrors and reverses the cold similes of Stave One.
Scrooge becomes 'a second father' to Tiny Tim, and Tiny Tim 'did NOT die'.
The cyclical structure returns to Christmas Day, transformed.
Dickens's didactic purpose requires a decisive, hopeful ending to persuade readers that change is possible.

lessons.title: Thematic threads: redemption, social responsibility, family, time, isolation

Choosing quotations that are famous rather than useful

misconceptions: Ignoring form and structure and writing only about language
Not knowing why Dickens chose 'stave' rather than 'chapter'
Treating structure as plot summary

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B 19th-century novel (extract plus whole-text essay)

knowledgeComponents.statement: The central themes of A Christmas Carol are redemption, social responsibility, poverty, family, isolation and time.
Tracing a theme means showing how it develops, not listing where it appears.
The strongest quotations are short, analysable and connected to a method.
A thesis statement in the opening paragraph controls the whole essay.
Dickens links personal redemption to social reform: Scrooge's change is a model for society.
A novella is longer than a short story and shorter than a novel.
Calling the sections 'staves' likens the novella to a carol, reinforcing the Christmas framing.
The five-stave structure moves problem, past, present, future, resolution.
The structure is cyclical: the novella opens and closes at Christmas with Scrooge transformed.
A didactic text sets out to teach a moral lesson.
Form and structure are explicitly credited under AO2 alongside language.
Dickens's short form made the text cheap and widely readable, serving his campaigning purpose.

Writing a history lesson instead of literary analysis

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Paper 1 Section B question begins 'Starting with this extract, how does Dickens present...'.
Roughly the first third of the answer should analyse the extract closely.
The remainder should trace the same idea across the whole novella.
A line of argument means every paragraph advances a single controlling thesis.
A topic sentence states the paragraph's argument before any quotation.
Level 6 (top band) responses are conceptualised: they treat the text as a deliberate construct.
Context is only credited when it illuminates the writer's choices, not when it is recited.
Integrated context appears within an analytical sentence, not in a separate paragraph.
A strong analytical paragraph moves: argument, evidence, method, effect, purpose.
Authorial intention frames analysis as 'Dickens does X in order to Y'.
Paper 1 Section B does not carry the AO4 SPaG marks; those sit on Section A.
The question is worth 30 marks and should take about 50 minutes including the Shakespeare question timing.

Organising quotations only by stave and not by theme

assessment.type: Quotation retrieval test

knowledgeComponents.statement: Both English Literature papers are closed book: no copies of the texts are allowed.
Short quotations of a few words are easier to recall and more flexible in analysis.
A quotation bank should be organised by theme and by character, not only by chapter.
Spaced retrieval practice is far more effective than massed cramming for quotation recall.
An approximate quotation still earns AO1 credit if the reference is clearly accurate to the text.
Aim for about six to eight quotations per major character or theme.
Planning for two to three minutes protects the structure of a 45-minute essay.
A closed-book essay must show detailed textual knowledge across the whole text.
The extract is printed on the paper, so it provides free evidence for the opening section.
Time pressure is best managed by fixing in advance how many paragraphs to write.
Analysis of a well-chosen short quotation beats mention of a long one.
Reviewing quotations weekly across the whole of Year 10 prevents Year 11 cramming.

objectives: I can analyse the presentation of the witches and the play's opening atmosphere
I can analyse Macbeth's reaction to the prophecy
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2
misconceptions: Assuming the witches control Macbeth's actions
Missing the metrical difference between the witches' verse and the human characters'
Reading 'fair is foul' as a throwaway line

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Shakespeare present the witches

knowledgeComponents.statement: Macbeth was written around 1606, early in the reign of James I.
James I became patron of Shakespeare's company, which became the King's Men.
The divine right of kings held that a monarch is appointed by God, making regicide a sin against God.
The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 was an attempt to assassinate James I.
James I wrote Daemonologie, a treatise on witchcraft, in 1597.
The Great Chain of Being placed God, then the king, then nobles, then commoners in fixed order.
Banquo was believed to be an ancestor of James I, which shapes his flattering presentation.
The play opens with the witches, immediately establishing disorder.
'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' establishes the motif of equivocation and moral inversion.
The witches speak in trochaic tetrameter, distinct from the iambic pentameter of the human characters.
Equivocation is speech that is deliberately ambiguous and can be understood two ways.
Macbeth's first line, 'So foul and fair a day I have not seen', echoes the witches before he has met them.
An aside is a speech heard by the audience but not by other characters on stage.
Banquo questions the prophecy while Macbeth is immediately drawn to it, establishing a contrast.

weeks.unit: Macbeth: Act 1 continued - Lady Macbeth and the decision

lessons.title: Lady Macbeth's entrance and the 'unsex me here' soliloquy

lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Calling Lady Macbeth simply 'evil' without analysing method
Missing that she invokes spirits rather than commanding them
Applying modern feminism without noting Jacobean expectations

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Shakespeare present Lady Macbeth

lessons.title: Act 1 Scene 7: Macbeth's soliloquy and the persuasion scene
objectives: I can analyse Macbeth's moral reasoning in 'If it were done'
I can analyse how Lady Macbeth persuades him
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2
misconceptions: Thinking Macbeth never doubts the murder
Attributing the decision entirely to Lady Macbeth
Not noticing that Macbeth lists sound reasons against the murder

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character alone on stage voices their thoughts to the audience.
Lady Macbeth calls on spirits to 'unsex me here' and 'fill me from the crown to the toe top-full of direst cruelty'.
She asks that her milk be taken 'for gall', rejecting the maternal.
Jacobean women were expected to be obedient, pious and domestic; Lady Macbeth inverts this.
Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter, the standard verse form for noble characters.
Iambic pentameter is a line of five unstressed-stressed pairs.
Lady Macbeth invokes supernatural agency rather than claiming her own power, which complicates readings of her strength.
In Act 1 Scene 7 Macbeth lists reasons against the murder: kinsman, subject, host.
Macbeth says he has 'no spur to prick the sides of my intent, but only vaulting ambition'.
Lady Macbeth questions Macbeth's manhood to persuade him.
Lady Macbeth claims she would have dashed out her own child's brains rather than break such a promise.
A hamartia is the fatal flaw that leads to a tragic hero's downfall.
Macbeth's ambition is presented as his hamartia, but the play makes his choice deliberate.

weeks.unit: Macbeth: Act 2 - the murder of Duncan

lessons.title: Act 2 Scene 1: the dagger soliloquy
objectives: I can analyse the dagger soliloquy and its ambiguity
I can discuss whether the dagger is supernatural or psychological
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2
misconceptions: Insisting on one interpretation of the dagger
Missing the shift in Macbeth's language from hesitancy to resolve
Not tracking blood imagery from this point

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Shakespeare present Macbeth's state of mind

lessons.title: Act 2 Scenes 2-4: aftermath, guilt and disorder in nature
objectives: I can analyse the contrast between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth after the murder
I can analyse the pathetic fallacy and natural disorder following regicide
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Treating the disordered nature as coincidence rather than cosmic response
Missing that Lady Macbeth is initially the more composed
Not linking sleep imagery to conscience

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Macbeth asks 'Is this a dagger which I see before me?' before the murder.
The dagger can be read as supernatural prompting or as a projection of Macbeth's guilt.
Ambiguity in the dagger scene is deliberate and productive for analysis.
The murder of Duncan happens offstage, focusing attention on psychology rather than violence.
Blood becomes the play's dominant motif from Act 2 onwards.
Macbeth hears a voice cry 'Macbeth does murder sleep'.
Macbeth cannot say 'Amen', showing he is spiritually cut off.
Lady Macbeth says 'A little water clears us of this deed', which is ironically reversed in Act 5.
After the regicide, nature is disordered: horses eat each other, an owl kills a falcon, darkness covers the day.
Natural disorder dramatises the violation of the Great Chain of Being.
Stichomythia is rapid alternating single-line dialogue, used in Act 2 Scene 2 to convey panic.
The Porter scene provides comic relief and introduces the theme of equivocation and hell-gate.

I can analyse how Shakespeare separates Macbeth from Lady Macbeth
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2
misconceptions: Assuming Lady Macbeth plans Banquo's murder
Missing that Macbeth now acts without consulting her
Reading the escalation as sudden rather than gradual

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Shakespeare present Macbeth as a tyrant

lessons.title: Act 3 Scene 4: the banquet scene and the ghost of Banquo
objectives: I can analyse the dramatic function of the banquet scene
I can analyse the reversal of the Macbeths' roles
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2
misconceptions: Not noticing only Macbeth sees the ghost
Missing the significance of the disrupted feast as an image of disordered rule
Overlooking Lady Macbeth's attempt to control the scene

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Macbeth has Banquo murdered because of the prophecy that Banquo's descendants will be kings.
Fleance escapes, leaving the prophecy alive and Macbeth's fear unresolved.
Macbeth does not tell Lady Macbeth of the plan, marking their growing separation.
Macbeth says 'To be thus is nothing, but to be safely thus'.
Macbeth's violence escalates from a single reluctant murder to ordering the deaths of others.
A tyrant is a ruler who governs by fear and without legitimate authority.
Only Macbeth sees Banquo's ghost, which stages his private guilt in a public setting.
The banquet is a formal image of ordered society, which Macbeth's guilt destroys.
Lady Macbeth covers for Macbeth in front of the lords, briefly reprising her earlier control.
After the banquet, Lady Macbeth's influence declines sharply.
Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows more than the characters on stage.
Macbeth resolves after the banquet to return to the witches, showing his dependence on the supernatural.

lessons.title: Act 4 Scene 1: the apparitions and equivocation
objectives: I can analyse the three apparitions and their equivocal prophecies
I can explain how Shakespeare builds dramatic irony
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Taking the prophecies at face value as Macbeth does
Missing the flattery of James I in the show of eight kings
Not linking equivocation to the Gunpowder Plot trials

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Shakespeare present the supernatural

lessons.title: Act 4 Scenes 2-3: the murder of Lady Macduff and the England scene
objectives: I can analyse the effect of staging the Macduff murders
I can explain the function of the England scene in restoring order
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Treating the Lady Macduff scene as a digression
Finding the England scene 'boring' rather than structurally necessary
Missing Malcolm's deliberate testing of Macduff

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)

knowledgeComponents.statement: The first apparition, an armed head, warns Macbeth to beware Macduff.
The second apparition, a bloody child, says none of woman born shall harm Macbeth.
The third apparition, a crowned child with a tree, says Macbeth is safe until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane.
Both the second and third prophecies are equivocations that come true in unexpected ways.
The show of eight kings flatters James I by presenting Banquo's line stretching into the future.
Hubris is excessive pride or confidence, which the prophecies encourage in Macbeth.
Equivocation was topical after the Gunpowder Plot trials, where it was used as a defence.
Lady Macduff and her son are murdered on stage, the only on-stage killing of innocents.
The Macduff murders mark the point where the audience's remaining sympathy for Macbeth collapses.
Malcolm tests Macduff by pretending to be worse than Macbeth.
Malcolm's list of the king-becoming graces defines legitimate kingship against Macbeth's tyranny.
The England scene shifts the play towards restoration of the rightful order.

weeks.unit: Macbeth: Act 5 and the tragic arc

lessons.title: Act 5 Scene 1: Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking scene
objectives: I can analyse the reversal of Lady Macbeth's character
I can analyse the significance of her shift from verse to prose
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2
misconceptions: Missing that Lady Macbeth speaks in prose here, unlike earlier
Reading her madness as unmotivated
Not connecting 'out, damned spot' to 'a little water clears us'

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Shakespeare present Lady Macbeth

lessons.title: Act 5 Scenes 2-8: the fall of Macbeth and the tragic form
objectives: I can analyse the 'tomorrow and tomorrow' soliloquy
I can explain Macbeth as a tragedy and evaluate Macbeth as a tragic hero
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Reading the final speech as regret rather than nihilism
Assuming a tragic hero must be sympathetic throughout
Not evaluating whether Macbeth retains any heroic quality at the end

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: how does Shakespeare present Macbeth's downfall

knowledgeComponents.statement: Lady Macbeth sleepwalks, repeatedly washing her hands and saying 'Out, damned spot!'
Lady Macbeth speaks in prose in Act 5 Scene 1, signalling her psychological breakdown.
Her fragmented syntax contrasts with her controlled rhetoric in Act 1.
'All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand' reverses her earlier dismissal of guilt.
The Doctor concludes she needs 'the divine more than the physician', linking guilt to sin.
Lady Macbeth dies offstage, reportedly by her own hand.
Macbeth responds to her death with 'She should have died hereafter' and the 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow' soliloquy.
The 'Tomorrow' soliloquy presents life as 'a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing'.
Birnam Wood 'comes' to Dunsinane when the army carries branches as camouflage.
Macduff was 'from his mother's womb untimely ripped', so was not 'of woman born'.
A tragic hero is a figure of high status whose flaw brings about their downfall.
Malcolm calls Macbeth and Lady Macbeth 'this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen', a judgement students may challenge.
Order is restored at the end with Malcolm's coronation, satisfying Jacobean expectations.

weeks.unit: Macbeth: themes, and Autumn 2 assessment

Listing rather than arguing

Misremembering quotations

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)
commandWords: starting with this extract, how does Shakespeare present

knowledgeComponents.statement: The main themes of Macbeth are ambition, guilt and conscience, kingship and tyranny, the supernatural, gender, and appearance versus reality.
A thematic essay should draw evidence from across all five acts.
Motifs in Macbeth include blood, sleep, darkness, clothing and children.
The clothing motif presents Macbeth's kingship as ill-fitting, 'like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief'.
The children motif connects Macbeth's lack of an heir to his political insecurity.
Tracking a motif across acts demonstrates whole-text knowledge, which the mark scheme rewards.
Paper 1 Section A carries the AO4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar on Paper 1.
AO4 is worth 4 marks on the Shakespeare question.
AO4 rewards a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation.
Spelling characters' names and literary terms correctly is part of AO4.
The Shakespeare question is worth 34 marks in total including AO4.
Around 45-50 minutes is the realistic allocation for the Shakespeare question within Paper 1's 1 hour 45.

weeks.unit: Macbeth: critical interpretations and essay refinement

lessons.title: Critical readings of Macbeth: feminist, psychological and political
objectives: I can consider more than one interpretation of a character or scene
I can use alternative readings to develop rather than replace my argument

Presenting one reading as the correct answer
Using 'some critics say' without evidence from the text

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)

lessons.title: Refining Shakespeare essays: conceptual argument and precise analysis
objectives: I can write with a conceptualised thesis about Shakespeare's purpose

lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A; AO1, AO2
misconceptions: Analysing only language and never dramatic form
Treating characters as real people rather than constructs
Writing a strong opening and a weak final third

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare (extract plus whole-text essay)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Multiple defensible interpretations are a feature of literary texts, not a problem.
A feminist reading examines how the play constructs and polices gender roles.
A psychological reading treats the supernatural as externalised guilt and desire.
A political reading emphasises the play's endorsement of legitimate kingship under James I.
Alternative interpretations should be introduced with textual evidence, not with a critic's name alone.
The phrase 'this could also suggest' is a simple way to open an alternative reading.
A conceptualised response argues about what Shakespeare is doing and why.
Dramatic methods include staging, entrances and exits, asides, soliloquy, verse form and stage violence.
Verse and prose choices are dramatic methods that carry meaning about status and state of mind.
Characters in a play are constructs; writing 'Shakespeare presents' rather than 'Macbeth feels' signals this.
The final third of an essay is where most marks are lost through rushing.
A conclusion should extend the argument, not repeat the introduction.

commandWords: how does Priestley present ideas about

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section A Modern texts (essay from a choice of two)
commandWords: how does Priestley present Mr Birling

knowledgeComponents.statement: An Inspector Calls is set in 1912 and was first performed in 1945.
The 1912 setting places the action before two world wars, the general strike and the Titanic sinking.
Priestley was a socialist who believed in collective responsibility.
The 1945 audience had just elected a Labour government committed to a welfare state.
Capitalism prioritises private profit; socialism prioritises collective welfare.
A morality play uses characters to represent moral positions, a form the play echoes.
Priestley's purpose is to persuade a 1945 audience to reject pre-war social attitudes.
Birling calls the Titanic 'unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable'.
Birling dismisses the possibility of war, saying 'The Germans don't want war'.
Dramatic irony here destroys Birling's credibility before the Inspector arrives.
The opening stage directions specify lighting that should be 'pink and intimate' until the Inspector arrives, then 'brighter and harder'.
The setting is described as 'substantial and heavily comfortable, but not cosy and homelike'.
Birling's speech about a man having to 'look after himself and his own' states the position the play refutes.

Missing his control of the pace and order of revelations

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section A Modern texts (essay from a choice of two)

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Inspector's name, Goole, puns on 'ghoul', hinting at the supernatural.
Priestley's stage directions say the Inspector creates 'an impression of massiveness, solidity and purposefulness'.
The Inspector shows one photograph to one person at a time, controlling the investigation.
The Inspector functions as Priestley's mouthpiece for the play's moral argument.
The Inspector's final speech warns of 'fire and blood and anguish'.
Interpretations of the Inspector include a ghost, a socialist conscience, a time-traveller and a moral device.
Sheila had Eva Smith dismissed from Milwards out of jealousy over a dress.
Sheila is the first character to accept responsibility fully.
Sheila says 'But these girls aren't cheap labour - they're people'.
Sheila begins to anticipate the Inspector's method, warning her mother not to 'build up a kind of wall'.
Sheila and Eric represent the younger generation's capacity for change, which Priestley presents as hopeful.
Sheila returns the engagement ring, asserting independence from Gerald.

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section A Modern texts (essay from a choice of two)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Gerald kept Eva, under the name Daisy Renton, as his mistress and then ended the relationship.
Gerald presents his actions as kindness, which the play invites the audience to question.
Mrs Birling chaired the Brumley Women's Charity Organisation and refused Eva's appeal for help.
Mrs Birling refused help partly because Eva had used the name 'Mrs Birling'.
Mrs Birling insists the father of the child should be made 'entirely responsible', unaware it is Eric.
Mrs Birling's charity is presented as class-based gatekeeping rather than genuine philanthropy.
Gerald is the one who discovers the Inspector may not be real, and uses this to escape responsibility.
Eric got Eva pregnant and stole money from his father's office to support her.
Eric's drinking is established early through Sheila's and Gerald's comments.
Eric says of his father 'you're not the kind of father a chap could go to when he's in trouble'.
Eric and Sheila both retain their guilt after the Inspector leaves, unlike their parents.
Priestley divides the family by generation rather than by gender or wealth.

knowledgeComponents.statement: The play is in three acts, performed continuously, observing unity of time and place.
Each act ends on a revelation or cliffhanger that maintains tension.
A well-made play uses tight plotting, escalating revelations and a decisive climax.
The final telephone call reveals a girl has died and an inspector is on his way.
The cyclical ending suggests the family will be forced to face the lesson again.
The ending denies the older Birlings the escape they thought they had secured.
Eva Smith never appears on stage and speaks only through others' accounts.
Eva's absence makes her a symbol of all exploited working people rather than an individual.
The Inspector says 'There are millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths still left with us'.
The Inspector's central claim is 'We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other.'
A polemic is a strongly argued attack on a position.
Evaluating a play's argument means judging how effectively it persuades, not only what it says.

Choosing the question with the strongest available evidence is more important than which looks easier.
A quick plan listing four paragraph arguments is worth the two minutes it takes.

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section B Poetry anthology (named poem plus one of choice, comparative)

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Power and Conflict cluster contains 15 poems.
Paper 2 Section B prints ONE named poem; the poem chosen for comparison must be recalled from memory.
The poetry comparison question is worth 30 marks.
Comparison should cover ideas, attitudes AND methods.
The cluster ranges from Romantic poetry to contemporary poems about conflict and identity.
Ozymandias was written by Percy Bysshe Shelley in 1818.
The poem is a sonnet with an irregular rhyme scheme that fits neither Petrarchan nor Shakespearean form.
The irregular form mirrors the crumbling of Ozymandias's power.
The inscription reads 'Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!'
The irony is that nothing beside the ruin remains: 'boundless and bare, the lone and level sands stretch far away'.
The frame narrative distances the reader from Ozymandias, diminishing him further.
Shelley was a Romantic poet critical of tyranny and inherited power.
'The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed' shows the sculptor's art outlasting the king.

objectives: I can analyse Blake's use of repetition and structure

objectives: I can analyse Wordsworth's presentation of nature
I can explain the Romantic concept of the sublime
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Treating the mountain as literally moving rather than as perceived
Missing the shift from confidence to fear
Confusing The Prelude's blank verse with prose

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section B Poetry anthology (named poem plus one of choice, comparative)

knowledgeComponents.statement: London was published in Blake's Songs of Experience in 1794.
Blake repeats 'chartered' to suggest that even the Thames has been mapped, owned and controlled.
Anaphora on 'In every' emphasises the universality of suffering.
'Mind-forg'd manacles' suggests oppression is partly internalised and self-imposed.
Blake criticises the Church ('black'ning Church appalls') and the monarchy ('Palace walls').
The regular ABAB quatrains create a relentless, trapped rhythm mirroring the speaker's circular walk.
Blake was writing in the aftermath of the French Revolution and amid British industrial poverty.
The Prelude extract is from Wordsworth's autobiographical poem, published 1850.
The extract is written in blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter.
The speaker steals a boat and rows out confidently before a 'huge peak, black and huge' seems to rise up.
The sublime is the Romantic experience of awe mixed with terror before nature's vastness.
The poem shifts from confident, active verbs to troubled, passive reflection.
Wordsworth presents nature as a moral teacher that humbles human pride.

lessons.title: My Last Duchess (Browning): the dramatic monologue and controlling power
objectives: I can analyse Browning's use of the dramatic monologue form
I can analyse how the Duke condemns himself through his own words
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Taking the Duke's account at face value
Missing how enjambment undercuts the controlled rhyming couplets
Not noticing the Duke is negotiating a new marriage

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section B Poetry anthology (named poem plus one of choice, comparative)

lessons.title: The Charge of the Light Brigade (Tennyson): heroism, duty and the poet as public voice
objectives: I can analyse Tennyson's use of rhythm and repetition
I can explain the poem's context as a public response to the Crimean War
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Reading the poem as straightforward anti-war protest
Missing the criticism in 'Someone had blunder'd'
Ignoring the galloping rhythm as a deliberate device

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section B Poetry anthology (named poem plus one of choice, comparative)
commandWords: compare how poets present the reality of war

knowledgeComponents.statement: My Last Duchess was published by Robert Browning in 1842 and is set in Renaissance Italy.
A dramatic monologue is a poem spoken by a single character to a silent listener.
The poem is written in iambic pentameter with rhyming couplets.
Enjambment across the couplets suggests the Duke's control is less complete than he claims.
The Duke says 'I gave commands; then all smiles stopped together', implying he had the Duchess killed.
The Duke keeps the portrait behind a curtain that only he draws, controlling her image after death.
The listener is an envoy negotiating the Duke's next marriage, which makes the story a warning.
The Charge of the Light Brigade was written by Tennyson in 1854, days after reading a newspaper report.
Tennyson was Poet Laureate, writing in an official public voice.
The dactylic rhythm imitates the galloping of horses.
'Someone had blunder'd' acknowledges military incompetence within a poem of praise.
The repeated 'Rode the six hundred' functions as a refrain and an elegy.
'Valley of Death' alludes to Psalm 23, elevating the soldiers' sacrifice.

weeks.unit: Power and Conflict: Exposure and Storm on the Island

lessons.title: Exposure (Owen): the war of weather, futility and stasis
objectives: I can analyse Owen's use of pararhyme and structure
I can explain how Owen presents nature as the enemy
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Assuming the poem describes battle
Missing the refrain 'But nothing happens' as structural
Not identifying pararhyme correctly

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section B Poetry anthology (named poem plus one of choice, comparative)
commandWords: compare how poets present the experience of war

lessons.title: Storm on the Island (Heaney): nature, community and implicit conflict
objectives: I can analyse Heaney's use of blank verse and military imagery
I can discuss the possible reading of the title as 'Stormont'
lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Reading the poem only as a literal storm
Overstating the political reading without textual support
Missing the shift from confidence to fear

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section B Poetry anthology (named poem plus one of choice, comparative)
commandWords: compare how poets present the power of nature

knowledgeComponents.statement: Exposure was written by Wilfred Owen in 1917-18 during the First World War.
Pararhyme is half-rhyme where consonants match but vowels differ, such as 'knive us' and 'nervous'.
Owen's pararhyme creates a sense of dissonance and unresolved tension.
The refrain 'But nothing happens' ends several stanzas, conveying futility and stasis.
The opening line is 'Our brains ache, in the merciless iced east winds that knive us'.
Owen personifies the wind and weather as the true enemy rather than the German army.
Owen died a week before the Armistice in November 1918.
Storm on the Island was published by Seamus Heaney in 1966.
The poem is written in blank verse with a colloquial, conversational register.
Heaney uses military imagery: the sea 'exploding', wind 'strafes', 'bombarded'.
The first eight letters of the title spell 'Stormont', the Northern Ireland parliament, supporting a political reading.
The poem shifts from confident preparation ('we are prepared') to the admission of fear at the close.
The final line, 'it is a huge nothing that we fear', echoes Exposure's concern with invisible threat.

lessons.title: Writing the comparative poetry essay
objectives: I can structure a comparative essay that integrates both poems

Comparing content only
Choosing a comparison poem that shares only a superficial link

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment: comparative poetry essay
objectives: I can write a 30-mark comparative poetry response in 45 minutes

Selecting a comparison poem without thinking about the question focus

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section B Poetry anthology (named poem plus one of choice, comparative)

knowledgeComponents.statement: One poem is printed on the exam paper; the second must be chosen and recalled by the candidate.
The comparison must address ideas, attitudes and the methods used to convey them.
Integrated comparison discusses both poems within each paragraph.
Choosing a comparison poem that genuinely fits the question focus is a key exam decision.
Useful comparative connectives are 'similarly', 'whereas', 'by contrast', 'in the same way'.
A thesis should state the key similarity or difference the essay will argue.
Form and structure comparisons (sonnet versus blank verse, regular versus irregular) are high-value.
Poems should be compared on effect, not just on the presence of a technique.
Around 45 minutes suits the 30-mark poetry comparison within Paper 2's 2 hours 15 minutes.
Learning six to eight quotations per poem allows flexible choice under exam conditions.
Knowing four or five poems extremely well is better than knowing all fifteen superficially.
Context in poetry answers should explain the poet's purpose, not narrate history.

lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3

lessons.specRef: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section B; AO1, AO2, AO3
misconceptions: Treating the casual tone as indifference rather than as trauma

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section B Poetry anthology (named poem plus one of choice, comparative)
commandWords: compare how poets present the effects of conflict

knowledgeComponents.statement: Bayonet Charge was written by Ted Hughes, published in 1957.
The poem opens in medias res: 'Suddenly he awoke and was running'.
Hughes uses a nameless third-person soldier to universalise the experience.
'King, honour, human dignity, etcetera' dismisses patriotic abstractions as useless in battle.
The soldier is compared to 'a man who has jumped up in the dark and runs', conveying disorientation.
Enjambment and caesura create a broken, breathless rhythm.
The yellow hare is a moment of natural suffering that jolts the soldier's perception.
Remains was published by Simon Armitage in 2008 in the collection The Not Dead.
The poem is based on testimony from a soldier who served in Basra, Iraq.
The colloquial register ('legs it up the road', 'myself and somebody else and somebody else') creates authentic voice.
The repeated line 'probably armed, possibly not' conveys unresolved guilt.
The structure moves from the street to the speaker's home and mind, showing trauma following him.
PTSD is post-traumatic stress disorder; the poem dramatises intrusive memory.

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section C Unseen poetry Question 1 (analysis of one unseen poem)
commandWords: what does the poet suggest about

knowledgeComponents.statement: War Photographer was published by Carol Ann Duffy in 1985.
The poem has four regular six-line stanzas, whose order contrasts with the chaos it describes.
The darkroom is described with religious imagery: 'as though this were a church and he a priest preparing to intone a Mass'.
'Spools of suffering set out in ordered rows' contrasts order with horror.
The list 'Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh.' uses caesura to give each conflict equal weight.
'Rural England' with its 'ordinary pain' is juxtaposed with the war zones.
The editor will pick 'five or six' images from a hundred, and readers' 'eyeballs prick with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers'.
Paper 2 Section C Question 1 is worth 24 marks and analyses ONE unseen poem.
Paper 2 Section C Question 2 is worth 8 marks and compares the methods of two unseen poems.
No context is required or credited on unseen poetry questions.
Reading an unseen poem three times - for sense, for voice, for method - is an efficient routine.
Identifying the shift or turn in an unseen poem is the fastest route to a structural point.
The title of an unseen poem is part of the poem and should be analysed.

Writing as much for 8 marks as for 24

assessment.type: Paper 2 Section C Unseen poetry Question 2 (comparison of two unseen poems)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Section C Question 1 focuses on ONE unseen poem and is worth 24 marks.
Section C Question 2 compares the methods of the two unseen poems and is worth 8 marks.
Question 1 assesses AO1 and AO2; Question 2 assesses AO2 only.
Context is not assessed anywhere in Section C.
The question names a focus, such as the speaker's feelings about a subject, which must be addressed.
An unseen analysis should cover voice, imagery, form and structure.
A tonal shift is usually the most productive structural feature to identify.
About 30 minutes suits Question 1 and about 15 minutes suits Question 2.
Question 2 asks specifically about METHODS, not ideas.
Two or three comparative points is enough for 8 marks.
Section C is worth 32 of the 96 marks on Paper 2.
Regular practice with unfamiliar poems is the only preparation possible for Section C.

A microcosm is a small thing that represents something much larger.
A motif is a recurring image or idea that develops a theme.
Form terminology includes sonnet, dramatic monologue, blank verse, novella, three-act play.
Structural terminology includes volta, enjambment, caesura, cyclical structure, in medias res.
Essay quality typically declines in the final third; deliberate pacing counters this.
Full timed essays, not plans, build the stamina the exam requires.
Four full essays are required across the two papers, totalling four hours of writing.
Paper 2 requires three responses in 2 hours 15 minutes: modern text, poetry comparison and unseen poetry.
Practising to time reveals whether an essay plan is realistic.

knowledgeComponents.statement: Fred embodies persistent goodwill and forgiveness, contrasting with Scrooge's rejection of family.

Bob Cratchit toasts Scrooge as 'the Founder of the Feast' despite his treatment.
Minor characters in the novella function as moral positions rather than psychological studies.
The charity collectors offer a model of active social responsibility.
Belle's later happy family life shows what Scrooge chose to give up.
A radical reading argues Dickens exposes structural injustice through Ignorance and Want.
A conservative reading argues Dickens's solution is individual charity rather than systemic change.
Both readings can be supported from the text, which is why the debate is productive.

Evaluating a text's effectiveness is different from summarising its message.

The play's short length and fast pace suit the sense of headlong moral collapse.

subjects.name: GCSE Combined Science: Trilogy
subjects.notes: AQA GCSE Combined Science: Trilogy 8464, Higher tier. This is a DOUBLE award: it is worth two GCSE grades, reported as a pair (for example 7-7 or 7-6), and it counts as two subjects. It was confirmed on aqa.org.uk on 30 August 2026 that 8464 remains the current specification and has NOT been reformed for summer 2028; the Curriculum and Assessment Review will change GCSE science content, but reformed specifications are for first teaching after September 2026, so a candidate starting Year 10 in September 2026 sits 8464 throughout. Assessment is six written papers, each 1 hour 15 minutes and 70 marks, each worth 16.7%: Biology 1 (topics 4.1-4.4), Biology 2 (4.5-4.7), Chemistry 1 (5.1-5.5), Chemistry 2 (5.6-5.10), Physics 1 (6.1-6.4) and Physics 2 (6.5-6.7). Questions are multiple choice, structured, closed short answer and open response. Assessment objectives are AO1 40%, AO2 40%, AO3 20%. At least 15% of the marks assess the knowledge, skills and understanding gained from the 21 required practical activities, and at least 20% of the marks assess mathematical skills at Key Stage 3 standard or above. IMPORTANT for revision planning: Ofqual decided (consultation outcome published on GOV.UK) that exam boards must provide an equations sheet for GCSE physics and combined science from the 2028 series onwards, for the lifetime of the current specifications, with clean copies supplied in the exam and the sheet published by 1 September of the preceding year. Sol WILL therefore have a physics equations sheet in summer 2028. The memorisation load shifts from recalling equations to SELECTING the right equation, rearranging it, converting units and knowing what each symbol means - which is what the knowledge components in this scheme drill. The historic recall list is still worth learning for fluency and speed. Higher tier is assumed to match the Higher tier maths in this file. That is a reasonable but reviewable choice: Higher awards 9-9 down to 4-4 (with an allowed 3-3), Foundation awards 5-5 down to 1-1, and the tier decision is normally confirmed in the spring of Year 11. Year 10 therefore teaches the whole Foundation core first and layers the Higher-only content (moles and reacting masses, limiting reactants, half equations, strong and weak acids, bond energy calculations, oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons) on top, so either decision remains open. The Higher-only content deferred to Year 11 is equilibrium and Le Chatelier, momentum, and Fleming's left-hand rule and electric motors. Teaching order: this scheme runs the conventional Year 10 = Paper 1 content, Year 11 = Paper 2 content split, and rotates in two-to-three week blocks between biology, chemistry and physics so that all three disciplines stay live for retrieval practice rather than being taught as three sealed blocks.

verifiedLiveOnAqaOrgUkOrGovUk: AQA 8464 remains the current GCSE Combined Science: Trilogy specification; the live specification pages were read on 30 August 2026 and show no reform for the 2028 series.

Specification at a glance: six papers - Biology Paper 1 (topics 1-4), Biology Paper 2 (5-7), Chemistry Paper 1 (8-12), Chemistry Paper 2 (13-17), Physics Paper 1 (18-21), Physics Paper 2 (22-24); each 1 hour 15 minutes, 70 marks, 16.7% of the GCSE; multiple choice, structured, closed short answer and open response.

Scheme of assessment: linear qualification, all assessments at the end of the course in the same series; AO1 approximately 40%, AO2 approximately 40%, AO3 approximately 20%; 70 raw marks per paper scaled to 170, 4200 scaled marks in total.
Foundation and Higher tiers are both available (confirmed from the 8464 specification document).

The full biology subject content tree 4.1 to 4.7 with every sub-topic reference from 4.1.1.1 to 4.7.3.6, including the HT-only markings on 4.5.3.5 and 4.5.3.6, verified on the AQA biology subject content page.

The full chemistry subject content tree 5.1 to 5.10 with every sub-topic reference, including the HT-only markings on 5.3.2.1-5.3.2.4, 5.4.1.4, 5.4.2.5, 5.4.3.5, 5.5.1.3, 5.6.2.4-5.6.2.7 and 5.10.1.4, verified on the AQA chemistry subject content page.

The full physics subject content tree 6.1 to 6.7 with every sub-topic reference, including the HT-only markings on 6.5.5, 6.7.2.2 and 6.7.2.3, and confirmation that topic 6.7 ends at electric motors so Trilogy contains no transformers or generators, verified on the AQA physics subject content page.
There are 21 required practical activities (7 biology, 6 chemistry, 8 physics) and their titles, verified on the AQA practical assessment page.
Practical questions count for at least 15% of the overall marks of the qualification, verified on the AQA practical assessment page.

Centres must submit a true and accurate written statement confirming that each student has completed the required practical activities and made a contemporaneous record of that work; failure to submit it constitutes malpractice. Verified on the AQA practical assessment page.

Ofqual consultation outcome on GOV.UK: exam boards must provide equations sheets for GCSE physics and combined science from 2028 onwards 'for the lifetime of the current specifications, including any resit opportunities', with clean copies supplied in the exam. This directly affects this candidate.
The contents of the AQA 8464/8465 physics equations sheet were read from the published AQA sheet, including the Higher-tier markings on momentum and F = BIl.
fromGeneralCurriculumKnowledgeNotVerifie: That the qualification is worth TWO GCSE grades reported as a pair on a 17-point scale from 9-9 down to 1-1, that Higher tier covers 9-9 to 4-4 with an allowed 3-3, that Foundation covers 5-5 to 1-1, and that the two grades are never more than one grade apart. This is long established and stable for combined science, but the specific AQA page stating it could not be read during this build. CONFIRM with AQA before entry.
That mathematical skills are at least 20% of the marks for combined science. The 15% practical figure WAS verified; the maths percentage was not.

The split of physics equations into those that must be RECALLED (21 for Trilogy) and those GIVEN in the exam (6 for Trilogy). The equivalent split was read from the AQA GCSE Physics 8463 Appendix A page and the Trilogy subset was derived from it by removing the physics-only equations (moments, pressure, pressure in a liquid column, magnification, F = m dv/dt and the transformer equation). Because a full equations sheet is provided from 2028 this split now matters for fluency rather than for compliance, but CHECK it against the 8464 specification Appendix B if exact recall lists are wanted.

The assignment of required practical 14 (specific heat capacity) to topic 6.1 Energy. AQA's own practical assessment page confirms the practical exists and its title; one AQA page summary placed it differently. Either way it sits in Physics Paper 1 content and so falls in Year 10, so the teaching plan is unaffected.

The paper durations of 1 hour 15 minutes were verified on the specification at a glance page; the internal question-type mark splits within each paper were not, so the per-lesson tariffs given here are typical AQA science tariffs from past papers rather than a published table. CHECK against a current AQA past paper before using them for timed practice.

The command words listed against each lesson, and the misconceptions. Misconceptions are drawn from examiners' reports and long-standing science education research (for example the 'energy is used up', 'plants get their mass from the soil', 'strong means concentrated', and 'current is used up' misconceptions) rather than from a single verified page.

The conventional Year 10 / Year 11 split. AQA does not prescribe a teaching order. Teaching Paper 1 content in Year 10 and Paper 2 content in Year 11 is the most common approach in English schools and is what this scheme uses.

All chemical and biological factual detail, formulae, equations and data values. These are standard GCSE content and should be cross-checked against a current AQA-endorsed textbook as they are learned.
couldNotVerify: AQA's specific published policy for PRIVATE CANDIDATES and the required practicals. What was verified is the centre requirement: the centre must submit a signed statement that the candidate has completed the required practical activities and kept a contemporaneous record. AQA's private candidate guidance page could not be read during this build. This is the single largest practical risk for this subject and must be resolved with a named exam centre before September 2026.

Whether any specific exam centre will accept Sol as a private candidate for 8464. Centres that accept private candidates for science vary widely: some run a required-practical week, some require the candidate to attend all practicals, and some will not accept science private candidates at all. Identify and contact a centre in autumn 2026, not in Year 11.

The 2028 equations sheet itself, which under the Ofqual decision must be published by 1 September 2027. Download it as soon as it is published and use THAT version for revision, not the 2025-2027 sheets.
practicalRisksForAPrivateCandidate: REQUIRED PRACTICALS ARE THE MAIN RISK. There is no coursework and no practical exam, but the centre must sign a statement that the 21 required practicals were completed and contemporaneously recorded, and failure to submit it constitutes malpractice. Sol must actually do the practicals and keep a dated lab book with method, results, graphs and conclusions for each one. Keep that lab book from week 2 of Year 10.
Twelve of the 21 required practicals fall in Year 10 under this plan: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (biology), 8, 9, 10 (chemistry) and 14, 15, 16, 17 (physics). Nine are deferred to Year 11.

Equipment needed at home for the Year 10 practicals: a light microscope with prepared and self-made slides, a balance reading to 0.01 g, a cork borer and scalpel, Benedict's solution and a water bath, iodine and biuret reagents, buffer solutions, pondweed and a lamp, dilute acids and insoluble bases, a filter funnel and evaporating basin, a low-voltage power supply with graphite electrodes, expanded polystyrene cups, an ammeter and voltmeter, a variable resistor, a filament lamp and a diode, a eureka can and measuring cylinders, and an immersion heater with a metal block and thermometer. Some of this needs a supplier that sells to home educators.

Practical work carries real hazards: dilute acids and alkalis, hot water baths, mains-adjacent electricity work (all circuit practicals here are low voltage), and chlorine gas during electrolysis of sodium chloride solution, which must be done in a well ventilated space and only in small quantities. Write a risk assessment for each practical as part of the lab book; this also earns marks in the exam.
There is no non-exam assessment and no spoken component, so apart from the practical statement 8464 is a straightforward private-candidate entry - unlike Design and Technology in this same file.

Entry note: Combined Science: Trilogy is entered as a single entry that yields two grades. It cannot be split, and a candidate cannot switch to separate sciences (8461/8462/8463) at short notice, as those cover substantially more content.
sourceNotes.howToUseThisFile: Lesson ids are sci-<term>-w<week>-l<n> and knowledge component ids are kc-sci-w<week>-<nn>, matching the convention used by the other subjects in this file. Every knowledge component carries a 'lesson' field pointing at the lesson that introduces it. Lessons flagged bigRock:true are the highest-yield content. Lessons with a 'requiredPractical' field must actually be carried out and written up. Science is far more memorisation-dense than most subjects: the knowledge components deliberately include definitions, units, equations, required-practical methods, reagent colours, the reactivity series and the standard reaction patterns, all written as atomic individually-testable statements for direct import into a spaced-repetition system. Statements marked (HT) are Higher tier only and can be suspended if the tier decision later moves to Foundation.

higherTierOnlyContent: 4.5.3.5 The use of hormones to treat infertility (Year 11)
5.3.2.1 Moles; 5.3.2.2 amounts of substances in equations; 5.3.2.3 using moles to balance equations (Year 10, weeks 27-28)
5.4.1.4 Oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons (Year 10, week 29)
5.4.3.5 Representation of reactions at electrodes as half equations (Year 10, week 31)
5.5.1.3 The energy change of reactions from bond energies (Year 10, week 33)
5.6.2.4 to 5.6.2.7 The effect of changing concentration, temperature and pressure on equilibrium (Year 11)
5.10.1.4 Alternative methods of extracting metals: phytomining and bioleaching (Year 11)

In addition, individual HT-only statements appear inside topics that are otherwise shared - for example the inverse square law for light intensity in 4.4.1.2, and the removal of lactic acid by the liver in 4.4.2.2. These are flagged in the lesson objectives with (HT).

equations.note: Ofqual has confirmed that an equations sheet is provided in GCSE combined science exams from the 2028 series onwards for the lifetime of the current specification, so Sol will have every equation below in front of him. The examinable skill is therefore selection, rearrangement, unit conversion and knowing what each symbol means; questions may not be answerable purely by copying from the sheet. The recall/given split below is the split written into the 8464 specification itself and is retained here because fluent recall is still much faster in the exam and underpins multi-step questions.
mustBeRecalledInTheSpecification: weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = mg)
work done = force x distance along the line of action of the force (W = Fs)
force applied to a spring = spring constant x extension (F = ke)
distance travelled = speed x time (s = vt)
acceleration = change in velocity / time taken (a = change in v / t)
resultant force = mass x acceleration (F = ma)
momentum = mass x velocity (p = mv) - Higher tier only
kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)squared (Ek = 0.5mv^2)
gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height (Ep = mgh)
power = energy transferred / time (P = E/t)
power = work done / time (P = W/t)
efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer
efficiency = useful power output / total power input
wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda)
charge flow = current x time (Q = It)
potential difference = current x resistance (V = IR)
power = potential difference x current (P = VI)
power = (current)squared x resistance (P = I^2 R)
energy transferred = power x time (E = Pt)
energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference (E = QV)
density = mass / volume (rho = m/V)
givenInTheExam: elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)squared (Ee = 0.5ke^2)
change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change (dE = mc x d theta)
thermal energy for a change of state = mass x specific latent heat (E = mL)
(final velocity)squared - (initial velocity)squared = 2 x acceleration x distance (v^2 - u^2 = 2as)
force on a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field carrying a current = magnetic flux density x current x length (F = BIl) - Higher tier only
equations.notInTrilogy: The shared 8464/8465 equations sheet also prints the transformer equation Vp x Ip = Vs x Is. Transformers, generators, loudspeakers and induced potential are NOT in the Trilogy subject content (topic 6.7 ends at electric motors, HT only), so do not spend revision time on them. Moments, pressure (p = F/A), pressure in a column of liquid, magnification of a lens and F = m x change in v / change in t are GCSE Physics 8463 content and are also not in Trilogy.

Chemistry 5.7 Organic chemistry: crude oil, hydrocarbons, alkanes, fractional distillation, properties of hydrocarbons, combustion, and cracking and alkenes - Year 11, Chemistry Paper 2.

Physics 6.5 Forces: scalars and vectors, contact and non-contact forces, gravity and weight, resultant forces, work done, forces and elasticity, distance and displacement, speed, velocity, distance-time and velocity-time graphs, acceleration, Newton's three laws, stopping distance, reaction time, braking, and the HT-only 6.5.5 momentum and conservation of momentum - Year 11, Physics Paper 2. This is the single largest deferred physics block and it depends on the gradient, area-under-graph and rearrangement fluency built in Year 10 maths and in the Year 10 energy topic.

Physics 6.6 Waves: transverse and longitudinal waves, wave properties and the wave equation, the electromagnetic spectrum, properties and uses of electromagnetic waves, and the hazards of ionising radiation - Year 11, Physics Paper 2.

Physics 6.7 Magnetism and electromagnetism: poles of a magnet, magnetic fields, the field around a wire, solenoids, the motor effect, and the HT-only 6.7.2.2 Fleming's left-hand rule and 6.7.2.3 electric motors - Year 11, Physics Paper 2. Note that Trilogy does NOT include transformers, generators, loudspeakers or the induced potential (those are GCSE Physics 8463 only), even though the shared 8464/8465 equations sheet prints the transformer equation.

Physics required practicals 18 (force and extension for a spring), 19 (effect of force and mass on acceleration), 20 (measuring the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves) and 21 (infrared radiation absorbed and radiated by different surfaces) - Year 11, because they belong to topics 6.5 and 6.6.

weeks.unit: Working scientifically; Biology 4.1 Cell biology: cell structure

lessons.title: Working scientifically: variables, apparatus, accuracy and uncertainty
objectives: I can identify the independent, dependent and control variables in an investigation
I can explain the difference between accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility
I can estimate uncertainty as half the range of a set of repeat readings
lessons.specRef: Working scientifically (AQA 8464 section 6); assessed across all six papers
misconceptions: Thinking accuracy and precision mean the same thing - a set of readings can be precise (closely grouped) but all wrong
Believing a repeated result proves a result is correct; repeatability only shows random error is small
Calling any unexpected value an anomaly, rather than one that lies well outside the pattern of the others

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.title: Eukaryotes and prokaryotes; animal and plant cell structure
objectives: I can describe the differences between a eukaryotic cell and a prokaryotic cell
I can name the sub-cellular structures of animal and plant cells and state the function of each
I can express the relative size of a bacterium and an animal cell in standard form
misconceptions: Thinking bacteria have a nucleus - prokaryotes have a single loop of chromosomal DNA plus plasmids, never a nucleus
Believing all plant cells contain chloroplasts; root hair cells do not
Confusing the cell wall with the cell membrane, or thinking animal cells have a cell wall

assessment.type: Multiple choice / closed short answer, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The independent variable is the one you deliberately change; the dependent variable is the one you measure.
A control variable is a variable kept the same so it does not affect the dependent variable.
Accuracy means how close a measurement is to the true value; precision means how closely repeated readings agree.
Resolution is the smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect.
Uncertainty from a set of repeats is estimated as half the range: (largest - smallest) / 2.
An anomalous result should be identified and excluded before calculating a mean.
A hazard is something that could cause harm; a risk is the chance that the hazard causes harm.
Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus; prokaryotic cells do not.
Prokaryotic cells carry a single loop of chromosomal DNA plus small rings of DNA called plasmids.
The nucleus contains the genetic material and controls the activities of the cell.
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which transfers energy for the cell.
Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.
Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, a permanent vacuole, and usually chloroplasts, in addition to the structures found in animal cells.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis.
A typical animal cell is about 10-100 micrometres across; a bacterium is about 1-5 micrometres.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.1 Cell biology: microscopy and specialisation

lessons.title: Microscopy and magnification calculations (Required practical 1)
objectives: I can use a light microscope to observe, draw and label plant and animal cells
I can use the equation magnification = size of image / size of real object and rearrange it
I can explain why electron microscopes have allowed a greater understanding of sub-cellular structures
misconceptions: Confusing magnification with resolution - an electron microscope wins mainly on resolving power
Forgetting to convert units before substituting, so mixing mm and micrometres in one calculation
Drawing biological diagrams with shading and sketchy lines instead of single clear pencil lines and labels

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 1: use a light microscope to observe, draw and label a selection of plant and animal cells, including a magnification scale.

lessons.title: Cell specialisation and cell differentiation
objectives: I can explain how sperm, nerve, muscle, root hair, xylem and phloem cells are adapted to their function
I can explain what differentiation is and when it occurs in animals compared with plants
misconceptions: Thinking differentiated cells contain different genes - they contain the same genes but express different ones
Believing plant cells lose the ability to differentiate as animal cells do; many plant cells keep it for life
Describing xylem as living tissue - mature xylem vessels are dead, hollow and lignified

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: magnification = size of image / size of real object.
To find the real size of an object, divide the image size by the magnification.
1 millimetre = 1000 micrometres, and 1 micrometre = 1000 nanometres.
Total magnification of a light microscope = eyepiece lens magnification x objective lens magnification.
Resolution is the ability to distinguish two separate points as separate.
Electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolving power than light microscopes, so they reveal sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes.
A biological drawing uses clear single unbroken pencil lines, no shading, and labels with straight ruled lines that do not cross.
Iodine solution is used as a stain to make plant cell structures visible under a light microscope.
Differentiation is the process by which a cell changes to become specialised for a particular job.
Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage; many plant cells keep the ability to differentiate throughout life.
In mature animals, cell division is mainly for repair and replacement rather than growth.
A sperm cell is adapted with a tail for swimming, many mitochondria for energy, and enzymes in the acrosome to digest the egg membrane.
A root hair cell has a long extension that increases surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions.
Xylem cells are dead, hollow and strengthened with lignin so water can flow through them.
Phloem cells have sieve plates with pores and companion cells to supply energy for translocation.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.1 Cell biology: cell division and stem cells

lessons.title: Chromosomes, mitosis and the cell cycle
objectives: I can describe chromosomes as coiled DNA carrying a large number of genes, found in pairs
I can describe the three stages of the cell cycle including mitosis
I can explain the importance of mitosis in growth, repair and asexual reproduction
misconceptions: Saying mitosis is cell division - mitosis is one stage of the cell cycle; the cell cycle also includes growth, DNA replication and cytokinesis
Thinking mitosis produces gametes or genetically varied cells; it produces two genetically identical diploid cells
Thinking chromosome number halves in mitosis - that is meiosis

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Stem cells: embryonic, adult, meristem and therapeutic cloning
objectives: I can describe what stem cells are and where embryonic, adult and plant meristem stem cells are found
I can describe therapeutic cloning and explain why it reduces the risk of rejection
I can evaluate the benefits, risks and ethical objections to the use of stem cells
misconceptions: Thinking adult stem cells can become any cell type - they form only a limited range, mainly blood cells from bone marrow
Thinking therapeutic cloning creates a baby; the embryo is a source of stem cells only
Believing stem cell treatment is risk free - transfer of viral infection and, historically, rejection are real risks

assessment.type: Extended response (6 mark, levels of response), written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: A chromosome is a long molecule of DNA, coiled up, carrying a large number of genes.
Body cells contain chromosomes in pairs; human body cells have 23 pairs.
The cell cycle has three stages: growth and DNA replication, mitosis, and cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm and membranes).
Before mitosis the DNA replicates and the number of sub-cellular structures such as mitochondria and ribosomes increases.
In mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.
Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
Mitosis is needed for growth, for repair of damaged tissue, and for asexual reproduction.
A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to give rise to more cells of the same type or to differentiate into other cell types.
Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into most kinds of human cell; adult stem cells from bone marrow form only a limited range, mainly blood cells.
Meristem tissue in plants can differentiate into any plant cell type throughout the life of the plant.
Plant clones from meristems can be produced quickly and economically to preserve rare species or to produce identical crop plants.
