In therapeutic cloning an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient, so the stem cells are not rejected.
Risks of stem cell treatment include transfer of viral infection from the culture.
Ethical objections to embryonic stem cell use centre on the destruction of a potential human life.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.1 Cell biology: transport in cells

lessons.title: Diffusion and surface area to volume ratio
objectives: I can define diffusion as the spreading out of particles from high to low concentration down a concentration gradient
I can explain how concentration gradient, temperature and surface area affect the rate of diffusion
I can calculate a surface area to volume ratio and explain why large organisms need exchange surfaces
misconceptions: Saying particles 'want' or 'try' to move to where there are fewer of them - diffusion is random motion producing a net movement
Thinking diffusion needs energy from respiration; it is passive
Thinking a bigger organism has a bigger surface area to volume ratio - as size increases the ratio falls

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Osmosis and the effect of solution concentration on plant tissue (Required practical 2)
objectives: I can define osmosis as the diffusion of water from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
I can investigate the effect of a range of concentrations of salt or sugar solutions on the mass of plant tissue
I can calculate and interpret percentage change in mass
misconceptions: Saying osmosis is the movement of water from high to low concentration without saying concentration of WATER, not of solute
Forgetting that osmosis moves water only - solute particles do not cross the partially permeable membrane
Using change in mass rather than percentage change in mass, so different starting masses cannot be compared

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 2: investigate the effect of a range of concentrations of salt or sugar solutions on the mass of plant tissue.

knowledgeComponents.statement: Diffusion is the spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
Diffusion is a passive process; it does not require energy from respiration.
The rate of diffusion increases with a steeper concentration gradient, a higher temperature, and a larger surface area of the membrane.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out of cells by diffusion; urea diffuses from cells into the blood plasma.
Surface area to volume ratio = total surface area / volume.
As an organism gets larger its surface area to volume ratio gets smaller, so it needs specialised exchange surfaces and a transport system.
Effective exchange surfaces have a large surface area, thin membranes for a short diffusion path, and in animals a good blood supply and ventilation.
Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
In osmosis only water moves; solute particles cannot cross the partially permeable membrane.
Plant tissue placed in a concentrated sugar solution loses water by osmosis and loses mass.
percentage change in mass = (change in mass / starting mass) x 100.
Percentage change in mass is used rather than change in mass so that samples with different starting masses can be compared fairly.
The concentration at which there is no change in mass equals the concentration of the cell contents (the isotonic point).
In the osmosis practical, potato cylinders must be blotted dry before weighing to remove surface liquid.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.1 Cell biology: active transport; Chemistry 5.1 Atomic structure: atoms and equations

lessons.title: Active transport
objectives: I can describe active transport as movement against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration
I can explain the role of active transport in root hair cells and in the small intestine
misconceptions: Thinking active transport is just fast diffusion - it moves substances the 'wrong way' up a gradient
Forgetting to state that the energy comes from respiration
Thinking active transport happens in plants only

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Atoms, elements, compounds and writing balanced chemical equations
objectives: I can describe the difference between an atom, an element and a compound
I can write and balance symbol equations, including state symbols
misconceptions: Changing a formula (for example writing H2O2) to balance an equation instead of changing the big numbers in front
Thinking a compound is the same as a mixture
Reading 2H2O as meaning 2 hydrogen atoms; it is 2 molecules, so 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Active transport moves substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution, against a concentration gradient.
Active transport requires energy transferred by respiration.
Root hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from very dilute soil solutions.
The small intestine uses active transport to absorb glucose when the concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood.
Cells that carry out a lot of active transport contain many mitochondria.
An element is a substance made of only one type of atom; a compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions, or by electrolysis.
In a balanced symbol equation the number of atoms of each element must be the same on both sides.
To balance an equation you may only change the large numbers in front of formulae, never the small subscript numbers inside them.
The state symbols are (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) aqueous (dissolved in water).
2H2O means two molecules of water: four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms.
The chemical formula of water is H2O, of carbon dioxide CO2, of ammonia NH3 and of methane CH4.
Hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine exist as diatomic molecules.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.1 Atomic structure: mixtures, separation and the developing model of the atom

lessons.title: Mixtures and separation: filtration, crystallisation, distillation and chromatography
objectives: I can describe filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation and chromatography
I can choose an appropriate separation technique for a given mixture and justify the choice
misconceptions: Thinking separation techniques involve chemical reactions; they are physical processes
Thinking distillation separates by melting point rather than boiling point
Thinking filtration can separate a dissolved salt from water

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: The development of the model of the atom
objectives: I can describe how the model of the atom changed from Dalton's spheres to the nuclear model
I can explain how the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the nuclear model
I can describe the contributions of Bohr and Chadwick
misconceptions: Thinking scientists 'proved' the earlier models wrong by argument rather than by new experimental evidence
Thinking the plum pudding model had a nucleus
Thinking Rutherford discovered the neutron; that was Chadwick, about 20 years later

assessment.type: Extended response (6 mark, levels of response), written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined, so the chemical properties of each substance are unchanged.
Mixtures can be separated by physical processes that do not involve chemical reactions.
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; the solid left in the filter paper is the residue and the liquid that passes through is the filtrate.
Crystallisation separates a soluble solid from its solution by evaporating the solvent.
Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution; fractional distillation separates liquids with different boiling points.
Chromatography separates substances by their different solubilities in the moving solvent.
Dalton described atoms as solid spheres and thought different spheres made up the different elements.
The discovery of the electron by J J Thomson led to the plum pudding model: a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
In the alpha particle scattering experiment most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, some were deflected, and a very few bounced back.
Alpha scattering showed that the mass and positive charge of an atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus, so the plum pudding model was replaced by the nuclear model.
Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances in fixed energy levels.
James Chadwick provided the experimental evidence for the existence of the neutron, about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.
Scientific models change when new experimental evidence cannot be explained by the existing model.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.1 Atomic structure: subatomic particles, isotopes and electronic structure

lessons.title: Subatomic particles, atomic number, mass number and isotopes
objectives: I can state the relative charge and relative mass of protons, neutrons and electrons
I can work out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons from atomic and mass numbers
I can explain what isotopes are and calculate relative atomic mass from abundances
misconceptions: Thinking isotopes have different numbers of protons; they differ only in neutrons
Thinking the mass number is the same as the relative atomic mass; RAM is a weighted mean over isotopes
Thinking an atom has an overall charge - the number of protons equals the number of electrons

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

lessons.title: Electronic structure
objectives: I can write the electronic structure of the first 20 elements as numbers and as a diagram
I can relate the number of outer electrons to the group and the number of shells to the period
misconceptions: Filling the third shell with 18 electrons at GCSE - at this level it is 2, 8, 8
Thinking electrons are randomly scattered rather than in energy levels
Losing count so that the electron total no longer matches the atomic number

assessment.type: Multiple choice / closed short answer, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: A proton has relative charge +1 and relative mass 1; a neutron has relative charge 0 and relative mass 1; an electron has relative charge -1 and a relative mass of very nearly 0.
The atomic number is the number of protons, and it defines the element.
The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons.
number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number.
In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so there is no overall charge.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The radius of an atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m, and the radius of the nucleus is less than 1/10000 of that.
relative atomic mass = sum of (isotope abundance x isotope mass number) / 100.
Electrons occupy the lowest available energy level (shell) first.
The first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second and third shells hold up to 8 each at GCSE.
The electronic structure of an atom is written as numbers separated by commas, for example sodium is 2,8,1.
The number of electrons in the outer shell equals the group number for Groups 1 to 7.
The number of occupied shells equals the period number.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.1 The periodic table: development, metals and non-metals, and group trends

lessons.title: The periodic table, its development, metals and non-metals
objectives: I can explain how the modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number and by group
I can explain why Mendeleev left gaps and reordered some elements, and how isotopes explained the anomalies
I can distinguish metals from non-metals and relate this to electron loss or gain
misconceptions: Thinking Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic number; that came later, atomic weight was used
Thinking all elements on the left are reactive and all on the right are unreactive - Group 0 sits on the far right
Thinking metals gain electrons

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Group 0, Group 1 and Group 7: properties and trends
objectives: I can explain the unreactivity of the noble gases in terms of full outer shells
I can describe and explain the trend in reactivity down Group 1 and down Group 7
I can predict and explain halogen displacement reactions
misconceptions: Saying reactivity increases down Group 7 - it decreases, because the outer shell is further from the nucleus so an electron is gained less easily
Explaining trends by 'more electrons' rather than by distance from the nucleus, shielding and force of attraction
Thinking noble gases are unreactive because they have 8 electrons; helium has only 2

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
Elements in the same group have the same number of outer shell electrons and so have similar chemical properties.
Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of atomic weight, left gaps for undiscovered elements, and swapped the order of some elements to fit properties.
The discovery of isotopes explained why ordering by atomic weight sometimes put elements in the wrong place.
Metals are on the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table; non-metals are on the right and towards the top.
Metals react by losing electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions.
The noble gases in Group 0 are unreactive because they have a full outer shell of electrons.
Boiling points of the noble gases increase going down Group 0 as the relative atomic mass increases.
Group 1 alkali metals react with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen.
Reactivity increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.
Reactivity decreases down Group 7 because the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so an electron is gained less easily.
Melting and boiling points of the halogens increase down Group 7.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
The halogens exist as diatomic molecules: F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.1 Energy: stores, systems and energy calculations

lessons.title: Energy stores, systems and energy transfers
objectives: I can name the energy stores and describe how energy is transferred between them
I can describe the changes in energy stores in a falling object, a car braking and a kettle
misconceptions: Using the outdated 'types of energy' language such as sound energy or light energy; AQA requires stores and transfer pathways
Saying energy is used up or lost; in a closed system the total is constant, energy is dissipated to less useful stores
Thinking energy and force are the same thing

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy calculations
objectives: I can recall and apply Ek = 0.5 x m x v squared
I can recall and apply Ep = m x g x h
I can use conservation of energy to link a drop in one store to a rise in another
misconceptions: Forgetting to square the speed, or squaring the whole expression 0.5mv
Doubling speed and expecting kinetic energy to double; it becomes four times as large
Using the distance travelled along a slope rather than the vertical height for gravitational potential energy

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The energy stores are kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational potential, elastic potential, nuclear, magnetic and electrostatic.
Energy is transferred between stores mechanically, electrically, by heating, or by radiation.
A closed system is one in which neither matter nor energy can enter or leave; the net change in total energy of a closed system is always zero.
When a car brakes, energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes and surroundings.
kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)squared, Ek = 0.5mv^2, in joules.
gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height, Ep = mgh.
On Earth the gravitational field strength g is about 9.8 N/kg.
Doubling the speed of an object makes its kinetic energy four times as large.
In gravitational potential energy calculations, h is the vertical height gained or lost, not the distance travelled along a slope.
For a falling object with no air resistance, the energy lost from the gravitational potential store equals the energy gained by the kinetic store.
To find the speed of a falling object, set mgh = 0.5mv^2, cancel the mass, and rearrange to v = square root of (2gh).
The unit of energy is the joule (J).
Always convert grams to kilograms and centimetres to metres before substituting into a physics equation.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.1 Energy: elastic and thermal energy, and power

lessons.title: Elastic potential energy and specific heat capacity (Required practical 14)
objectives: I can select and apply the elastic potential energy equation Ee = 0.5 x k x e squared
I can select and apply the equation for a change in thermal energy, dE = m x c x d(theta)
I can determine the specific heat capacity of a material experimentally
misconceptions: Confusing specific heat capacity with specific latent heat
Thinking a material with a high specific heat capacity heats up quickly; it heats up slowly
Not allowing for energy transferred to the surroundings, which makes the measured value too high

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 14: an investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials, linking the decrease of one energy store to the increase in temperature and thermal energy stored.

lessons.title: Power as the rate of energy transfer
objectives: I can recall and apply P = E / t and P = W / t
I can explain what a power of one watt means and compare devices doing the same work in different times
misconceptions: Thinking a more powerful device always transfers more energy overall; it transfers energy faster
Confusing the units of energy (joule) and power (watt)
Forgetting to convert minutes to seconds before substituting

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)squared, Ee = 0.5ke^2. This equation is given on the equation sheet.
change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change, dE = mc(d theta). This equation is given on the equation sheet.
Specific heat capacity is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
The unit of specific heat capacity is J/kg C.
A substance with a high specific heat capacity needs a lot of energy to change its temperature, so it heats up and cools down slowly.
In the specific heat capacity practical the block is insulated and oil is placed in the thermometer hole to improve thermal contact.
Energy transferred to the surroundings makes the experimental value of specific heat capacity higher than the true value.
power = energy transferred / time, P = E/t.
power = work done / time, P = W/t.
The unit of power is the watt (W), and one watt is one joule per second.
Two devices that transfer the same total energy have different powers if they take different times.
1 kilowatt = 1000 watts.
Time must be in seconds when using P = E/t.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.1 Energy: conservation, dissipation and efficiency

lessons.title: Conservation and dissipation of energy: lubrication, insulation and thermal conductivity
objectives: I can state the principle of conservation of energy and explain what dissipated energy means
I can explain how lubrication, streamlining, insulation and thickness reduce unwanted energy transfer
I can explain how thermal conductivity affects the rate of cooling of a building
misconceptions: Saying energy is lost rather than dissipated to the surroundings, usually as thermal energy
Thinking a good insulator has a high thermal conductivity
Thinking insulation stops heat transfer completely rather than slowing the rate

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Efficiency
objectives: I can recall and apply the two efficiency equations, using energy or using power
I can express efficiency as a decimal or a percentage and interpret Sankey-style information
I can suggest ways of increasing the efficiency of an energy transfer
misconceptions: Producing an efficiency greater than 1 or over 100%, which is impossible
Using total output rather than USEFUL output on the top of the fraction
Giving efficiency units

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The principle of conservation of energy states that energy can be transferred, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.
Dissipated energy is energy transferred to the surroundings in a way that is not useful; it is often described as wasted.
Lubrication reduces friction between moving surfaces and so reduces unwanted energy transfer.
Thermal insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating from a building.
The rate of cooling of a building depends on the thickness and the thermal conductivity of its walls.
The higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across it.
Cavity wall insulation and double glazing trap air, which has a low thermal conductivity.
efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer.
efficiency = useful power output / total power input.
Efficiency has no units and can be given as a decimal or as a percentage.
Efficiency can never be greater than 1, or 100%.
To convert an efficiency decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100.
Efficiency can be increased by reducing wasted energy transfers, for example by lubrication or better insulation.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.1 Energy resources; Biology 4.2 Organisation: levels of organisation and digestion

lessons.title: National and global energy resources
objectives: I can name the main energy resources and classify them as renewable or non-renewable
I can compare energy resources for reliability, environmental impact and cost
I can explain why patterns of energy use have changed and evaluate the political and ethical issues
misconceptions: Thinking nuclear power is renewable, or that it produces carbon dioxide during generation
Thinking renewable means reliable; wind and solar are not reliable
Thinking biofuels are carbon neutral without qualification

assessment.type: Extended response (6 mark, levels of response), written paper

lessons.title: Principles of organisation and the human digestive system
objectives: I can order cells, tissues, organs and organ systems as levels of organisation
I can name the organs of the digestive system and state the function of each
misconceptions: Thinking food is 'inside the body' once swallowed - it is inside the gut until it is absorbed
Thinking the liver makes insulin (that is the pancreas) or that bile is made in the gall bladder (it is made in the liver and stored there)
Confusing digestion (breakdown) with absorption (movement into the blood)

assessment.type: Multiple choice / closed short answer, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The non-renewable energy resources are coal, oil, natural gas and nuclear fuel.
The renewable energy resources are biofuel, wind, hydroelectricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves.
A renewable energy resource is one that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which contributes to global warming, and sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain.
Wind and solar are unreliable because they depend on the weather; tidal and geothermal are reliable.
Nuclear power produces no carbon dioxide during generation but produces radioactive waste that must be stored for a very long time.
The trend in the UK has been away from coal and towards renewables, driven by concern about carbon dioxide emissions.
The levels of organisation are cells, tissues, organs, organ systems and the whole organism.
A tissue is a group of cells with a similar structure and function working together.
An organ is an aggregation of tissues performing specific functions.
The digestive system is an organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food.
Digestion is the breakdown of large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones; absorption is their movement into the bloodstream.
The pancreas produces amylase, protease and lipase, which act in the small intestine.
The liver produces bile, which is stored in the gall bladder.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.2 Organisation: enzymes and food tests

lessons.title: Enzymes, the lock and key model, and the effect of pH on amylase (Required practical 4)
objectives: I can explain enzyme action using the lock and key model, including the active site and substrate
I can explain how temperature and pH affect enzyme activity, including denaturing
I can investigate the effect of pH on the rate at which amylase breaks down starch
misconceptions: Saying an enzyme is 'killed' at high temperature - enzymes are not alive, they are denatured
Thinking denaturing breaks the peptide bonds; the shape of the active site changes so the substrate no longer fits
Thinking a higher temperature always means a faster reaction, ignoring the drop after the optimum
Thinking enzymes are used up in the reaction

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 4: investigate the effect of pH on the rate of reaction of amylase enzyme.

lessons.title: Food tests for carbohydrates, lipids and proteins (Required practical 3)
objectives: I can carry out and describe the Benedict's, iodine, biuret and ethanol/Sudan III tests
I can state the positive and negative result for each qualitative food test
misconceptions: Reporting the colour of the reagent rather than the colour change (Benedict's is blue and turns brick red)
Forgetting that Benedict's needs heating in a water bath
Thinking iodine turns black - the accepted answer is blue-black, and it stays orange-brown if starch is absent

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 3: use qualitative reagents to test for a range of carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.

knowledgeComponents.statement: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions without being used up.
In the lock and key model the substrate fits into the active site of the enzyme, which is a complementary shape.
If the temperature or pH goes too far from the optimum, the shape of the active site changes and the enzyme is denatured, so the substrate no longer fits.
Enzymes are not alive, so they cannot be killed; they are denatured.
Increasing temperature increases the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction up to the optimum, after which the rate falls sharply.
In the amylase practical, iodine solution stays orange-brown when all the starch has been digested.
Buffer solutions are used in the amylase practical to keep the pH constant at a set value.
rate of reaction in the amylase practical = 1000 / time in seconds.
Benedict's solution tests for reducing sugars: heat in a water bath at 75 C, and a positive result changes blue to brick red.
Iodine solution tests for starch: a positive result changes orange-brown to blue-black.
Biuret reagent tests for protein: a positive result changes blue to purple or lilac.
Sudan III stain or the ethanol emulsion test detects lipids: a positive result gives a red-stained layer or a cloudy white emulsion.
Food samples must be broken up and mixed with distilled water before a food test is carried out.
Benedict's test requires heating in a water bath rather than over a naked flame.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.2 Organisation: digestive enzymes, bile and the heart

lessons.title: Digestive enzymes, bile, and the products of digestion
objectives: I can name the enzymes that digest carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, where they are made, and their products
I can explain how bile emulsifies fat and neutralises stomach acid, and why this increases the rate of digestion
misconceptions: Calling bile an enzyme - it is an alkaline emulsifier and contains no enzymes
Saying bile breaks down fat - it breaks fat into droplets, increasing surface area for lipase
Thinking protease works best in alkaline conditions everywhere; stomach protease works at about pH 2

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: The heart, the double circulatory system and the blood vessels
objectives: I can describe the structure of the heart and the path of blood through the double circulatory system
I can explain how the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries relates to their function
I can explain the role of the natural pacemaker and of artificial pacemakers
misconceptions: Thinking arteries always carry oxygenated blood - the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood
Thinking the heart is on the left of the chest, and mislabelling left and right on a diagram drawn as if facing the patient
Thinking blood passes through the heart once per circuit; it passes through twice in a double circulatory system
Thinking veins have thicker walls than arteries

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Carbohydrase enzymes such as amylase break down starch into simple sugars.
Protease enzymes break down proteins into amino acids.
Lipase enzymes break down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.
Amylase is produced in the salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine.
Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and released into the small intestine.
Bile is alkaline, so it neutralises the hydrochloric acid from the stomach and gives enzymes their optimum pH.
Bile emulsifies fat into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase and so increasing the rate of digestion.
The heart has four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle.
Blood enters the right atrium from the vena cava and the left atrium from the pulmonary vein.
The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall because it pumps blood around the whole body.
Arteries have thick muscular elastic walls and a narrow lumen to withstand high pressure; veins have thin walls, a wide lumen and valves.
Capillaries are one cell thick to give a short diffusion path for exchange of substances.
The natural resting heart rate is controlled by a group of cells in the right atrium that act as a pacemaker.
The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.2 Organisation: blood and coronary heart disease

lessons.title: Blood: plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
objectives: I can name the four components of blood and give the function of each
I can explain how red blood cells are adapted to transport oxygen
misconceptions: Thinking platelets are cells - they are cell fragments
Thinking red blood cells have a nucleus in humans; they lose it to carry more haemoglobin
Thinking plasma carries oxygen; plasma mainly carries carbon dioxide, urea, glucose, hormones and heat

assessment.type: Multiple choice / closed short answer, written paper

lessons.title: Coronary heart disease, faulty valves and treatments
objectives: I can explain how the build-up of fatty material in the coronary arteries causes coronary heart disease
I can evaluate the use of stents, statins, mechanical and biological valves, and heart transplants
misconceptions: Thinking a stent lowers cholesterol - it physically widens the artery; statins lower cholesterol
Thinking statins have no drawbacks; they must be taken long term and can cause side effects
Thinking an artificial heart is a permanent cure rather than usually a bridge to transplant

assessment.type: Extended response (6 mark, levels of response), written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Blood is a tissue consisting of plasma with red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets suspended in it.
Plasma transports carbon dioxide, urea, glucose, hormones, antibodies and heat around the body.
Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin in the lungs.
Red blood cells have no nucleus and are biconcave, which increases surface area and space for haemoglobin.
White blood cells defend against infection by phagocytosis, by producing antibodies, and by producing antitoxins.
Platelets are cell fragments that help the blood to clot at a wound.
Coronary heart disease is caused by layers of fatty material building up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow to the heart muscle.
A stent is a mesh tube inserted to keep a narrowed coronary artery open.
Statins are drugs that reduce blood cholesterol, slowing the rate of fatty deposit formation.
Mechanical replacement valves last longer but require the patient to take anticoagulant drugs for life; biological valves do not, but wear out sooner.
In heart failure a donor heart, or a heart and lungs, may be transplanted; an artificial heart may be used temporarily.
Artificial hearts reduce the chance of rejection because they are not made of living tissue.
Any surgical treatment carries a risk of infection, bleeding and rejection of donor tissue.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.2 Bonding: ionic bonding and ionic compounds

lessons.title: Chemical bonds and ionic bonding
objectives: I can name the three types of strong chemical bond and state which particles they occur between
I can explain ionic bonding as the transfer of electrons producing oppositely charged ions
I can draw dot and cross diagrams for simple ionic compounds
misconceptions: Saying ions 'share' electrons in ionic bonding - electrons are transferred
Thinking the ionic bond is the transfer itself; the bond is the electrostatic attraction between the ions afterwards
Forgetting to write the charge and square brackets on ions in a dot and cross diagram

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Ionic compounds: giant lattices, formulae and properties
objectives: I can describe an ionic compound as a giant lattice held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions
I can deduce the formula of an ionic compound from the charges on its ions
I can explain why ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct only when molten or dissolved
misconceptions: Saying ionic compounds conduct because electrons move; the charge carriers are the mobile IONS
Saying you break bonds when melting an ionic solid without saying that many strong electrostatic forces must be overcome
Reading a ball and stick diagram as showing the true spacing of ions

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The three types of strong chemical bond are ionic, covalent and metallic.
Ionic bonding occurs between a metal and a non-metal; covalent bonding between non-metals; metallic bonding in metals and alloys.
In ionic bonding electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom, producing oppositely charged ions.
An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, acting in all directions.
Metals in Group 1 form 1+ ions, Group 2 form 2+ ions; non-metals in Group 6 form 2- ions and Group 7 form 1- ions.
In a dot and cross diagram of an ion, the ion is drawn in square brackets with its charge outside the bracket.
Ions formed by metals and non-metals in Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas.
An ionic compound is a giant lattice of ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions.
Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points because a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the many strong electrostatic forces.
Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water because the ions are then free to move and carry charge.
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity because the ions are held in fixed positions.
The formula of an ionic compound is deduced by balancing the total positive and negative charge, for example MgCl2.
Ball and stick models show the arrangement of ions but exaggerate the spacing and do not show the true size of the lattice.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.2 Bonding: covalent bonding, small molecules, giant covalent structures and polymers

lessons.title: Covalent bonding and the properties of small molecules
objectives: I can explain covalent bonding as a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms
I can draw dot and cross diagrams for H2, Cl2, O2, H2O, NH3, CH4 and HCl
I can explain why small molecules have low melting and boiling points and do not conduct
misconceptions: Saying the covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance melts or boils; only the weak intermolecular forces are overcome
Thinking intermolecular forces are a kind of bond as strong as a covalent bond
Thinking bigger molecules have weaker intermolecular forces; forces increase with molecule size

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Giant covalent structures and polymers
objectives: I can explain why giant covalent structures have very high melting points
I can explain why polymers are solid at room temperature but soften more easily than giant covalent structures
I can represent a polymer using the repeating unit notation
misconceptions: Thinking a polymer is a giant covalent structure in the same sense as diamond; polymer chains are held to each other by relatively strong intermolecular forces
Thinking silicon dioxide is a molecule rather than a giant structure
Forgetting the brackets and the n in the repeating unit

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
Covalent bonds are strong, but the intermolecular forces between small molecules are weak.
Substances made of small molecules have low melting and boiling points because only the weak intermolecular forces are overcome when they melt or boil.
When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, the covalent bonds inside the molecules do NOT break.
Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecule, so melting and boiling points increase.
Substances made of small molecules do not conduct electricity because the molecules have no overall electric charge.
The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas, and the particle model represents them as small solid spheres.
Polymers are very large molecules in which atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds in long chains.
Polymers are solid at room temperature because the intermolecular forces between the long chains are relatively strong.
A polymer is represented by its repeating unit written inside brackets with an n outside.
Giant covalent structures are solids with very high melting points because all the atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds.
Diamond, silicon dioxide and graphite are giant covalent structures.
Melting a giant covalent structure requires breaking many strong covalent bonds, which needs a very large amount of energy.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.2 Bonding: metallic bonding, alloys and the structures of carbon

lessons.title: Metallic bonding, the properties of metals, and alloys
objectives: I can describe metallic bonding as positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
I can explain why metals conduct electricity and heat and why they are malleable
I can explain why alloys are harder than pure metals
misconceptions: Saying metals conduct because the ions move; the ions stay in place and the delocalised electrons move
Thinking an alloy is a compound rather than a mixture
Thinking alloys are harder because they are 'stronger metals' rather than because differently sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Diamond, graphite, graphene and fullerenes; the three states of matter
objectives: I can explain the properties of diamond and graphite from their structure and bonding
I can describe graphene, fullerenes and carbon nanotubes and give a use of each
I can use the particle model to explain melting, boiling and the limitations of the model
misconceptions: Saying graphite conducts because it is a metal; it conducts because each carbon forms three bonds leaving one delocalised electron
Saying the layers in graphite are held by covalent bonds; they are held by weak intermolecular forces so they slide
Thinking diamond conducts electricity because it is shiny and hard

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Metals consist of giant structures of positive ions arranged in a regular pattern with a sea of delocalised electrons.
The metallic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
Metals conduct electricity and thermal energy because the delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure.
Pure metals are malleable because the layers of atoms are the same size and can slide over each other.
An alloy is a mixture of a metal with at least one other element.
Alloys are harder than pure metals because the different sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide over each other easily.
In diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in a giant structure, making it very hard with a very high melting point.
In graphite each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds, forming layers of hexagonal rings with no covalent bonds between the layers.
Graphite conducts electricity and thermal energy because one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.
Graphite is soft and slippery because the layers are held by weak intermolecular forces and can slide over each other.
Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick, and it is strong and conducts electricity.
Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes based on hexagonal rings; the first discovered was buckminsterfullerene, C60.
Carbon nanotubes have a very high length to diameter ratio, conduct electricity, and are useful in nanotechnology and as reinforcement in materials.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.2 Electricity: charge, current, potential difference and resistance

lessons.title: Circuit symbols, electrical charge and current
objectives: I can draw and interpret standard circuit diagram symbols
I can define current as the rate of flow of charge and recall and apply Q = I x t
I can explain why a closed loop and a source of potential difference are needed
misconceptions: Thinking current is used up as it goes round a series circuit; current is the same everywhere in a series circuit
Connecting an ammeter in parallel rather than in series
Thinking charge and current mean the same thing

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Potential difference, resistance and factors affecting resistance (Required practical 15)
objectives: I can recall and apply V = I x R and rearrange it
I can investigate how the length of a wire affects resistance, and how resistors combine in series and parallel
I can explain the relationship between resistance and length for a metal wire at constant temperature
misconceptions: Thinking voltage flows through a component; potential difference is across a component
Thinking adding resistors in parallel increases total resistance; it decreases it
Forgetting that a wire heats up as current passes, which changes the resistance

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 15: use circuit diagrams to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits, including the length of a wire at constant temperature and combinations of resistors in series and parallel.

knowledgeComponents.statement: Electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge.
charge flow = current x time, Q = It, with charge in coulombs, current in amperes and time in seconds.
For charge to flow through a circuit there must be a complete closed loop and a source of potential difference.
The current through a single closed loop is the same at every point in that loop.
An ammeter is connected in series with a component; a voltmeter is connected in parallel across it.
potential difference = current x resistance, V = IR, with pd in volts, current in amperes and resistance in ohms.
Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge, measured across a component.
The resistance of a length of uniform wire at constant temperature is directly proportional to its length.
Adding resistors in series increases the total resistance because the pd is shared and the current is reduced.
Adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance because there are more paths for the current.
In the resistance practical, the current is switched off between readings to stop the wire heating up and changing its resistance.
An ohmic conductor at constant temperature has a resistance that stays the same as current changes, so I is directly proportional to V.
To rearrange V = IR for resistance, R = V / I.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.2 Electricity: I-V characteristics, thermistors and LDRs

lessons.title: I-V characteristics of circuit elements (Required practical 16)
objectives: I can investigate the I-V characteristics of a resistor at constant temperature, a filament lamp and a diode
I can explain the shape of each I-V graph in terms of resistance
misconceptions: Reading the gradient of an I-V graph as the resistance rather than as 1/R
Thinking a filament lamp is ohmic because it is a simple component; its resistance rises as it heats
Thinking a diode has zero resistance in the forward direction

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 16: use circuit diagrams to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I-V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature.

lessons.title: Resistors, thermistors and light dependent resistors
objectives: I can describe how the resistance of a thermistor changes with temperature and of an LDR with light intensity
I can explain the use of thermistors and LDRs in sensing circuits
misconceptions: Thinking the resistance of a thermistor increases as it gets hotter; it decreases
Thinking an LDR has high resistance in bright light; resistance falls as light intensity rises
Confusing an LDR with an LED

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The I-V graph of a resistor at constant temperature is a straight line through the origin.
The I-V graph of a filament lamp is an S-shaped curve because resistance increases as the filament heats up.
The I-V graph of a diode shows almost no current in the reverse direction because the resistance is very high one way round.
A diode allows current to flow in one direction only.
In an I-V graph, a steeper line means a lower resistance.
To find resistance from an I-V graph, read a pair of values and calculate R = V / I; do not use the gradient directly.
In the I-V characteristics practical, a variable resistor is used to change the current through the component.
Readings should be taken with the supply reversed so that negative values of current and potential difference can be plotted.
The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases.
The resistance of a light dependent resistor decreases as light intensity increases.
Thermistors are used in thermostats and temperature-sensing circuits.
Light dependent resistors are used in switching circuits such as automatic street lighting.
An LDR is a sensor whose resistance changes with light; an LED is a diode that emits light.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.2 Electricity: series and parallel circuits, and mains electricity

lessons.title: Series and parallel circuits
objectives: I can state the rules for current, potential difference and resistance in series and in parallel circuits
I can calculate total resistance in series, and explain why parallel resistors reduce total resistance
I can solve multi-step circuit problems
misconceptions: Thinking current is shared equally between unequal parallel branches
Thinking two lamps in parallel are dimmer than one because the current is shared
Adding parallel resistances as if they were in series

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

lessons.title: Direct and alternating potential difference; mains electricity and safety
objectives: I can explain the difference between direct and alternating potential difference
I can state that UK mains is 230 V at 50 Hz and describe the three-core cable
I can explain why a live wire is dangerous even when a switch is open, and the role of the earth wire
misconceptions: Thinking the earth wire carries current in normal use; it is a safety wire
Thinking the neutral wire is at a dangerous potential; it is at about 0 V
Thinking a switch on the neutral side makes an appliance safe

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: In a series circuit the current is the same through every component.
In a series circuit the total potential difference of the supply is shared between the components.
In a series circuit the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances, R total = R1 + R2.
In a parallel circuit the potential difference across each branch is the same and equals the supply pd.
In a parallel circuit the total current is the sum of the currents through the separate branches.
The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smaller individual resistor.
Adding a lamp in parallel does not make the other lamps dimmer, because each branch still has the full supply pd across it.
Direct potential difference gives a current that is always in the same direction; alternating potential difference repeatedly reverses direction.
UK mains electricity is an alternating supply at about 230 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.
In a three-core cable the live wire is brown, the neutral wire is blue, and the earth wire is green and yellow.
The live wire carries the alternating potential difference from the supply; the neutral wire completes the circuit and is at about 0 V.
The earth wire is a safety wire that carries a current only if there is a fault.
Touching the live wire is dangerous even when a switch is open, because a large potential difference exists between the live wire and the body at 0 V, so a current flows through the body.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.2 Electrical power and the National Grid; Biology 4.2 health and risk factors

lessons.title: Electrical power, energy transfers in appliances and the National Grid
objectives: I can recall and apply P = V x I and P = I squared x R
I can recall and apply E = P x t and E = Q x V
I can explain why the National Grid transmits at high potential difference and low current
misconceptions: Thinking the grid uses high current to deliver more power; high pd and low current reduce heating losses
Thinking a transformer changes power; an ideal transformer changes pd and current, not power
Confusing the kilowatt (power) with the kilowatt hour (energy)

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

lessons.title: Health, risk factors and non-communicable disease
objectives: I can define health as a state of physical and mental wellbeing
I can explain how diet, smoking, alcohol and exercise are risk factors for non-communicable diseases
I can explain the difference between a correlation and a causal mechanism
misconceptions: Treating correlation as proof of cause - a causal mechanism must be shown
Thinking health means only the absence of disease
Thinking diseases never interact - a virus can trigger cancer, and immune reactions can cause allergies

assessment.type: Extended response (6 mark, levels of response), written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: power = potential difference x current, P = VI.
power = (current)squared x resistance, P = I^2 R.
energy transferred = power x time, E = Pt.
energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference, E = QV.
The amount of energy an appliance transfers depends on how long the appliance is switched on and the power of the appliance.
The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
Step-up transformers increase the potential difference for transmission, which reduces the current and therefore reduces energy wasted by heating in the cables.
Step-down transformers reduce the potential difference to a safe level for domestic use.
Health is a state of physical and mental wellbeing.
Diseases are a major cause of ill health, but diet, stress and life situations also affect physical and mental health.
Different types of disease may interact: a weakened immune system makes infection more likely, some viruses trigger cancers, and immune reactions can cause allergies.
A risk factor is a variable linked to an increased rate of a disease.
A correlation between a factor and a disease does not prove cause; a causal mechanism must be shown.
Risk factors for non-communicable disease include obesity for type 2 diabetes, alcohol for liver and brain damage, and smoking for lung disease and lung cancer.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.2 Organisation: cancer and plant tissues and transport

lessons.title: Cancer: benign and malignant tumours
objectives: I can explain that cancer is the result of uncontrolled cell division forming a tumour
I can describe the difference between benign and malignant tumours
I can identify genetic and lifestyle risk factors for cancer
misconceptions: Thinking all tumours are cancer - benign tumours do not invade other tissues
Thinking cancer is caught or inherited in every case; most cancers arise from mutations with lifestyle and genetic risk factors
Thinking benign tumours are always harmless; they can still damage tissue by pressing on it

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Plant tissues and the plant organ system: transpiration and translocation
objectives: I can name the tissues of a leaf and relate each to its function
I can explain how the structure of xylem and phloem suits transport of water and of dissolved sugars
I can explain how temperature, humidity, air movement and light intensity affect the rate of transpiration
misconceptions: Saying stomata are on the top of the leaf; most are on the lower epidermis to reduce water loss
Confusing transpiration (water, in xylem, upwards) with translocation (dissolved sugars, in phloem, both ways)
Thinking plants take in oxygen only at night; they respire continuously

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division, forming a tumour.
Benign tumours grow in one place within a membrane and do not invade other parts of the body.
Malignant tumour cells are cancers; they invade neighbouring tissues and spread in the blood to form secondary tumours.
Risk factors for cancer include smoking, obesity, UV exposure, ionising radiation, viral infection and inherited genetic factors.
The tissues of a leaf are epidermal tissue, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem, and meristem tissue at growing tips.
Palisade mesophyll cells contain the most chloroplasts and are near the top of the leaf for maximum light absorption.
Spongy mesophyll has air spaces that increase the surface area for gas exchange by diffusion.
Stomata are mainly on the lower surface of the leaf; guard cells open and close them to control gas exchange and water loss.
Transpiration is the movement of water from the roots through the xylem and out of the leaves.
Xylem transports water and mineral ions upwards only; phloem transports dissolved sugars in both directions by translocation.
Xylem is made of dead hollow cells strengthened by lignin; phloem is made of living cells with sieve plates.
The rate of transpiration increases with higher temperature, higher light intensity, more air movement and lower humidity.
Guard cells close the stomata when the plant is short of water, which reduces water loss but also reduces photosynthesis.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.3 Infection and response: pathogens, viral, bacterial, fungal and protist disease

lessons.title: Communicable disease, pathogens and viral diseases
objectives: I can describe how pathogens are spread by direct contact, by water and by air
I can describe measles, HIV and tobacco mosaic virus, including their symptoms and spread
misconceptions: Thinking bacteria and viruses are the same kind of thing; viruses reproduce inside cells and burst them, bacteria produce toxins
Thinking HIV and AIDS are the same - AIDS is the late stage when the immune system is badly damaged
Thinking antibiotics can treat viral disease

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Bacterial, fungal and protist diseases
objectives: I can describe salmonella and gonorrhoea, their symptoms, spread and control
I can describe rose black spot and malaria, including the role of the mosquito as a vector
misconceptions: Saying mosquitoes cause malaria - the mosquito is the vector and a protist is the pathogen
Thinking rose black spot is bacterial; it is a fungal disease spread by water and wind
Thinking gonorrhoea is still easily treated with penicillin - resistant strains have appeared

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease, and include bacteria, viruses, protists and fungi.
Bacteria make you feel ill by producing toxins that damage tissues and cells.
Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage when the cell bursts.
Pathogens can be spread by direct contact, by water and by air.
Measles is a viral disease spread by inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs; symptoms are fever and a red skin rash, and it can be fatal.
Most young children are vaccinated against measles.
HIV is spread by sexual contact or exchange of body fluids such as blood when drug users share needles; it is controlled with antiretroviral drugs.
Late stage HIV, or AIDS, occurs when the virus attacks the body's immune cells so badly that the body can no longer deal with other infections.
Tobacco mosaic virus is a widespread plant pathogen that gives a distinctive mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves, reducing photosynthesis and growth.
Salmonella is a bacterium causing food poisoning; symptoms are fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea caused by toxins.
In the UK poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.
Gonorrhoea is a bacterial sexually transmitted disease with a thick yellow or green discharge and pain on urinating; it was treated with penicillin until resistant strains appeared.
Rose black spot is a fungal disease that causes purple or black spots on rose leaves, which then turn yellow and drop; it is spread by water and wind and treated with fungicides.
Malaria is caused by a protist pathogen carried by mosquitoes acting as vectors; it causes recurrent episodes of fever and can be fatal.
Malaria is controlled by preventing the mosquito vector from breeding and by using mosquito nets.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.3 Infection and response: defence systems, vaccination and antibiotics

lessons.title: Human defence systems: non-specific defences and the immune system
objectives: I can describe the skin, nose, trachea, bronchi and stomach as non-specific defences
I can explain how phagocytes and lymphocytes destroy pathogens
misconceptions: Thinking white blood cells 'eat germs' as a single process - phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxin production are three distinct roles
Confusing antibodies with antibiotics
Thinking antibodies destroy the pathogen directly; they are specific to one antigen and mark or clump pathogens

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Vaccination, antibiotics and painkillers
objectives: I can explain how a vaccine produces immunity using dead or inactive pathogen and memory lymphocytes
I can explain herd immunity, and evaluate the use of vaccination
I can explain why antibiotics do not treat viruses and why resistance is increasing
misconceptions: Thinking a vaccine contains antibodies - it contains dead or inactive pathogen, and the body makes the antibodies
Thinking a vaccine gives you a mild dose of the disease
Saying bacteria 'become resistant because they are exposed' rather than because resistant mutants survive and reproduce
Thinking painkillers cure infection - they only treat symptoms

assessment.type: Extended response (6 mark, levels of response), written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The skin acts as a barrier, produces antimicrobial secretions and scabs over cuts.
The nose has hairs and mucus that trap particles containing pathogens.
The trachea and bronchi secrete mucus and are lined with cilia that waft mucus up to the throat to be swallowed.
The stomach produces hydrochloric acid, which kills most pathogens in food and drink.
Phagocytes ingest and digest pathogens by phagocytosis.
Lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to the antigens on a particular pathogen, and produce antitoxins that neutralise toxins.
An antigen is a marker molecule on the surface of a pathogen, and an antibody is specific to one antigen.
Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen to stimulate white blood cells to produce antibodies.
If the same pathogen re-enters the body, memory white blood cells produce the correct antibodies rapidly, preventing infection.
If a large proportion of the population is immune, the spread of the pathogen is much reduced; this is herd immunity.
Antibiotics such as penicillin kill bacteria inside the body but do not kill viruses.
Specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics.

Strains of bacteria resistant to antibiotics have emerged because resistant mutants survive treatment and reproduce, and resistance is increasing because of overuse and inappropriate use of antibiotics.
Painkillers and other medicines treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.3 drug development; Chemistry 5.3 Quantitative chemistry: conservation of mass and Mr

lessons.title: Discovery and development of drugs; preclinical and clinical trials
objectives: I can describe the plant and microorganism origins of digitalis, aspirin and penicillin
I can describe how new drugs are tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose
I can explain the use of placebos, and of double blind trials, and peer review
misconceptions: Thinking new drugs are tested on humans first; preclinical testing uses cells, tissues and live animals
Thinking a placebo is a low dose of the drug
Thinking efficacy means safety - efficacy is whether the drug works

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Conservation of mass, balanced equations and relative formula mass
objectives: I can explain the law of conservation of mass in terms of atoms being rearranged
I can calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of a compound from relative atomic masses
misconceptions: Thinking mass is lost in a reaction when a gas escapes; the atoms are still there
Forgetting to multiply by the subscript when calculating Mr, for example Ca(OH)2
Thinking Mr has units; relative masses have no units

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Digitalis, a heart drug, originates from foxgloves.
Aspirin, a painkiller, originates from willow.
Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould.
New drugs are tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose.
Preclinical testing is done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals.
Clinical trials use healthy volunteers first, at very low doses, to test for safety, then patients to find the optimum dose.
In a double blind trial some patients are given a placebo and neither the doctors nor the patients know who has received the real drug.
Results of drug testing are published only after peer review, which helps to prevent false claims.
The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction, so the total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants.
The relative formula mass Mr of a compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in its formula.
In Ca(OH)2 the subscript 2 applies to everything in the bracket, so there are two oxygen atoms and two hydrogen atoms.
Relative atomic mass and relative formula mass have no units.
In a balanced equation the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants, taking account of the balancing numbers, equals that of the products.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.3 Quantitative chemistry: mass changes, uncertainty and moles (HT)

lessons.title: Mass changes when a reactant or product is a gas; chemical measurements and uncertainty
objectives: I can explain an apparent increase or decrease in mass in a non-enclosed system
I can represent the distribution of a set of results and use range to estimate uncertainty
misconceptions: Saying mass has been created when a metal is heated in air; the gain is the mass of oxygen added
Reporting uncertainty as the range rather than half the range
Including an anomaly when calculating a mean

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

lessons.title: Moles, the Avogadro constant and reacting masses (Higher tier only)
objectives: I can use the relationship mass = relative formula mass x number of moles
I can calculate the masses of reactants and products from a balanced equation
I can use masses to deduce the balancing numbers in an equation
misconceptions: Confusing the number of moles with the number of particles
Using the ratio of masses instead of the ratio of moles when working from a balanced equation
Forgetting that mole ratio comes from the big numbers in the equation, not the subscripts

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: If the mass of a reaction mixture increases in a non-enclosed system, a gas from the air such as oxygen has been added to the reactants.
If the mass of a reaction mixture decreases in a non-enclosed system, a gas has been produced and has escaped.
Whenever a measurement is made there is always some uncertainty about the result.
The mean of a set of results is calculated after excluding any anomalous result.
The uncertainty of a mean is estimated as half the range of the concordant results.
One mole of a substance contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles, the Avogadro constant. (HT)
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass. (HT)
number of moles = mass in grams / relative formula mass. (HT)
The balancing numbers in a symbol equation give the ratio of the numbers of MOLES of each substance, not the ratio of masses. (HT)
To find a reacting mass: convert the known mass to moles, use the mole ratio from the equation, then convert back to mass. (HT)
Masses of reactants and products can be used to deduce the balancing numbers of an equation by converting each mass to moles and finding the simplest whole number ratio. (HT)
The symbol for the unit of amount of substance is mol. (HT)

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.3 limiting reactants and concentration; 5.4 Chemical changes: reactivity of metals

lessons.title: Limiting reactants (HT) and concentration of solutions
objectives: I can explain what a limiting reactant is and identify it from a balanced equation (HT)
I can calculate the concentration of a solution in g/dm3 and convert cm3 to dm3
misconceptions: Assuming the reactant with the smaller mass is limiting without using mole ratios
Forgetting to convert cm3 to dm3, giving an answer 1000 times too small or too large
Thinking a more concentrated solution always means a larger volume

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

lessons.title: Metal oxides, oxidation and the reactivity series
objectives: I can define oxidation as gain of oxygen and reduction as loss of oxygen
I can place metals in order of reactivity from their reactions with water and dilute acid
I can explain reactivity in terms of the tendency of a metal atom to form a positive ion
misconceptions: Thinking reduction means the substance gets smaller
Thinking gold and platinum are unreactive because they are rare or valuable, rather than because they resist forming ions
Forgetting that carbon and hydrogen are placed in the reactivity series for comparison

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The limiting reactant is the reactant that is completely used up first and so limits the amount of product formed. (HT)
The reactant that is not completely used up is said to be in excess. (HT)
The amount of product formed is directly proportional to the amount of the limiting reactant. (HT)
To identify the limiting reactant, convert both masses to moles and compare with the mole ratio in the equation. (HT)
concentration in g/dm3 = mass of solute in g / volume of solution in dm3.
1 dm3 = 1000 cm3, so to convert cm3 to dm3 divide by 1000.
The mass of solute and the volume of solution must both be known to calculate concentration.
Oxidation is the gain of oxygen and reduction is the loss of oxygen.
When a metal reacts with oxygen it is oxidised to form a metal oxide.
The reactivity series in order of decreasing reactivity is potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper.
Carbon and hydrogen are included in the reactivity series as non-metals for comparison.
The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form a positive ion.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound.
Unreactive metals such as gold are found in the Earth as the metal itself.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.4 Chemical changes: extraction of metals, redox and reactions of acids

lessons.title: Extraction of metals by reduction; oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons (HT)
objectives: I can explain why metals below carbon can be extracted by reduction with carbon
I can identify oxidation and reduction in terms of electron loss and gain using OIL RIG (HT)
I can write ionic equations for displacement reactions (HT)
misconceptions: Thinking all metals can be extracted with carbon; metals above carbon must be extracted by electrolysis
Reversing OIL RIG, so calling electron gain oxidation
Leaving spectator ions in an ionic equation

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Reactions of acids with metals, bases and carbonates; neutralisation and salts
objectives: I can write general equations for acid + metal, acid + base, acid + carbonate
I can name the salt produced by a given acid, and write the ionic equation for neutralisation
I can name common acids and alkalis and their ions
misconceptions: Thinking all bases are alkalis; an alkali is a soluble base
Forgetting that acid + carbonate also makes carbon dioxide and water
Writing the wrong salt, for example calling the salt from sulfuric acid a sulfide

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon.
Metals more reactive than carbon must be extracted by electrolysis of a molten compound.
In a reduction with carbon, the metal oxide loses oxygen and the carbon gains oxygen and is oxidised.
OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons. (HT)
In an ionic equation, spectator ions that appear unchanged on both sides are left out. (HT)
In the displacement of copper by magnesium, magnesium is oxidised (loses electrons) and copper ions are reduced (gain electrons). (HT)
acid + metal gives a salt + hydrogen.
acid + metal oxide, or acid + metal hydroxide, gives a salt + water.
acid + metal carbonate gives a salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, sulfuric acid produces sulfates and nitric acid produces nitrates.
A base is a substance that neutralises an acid; an alkali is a base that is soluble in water.
Acids produce hydrogen ions, H+, in aqueous solution; alkalis produce hydroxide ions, OH-.
The ionic equation for neutralisation is H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) gives H2O (l).

weeks.dates: Mon 3 May - Fri 7 May 2027 (bank holiday Mon 3 May)
weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.4 Chemical changes: making a soluble salt, the pH scale and strong and weak acids

lessons.title: Preparing a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt (Required practical 8)
objectives: I can prepare a pure dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate
I can explain each step: warming the acid, adding excess base, filtering and crystallising
misconceptions: Thinking excess base is a mistake; excess ensures all the acid reacts, and it is then filtered off
Evaporating to dryness over a flame, which decomposes the crystals - the solution should be evaporated to the crystallisation point and left to cool
Thinking the filtrate is thrown away; the filtrate contains the salt

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 8: preparation of a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate.

lessons.title: The pH scale, neutralisation, and strong and weak acids (HT)
objectives: I can use the pH scale and universal indicator to classify solutions
I can describe how to carry out a titration to find the volume needed for neutralisation
I can explain the difference between a strong and a weak acid, and between concentrated and dilute (HT)
misconceptions: Using 'strong' to mean 'concentrated' - strong refers to how completely the acid ionises, concentrated to how much acid is in a given volume
Thinking a weak acid cannot be dangerous
Thinking pH changes by one unit means the hydrogen ion concentration changes by one unit; it changes by a factor of ten (HT)

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: A soluble salt can be made by reacting an acid with an insoluble metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate.
The acid is warmed gently before adding the insoluble base, to speed up the reaction.
The insoluble base is added until it is in excess, which shows that all the acid has reacted.
Excess solid is removed by filtration, leaving a solution of the salt as the filtrate.
The salt solution is evaporated to the point of crystallisation and then left to cool so that crystals form slowly.
Crystals are dried by patting between filter paper or in a warm oven, not by strong heating, which would decompose them.
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is; 7 is neutral.
Acids have a pH below 7 and alkalis have a pH above 7.
pH can be measured with universal indicator, which gives an approximate value from its colour, or with a pH probe, which is more accurate.
In a titration, an indicator shows the end point when exactly enough acid has been added to neutralise the alkali.
A strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution; hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids are strong acids. (HT)
A weak acid is only partially ionised in aqueous solution; ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are weak acids. (HT)
Strong and weak describe the degree of ionisation; concentrated and dilute describe the amount of acid in a given volume of solution. (HT)
As the pH decreases by one unit, the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10. (HT)

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.4 Chemical changes: electrolysis of molten compounds and of aqueous solutions

lessons.title: Electrolysis of molten ionic compounds, extraction of aluminium, and half equations (HT)
objectives: I can explain why an ionic compound must be molten or dissolved to be electrolysed
I can predict the products of electrolysis of a molten binary ionic compound
I can explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis, the role of cryolite, and write half equations (HT)
misconceptions: Mixing up the electrodes - cations (positive ions) go to the cathode (negative electrode)
Thinking electrolysis works on a solid ionic compound; the ions must be free to move
Not balancing charge in a half equation, for example writing Al3+ + e- gives Al

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions (Required practical 9)
objectives: I can predict the products of electrolysis of aqueous solutions using inert electrodes
I can investigate what happens when aqueous solutions are electrolysed and test the gases produced
misconceptions: Forgetting that water provides H+ and OH- ions, so hydrogen or oxygen may be produced instead of the metal
Predicting the metal at the cathode when the metal is more reactive than hydrogen
Thinking oxygen relights a glowing splint only in a mixture; the test is a glowing splint relighting

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 9: investigate what happens when aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert electrodes.

knowledgeComponents.statement: Electrolysis is the breaking down of an ionic compound using electricity.
An ionic compound must be molten or dissolved in water before it can be electrolysed, so that the ions are free to move.
The negative electrode is the cathode and the positive electrode is the anode.
Positive ions move to the cathode and are reduced; negative ions move to the anode and are oxidised.
When a molten binary ionic compound is electrolysed, the metal is produced at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.
Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of aluminium oxide because aluminium is more reactive than carbon.
Aluminium oxide is mixed with cryolite to lower the melting point, which reduces the energy needed and the cost.
The carbon anodes in aluminium extraction must be replaced regularly because they react with the oxygen produced.
A half equation shows what happens at one electrode; for example, Al3+ + 3e- gives Al at the cathode. (HT)
In the electrolysis of an aqueous solution, hydrogen is produced at the cathode if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
