In the electrolysis of an aqueous solution, oxygen is produced at the anode unless the solution contains halide ions, in which case the halogen is produced.
The test for hydrogen is a lighted splint giving a squeaky pop.
The test for oxygen is that it relights a glowing splint.
The test for chlorine is that it bleaches damp litmus paper white.
Inert electrodes such as graphite are used so that they do not react with the electrolyte or the products.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.5 Energy changes: exothermic and endothermic reactions

lessons.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
objectives: I can distinguish exothermic and endothermic reactions by the temperature change of the surroundings
I can give everyday applications: self-heating cans, hand warmers and sports injury packs
misconceptions: Thinking endothermic reactions feel hot because energy is taken in; they feel cold
Thinking energy is created or destroyed in a chemical reaction
Thinking all reactions that need heating to start are endothermic - combustion needs a spark but is exothermic

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Investigating temperature changes in reacting solutions (Required practical 10)
objectives: I can investigate the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions
I can plot and interpret results and identify the point of neutralisation from a temperature graph
misconceptions: Thinking a bigger volume always gives a bigger temperature rise
Not insulating the cup and blaming an anomaly rather than heat loss to the surroundings
Recording the final temperature rather than the maximum temperature reached

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 10: investigate the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions, such as acid plus alkali or displacement of metals.

knowledgeComponents.statement: An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Combustion, oxidation and neutralisation are exothermic reactions.
Thermal decomposition and the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate are endothermic.
Self-heating cans and hand warmers use exothermic reactions; some sports injury packs use endothermic reactions.
Energy is conserved in a chemical reaction; it is transferred, not created or destroyed.
In the energy changes practical, a polystyrene cup with a lid is used to reduce energy transfer to the surroundings.
The maximum temperature reached, not the final temperature, is recorded in the energy changes practical.
When acid is added to alkali in stages, the temperature rises to a maximum at the point of neutralisation and then falls as excess cold reagent is added.
A thermometer with a smaller scale division has a higher resolution and gives a more precise temperature reading.
Variables that affect the temperature change include the concentrations of the solutions, the volumes used and the identity of the metal or acid.
Energy transferred to the surroundings makes the measured temperature rise smaller than the true value.

weeks.unit: Chemistry 5.5 reaction profiles and bond energies; Physics 6.3 Particle model: density

lessons.title: Reaction profiles, activation energy and bond energy calculations (HT)
objectives: I can draw and label reaction profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions
I can explain activation energy as the minimum energy needed for particles to react
I can calculate the overall energy change of a reaction from bond energies (HT)
misconceptions: Thinking bond breaking releases energy - breaking bonds is endothermic, making bonds is exothermic
Drawing the activation energy from the axis rather than from the reactant energy level to the peak
Getting the sign wrong: a negative overall energy change means exothermic

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

lessons.title: Density of solids and liquids (Required practical 17)
objectives: I can recall and apply density = mass / volume
I can determine the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids
I can use the particle model to explain the different densities of solids, liquids and gases
misconceptions: Thinking a heavier object is always denser, ignoring volume
Thinking particles expand when a substance is heated; the particles stay the same size and the spacing increases
Mixing up units, for example dividing grams by cubic metres

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 17: use appropriate apparatus to make and record the measurements needed to determine the densities of regular and irregular solid objects and liquids.

knowledgeComponents.statement: A reaction profile shows the relative energies of reactants and products and the activation energy.
In an exothermic reaction profile the products are at a lower energy than the reactants.
In an endothermic reaction profile the products are at a higher energy than the reactants.
Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react, measured from the reactant energy level to the peak.
Breaking bonds is an endothermic process and making bonds is an exothermic process.
overall energy change = energy taken in to break bonds - energy released when bonds are made. (HT)
A negative overall energy change means the reaction is exothermic; a positive value means it is endothermic. (HT)
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy and is not used up.
density = mass / volume, with density in kg/m3 or g/cm3.
The density of a regular solid is found by measuring its mass on a balance and calculating its volume from its dimensions.
The volume of an irregular solid is found by displacement, using a eureka can or a measuring cylinder of water.
The density of a liquid is found by measuring the mass of a known volume, remembering to subtract the mass of the empty measuring cylinder.
Solids are usually denser than liquids, and gases are far less dense, because of the spacing of the particles.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.3 Particle model: changes of state, internal energy and specific heat capacity

lessons.title: Changes of state and the particle model
objectives: I can name the changes of state and describe them as physical changes
I can explain why mass is conserved in a change of state and why the change is reversible
misconceptions: Thinking a change of state is a chemical change because a new substance appears different
Thinking mass changes when ice melts
Thinking evaporation happens only at the boiling point

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Internal energy and specific heat capacity
objectives: I can describe internal energy as the total kinetic and potential energy of the particles in a system
I can explain what happens to internal energy when a system is heated
I can select and apply dE = m x c x d(theta) in multi-step problems
misconceptions: Thinking heat and temperature are the same; temperature is a measure of average particle kinetic energy
Thinking a large object at a low temperature has less internal energy than a small object at a high temperature
Forgetting to use the CHANGE in temperature rather than the final temperature

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The changes of state are melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and sublimating.
A change of state is a physical change, not a chemical change, because the substance recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.
Mass is conserved in a change of state, because the number of particles does not change.
In a change of state the particles themselves do not change; only their arrangement, spacing and motion change.
Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
Heating a system increases the internal energy, which either raises the temperature or produces a change of state.
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, whereas internal energy is the total energy of all the particles.
change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change, dE = mc(d theta).
In dE = mc(d theta), the temperature term is the CHANGE in temperature, not the final temperature.
A change of 1 degree Celsius is the same size as a change of 1 kelvin, so temperature differences can be used directly.
To find specific heat capacity from experimental data, rearrange to c = dE / (m x d theta).
A large object at a low temperature can have more internal energy than a small object at a high temperature.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.3 Particle model: specific latent heat and particle motion in gases

lessons.title: Specific latent heat and heating and cooling graphs
objectives: I can define specific latent heat of fusion and of vaporisation
I can select and apply E = m x L
I can interpret the flat sections of a temperature-time graph during a change of state
misconceptions: Thinking the temperature keeps rising while a substance melts; it stays constant during a change of state
Thinking energy is not being supplied during the flat part of the graph
Confusing specific latent heat (J/kg) with specific heat capacity (J/kg C)

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

lessons.title: Particle motion in gases and gas pressure
objectives: I can explain gas pressure as the result of collisions of particles with the container walls
I can explain why increasing temperature at constant volume increases pressure
I can relate the temperature of a gas to the average kinetic energy of its molecules
misconceptions: Thinking gas particles push each other apart or repel; pressure comes from collisions with the walls
Thinking particles get bigger when a gas is heated
Thinking all particles in a gas move at the same speed

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Specific latent heat is the amount of energy required to change the state of one kilogram of a substance with no change in temperature.
energy for a change of state = mass x specific latent heat, E = mL. This equation is given on the equation sheet.
Specific latent heat of fusion is for the change between solid and liquid; specific latent heat of vaporisation is for the change between liquid and vapour.
The unit of specific latent heat is J/kg.
During a change of state the temperature stays constant, giving a flat section on a heating or cooling graph, even though energy is still being transferred.
During the flat section of a heating graph the energy supplied is used to break the forces between particles, increasing potential energy not kinetic energy.
Specific heat capacity is measured in J/kg C and involves a temperature change; specific latent heat is measured in J/kg and involves no temperature change.
The pressure of a gas is caused by the collisions of its particles with the walls of the container.
The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion with a range of different speeds.
The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules.
Increasing the temperature of a gas at constant volume increases the pressure, because the particles move faster and collide with the walls more often and harder.
Gas pressure produces a net force at right angles to any surface in contact with the gas.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.4 Atomic structure: the atom, isotopes and the development of the model

lessons.title: The structure of the atom; mass number, atomic number and isotopes
objectives: I can describe the atom as a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in energy levels
I can state that the radius of an atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m and the nucleus is about 1/10000 of that
I can explain what an isotope is and how electron absorption or emission changes the energy level
misconceptions: Drawing the nucleus far too large relative to the atom
Thinking an isotope is a different element
Thinking an atom becomes an ion by gaining or losing a proton; it gains or loses electrons

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: The development of the model of the atom in physics
objectives: I can describe how the plum pudding model was replaced by the nuclear model
I can explain how alpha particle scattering provided the evidence for a small, charged, massive nucleus
I can describe the contributions of Bohr and of Chadwick
misconceptions: Thinking most alpha particles bounced back; nearly all passed straight through
Thinking the model changed because scientists preferred it, rather than because of experimental evidence
Confusing the physics account with the chemistry account - they are the same story and should be revised together

assessment.type: Extended response (6 mark, levels of response), written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: An atom consists of a tiny central nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in energy levels.
The radius of an atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m; the radius of the nucleus is less than 1/10000 of the radius of the atom.
Almost all of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
The atomic number is the number of protons; all atoms of a given element have the same atomic number.
The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
An atom becomes a positive ion by losing one or more electrons from its outer shells.
Electrons can move to a higher energy level by absorbing electromagnetic radiation, and move to a lower level by emitting it.
The plum pudding model described the atom as a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
The alpha particle scattering experiment showed that most of an atom is empty space with a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
Nearly all alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil; only a very small number were deflected through large angles.
Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances in fixed energy levels, and his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.
Later experiments established that the positive charge of a nucleus is divided into particles called protons, and Chadwick provided evidence for the neutron.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.4 Atomic structure: radioactive decay and nuclear equations

lessons.title: Radioactive decay: alpha, beta, gamma and neutron emission
objectives: I can describe alpha, beta, gamma and neutron radiation and compare their range, penetration and ionising power
I can define activity and count-rate and state their units
I can explain that radioactive decay is random
misconceptions: Thinking alpha is the least dangerous in all circumstances; it is the most dangerous if the source is inside the body
Thinking gamma is not ionising because it penetrates far; it is weakly ionising but very penetrating
Thinking you can predict when a particular nucleus will decay

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Nuclear equations
objectives: I can write and balance nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay
I can state the effect of each type of decay on the mass number and atomic number of the nucleus
misconceptions: Thinking gamma emission changes the mass number or the atomic number; it changes neither
Thinking a beta particle comes from the electron shells; it is emitted when a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton
Getting alpha decay wrong by subtracting 2 from the mass number instead of 4

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and give out radiation as they change to become more stable; this is radioactive decay.
Radioactive decay is a random process, so it is impossible to predict when a given nucleus will decay.
Activity is the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, measured in becquerel (Bq).
Count-rate is the number of decays recorded each second by a detector such as a Geiger-Muller tube.
An alpha particle consists of two neutrons and two protons, the same as a helium nucleus.
A beta particle is a high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton.
Alpha radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma by thick lead.
Alpha has a range in air of a few centimetres, beta a few metres, and gamma travels a very long distance.
Alpha is the most strongly ionising and gamma the least, so alpha is the most dangerous if the source is inside the body.
Alpha decay decreases the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.
Beta decay increases the atomic number by 1 and does not change the mass number.
Gamma emission does not change the mass number or the atomic number of the nucleus.
An alpha particle is written in a nuclear equation as helium with mass number 4 and atomic number 2.
A beta particle is written in a nuclear equation as an electron with mass number 0 and charge -1.

weeks.unit: Physics 6.4 half-life and contamination; Biology 4.4 Bioenergetics: photosynthesis

lessons.title: Half-life, and radioactive contamination and irradiation
objectives: I can define half-life and use it to determine the net decline in activity after a whole number of half-lives
I can explain the difference between contamination and irradiation and the hazards of each
I can explain why findings on the effects of radiation must be published and peer reviewed
misconceptions: Thinking half-life is the time for a source to become completely safe
Thinking an irradiated object becomes radioactive; irradiation does not make an object a source
Halving the count-rate the wrong number of times, or forgetting to subtract background radiation

assessment.type: Structured calculation question, written paper

lessons.title: Photosynthesis: the reaction and the uses of glucose
objectives: I can write the word and symbol equation for photosynthesis and state that it is endothermic
I can describe the five uses of the glucose made in photosynthesis
misconceptions: Thinking plants photosynthesise instead of respiring; plants do both, and respire all the time
Thinking plants get their food or mass from the soil, rather than mainly from carbon dioxide
Thinking photosynthesis is exothermic because it involves light; it is endothermic, energy is transferred IN

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: Half-life is the time it takes for the number of nuclei of an isotope in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count-rate to fall to half its initial level.
After n half-lives the remaining activity is the initial activity divided by 2 to the power n.
The net decline is often expressed as a ratio, for example a fall to one eighth after three half-lives is a ratio of 1:8.
Background radiation must be subtracted from the measured count-rate before calculating half-life.
Radioactive contamination is the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on or in other materials.
Irradiation is the process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation; the object does not become radioactive.
Suitable precautions must be taken to protect against any hazard the radioactive source used in the process of irradiation may present.
Findings about the effects of radiation on humans must be published and shared with other scientists so that they can be checked by peer review.
The word equation for photosynthesis is carbon dioxide + water gives glucose + oxygen, using light.
The symbol equation for photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O gives C6H12O6 + 6O2.
Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in which energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.

Glucose from photosynthesis is used for respiration, converted into starch for storage, converted into cellulose to strengthen cell walls, used to make lipids for storage in seeds, and combined with nitrate ions to make amino acids for protein synthesis.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.4 Bioenergetics: rate of photosynthesis and respiration

lessons.title: Rate of photosynthesis, limiting factors and the inverse square law (Required practical 5)
objectives: I can explain how light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature and chlorophyll limit the rate of photosynthesis
I can investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using pondweed
I can use the inverse square law to explain how light intensity changes with distance (HT)
misconceptions: Thinking the graph plateaus because the plant is 'full'; another factor has become limiting
Thinking light intensity halves when distance doubles; by the inverse square law it falls to one quarter
Not controlling temperature when the lamp itself heats the water

assessment.type: Required practical / practical skills question (AO2/AO3), written paper

lessons.requiredPractical: Required practical 5: investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using an aquatic organism such as pondweed.

lessons.title: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration
objectives: I can write the word and symbol equation for aerobic respiration and state that it is exothermic
I can compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in muscle and in yeast
I can state the three uses of the energy transferred by respiration
misconceptions: Thinking respiration is breathing - respiration is a chemical reaction in every cell
Thinking respiration 'makes' or 'produces' energy; energy is transferred, not created
Thinking anaerobic respiration releases more energy than aerobic because it feels harder; it releases much less per glucose molecule

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: The rate of photosynthesis is affected by temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll.
A limiting factor is the factor that is in shortest supply and so controls the rate of photosynthesis at that moment.
When a graph of rate against a factor levels off, another factor has become limiting.
Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source, so doubling the distance quarters the intensity. (HT)
In the photosynthesis practical, the number of bubbles of oxygen released by pondweed in a fixed time is counted at different distances from a lamp.
A glass tank or heat shield of water is placed between the lamp and the pondweed so that the lamp does not warm the water and change the temperature.
Greenhouse growers control temperature, light and carbon dioxide levels to increase the rate of photosynthesis and so increase crop yield.
The word equation for aerobic respiration is glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water.
The symbol equation for aerobic respiration is C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O.
Respiration is an exothermic reaction that occurs continuously in all living cells, mainly in the mitochondria.
Energy transferred by respiration is used for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, for movement, and for keeping warm.
Anaerobic respiration in muscle produces lactic acid, and releases much less energy per glucose molecule because the oxidation of glucose is incomplete.
Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells is called fermentation and produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

weeks.unit: Biology 4.4 Bioenergetics: response to exercise and metabolism

lessons.title: Response to exercise and oxygen debt
objectives: I can describe how heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase during exercise and explain why
I can explain what oxygen debt is and how lactic acid is removed (HT)
misconceptions: Thinking lactic acid causes muscle soreness days later, rather than fatigue during exercise
Thinking oxygen debt is a shortage of oxygen in the air
Thinking you stop breathing hard the instant exercise ends; extra oxygen is still needed to repay the debt

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

lessons.title: Metabolism
objectives: I can define metabolism as the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body
I can give examples of synthesis and breakdown reactions in metabolism
misconceptions: Thinking metabolism means only how fast you burn calories
Thinking proteins can be stored in the body; excess amino acids are deaminated and converted to urea
Thinking one lipid is made from one glycerol and one fatty acid; it is one glycerol and three fatty acids

assessment.type: Structured question, written paper

knowledgeComponents.statement: During exercise the heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.
If insufficient oxygen is supplied, anaerobic respiration takes place in muscles and lactic acid builds up, causing muscle fatigue.
Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.
Blood flowing through the muscles transports lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose. (HT)
Long periods of vigorous activity cause muscles to become fatigued so that they stop contracting efficiently.
Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or in the body.
The energy transferred by respiration is used to make new molecules in metabolic reactions.
Glucose molecules are joined to form starch, glycogen and cellulose.
A lipid molecule is made from one molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acid.
Glucose is combined with nitrate ions to make amino acids, which are then used to synthesise proteins.
Excess protein cannot be stored, so it is broken down to produce urea for excretion.
Respiration is a metabolic reaction that breaks down glucose to release energy for other metabolic processes.

subjects.name: GCSE Geography
subjects.notes: AQA GCSE Geography 8035 - the specification named by the family. 8035 has NOT been reformed for 2028 exams; it remains the 2016 first-teaching specification. Assessment (verified on the AQA scheme-of-assessment page): Paper 1 'Living with the physical environment' 88 raw marks, 35%; Paper 2 'Challenges in the human environment' 88 raw marks, 35%; Paper 3 'Geographical applications' 76 raw marks, 30%; 252 scaled marks in total. Paper durations (1h30, 1h30, 1h15) and the SPaG allocations (3, 3 and 6 marks) are from established practice, not verified on a live page during this build. Assessment objectives: AO1 knowledge 15%, AO2 understanding 25%, AO3 application and analysis 35% (including 10% fieldwork context), AO4 skills 25% (including 5% fieldwork data). OPTION CHOICES made in this scheme, all permitted by the specification: The Living World - Tropical rainforests (compulsory) PLUS Hot deserts (rather than Cold environments); Physical landscapes in the UK - Coastal landscapes PLUS River landscapes (rather than Glacial); Resource management - Water (rather than Food or Energy), taught in Year 11. Case studies and named examples selected: Nepal 2015 and Chile 2010 (contrasting tectonic hazards), Typhoon Haiyan 2013, Somerset Levels 2013-14 (UK extreme weather), the Amazon (rainforest deforestation), the Western Desert USA and the Sahel (hot deserts and desertification), the Dorset/Jurassic Coast and Lyme Regis (coasts), the River Tees and Banbury (rivers), Rio de Janeiro and Bristol (urban). IMPORTANT FOR A HOME-EDUCATED CANDIDATE: 3.3.2 fieldwork requires TWO enquiries involving primary data collection in CONTRASTING environments, carried out outside the classroom and school grounds on at least two occasions, at least one showing physical and human interaction. The exam centre must submit a signed written statement giving dates, locations, the questions investigated and the specification links; failure to provide this constitutes malpractice. Not all centres accept private candidates for Geography because of this. The fieldwork must therefore be planned, carried out and fully documented in Year 10 (Summer 1 and Summer 2 in this scheme) with the chosen centre's agreement secured in advance.
deferredToYear11: 3.2.2 The changing economic world in full - global development variations and measures (GNI, HDI, DTM), causes and consequences of uneven development, strategies to reduce the development gap, the LIC/NEE rapid development case study (e.g. Nigeria or India), and economic change in the UK - Year 11. This is the conventional split: Year 10 does all of Paper 1 plus the first Paper 2 topic, Year 11 does the remaining two Paper 2 topics.
3.2.3.1 Resource management overview - the significance of food, water and energy and UK resource demands - Year 11.
3.2.3.3 Water (the chosen resource option) - water security and insecurity, supply strategies, a large-scale water transfer scheme, and a sustainable local scheme in an LIC or NEE - Year 11.
3.3.1 Issue evaluation (Paper 3 Section A) - this CANNOT be taught in Year 10 because AQA releases the pre-release resource booklet only 12 weeks before the exam, in the spring of Year 11.
Decision-making technique for the issue evaluation: weighing options, justifying a choice and considering stakeholder conflict against an unseen resource booklet - Year 11.
Full past-paper practice across all three papers under exam conditions - Year 11.
Extended case study consolidation and retrieval across all Paper 1 and Paper 2 content - Year 11.

Glacial landscapes in the UK (3.1.3.4) and Cold environments (3.1.2.4) are NOT taught at all, because the specification requires only two of the three UK landscape options and one of the two living world options.
Food (3.2.3.2) and Energy (3.2.3.4) are NOT taught at all, because only one resource option is required.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1.1 Natural hazards and hazard risk

lessons.title: What is a natural hazard? Types and classification
objectives: I can define a natural hazard and distinguish it from a natural event
I can classify hazards as tectonic, atmospheric or geomorphological
misconceptions: Calling any natural event a hazard even when no people are threatened
Confusing hazard (the threat) with disaster (the realised impact)
Assuming hazards only affect poor countries

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Factors affecting hazard risk
objectives: I can explain how urbanisation, poverty, climate change and farming affect hazard risk
I can explain why people continue to live in hazardous areas
misconceptions: Thinking hazard risk depends only on the physical event
Assuming everyone in a hazardous area has a choice about living there
Confusing magnitude with impact

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: A natural hazard is a natural event that threatens people or property.
A natural event only becomes a hazard when people are exposed to it.
A natural disaster is a hazard that has actually caused significant damage, injury or death.
Tectonic hazards include earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.
Atmospheric hazards include tropical storms, droughts and extreme weather.
Geomorphological hazards include landslides and flooding.
Hazard risk is the probability that people will be adversely affected by a hazard.
Urbanisation increases hazard risk by concentrating population and property in one place.
Poverty increases hazard risk because people build in unsafe locations with poor-quality materials.
Farming increases hazard risk because fertile floodplains and volcanic soils attract settlement.
Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of some atmospheric hazards.
Magnitude is the size or strength of a hazard; frequency is how often it occurs.
Wealthier countries generally have greater capacity to cope, reducing the impact of the same magnitude event.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1.2 Tectonic hazards: plate tectonics and plate margins

lessons.title: Plate tectonics theory and the global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes
objectives: I can describe the global distribution of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions
I can explain the distribution using plate tectonics theory
misconceptions: Describing distribution without using named locations or directions
Saying earthquakes only happen at destructive margins
Confusing plates with continents

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Processes at constructive, destructive and conservative plate margins
objectives: I can describe the processes at each type of plate margin
I can explain why earthquakes and volcanoes occur at each margin
misconceptions: Thinking volcanoes occur at conservative margins
Confusing constructive and destructive margins
Believing continental crust subducts beneath oceanic crust

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Earth's lithosphere is divided into tectonic plates that move relative to one another.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur in narrow belts along plate margins.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is the most active tectonic belt on Earth.
Plate movement is driven by convection currents in the mantle and by slab pull at subduction zones.
Oceanic crust is thinner and denser than continental crust.
Continental crust is thicker, older and less dense than oceanic crust.
At a constructive margin, plates move apart, magma rises, and shield volcanoes and shallow earthquakes form.
At a destructive margin, oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust, causing composite volcanoes and powerful earthquakes.
At a conservative margin, plates slide past each other; earthquakes occur but there are no volcanoes.
Subduction is the sinking of denser oceanic crust into the mantle at a destructive margin.
The San Andreas Fault in California is an example of a conservative margin.
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is an example of a constructive margin.
Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and over a hot spot.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1.2 Tectonic hazards: contrasting case studies

lessons.title: Effects of a tectonic hazard in a lower-income country: Nepal earthquake, 2015
objectives: I can describe the primary and secondary effects of the Nepal earthquake
I can use named place detail and statistics in my answer
misconceptions: Confusing primary effects (immediate, direct) with secondary effects (knock-on)
Giving generic effects with no Nepal-specific detail
Confusing effects with responses

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Effects of a tectonic hazard in a higher-income country: Chile earthquake, 2010
objectives: I can describe the effects of the Chile earthquake
I can compare the effects in Chile and Nepal and explain the differences
misconceptions: Assuming the higher-magnitude event always causes more deaths
Explaining differences only by wealth without mentioning preparedness or building codes
Not using data from both places

assessment.type: 6-mark extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Primary effects happen immediately as a direct result of the hazard, such as buildings collapsing.
Secondary effects happen later as a knock-on consequence, such as disease or economic decline.
The Nepal earthquake of April 2015 measured 7.8 on the moment magnitude scale.
Around 9,000 people died in the Nepal earthquake and about 8 million were affected.
The Nepal earthquake triggered avalanches on Mount Everest and widespread landslides.
Nepal is a lower-income country with limited building regulation and difficult mountain access.
Historic buildings including Durbar Square in Kathmandu were destroyed.
The Chile earthquake of February 2010 measured 8.8, far stronger than Nepal's.
Around 500 people died in Chile despite the greater magnitude.
Chile has strict earthquake-resistant building codes and a well-funded emergency service.
The Chile earthquake triggered a tsunami that damaged coastal towns.
The Nepal-Chile comparison shows that level of development affects impact more than magnitude alone.
Chile's economy could largely fund its own recovery; Nepal depended heavily on international aid.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1.2 Tectonic hazards: responses and management

lessons.title: Immediate and long-term responses to tectonic hazards
objectives: I can distinguish immediate from long-term responses
I can compare responses in Nepal and Chile
misconceptions: Confusing responses with effects
Assuming all aid is effective
Placing reconstruction as an immediate response

assessment.type: 6-mark extended response

lessons.title: Reducing the risk: monitoring, prediction, protection and planning
objectives: I can explain the four management strategies for tectonic hazards
I can evaluate which strategy is most effective
misconceptions: Believing earthquakes can be accurately predicted
Confusing protection (building design) with planning (organisation)
Evaluating without reaching a judgement

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Immediate responses occur in the hours and days after a hazard: search and rescue, emergency aid, medical care.
Long-term responses occur over months and years: rebuilding, economic recovery, improved planning.
In Nepal, helicopters rescued people from remote areas and India and China sent emergency aid.
In Chile, the government rehoused nearly 200,000 people and rebuilt within about four years.
Chile could fund its own recovery, while Nepal relied on international NGOs and aid.
Monitoring uses seismometers, tiltmeters and gas sensors to track tectonic activity.
Volcanic eruptions can often be predicted; earthquakes currently cannot be predicted reliably.
Protection means designing buildings and infrastructure to withstand shaking, using cross-bracing, rubber shock absorbers and deep foundations.
Planning means preparing people: hazard maps, evacuation routes, drills and emergency supplies.
Japan holds an annual national Disaster Prevention Day drill.
Prediction is only useful if people act on the warning, which depends on planning.
A 9-mark evaluate question requires a judgement supported by evidence from more than one strategy.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1.3 Weather hazards: global atmospheric circulation and tropical storms

lessons.title: Global atmospheric circulation: pressure belts and surface winds
objectives: I can describe the general atmospheric circulation model
I can explain how circulation cells create global climate zones
misconceptions: Thinking air rises at high pressure
Confusing the direction of surface winds with high-altitude winds
Not linking circulation to deserts at 30 degrees latitude

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: The formation and structure of tropical storms
objectives: I can explain the conditions required for a tropical storm to form
I can describe the structure and sequence of a tropical storm
misconceptions: Thinking tropical storms form over land
Confusing the calm eye with the destructive eyewall
Ignoring the required sea temperature and depth conditions

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Global atmospheric circulation consists of three cells in each hemisphere: Hadley, Ferrel and Polar.
At the equator, intense heating causes air to rise, creating low pressure and heavy rainfall.
At about 30 degrees latitude, air sinks, creating high pressure, clear skies and the world's hot deserts.
At about 60 degrees latitude, warm and cold air meet and air rises, creating low pressure and unsettled weather.
At the poles, cold dense air sinks, creating high pressure and very low precipitation.
The Coriolis effect deflects winds to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern.
Trade winds blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equator.
Tropical storms form over oceans with a surface temperature above 27 degrees Celsius to a depth of about 70 metres.
Tropical storms form between 5 and 30 degrees north and south of the equator, where the Coriolis effect is sufficient.
Latent heat released as water vapour condenses provides the energy that powers a tropical storm.
The eye is a calm area of sinking air at the centre; the eyewall has the most intense winds and rain.
Tropical storms are called hurricanes in the Atlantic, cyclones in the Indian Ocean and typhoons in the western Pacific.
Tropical storms weaken over land because their energy source, warm ocean water, is removed.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1.3 Weather hazards: Typhoon Haiyan and tropical storm management

lessons.title: Typhoon Haiyan, Philippines 2013: effects and responses
objectives: I can describe the primary and secondary effects of Typhoon Haiyan
I can describe the immediate and long-term responses
misconceptions: Giving generic typhoon effects with no Philippines detail
Confusing storm surge with heavy rainfall flooding
Not distinguishing immediate from long-term responses

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Reducing the effects of tropical storms and the impact of climate change
objectives: I can explain how monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce tropical storm impacts
I can explain how climate change may affect tropical storm distribution, frequency and intensity
misconceptions: Assuming climate change will simply create more storms everywhere
Confusing intensity with frequency
Believing prediction alone prevents damage

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Typhoon Haiyan struck the Philippines in November 2013 as a Category 5 storm.
Haiyan's winds reached around 275 km per hour.
A storm surge of up to about 5 metres devastated the city of Tacloban.
Around 6,300 people died and over 600,000 were displaced.
Secondary effects included shortages of food and water, looting, and outbreaks of disease.
Immediate responses included international aid, emergency shelter and the deployment of field hospitals.
Long-term responses included the 'Build Back Better' programme and replanting mangroves.
A storm surge is a rise in sea level caused by low pressure and strong onshore winds.
Tropical storms are monitored by satellites and aircraft, allowing several days of warning.
Protection includes storm-resistant buildings on stilts, sea walls and flood defences.
Planning includes evacuation routes, storm shelters, education and emergency supplies.
Warmer oceans may increase the intensity of tropical storms and widen the area where they can form.
Evidence for a change in tropical storm frequency is less clear than evidence for a change in intensity.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1.3 Weather hazards in the UK

lessons.title: Types of UK weather hazard and evidence of increasing extremes
objectives: I can identify the main weather hazards affecting the UK
I can evaluate the evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme
misconceptions: Assuming one extreme event proves a trend
Confusing weather with climate
Listing hazards without evidence of change

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: UK extreme weather event: Somerset Levels floods, winter 2013-14
objectives: I can explain the physical and human causes of the Somerset Levels floods
I can describe the social, economic and environmental impacts and the management response
misconceptions: Giving only physical causes and ignoring human factors such as lack of dredging
Confusing impacts with causes
Not using Somerset-specific detail

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

knowledgeComponents.statement: The UK experiences hazards including storms, heavy rain and flooding, drought, extreme heat, heavy snow and strong winds.
Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions; climate is the average over about 30 years.
Evidence for increasing UK extremes includes record-breaking temperatures, wetter winters and more frequent named storms.
A single extreme event is weather, not proof of climate change; trends over decades are needed.
The UK's variable weather results from its position where several air masses meet.
The Somerset Levels floods occurred over the winter of 2013 to 2014.
Physical causes included prolonged heavy rainfall, high tides, saturated ground and the low-lying floodplain.
A human cause was that rivers had not been dredged for around 20 years, reducing channel capacity.
Over 600 houses were flooded and around 14,000 hectares of farmland were under water for weeks.
Villages such as Moorland were evacuated and roads were cut off.
Economic impacts included losses of over 10 million pounds and the death of livestock.
The response included the Somerset Levels and Moors Flood Action Plan, dredging 8 km of rivers and raising road levels.
Environmental impacts included contaminated floodwater and damage to habitats and soil.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1.4 Climate change (Autumn 1 assessment)

lessons.title: Evidence and causes of climate change
objectives: I can describe the evidence for climate change from the Quaternary period to the present
I can explain natural and human causes of climate change
misconceptions: Confusing the natural greenhouse effect with the enhanced greenhouse effect
Ignoring natural causes entirely
Confusing evidence with causes

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Managing climate change: mitigation and adaptation, and Autumn 1 assessment
objectives: I can distinguish mitigation from adaptation and give examples of each
I can evaluate the effectiveness of different management strategies
misconceptions: Confusing mitigation (reducing causes) with adaptation (coping with effects)
Assuming international agreements are automatically effective
Evaluating without a conclusion

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)
commandWords: to what extent do you agree

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Quaternary period covers approximately the last 2.6 million years.
Evidence for climate change includes ice cores, tree rings, pollen analysis, historical records and temperature data.
Ice cores trap air bubbles that reveal past atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations.
Natural causes of climate change include orbital changes (Milankovitch cycles), volcanic activity and variation in solar output.
Human causes include burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture, especially methane from livestock and rice paddies.
The enhanced greenhouse effect is the additional warming caused by human-produced greenhouse gases.
Effects of climate change include sea level rise, ice melt, changed rainfall patterns and shifting ecosystems.
Mitigation reduces the causes of climate change, for example by cutting emissions.
Adaptation reduces the effects of climate change, for example by building flood defences.
Mitigation strategies include alternative energy, carbon capture and storage, planting trees and international agreements.
Adaptation strategies include changing agricultural systems, managing water supply and reducing the risk from rising sea levels.
The Paris Agreement of 2015 committed countries to limiting global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius.
International agreements are hard to enforce because countries differ in wealth and emissions responsibility.

weeks.unit: 3.1.2.1 Ecosystems

lessons.title: Ecosystem components, food chains and nutrient cycling
objectives: I can identify biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem
I can explain food chains, food webs and nutrient cycling
misconceptions: Confusing a food chain (single line) with a food web (interconnected)
Thinking decomposers are consumers
Ignoring abiotic components such as soil and climate

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Small-scale UK ecosystem and the effect of change; global ecosystem distribution
objectives: I can describe interrelationships in a small-scale UK ecosystem such as a freshwater pond
I can describe the global distribution and characteristics of major biomes
misconceptions: Assuming a change in one component affects nothing else
Confusing biome with ecosystem
Placing biomes at the wrong latitudes

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

knowledgeComponents.statement: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with their non-living environment.
Biotic components are living: plants, animals, bacteria. Abiotic components are non-living: water, soil, climate, light.
Producers make their own food by photosynthesis and form the base of a food chain.
Consumers eat other organisms; decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil.
A food chain shows one line of feeding relationships; a food web shows many interconnected chains.
Nutrient cycling moves nutrients between biomass, litter and soil stores.
Interdependence means that a change to one component of an ecosystem affects the others.
A UK freshwater pond ecosystem includes pondweed (producer), insects and fish (consumers) and bacteria (decomposers).
A biome is a large-scale global ecosystem defined by its climate and vegetation.
Tropical rainforests lie in a belt around the equator.
Hot deserts lie around 30 degrees north and south, beneath descending air of the Hadley cell.
Tundra is found in high latitudes of the northern hemisphere, largely north of the Arctic Circle.
Temperate deciduous forest is found in mid-latitudes such as western Europe.

weeks.unit: 3.1.2.2 Tropical rainforests: characteristics and adaptations

lessons.title: Physical characteristics and interdependence in tropical rainforests
objectives: I can describe the climate, soil and vegetation structure of a tropical rainforest
I can explain the interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people
misconceptions: Assuming rainforest soils are fertile because vegetation is dense
Confusing the canopy with the emergent layer
Thinking rainforest climate has distinct seasons

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Plant and animal adaptations, and biodiversity
objectives: I can explain how plants and animals are adapted to rainforest conditions
I can explain why rainforest biodiversity is high and why it matters
misconceptions: Describing an adaptation without explaining why it helps
Confusing buttress roots with drip tips
Assuming high biodiversity means the ecosystem is robust

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Tropical rainforests have high temperatures around 26-28 degrees Celsius all year and over 2000 mm of rain annually.
Rainforests have no distinct seasons because of their equatorial location.
The rainforest has four layers: emergent, canopy, under-canopy and shrub layer.
Rainforest soils are thin and infertile because heavy rainfall leaches nutrients away.
Most rainforest nutrients are stored in the biomass, not the soil.
Rapid decomposition in hot, humid conditions cycles nutrients quickly back into plants.
Deforestation breaks the nutrient cycle because the main nutrient store is removed.
Drip tips allow leaves to shed heavy rainfall quickly, preventing rot and algae growth.
Buttress roots give tall trees stability in shallow soil.
Lianas climb existing trees to reach the light without investing in a thick trunk.
Epiphytes grow on other plants to access light in the canopy.
Tropical rainforests cover about 6% of the Earth's surface but contain over half of all known species.
Endemic species are found nowhere else, so their loss is permanent extinction.

weeks.unit: 3.1.2.2 Tropical rainforests: deforestation case study (the Amazon)

lessons.title: Causes of deforestation in the Amazon
objectives: I can explain the causes of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest
I can use named place and statistical detail
misconceptions: Listing causes without explaining the process
Assuming subsistence farming is the main cause in the Amazon
Giving no named locations or figures

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Impacts of deforestation: economic development, soil erosion and climate change
objectives: I can explain the environmental and economic impacts of deforestation
I can evaluate whether the economic benefits outweigh the environmental costs
misconceptions: Presenting deforestation as having only negative impacts
Confusing soil erosion with soil infertility
Not reaching a judgement in an evaluation

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Amazon rainforest covers around 5.5 million square kilometres, mostly in Brazil.
Cattle ranching is the largest single cause of Amazon deforestation.
Commercial farming, especially soya production, clears large areas of forest.
Logging removes valuable hardwoods such as mahogany, and roads built for logging open access for others.
Mineral extraction, including the Carajas iron ore mine, clears forest and pollutes rivers.
The Trans-Amazonian Highway opened large areas of forest to settlement.
Hydroelectric dams such as Belo Monte flood large areas of forest.
Population growth and government resettlement schemes increased pressure on the forest.
Deforestation causes soil erosion because tree roots no longer bind the soil and rain hits bare ground.
The Amazon is a major carbon sink; deforestation releases stored carbon and reduces future absorption.
Reduced transpiration lowers rainfall, which can dry out the remaining forest.
Deforestation brings economic development through exports, jobs, taxes and infrastructure.
Indigenous peoples are displaced and their way of life destroyed by deforestation.

weeks.unit: 3.1.2.2 Tropical rainforests: sustainable management

lessons.title: Value of the rainforest and sustainable management strategies
objectives: I can explain the value of tropical rainforests to people and the environment
I can explain sustainable management strategies
misconceptions: Assuming sustainable management means stopping all use
Confusing selective logging with clear felling
Not explaining how a strategy actually works

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Evaluating sustainable management of the rainforest
objectives: I can evaluate the effectiveness of different management strategies
I can consider the interests of different stakeholders
misconceptions: Evaluating one strategy only
Assuming international agreements are always enforced
Ignoring the economic needs of the host country

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Rainforests provide medicines, timber, food, water regulation and carbon storage.
Around a quarter of modern medicines originate from rainforest plants.
Selective logging removes only mature or valuable trees, allowing the forest to regenerate.
Replanting requires felled areas to be replanted, often with native species.
Conservation designates protected areas such as national parks and reserves.
Ecotourism generates income while conserving the forest and employing local people.
Education helps local people and tourists understand the value of the forest.
International hardwood agreements such as FSC certification promote sustainably sourced timber.
Debt-for-nature swaps cancel part of a country's debt in return for conservation commitments.
Sustainable management means meeting present needs without compromising future generations.
Enforcement is difficult over vast, remote areas with limited government resources.
Stakeholders in rainforest management include indigenous peoples, loggers, farmers, governments, NGOs and consumers.
Strategies work best in combination rather than in isolation.

weeks.unit: 3.1.2.3 Hot deserts: characteristics, adaptations and opportunities

lessons.title: Physical characteristics of hot deserts and plant and animal adaptations
objectives: I can describe the climate, soils and vegetation of hot deserts
I can explain how plants and animals are adapted to desert conditions
misconceptions: Assuming deserts are always hot, including at night
Describing adaptations without explaining the benefit
Thinking desert soils are always sandy

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Development opportunities in a hot desert: the Western Desert, USA
objectives: I can describe the opportunities for development in the Western Desert
I can use named place detail for mineral extraction, energy, farming and tourism
misconceptions: Giving generic desert opportunities without USA detail
Confusing opportunities with challenges
Missing the water supply issue underlying all of them

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

knowledgeComponents.statement: Hot deserts receive less than 250 mm of rainfall per year.
Hot deserts have a very large diurnal temperature range: very hot days and cold nights.
The lack of cloud cover allows intense daytime heating and rapid night-time heat loss.
Desert soils are thin, sandy or stony, low in organic matter and often salty.
Desert vegetation is sparse, with bare ground between plants competing for water.
Cacti store water in thick stems, have waxy skin to reduce transpiration and spines instead of leaves.
Some desert plants have long taproots to reach deep groundwater; others have wide shallow roots to catch surface rain.
Many desert animals are nocturnal to avoid daytime heat, and some can survive without drinking.
The Western Desert of the USA covers parts of Arizona, California, Nevada, New Mexico and Utah.
The Colorado River, dammed at the Hoover Dam to form Lake Mead, supplies water and hydroelectric power.
The Central Arizona Project canal transfers Colorado River water to Phoenix and Tucson.
Irrigation supports high-value farming of fruit, vegetables and cotton in the Coachella and Imperial valleys.
Copper mining at Morenci, Arizona, is a major economic activity.
Tourism centres on Las Vegas and the Grand Canyon, and solar energy exploits high insolation.

weeks.unit: 3.1.2.3 Hot deserts: challenges and desertification

lessons.title: Challenges of development in the Western Desert
objectives: I can explain the challenges of extreme temperature, water supply and inaccessibility
I can evaluate whether desert development is sustainable
misconceptions: Listing challenges without explaining their consequences
Ignoring the long-term water supply problem
Assuming technology solves all challenges

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Desertification: causes and reduction strategies
objectives: I can explain the causes of desertification on the fringes of hot deserts
I can evaluate strategies to reduce the risk of desertification
misconceptions: Confusing desertification with desert expansion caused only by climate
Ignoring human causes
Describing a strategy without explaining how it works

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Water supply is the fundamental challenge of desert development, and demand often exceeds sustainable supply.
Over-abstraction from the Colorado River means it now rarely reaches the sea.
Lake Mead water levels have fallen substantially, threatening water and power supply.
Extreme summer temperatures over 40 degrees Celsius increase energy demand for air conditioning.
Inaccessibility and the cost of building roads and services limit development in remote desert areas.
Desert development is not sustainable if it depends on depleting aquifers laid down thousands of years ago.
Desertification is the process by which land becomes increasingly arid and loses its productivity.
Causes of desertification include climate change, population growth, removal of fuel wood, overgrazing, over-cultivation and soil erosion.
The Sahel, on the southern fringe of the Sahara, is the classic example of desertification.
Water management strategies include drip irrigation and small earth dams to capture rainwater.
Soil management strategies include contour ploughing, terracing and using manure to improve structure.
Tree planting stabilises soil, provides shade and reduces wind erosion.
Appropriate technology such as 'magic stones' (stone lines) slows run-off and traps soil, and is cheap and locally maintainable.

weeks.unit: The living world: review and Autumn 2 assessment

lessons.title: Comparing biomes: rainforest and desert
objectives: I can compare the characteristics, opportunities and challenges of two biomes
I can use appropriate comparative language and data
misconceptions: Describing each biome separately without comparing
Comparing only climate and ignoring people
Not using data to support comparisons

assessment.type: 6-mark extended response

lessons.title: Autumn 2 assessment: natural hazards and the living world
objectives: I can answer Paper 1 Sections A and B questions under timed conditions
I can deploy case study detail accurately
misconceptions: Writing generic answers with no place-specific detail
Misreading the command word
Running out of time on the 9-mark question

assessment.type: Timed Paper 1 Sections A and B assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: Rainforests have high rainfall and high biodiversity; deserts have very low rainfall and low biodiversity.
Both biomes have nutrient-poor soils but for different reasons: leaching in rainforests, lack of organic matter in deserts.
Both biomes face pressure from resource extraction and population growth.
Comparative answers should use connectives such as 'whereas', 'in contrast' and 'similarly'.
Adaptations in both biomes solve the limiting factor: light in rainforests, water in deserts.
Case studies require named places, figures and dates to gain full marks.
'Describe' asks what something is like; 'explain' asks why.
'Evaluate' and 'assess' require a judgement, not just a list of points.
'To what extent do you agree' requires an explicit degree of agreement.
9-mark questions are marked in three levels and require a conclusion.
Three SPaG marks are attached to one extended question per paper.
Roughly one mark per minute is a reasonable pace on a Geography paper.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.1 UK physical landscapes and 3.1.3.2 coastal processes

lessons.title: UK physical landscapes: upland, lowland and major rivers
objectives: I can locate the major upland and lowland areas of the UK
I can locate the major UK river systems
misconceptions: Confusing uplands with mountains only
Placing the Pennines in the wrong part of England
Not being able to use a UK relief map

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

lessons.title: Wave types, weathering and mass movement
objectives: I can describe the characteristics of constructive and destructive waves
I can explain mechanical and chemical weathering and types of mass movement
misconceptions: Mixing up swash and backwash dominance in the two wave types
Confusing weathering (in situ breakdown) with erosion (removal)
Confusing slumping with sliding

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: The main UK upland areas are the Scottish Highlands and Grampians, the Southern Uplands, the Pennines, the Lake District, Snowdonia and Dartmoor.
Most UK lowland is in the south and east, including the Fens, the London Basin and the East Anglian plain.
The Tees-Exe line is a common way of dividing upland from lowland Britain.
Major UK rivers include the Severn, Thames, Trent, Tyne, Tees and Ouse.
Constructive waves are low with a long wavelength; their strong swash builds beaches up.
Destructive waves are tall and steep with a strong backwash that removes material from beaches.
Fetch is the distance of open water over which the wind blows; a longer fetch creates bigger waves.
Weathering is the in-situ breakdown of rock; erosion is the wearing away and removal of material.
Freeze-thaw weathering occurs when water in cracks freezes, expands by about 9% and widens the crack.
Chemical weathering includes carbonation, where slightly acidic rainwater dissolves limestone.
Mass movement is the downhill movement of material under gravity.
Slumping involves rotational movement of saturated material along a curved surface.
Rock fall occurs when fragments break away from a cliff face, often after freeze-thaw.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.2 Coastal erosion, transportation and deposition

lessons.title: Processes of coastal erosion
objectives: I can explain hydraulic power, abrasion, attrition and solution
I can explain how geology and rock type influence the rate of erosion
misconceptions: Confusing abrasion (rocks scraping the cliff) with attrition (rocks hitting each other)
Thinking solution affects all rock types equally
Confusing discordant and concordant coastlines

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Transportation and deposition: longshore drift
objectives: I can explain longshore drift using a labelled diagram
I can explain why deposition occurs in sheltered coastal areas
misconceptions: Drawing swash and backwash at the same angle
Thinking longshore drift moves material out to sea
Confusing the four transport processes

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Hydraulic power is the force of water compressing air in cracks, causing rock to break apart.
Abrasion is the wearing away of a cliff by material thrown against it by waves.
Attrition is the wearing down of rock fragments as they collide with each other, becoming smaller and rounder.
Solution is the dissolving of soluble rock such as limestone and chalk by seawater.
A discordant coastline has alternating bands of hard and soft rock at right angles to the sea, forming headlands and bays.
A concordant coastline has bands of rock parallel to the sea, producing a straighter coastline.
More resistant rock erodes more slowly and stands out as headlands.
Longshore drift moves sediment along a coast in a zig-zag path.
In longshore drift, swash moves material up the beach at the angle of the prevailing wind, and backwash returns it straight down under gravity.
Traction rolls large material along the sea bed; saltation bounces smaller material.
Suspension carries fine material within the water; solution carries dissolved material.
Deposition occurs where waves lose energy, such as in sheltered bays or behind spits.
Sediment is deposited when the sea has too little energy to keep transporting it.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.2 Coastal landforms of erosion and deposition

lessons.title: Erosional landforms: headlands and bays, cliffs and wave-cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks
objectives: I can explain the formation of a wave-cut platform in sequence
I can explain the cave-arch-stack-stump sequence
misconceptions: Explaining a sequence out of order
Saying an arch collapses into a stump without the stack stage
Not naming the processes causing each stage

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Depositional landforms: beaches, spits, bars and sand dunes
objectives: I can explain the formation of a spit and a bar
I can explain the formation and succession of sand dunes
misconceptions: Thinking a spit forms across an open coastline rather than where the coast changes direction
Confusing a bar with a spit
Ignoring the role of a change in prevailing wind in forming a recurved end

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Waves erode a wave-cut notch at the base of a cliff, which undercuts and causes collapse; repeated retreat leaves a wave-cut platform.
Headlands form where resistant rock resists erosion; bays form where less resistant rock erodes faster.
Wave refraction concentrates wave energy on headlands and reduces it in bays.
The sequence at a headland is: crack, cave, arch, stack, stump.
Caves form when erosion widens a line of weakness such as a fault or joint.
Old Harry Rocks in Dorset is a well-known example of a stack.
A wave-cut platform is exposed at low tide and slopes gently seaward.
A spit forms where the coastline changes direction and longshore drift deposits material into open water.
A spit's end may be recurved by a change in wind direction, and a salt marsh may form in the sheltered water behind.
Spurn Head on the Holderness coast is a classic UK spit.
A bar forms when a spit grows across a bay, trapping a lagoon behind it.
A tombolo is a bar joining the mainland to an island, such as Chesil Beach to the Isle of Portland.
Sand dunes form when sand is blown inland and trapped by obstacles, developing through embryo, fore, yellow and grey dune stages.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.2 UK coastal landscape example and coastal management

lessons.title: A section of UK coastline: the Dorset (Jurassic) coast
objectives: I can identify major landforms of erosion and deposition on a named UK coastline
I can use an OS map to locate and describe coastal landforms
misconceptions: Not knowing whether the landform is erosional or depositional
Giving four-figure references when six figures are required
Describing landforms without linking to rock type

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

lessons.title: Coastal management: hard and soft engineering and managed retreat
objectives: I can describe hard and soft engineering strategies and managed retreat
I can explain the advantages and disadvantages of each
misconceptions: Confusing rock armour with gabions
Thinking soft engineering is always cheaper and better
Forgetting that groynes starve beaches further along the coast

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Dorset coast is a World Heritage Site known as the Jurassic Coast.
Lulworth Cove formed where the sea broke through resistant Portland limestone into softer clays behind.
Durdle Door is an arch formed in Portland limestone.
Old Harry Rocks are chalk stacks at the eastern end of the Isle of Purbeck.
Chesil Beach is a shingle tombolo linking the mainland to the Isle of Portland.
A six-figure grid reference locates a feature to within 100 metres.
On an OS map, contour lines close together indicate steep ground such as a cliff.
Sea walls reflect wave energy and are effective but expensive and can look intrusive.
Rock armour is large boulders that absorb wave energy; cheaper than a sea wall but can be hazardous.
Gabions are wire cages of rocks; cheap but less durable and unattractive.
Groynes trap sediment moving by longshore drift, widening the beach but starving beaches downdrift.
Beach nourishment adds sand to a beach; it looks natural but must be repeated regularly.
Managed retreat allows low-value land to flood, creating salt marsh that absorbs wave energy.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.2 Coastal management scheme and Spring 1 assessment

lessons.title: A UK coastal management scheme: Lyme Regis, Dorset
objectives: I can explain why a coastal management scheme was needed at Lyme Regis
I can evaluate the effects of the scheme and the conflicts it created
misconceptions: Describing the scheme without evaluating it
Not identifying any conflicts or drawbacks
Giving no named detail or costs

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Spring 1 assessment: coastal landscapes
objectives: I can answer coastal landform and management questions under timed conditions
I can draw and label a diagram to support an explanation
misconceptions: Drawing a diagram without labels or annotations
Missing steps out of a formation sequence
Not using the correct process terminology

assessment.type: Timed Paper 1 Section C assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: Lyme Regis lies on an unstable coastline of clay prone to landslips.
The Lyme Regis Environmental Improvement Scheme was carried out in phases from the 1990s.
Phase works included new sea walls, rock armour, beach nourishment and drainage to stabilise cliffs.
The scheme cost tens of millions of pounds, funded largely by the Environment Agency.
Positive effects included protecting homes and businesses and increasing visitor numbers.
Conflicts included the visual impact of defences, cost to taxpayers and effects on fossil exposure valued by geologists.
Some argue the scheme has increased erosion pressure on undefended coast nearby.
A cost-benefit analysis weighs the financial cost of defence against the value of land and property protected.
An annotated diagram explains a process; a labelled diagram only names features.
Formation questions must present stages in the correct sequence.
Naming the specific erosion process at each stage raises the level of a formation answer.
Diagrams can earn marks in their own right on Paper 1.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.3 River landscapes: processes and the long profile

lessons.title: The long profile and changing cross profile of a river
objectives: I can describe how a river's long and cross profiles change downstream
I can explain the changes using velocity, discharge and load
misconceptions: Thinking a river flows fastest in its upper course
Confusing the long profile with the cross profile
Assuming load size increases downstream

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Fluvial processes: erosion, transportation and deposition
objectives: I can explain hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution in rivers
I can explain vertical and lateral erosion and the four transport processes
misconceptions: Confusing vertical erosion (downwards, upper course) with lateral erosion (sideways, middle and lower course)
Confusing abrasion with attrition
Thinking deposition only happens at the river mouth

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: The long profile shows the gradient of a river from source to mouth and is typically concave.
The cross profile shows a section across the valley and channel at a point.
The upper course has a steep gradient, a narrow V-shaped valley and large angular load.
The lower course has a gentle gradient, a wide flat valley and fine, rounded load.
Velocity actually increases downstream because the channel becomes smoother and less friction acts on the water.
Discharge is the volume of water passing a point per second, measured in cumecs.
Discharge increases downstream as tributaries join the river.
Hydraulic action is the force of water forcing air into cracks in the bank and bed.
Abrasion is the river's load scraping against the bed and banks.
Attrition wears the load itself down, making it smaller and rounder downstream.
Vertical erosion deepens the channel and dominates in the upper course.
Lateral erosion widens the channel and dominates in the middle and lower courses.
Deposition occurs when a river loses energy: on the inside of meanders, on the floodplain and at the mouth.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.3 River landforms of erosion

lessons.title: Interlocking spurs, waterfalls and gorges
objectives: I can explain the formation of a waterfall and gorge in sequence
I can explain how interlocking spurs form
misconceptions: Missing the plunge pool and undercutting stages of waterfall formation
Thinking a gorge forms before the waterfall retreats
Confusing interlocking spurs with truncated spurs (glacial)

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Meanders and ox-bow lakes
objectives: I can explain the formation of a meander using erosion and deposition
I can explain the formation of an ox-bow lake in sequence
misconceptions: Placing the fastest flow on the inside of the meander bend
Missing the neck-narrowing stage before a cut-off
Confusing a river cliff with a slip-off slope

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Interlocking spurs form in the upper course where the river winds around areas of resistant rock it cannot erode laterally.
A waterfall forms where a band of hard rock lies over softer rock.
The softer rock is eroded faster, undercutting the hard rock and forming an overhang.
The overhang eventually collapses and the waterfall retreats upstream.
A plunge pool forms at the base through hydraulic action and abrasion by fallen rock.
Repeated retreat of a waterfall leaves a steep-sided gorge downstream.
High Force on the River Tees is a well-known UK waterfall.
On a meander, the fastest flow (the thalweg) is on the outside of the bend.
Erosion on the outside of a meander creates a steep river cliff.
Deposition on the inside of a meander creates a gentle slip-off slope of sand and shingle.
As meanders migrate, the neck between two bends narrows.
During a flood the river cuts through the neck, and deposition seals off the old bend to leave an ox-bow lake.
An ox-bow lake eventually dries out to become a meander scar.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.3 River landforms of deposition and a UK river example

lessons.title: Floodplains, levees and estuaries
objectives: I can explain the formation of a floodplain and a levee
I can describe the characteristics of an estuary
misconceptions: Thinking levees are always artificial
Confusing a floodplain with a delta
Not linking floodplain width to meander migration

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: A UK river valley example: the River Tees
objectives: I can identify landforms of erosion and deposition along the River Tees
I can use an OS map to identify river landforms
misconceptions: Not knowing where in the course each landform occurs
Confusing the Tees with other UK rivers
Misreading contour patterns on an OS map

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A floodplain is the flat area either side of a river that floods and receives alluvium.
Floodplains are widened by meander migration and built up by repeated flood deposition.
Levees are natural raised banks formed when a river floods and deposits its coarsest load closest to the channel.
Alluvium is fine, fertile sediment deposited by a river in flood.
An estuary is the tidal mouth of a river, where fresh and salt water mix and mudflats form.
Deposition in an estuary occurs because the river loses velocity on meeting the sea and the tide slows flow further.
The River Tees rises at Cross Fell in the Pennines.
High Force is a waterfall on the upper Tees formed where the resistant Whin Sill dolerite overlies softer limestone and shale.
Large meanders occur in the middle course of the Tees near Yarm.
The Tees estuary near Middlesbrough is heavily industrialised with mudflats and a wide tidal mouth.
