On an OS map, a river's blue line running between close contours indicates a steep upper course.
Widely spaced contours and a meandering blue line indicate a lower course floodplain.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.3 Flood risk and hydrographs

lessons.title: Physical and human factors increasing flood risk
objectives: I can explain how precipitation, geology, relief and land use affect flood risk
I can explain how urbanisation and deforestation increase flood risk
misconceptions: Thinking heavy rain alone causes flooding
Confusing permeable with impermeable rock
Ignoring antecedent conditions such as already-saturated ground

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Interpreting flood hydrographs
objectives: I can interpret a flood hydrograph and describe its features
I can explain why hydrographs differ between drainage basins
misconceptions: Confusing lag time with the time of peak discharge
Reading discharge off the rainfall axis
Thinking a short lag time is always caused by more rainfall

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Impermeable rock such as granite or clay prevents infiltration, increasing surface run-off and flood risk.
Steep relief increases the speed of run-off and reduces the time water takes to reach the river.
Prolonged rainfall saturates the soil so further rain becomes surface run-off.
Intense rainfall exceeds the infiltration capacity of the soil even when the ground is dry.
Urbanisation replaces permeable surfaces with tarmac and concrete and adds drains that carry water quickly to rivers.
Deforestation reduces interception and transpiration, increasing run-off.
A hydrograph shows river discharge and rainfall over time for a storm event.
Lag time is the time between peak rainfall and peak discharge.
The rising limb shows discharge increasing; the falling limb shows it returning to base flow.
Base flow is the normal discharge of the river between storm events.
A flashy hydrograph has a short lag time and high peak discharge, typical of urban or steep impermeable basins.
A subdued hydrograph has a long lag time and low peak, typical of permeable, gently sloping, vegetated basins.
Discharge is measured in cumecs, cubic metres per second.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.3 River management strategies

lessons.title: Hard engineering flood management
objectives: I can describe dams, reservoirs, channel straightening, embankments and flood relief channels
I can explain the costs and benefits of each
misconceptions: Thinking hard engineering always solves flooding permanently
Ignoring that straightening moves the flood problem downstream
Not considering the cost and environmental impact

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

lessons.title: Soft engineering flood management
objectives: I can describe flood warnings, floodplain zoning, tree planting and river restoration
I can compare hard and soft engineering approaches
misconceptions: Thinking soft engineering has no disadvantages
Confusing floodplain zoning with flood warning
Not comparing approaches when asked to compare

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Dams and reservoirs store water and release it in a controlled way, but are very expensive and flood land upstream.
Channel straightening speeds water through an area but increases flood risk downstream.
Embankments raise the banks so the channel holds more water, but can fail catastrophically.
Flood relief channels divert water around a settlement during high flow.
Hard engineering uses artificial structures; soft engineering works with natural processes.
Hard engineering has high capital cost and often high environmental impact.
Flood warnings give people time to prepare but do not prevent flooding or protect property.
Floodplain zoning restricts building on high-risk land, but is ineffective where development already exists.
Tree planting increases interception and reduces run-off, and is cheap and sustainable.
River restoration returns a straightened channel to a natural meandering state, slowing flow and creating habitat.
Soft engineering is generally cheaper and more sustainable but offers less certain protection.
An evaluation of flood management should consider cost, effectiveness, sustainability and impact on different groups.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3.3 UK flood management scheme and Spring 2 assessment

lessons.title: A UK flood management scheme: Banbury, Oxfordshire
objectives: I can explain why a flood management scheme was needed at Banbury
I can evaluate the social, economic and environmental issues of the scheme
misconceptions: Describing the scheme without evaluating it
Giving no cost or protection figures
Ignoring environmental benefits or drawbacks

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment: river landscapes
objectives: I can answer river landform, hydrograph and management questions under timed conditions
I can interpret an OS map extract of a river valley
misconceptions: Not using data from a resource when instructed to
Describing rather than explaining
Losing SPaG marks through careless writing

assessment.type: Timed Paper 1 Section C assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: Banbury on the River Cherwell has flooded repeatedly, notably in 1998 and 2007.
The Banbury flood scheme was completed in 2012 at a cost of around 18.5 million pounds.
The scheme created a flood storage reservoir holding around 3 million cubic metres of water.
A 2.9 km earth embankment and a new pumping station were built.
The scheme protects over 400 homes and businesses in Banbury.
Environmental benefits included new wetland habitat and improved biodiversity.
Costs included the loss of some agricultural land and the visual impact of the embankment.
The scheme also allowed the A361 road to be raised, keeping access open during floods.
Questions that say 'using Figure 1' require explicit use of the resource for full marks.
'Describe' means say what you see; 'explain' means give reasons.
SPaG marks are awarded on one extended question per paper, so clarity and spelling matter.
Naming a specific scheme with figures distinguishes a Level 3 answer from a Level 2 one.

weeks.unit: 3.2.1 Urbanisation and megacities

lessons.title: The global pattern of urban change
objectives: I can describe the global pattern of urbanisation
I can explain the difference in urban growth rates between HICs and LICs
misconceptions: Confusing urbanisation (proportion) with urban growth (absolute numbers)
Assuming HICs are not urbanising at all
Describing a map without quantifying

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

lessons.title: Causes of urban growth: migration and natural increase
objectives: I can explain rural-to-urban migration using push and pull factors
I can explain the role of natural increase in urban growth
misconceptions: Confusing push and pull factors
Ignoring natural increase as a cause of urban growth
Assuming migrants always improve their situation

assessment.type: Paper 2 (Challenges in the human environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Urbanisation is the increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities.
More than half the world's population now lives in urban areas.
Urbanisation is fastest in LICs and NEEs; HICs are already highly urbanised and growing slowly.
A megacity is an urban area with a population of over 10 million.
Most megacities are now in Asia, Africa and South America rather than Europe and North America.
Urban growth is the absolute increase in the number of people living in a city.
Push factors drive people away from rural areas: poverty, lack of services, drought, mechanisation of farming, conflict.
Pull factors attract people to cities: jobs, healthcare, education, entertainment and perceived opportunity.
Rural-to-urban migration is the movement of people from countryside to city.
Natural increase occurs where births exceed deaths, and is high in cities because migrants are typically young adults.
Cities often have better healthcare, lowering death rates and raising natural increase.
Perception of opportunity may exceed reality, leading to underemployment in the informal sector.

weeks.unit: 3.2.1 Urban growth in an LIC or NEE: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (opportunities)

lessons.title: Rio de Janeiro: location, importance and growth
objectives: I can describe the location and regional, national and international importance of Rio
I can explain the causes of Rio's growth
misconceptions: Not distinguishing regional, national and international importance
Describing Rio without locating it
Giving no figures for population or growth

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Opportunities in Rio: social and economic
objectives: I can explain the social opportunities in Rio: health, education, water and energy
I can explain the economic opportunities created by industry and services
misconceptions: Presenting the city as offering no opportunities
Confusing formal and informal employment
Giving generic opportunities with no Rio detail

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

knowledgeComponents.statement: Rio de Janeiro is on the south-east coast of Brazil, an NEE in South America.
Rio has a population of around 6.5 million in the city and about 12 million in the wider metropolitan area.
Regionally Rio is a centre of employment and services for south-east Brazil.
Nationally Rio is Brazil's second largest city and a major cultural and economic centre.
Internationally Rio hosted the 2014 World Cup and the 2016 Olympic Games and is a major tourist destination.
Rio's port handles a large share of Brazil's trade and it has major oil and service industries.
Rio grew through rural-to-urban migration from Brazil's poorer north-east and through natural increase.
Around 20% of Rio's population lives in favelas, informal settlements.
Social opportunities include better access to healthcare, schools, water and electricity than in rural Brazil.
School attendance in Rio is far higher than in rural areas of Brazil.
Economic opportunities come from the port, oil, tourism, service industries and manufacturing.
The informal economy provides unregulated, untaxed, insecure work for many favela residents.
Industrial development creates a multiplier effect, generating further jobs and services.

weeks.unit: 3.2.1 Rio de Janeiro: challenges and urban planning

lessons.title: Challenges in Rio: squatter settlements, services, unemployment, crime and pollution
objectives: I can explain the social and economic challenges facing Rio
I can explain the environmental challenges facing Rio
misconceptions: Assuming favelas are uniformly terrible with no community life
Confusing social with economic challenges
Giving no named or numerical detail

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Urban planning to improve the quality of life for the urban poor: the Favela Bairro Project
objectives: I can describe an urban planning scheme improving life for the urban poor
I can evaluate the success of the scheme
misconceptions: Describing the scheme without evaluating it
Assuming all residents benefited equally
Not identifying any limitations

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A favela is an informal settlement built on land the residents do not legally own.
Rocinha is Rio's largest favela, with a population of around 70,000.
Many favelas are built on steep hillsides at risk of landslides during heavy rain.
Around a third of favela homes historically lacked mains sanitation, causing disease.
High unemployment and reliance on the informal economy leave incomes low and insecure.
Drug gangs have controlled parts of some favelas, and murder rates in Rio have been high.
Guanabara Bay is heavily polluted by untreated sewage and industrial waste.
Traffic congestion contributes to serious air pollution in central Rio.
The Favela Bairro Project ran from 1995, investing hundreds of millions of dollars in favela upgrading.
The project paved and lit roads, installed sewerage and water, and built health and childcare facilities.
Residents were given legal ownership of their properties, encouraging investment.
Criticisms include insufficient funding for maintenance, limited resident involvement and the scale of remaining need.
Self-help and site-and-service schemes give residents materials and basic infrastructure to build their own homes.

weeks.dates: Mon 3 May - Fri 7 May 2027 (bank holiday Mon 3 May)
weeks.unit: 3.2.1 Urban change in a UK city: Bristol (opportunities)

lessons.title: The UK's population distribution and Bristol's importance
objectives: I can describe the distribution of population and major cities in the UK
I can explain the national and international importance of Bristol
misconceptions: Describing UK population distribution without reference to specific areas
Not distinguishing national from international importance
Giving no data

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Opportunities in Bristol: cultural mix, recreation, employment, transport and urban greening
objectives: I can explain the social and economic opportunities created by urban change in Bristol
I can explain how migration has affected Bristol's growth and character
misconceptions: Treating migration as only a challenge
Confusing social with economic opportunities
Giving no Bristol-specific detail

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

knowledgeComponents.statement: The UK population is concentrated in England, particularly London, the Midlands and the north-west.
Upland areas of Scotland and Wales are sparsely populated.
Bristol is in the south-west of England, with a population of around 460,000.
Bristol is nationally important for aerospace, financial services, the media and its two universities.
Bristol is internationally important through Airbus and Rolls-Royce, Bristol Port and its tourism.
Bristol was European Green Capital in 2015.
Around 16% of Bristol's population is from a black or minority ethnic background, and over 90 languages are spoken.
Migration has brought a young workforce and cultural diversity, including the St Pauls Carnival.
Recreational and cultural opportunities include the Harbourside, theatres, sport and music venues.
Bristol's integrated transport includes the MetroBus network, cycle routes and rail links.
Urban greening includes over 400 parks and green spaces and the Bristol Green Capital Partnership.
Employment opportunities are concentrated in high-tech, aerospace, creative and financial sectors.
Urban greening improves air quality, reduces flood risk and improves wellbeing.

weeks.unit: 3.2.1 Bristol: challenges, regeneration and urban sustainability

lessons.title: Challenges in Bristol: inequality, housing, dereliction and urban sprawl
objectives: I can explain the social and economic challenges of urban change in Bristol
I can explain the environmental challenges including brownfield versus greenfield development
misconceptions: Confusing brownfield with greenfield sites
Assuming all parts of a city experience the same conditions
Ignoring the rural-urban fringe

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Urban regeneration and sustainable urban living
objectives: I can describe an urban regeneration project and why it was needed
I can explain strategies for sustainable urban living
misconceptions: Describing a regeneration project without saying why it was needed
Listing sustainability strategies without explaining how they work
Not evaluating whether the strategies are effective

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Bristol has sharp inequality: life expectancy differs by around ten years between its richest and poorest wards.
Filwood and Hartcliffe are among the most deprived areas; Clifton and Stoke Bishop among the least.
Housing demand exceeds supply, pushing prices and rents beyond many residents' reach.
A brownfield site is previously developed land; a greenfield site has not been built on before.
Brownfield development reuses land and services but can be expensive to decontaminate.
Greenfield development is cheaper to build on but causes urban sprawl and loss of countryside.
Urban sprawl extends the city into the rural-urban fringe, increasing commuting and congestion.
The Bristol Temple Quarter Enterprise Zone regenerated derelict land around Temple Meads station.
Temple Quarter aimed to create thousands of jobs and new homes on brownfield land.
Sustainable urban living includes water and energy conservation, waste recycling and creating green space.
Bristol's SS Great Britain and Harbourside regeneration converted derelict docks into visitor attractions.
Transport strategies to reduce congestion include park and ride, bus lanes, cycle schemes and congestion charging.
A sustainable city meets the needs of current residents without damaging the environment for future ones.

weeks.unit: Fieldwork enquiry 1: physical geography (coastal or river)

lessons.title: Planning a physical fieldwork enquiry: question, theory and risk assessment
objectives: I can write a suitable geographical enquiry question linked to theory
I can complete a risk assessment for fieldwork
misconceptions: Writing a question that cannot be answered with the data available
Not linking the question to specification theory
Treating the risk assessment as a formality

assessment.type: Paper 3 Section B (Fieldwork) question

lessons.title: Collecting primary data in the field: methods and sampling
objectives: I can select and justify appropriate data collection methods
I can explain and apply random, systematic and stratified sampling
misconceptions: Confusing primary data (you collect it) with secondary data (someone else did)
Confusing random with systematic sampling
Collecting data without recording the method used

assessment.type: Paper 3 Section B (Fieldwork) question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Fieldwork must be carried out on at least two occasions in contrasting environments, outside the classroom and school grounds.
At least one enquiry must involve physical and human interaction.
A good enquiry question is specific, measurable and linked to a geographical theory.
An example coastal enquiry question is: how does beach profile change along a stretch of coastline?
An example river enquiry question is: how do river channel characteristics change downstream?
A risk assessment identifies hazards, who is at risk and the control measures taken.
Primary data is collected first-hand by the investigator.
Secondary data is collected by someone else, such as census data or Environment Agency records.
Quantitative data is numerical; qualitative data is descriptive such as photographs and field sketches.
Random sampling gives every location an equal chance of selection and avoids bias.
Systematic sampling selects at regular intervals, such as every 10 metres.
Stratified sampling divides the area into groups and samples each in proportion.
Repeating measurements improves reliability by reducing the effect of anomalies.

weeks.unit: Fieldwork enquiry 1: presentation, analysis and Summer 1 assessment

lessons.title: Processing and presenting fieldwork data
objectives: I can select appropriate presentation techniques for different data types
I can draw accurate graphs, maps and cross-sections
misconceptions: Choosing a pie chart for continuous data
Drawing graphs without titles, axis labels or units
Presenting data without any map context

assessment.type: Paper 3 Section B (Fieldwork) question

lessons.title: Analysing fieldwork data, drawing conclusions and evaluating
objectives: I can describe patterns and identify anomalies in my data
I can draw an evidence-based conclusion and evaluate the reliability of my enquiry
misconceptions: Describing data without linking it back to the enquiry question
Concluding beyond what the data supports
Evaluating by saying only 'it was rushed'

assessment.type: Paper 3 Section B (Fieldwork) question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Scatter graphs are used to show the relationship between two continuous variables.
Bar charts are used for discrete categories; line graphs for continuous change over time or distance.
A cross-section is used to present beach or river channel profiles.
Located bar charts place data on a base map to show geographical variation.
All graphs need a title, labelled axes, units and an appropriate scale.
Annotated photographs and field sketches present qualitative data effectively.
Analysis describes the pattern, quantifies it with data, and explains it using geographical theory.
An anomaly is a result that does not fit the general trend and should be identified and explained.
A conclusion must answer the original enquiry question using the evidence collected.
Evaluation should consider the data collection method, sample size, timing, weather and human error.
Reliability is improved by repeating measurements and increasing sample size.
A good evaluation suggests specific improvements and additional data that would strengthen the conclusion.
Fieldwork accounts for a substantial part of Paper 3, which is 30% of the GCSE.

weeks.unit: Fieldwork enquiry 2: human geography (urban)

lessons.title: Planning an urban fieldwork enquiry
objectives: I can design an urban enquiry investigating physical and human interaction
I can justify the choice of location and methods
misconceptions: Designing a questionnaire with leading questions
Choosing locations that are not genuinely contrasting
Not justifying the sampling strategy

assessment.type: Paper 3 Section B (Fieldwork) question

lessons.title: Collecting urban primary data: environmental quality, land use and perception
objectives: I can carry out an environmental quality survey and land use survey
I can collect qualitative data on people's perceptions
misconceptions: Ignoring the subjectivity of environmental quality scores
Asking closed questions when opinion is required
Collecting data at a time unrepresentative of normal conditions

assessment.type: Paper 3 Section B (Fieldwork) question

knowledgeComponents.statement: An urban enquiry investigating deprivation, environmental quality or regeneration meets the human-physical interaction requirement.
An example urban enquiry question is: how does environmental quality vary with distance from the city centre?
Contrasting locations should differ in a way relevant to the enquiry question.
Questionnaires should use clear, neutral wording and avoid leading questions.
A pilot survey tests a questionnaire before full data collection.
An environmental quality survey scores factors such as litter, noise, greenery and building condition on a bipolar scale.
A bipolar scale runs from a negative to a positive extreme, such as -3 to +3.
A land use survey records the function of each building on a base map.
Environmental quality scores are subjective, so multiple assessors improve reliability.
Data collected at one time of day may not represent typical conditions.
Bias occurs when the sample is unrepresentative of the population being studied.
Qualitative perception data adds depth that numerical data alone cannot capture.

weeks.unit: Fieldwork enquiry 2: analysis, conclusion and evaluation

lessons.title: Presenting and analysing urban fieldwork data
objectives: I can select suitable presentation techniques for urban data
I can analyse patterns and relate them to urban geography theory
misconceptions: Using an inappropriate technique for the data type
Analysing without reference to urban theory
Ignoring anomalies

assessment.type: Paper 3 Section B (Fieldwork) question

lessons.title: Conclusion, evaluation and comparing the two enquiries
objectives: I can draw an evidence-based conclusion for my urban enquiry
I can compare the strengths and limitations of my two enquiries
misconceptions: Making a conclusion the data does not support
Evaluating only the weather
Not suggesting realistic improvements

assessment.type: Paper 3 Section B (Fieldwork) question
commandWords: assess the reliability of your conclusion

knowledgeComponents.statement: A choropleth map shades areas by value and suits data grouped by district or ward.
A radar chart suits multi-factor index data such as environmental quality scores.
Analysis should relate observed patterns to urban geography theory such as land value or deprivation gradients.
Anomalies in urban data often reflect recent regeneration or local land use.
Quantifying a pattern with specific data values strengthens an analysis.
A conclusion must directly answer the enquiry question and reference the data.
Limitations include small sample size, subjectivity, time of day, weather and non-response bias.
Improvements should be specific and realistic, such as sampling at three different times of day.
Validity is whether the data actually measures what the enquiry intended to measure.
Reliability is whether repeating the method would give the same result.
Paper 3 Section B asks questions about the candidate's own fieldwork as well as unfamiliar fieldwork.
A signed written statement from the centre confirming the fieldwork dates and locations is required by AQA.

weeks.unit: 3.4 Geographical skills: cartographic and graphical

lessons.title: Cartographic skills: OS maps, atlas maps, GIS and sketch maps
objectives: I can use grid references, scale, direction and contours on an OS map
I can interpret different types of map including choropleth, isoline and flow-line maps
misconceptions: Reading eastings and northings in the wrong order
Confusing a four-figure with a six-figure reference
Misinterpreting contour patterns

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

lessons.title: Graphical skills: selecting, drawing and interpreting graphs
objectives: I can select the appropriate graph type for a data set
I can complete and interpret a range of graphs including divided bar, pie, scatter and population pyramid
misconceptions: Completing a graph without reading the existing scale
Drawing a line of best fit through the origin unnecessarily
Confusing correlation with causation

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Grid references are read along the bottom first (eastings), then up the side (northings).
A four-figure grid reference identifies a 1 km square; a six-figure reference locates to 100 metres.
On a 1:50 000 OS map, 2 cm represents 1 km.
On a 1:25 000 OS map, 4 cm represents 1 km.
Contour lines close together show steep slopes; widely spaced contours show gentle slopes.
A choropleth map uses shading density to show values by area.
An isoline map joins points of equal value, such as contours or isobars.
A flow-line map uses arrows of varying width to show movement.
GIS is a geographical information system that layers spatial data digitally.
Line graphs suit continuous data; bar charts suit discrete categories.
Scatter graphs show relationships between two variables and may show positive, negative or no correlation.
A population pyramid shows the age and sex structure of a population.
A line of best fit should follow the trend of the points, with roughly equal numbers either side.
Correlation does not prove causation.

weeks.unit: 3.4 Geographical skills: numerical and statistical

lessons.title: Numerical skills: percentages, proportion, ratio and magnitude
objectives: I can calculate percentages, percentage change and proportions from geographical data
I can use ratios and describe orders of magnitude
misconceptions: Calculating percentage change from the new value rather than the original
Confusing percentage with percentage point
Ignoring units in a density calculation

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

lessons.title: Statistical skills: measures of central tendency and dispersion
objectives: I can calculate mean, median, mode, range and interquartile range
I can identify anomalies and describe trends and relationships
misconceptions: Not ordering data before finding the median
Confusing range with interquartile range
Calling any high value an anomaly without justification

assessment.type: Geographical skills question (map, graph or statistics)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Percentage change = (change / original value) x 100.
A proportion can be expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage.
Population density = total population / area, usually in people per square kilometre.
Per capita means per person and allows fair comparison between places of different sizes.
An order of magnitude is a factor of ten.
A ratio compares two quantities, such as doctors per 1000 people.
The mean is the total divided by the number of values and is affected by extreme values.
The median is the middle value when data is ordered and is not distorted by extremes.
The mode is the most frequently occurring value.
The range is the highest value minus the lowest value.
The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile and shows the spread of the middle 50%.
The lower quartile is at the 25% position and the upper quartile at the 75% position of ordered data.
An anomaly should be identified with data and, where possible, explained geographically.

weeks.unit: Revision: Paper 1 physical geography

lessons.title: Revision: natural hazards and the living world
objectives: I can recall all case study detail for hazards and ecosystems
I can write high-quality 6- and 9-mark answers on Paper 1 Sections A and B
misconceptions: Recalling case studies without figures
Writing 9-mark answers without a conclusion
Missing the command word

assessment.type: Extended 9-mark evaluative question (plus 3 SPaG marks on one question per paper)

lessons.title: Revision: physical landscapes in the UK
objectives: I can recall the formation sequences of all coastal and river landforms
I can apply landform knowledge to an unfamiliar OS map or photograph
misconceptions: Learning landform sequences in the wrong order
Being unable to identify landforms on an unfamiliar map
Not naming processes within a formation answer

assessment.type: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment) structured question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 1 is 1 hour 30 minutes, 88 marks including 3 SPaG marks, and 35% of the GCSE.
Paper 1 has three sections: A the challenge of natural hazards, B the living world, C physical landscapes in the UK.
Nine-mark answers should have a clear structure with developed points and a final judgement.
Case study answers require named places, figures and dates.
Recall of specific data is what separates a Level 3 answer from a Level 2 one.
Command words determine the structure of the answer required.
Landform formation answers must present stages in the correct sequence with named processes.
The coastal erosion sequence is crack, cave, arch, stack, stump.
The waterfall sequence is hard rock over soft rock, undercutting, overhang, collapse, retreat, gorge.
The ox-bow lake sequence is meander migration, neck narrowing, cut-off during flood, deposition seals the bend.
Applying knowledge to an unfamiliar map or photograph is an AO3 skill and is heavily weighted.
AO3 (application and analysis) is the largest assessment objective at 35% of the qualification.

weeks.unit: Revision: urban issues, fieldwork and skills

lessons.title: Revision: urban issues and challenges
objectives: I can recall all case study detail for Rio de Janeiro and Bristol
I can compare urban issues in an LIC or NEE with those in a UK city
misconceptions: Mixing up detail between the two case studies
Giving opportunities when asked for challenges
Not comparing when asked to compare

assessment.type: Case study / example question requiring named place detail

lessons.title: Revision: fieldwork and geographical skills
objectives: I can answer questions about my own fieldwork with confidence
I can apply skills to unfamiliar resources under timed conditions
misconceptions: Not knowing the specific detail of your own methods and results
Failing to use the resource provided
Rushing calculation questions

assessment.type: Paper 3 Section B (Fieldwork) question

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 2 is 1 hour 30 minutes, 88 marks including 3 SPaG marks, and 35% of the GCSE.
Paper 3 is 1 hour 15 minutes, 76 marks including 6 SPaG marks, and 30% of the GCSE.
Paper 3 Section A is issue evaluation using a pre-release resource booklet; Section B is fieldwork.
The Paper 3 pre-release resource booklet is issued 12 weeks before the exam, in Year 11.
Paper 3 Section B asks about the candidate's own fieldwork AND about unfamiliar fieldwork situations.
Candidates must know their own enquiry questions, methods, results, conclusions and evaluations in detail.
Rio and Bristol case studies must be kept distinct: one LIC/NEE city, one UK city.
Comparison answers need explicit comparative language and evidence from both places.
Bristol's challenges include inequality, housing shortage, dereliction and urban sprawl.
Rio's challenges include favelas, sanitation, unemployment, crime and pollution.
The Favela Bairro Project and Bristol Temple Quarter are the two named regeneration examples.
Questions instructing 'using Figure X' award no marks for answers that ignore the resource.

weeks.unit: Year 10 end-of-year examination

lessons.title: Year 10 examination: Paper 1 (Living with the physical environment)
objectives: I can complete a full Paper 1 in 1 hour 30 minutes
I can deploy case study detail accurately across all three sections
misconceptions: Running out of time before the 9-mark question
Recalling the wrong case study
Losing SPaG marks through rushed writing

assessment.type: Full Paper 1 mock examination

lessons.title: Year 10 examination: urban issues, fieldwork and skills paper
objectives: I can answer urban issues, fieldwork and skills questions under exam conditions
I can identify my priorities for Year 11
misconceptions: Neglecting fieldwork revision because it feels less like content
Not using resources provided
Setting vague targets

assessment.type: Timed assessment on Paper 2 Section A and Paper 3 Section B

knowledgeComponents.statement: The full GCSE is 252 marks across three papers.
Paper 1 covers natural hazards, the living world and UK physical landscapes.
Case study recall is the single largest differentiator of grades in GCSE Geography.
Nine-mark questions carry the SPaG marks on Papers 1 and 2.
Time management should follow roughly one mark per minute.
By the end of Year 10 the candidate has completed the whole of Paper 1 content and the first Paper 2 topic.
Both fieldwork enquiries should be completed in Year 10 so Year 11 can focus on issue evaluation and revision.
The Paper 3 issue evaluation cannot be taught in Year 10 because the resource booklet is released only 12 weeks before the exam.
Year 11 covers the changing economic world, resource management and water, plus issue evaluation and revision.
Targets for Year 11 should name the topic, the skill and the action.
Fieldwork is worth a significant proportion of Paper 3 and should be revised as seriously as content.
Private candidates must confirm their centre will accept and sign the fieldwork statement.

subjects.name: GCSE Business
subjects.notes: BOARD CHOICE: AQA GCSE Business 8132, chosen over Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Business 1BS0. Both are 100% examined with no controlled assessment or NEA, which matters greatly for a home-educated candidate: either board can be sat as a private candidate at any centre that accepts external entries, with no coursework or centre-assessed component to arrange. Three reasons for AQA here. (1) Board consistency: this candidate is already sitting AQA for Maths, English Language, English Literature, Geography and Design & Technology. A single board means one set of command words, one house style of mark scheme, one exam-officer relationship and one entry deadline calendar - a genuine simplification for a family managing five subjects privately. (2) Structure that suits a two-year home-education split: AQA organises content into six free-standing topics (3.1 Business in the real world, 3.2 Influences on business, 3.3 Business operations, 3.4 Human resources, 3.5 Marketing, 3.6 Finance) with 3.1 and 3.2 examined on BOTH papers. That lets Year 10 teach the two cross-cutting topics first and then complete one whole paper's remaining content, so a genuine full-paper mock is possible at the end of Year 10. Edexcel's 1BS0 splits into Theme 1 (Investigating small business) and Theme 2 (Building a business), each examined on its own paper, which forces a rigid Theme 1 = Year 10, Theme 2 = Year 11 order and gives a Year 10 mock covering only half the qualification. (3) Assessment style: AQA's Section A carries 20 marks of multiple choice and short answer, which gives a home-educated candidate frequent low-stakes retrieval checkpoints and is well suited to a spaced-repetition system. ASSESSMENT (verified on the AQA specification-at-a-glance page): Paper 1 'Influences of operations and HRM on business activity' - 1h45, 90 marks, 50%, covering 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4. Paper 2 'Influences of marketing and finance on business activity' - 1h45, 90 marks, 50%, covering 3.1, 3.2, 3.5, 3.6. Each paper: Section A multiple choice and short answer (20 marks), Section B case study/data response (approx 34 marks), Section C case study/data response (approx 36 marks). Total 180 marks. Assessment objectives: AO1 knowledge, AO2 application, AO3 analysis, AO4 evaluation. A calculator is permitted. 8132 has NOT been reformed for 2028 exams.
deferredToYear11: 3.3 Business operations in full - 3.3.1 production processes (job and flow production, lean production, just-in-time), 3.3.2 the role of procurement (JIT vs JIC stock control, choosing suppliers, logistics, supply chain management), 3.3.3 the concept of quality (quality control, quality assurance, TQM, costs and benefits), 3.3.4 good customer service (methods, benefits, dangers of poor service, the role of ICT) - Year 11.

3.4 Human resources in full - 3.4.1 organisational structures (span of control, chain of command, delayering, delegation, centralisation, tall vs flat structures), 3.4.2 recruitment and selection (internal vs external, job analysis, job description, person specification, selection methods, contract types), 3.4.3 motivating employees (financial and non-financial methods, benefits of a motivated workforce), 3.4.4 training (induction, on-the-job, off-the-job, benefits and comparison) - Year 11.

Why this split is conventional: 3.1 and 3.2 are examined on BOTH papers and so must be taught first. Once they are secure, a school completes one paper's remaining content in Year 10 and the other paper's in Year 11. Taking Marketing and Finance in Year 10 completes Paper 2 exactly, so a full 90-mark Paper 2 mock is available at the end of Year 10; and Finance, which is the most quantitative and most commonly under-performed topic, then has a full extra year of spaced retrieval before the real exam.
Full past-paper practice on Paper 1 (which requires 3.3 and 3.4) - Year 11 only.
Interleaved revision across all six topics with both papers in play - Year 11.
Extended evaluation technique at the top of the mark range: weighing multiple factors, using explicit criteria and reaching conditional judgements - developed in Year 10, refined in Year 11.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1 The purpose and nature of business

lessons.title: Why businesses exist: needs, wants and the purpose of business
objectives: I can explain the purpose of business activity
I can distinguish between goods and services and between needs and wants
misconceptions: Confusing needs with wants
Thinking all businesses aim only to make profit
Confusing added value with profit

assessment.type: Section A multiple choice / short answer

lessons.title: Enterprise, entrepreneurs and risk
objectives: I can describe the characteristics and role of an entrepreneur
I can explain the risks and rewards of starting a business
misconceptions: Assuming entrepreneurs are always young or wealthy
Thinking risk-taking always means recklessness
Ignoring the opportunity cost of starting a business

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

knowledgeComponents.statement: The purpose of business activity is to produce goods and services that satisfy customer needs and wants.
A need is essential for survival; a want is desirable but not essential.
Goods are physical products; services are intangible activities provided for customers.
The factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Added value is the difference between the cost of inputs and the price charged for the output.
Added value can be created by branding, quality, convenience, design and customer service.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a decision is made.
An entrepreneur organises the other factors of production and takes the risk of the business failing.
Entrepreneurial characteristics include risk-taking, determination, creativity, organisation and confidence.
Rewards of enterprise include profit, independence and personal satisfaction.
Risks of enterprise include losing invested money, unlimited liability and a loss of regular income.
The dynamic business environment changes because of technology, economic conditions, legislation and environmental pressures.

weeks.unit: 3.1.2 Business ownership

lessons.title: Sole traders and partnerships
objectives: I can explain the features of a sole trader and a partnership
I can explain the advantages and disadvantages of each, including unlimited liability
misconceptions: Thinking a sole trader must work alone
Confusing unlimited liability with unlimited profit
Assuming partnerships always share profits equally

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Private and public limited companies and not-for-profit organisations
objectives: I can explain the features of a private limited company and a public limited company
I can explain limited liability and the aims of not-for-profit organisations
misconceptions: Thinking a plc is government-owned
Confusing limited liability with limited responsibility
Believing not-for-profits cannot make a surplus

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: A sole trader is a business owned and controlled by one person.
Unlimited liability means the owner's personal assets can be used to pay business debts.
Sole traders keep all the profit and make all decisions but bear all the risk.
A partnership is owned by two or more people, typically between 2 and 20.
A deed of partnership sets out how profits, responsibilities and decisions are shared.
Partnerships bring in more capital and shared expertise but can lead to disagreement.
Sole traders and partnerships are unincorporated: there is no legal separation between owner and business.
A private limited company (ltd) has shares sold privately and cannot sell shares on the stock exchange.
A public limited company (plc) can sell shares to the general public on the stock exchange.
Limited liability means shareholders can only lose the money they invested.
Companies are incorporated: the business is a separate legal entity from its owners.
A dividend is a share of profit paid to shareholders.
Not-for-profit organisations, including charities and social enterprises, reinvest surpluses to pursue a social aim.
Becoming a plc raises large amounts of capital but risks loss of control through takeover.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3 Business aims and objectives

lessons.title: Setting business aims and objectives
objectives: I can identify common business aims and objectives
I can explain why objectives differ between businesses
misconceptions: Confusing an aim (broad goal) with an objective (specific target)
Assuming all businesses aim to maximise profit
Thinking objectives never change

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: How and why objectives change over time
objectives: I can explain how objectives change as a business develops
I can explain how external factors force objectives to change
misconceptions: Assuming survival is only a start-up objective
Not linking a change in objective to a specific cause
Listing objectives without applying them to the case study business

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

knowledgeComponents.statement: An aim is a broad long-term goal; an objective is a specific, measurable target that helps achieve it.
Common business objectives are survival, profit, growth, market share, customer satisfaction, social and ethical goals.
SMART objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound.
Survival is usually the priority objective for a new business.
Market share is a business's sales as a percentage of total market sales.
Objectives differ by size, sector, ownership and stage of development.
Not-for-profit organisations set social rather than profit objectives.
Objectives change as a business moves from survival to growth and then to profit maximisation.
A recession may force a business to switch from a growth objective back to survival.
Customer loyalty objectives aim to increase repeat purchase and lifetime customer value.
Ethical objectives may reduce short-term profit but improve reputation and long-term sales.
Success against an objective can be measured by comparing actual performance to the target.

weeks.unit: 3.1.4 Stakeholders

lessons.title: Identifying stakeholders and their objectives
objectives: I can identify the main stakeholders of a business
I can explain what each stakeholder group wants from the business
misconceptions: Confusing stakeholders with shareholders
Assuming all stakeholders want the same thing
Forgetting the local community and government as stakeholders

assessment.type: Section A multiple choice / short answer

lessons.title: Stakeholder conflict and how businesses manage it
objectives: I can explain how stakeholder objectives conflict
I can analyse the impact of a business decision on different stakeholders
misconceptions: Describing conflict without explaining why the objectives clash
Assuming shareholders always win
Not applying the conflict to the case study business

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A stakeholder is any individual or group affected by or with an interest in a business.
Internal stakeholders include owners, managers and employees.
External stakeholders include customers, suppliers, the local community, government and pressure groups.
Shareholders want profit, dividends and a rising share price.
Employees want job security, fair pay, good conditions and training.
Customers want quality, value for money and good service.
Suppliers want prompt payment and regular, predictable orders.
The local community wants employment and minimal pollution and disruption.
Government wants tax revenue, employment and compliance with the law.
Conflict arises because meeting one stakeholder's objective often costs another.
Cutting costs to raise shareholder returns may reduce employee pay and job security.
Expanding a factory may create jobs but increase noise and traffic for the community.
Businesses prioritise stakeholders according to their power and influence over the business.

weeks.unit: 3.1.5 Business location

lessons.title: Factors affecting business location
objectives: I can explain the factors that influence where a business locates
I can explain how the importance of each factor varies by business type
misconceptions: Assuming the cheapest location is always best
Applying retail location factors to a manufacturer
Listing factors without applying them to the business in the case study

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: E-commerce, globalisation and changing location decisions
objectives: I can explain how e-commerce has changed location decisions
I can justify a location decision for a given business
misconceptions: Thinking location no longer matters for online businesses
Justifying without weighing alternatives
Ignoring the type of business when recommending a location

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Key location factors are proximity to the market, raw materials, labour, competitors and cost.
Retailers prioritise footfall and proximity to customers.
Manufacturers using bulky raw materials locate close to those materials to cut transport costs.
Businesses needing specialist skills locate near a suitable labour supply, such as near a university.
Locating near competitors can be beneficial where customers compare products, as on a high street.
Rent and business rates are usually much higher in city centres than out of town.
Good transport infrastructure reduces distribution costs and delivery times.
E-commerce allows businesses to sell nationally from a low-cost location.
Online retailers locate distribution centres near motorway networks rather than near customers.
Offshoring moves production abroad to reduce labour costs.
Government grants may encourage businesses to locate in areas of high unemployment.
A justified location decision weighs at least two options and reaches a supported conclusion.

weeks.unit: 3.1.6 Business planning and basic finance

lessons.title: The purpose and contents of a business plan
objectives: I can explain why a business produces a business plan
I can describe the main sections of a business plan
misconceptions: Thinking a business plan is only for start-ups
Believing a plan guarantees success
Confusing a business plan with a cash flow forecast

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Revenue, costs and profit calculations
objectives: I can calculate total revenue, total costs and profit
I can distinguish fixed costs from variable costs
misconceptions: Treating all costs as variable
Forgetting to multiply variable cost per unit by output
Confusing revenue with profit

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data

knowledgeComponents.statement: A business plan sets out objectives, market research, marketing, operations and financial forecasts.
A business plan helps secure finance from banks and investors.
A business plan reduces risk by forcing the owner to research and forecast before committing money.
A plan is a working document that should be revised as circumstances change.
Established businesses also use plans when launching products or seeking investment.
Revenue = selling price x quantity sold.
Fixed costs do not change with the level of output, for example rent and salaries.
Variable costs change directly with output, for example raw materials and packaging.
Total costs = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit x quantity).
Profit = total revenue - total costs.
A loss occurs when total costs exceed total revenue.
Fixed costs per unit fall as output rises, which is the basis of economies of scale.
Calculation answers should show working and include units or currency symbols.

weeks.unit: 3.1.7 Expanding a business

lessons.title: Methods of business growth: internal and external
objectives: I can explain internal growth methods including new locations, e-commerce and outsourcing
I can explain external growth through mergers, takeovers and franchising
misconceptions: Confusing a merger (agreed) with a takeover (may be hostile)
Confusing franchisor and franchisee roles
Thinking growth is always beneficial

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Economies and diseconomies of scale
objectives: I can explain economies of scale and their effect on unit costs
I can explain diseconomies of scale and evaluate whether growth is worthwhile
misconceptions: Thinking economies of scale reduce total costs rather than unit costs
Assuming growth always lowers costs
Not linking diseconomies to management and communication problems

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement
commandWords: do you think the business should expand

knowledgeComponents.statement: Internal (organic) growth comes from within the business: new products, new outlets, e-commerce.
External growth comes from combining with other businesses through merger or takeover.
A merger is an agreed combination of two businesses into one.
A takeover occurs when one business buys a controlling interest in another.
A franchisor sells the right to trade under its brand; the franchisee pays a fee and a share of revenue.
Franchising allows rapid expansion with limited capital risk for the franchisor.
Outsourcing pays another business to carry out an activity, reducing fixed costs.
E-commerce allows a business to reach national and international markets without new premises.
Economies of scale are reductions in average unit cost as output increases.
Purchasing economies come from bulk-buying discounts.
Technical economies come from using larger, more efficient machinery.
Diseconomies of scale are rises in unit cost when a business grows too large.
Diseconomies arise from poor communication, weaker coordination and lower staff motivation.
Growth may bring higher revenue but also higher risk, borrowing and loss of control.

weeks.unit: 3.1 Review and Autumn 1 assessment

lessons.title: Applying business in the real world to a case study
objectives: I can apply my knowledge of ownership, aims, stakeholders and growth to an unfamiliar business
I can build a chain of reasoning in an analyse question
misconceptions: Writing generic textbook answers with no reference to the case study
Making a point without developing the consequences
Ignoring data provided in the stimulus

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Autumn 1 assessment: business in the real world
objectives: I can answer multiple choice, short answer, calculation and extended questions on 3.1
I can structure a 9-mark justified response
misconceptions: Not reaching a judgement in a 9-mark answer
Writing at length for a 1-mark question
Failing to use the case study business name

assessment.type: Timed assessment on 3.1

knowledgeComponents.statement: Application means using specific detail from the case study business in the answer.
A chain of reasoning links a cause to a consequence and then to a further consequence.
Analyse questions require developed points, not lists.
Naming the business and referring to its data is the simplest way to secure application marks.
Case study data such as sales figures or costs should be used, not ignored.
AQA Business Papers 1 and 2 are each 1 hour 45 minutes and worth 90 marks (50% each).
Section A is multiple choice and short answer worth 20 marks.
Sections B and C are case study and data response, worth approximately 34 and 36 marks.
Nine-mark questions require analysis of both sides and a supported judgement.
A judgement should say which factor matters most and why, in the context of the business.
Answer length should be proportional to the mark tariff.
Multiple choice questions should always be attempted; there is no penalty for a wrong answer.

weeks.unit: 3.2.1 Technology

lessons.title: E-commerce and its impact on business
objectives: I can explain what e-commerce is and how it changes how businesses operate
I can analyse the benefits and drawbacks of e-commerce for a business
misconceptions: Thinking e-commerce only benefits businesses
Ignoring the set-up and delivery costs of selling online
Confusing e-commerce with digital communication

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Digital communication and its impact on business
objectives: I can explain how digital communication changes marketing and customer service
I can evaluate the risks of digital communication for a business
misconceptions: Assuming social media marketing is free and risk-free
Confusing promotion with communication
Not considering negative online reviews

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: E-commerce is buying and selling goods and services over the internet.
M-commerce is e-commerce carried out on mobile devices.
E-commerce allows 24-hour trading and access to national and global markets.
E-commerce reduces the need for expensive high-street premises.
E-commerce increases competition because customers can easily compare prices.
Drawbacks of e-commerce include website costs, delivery costs, returns and cyber security risks.
Digital communication includes social media, email, video conferencing and instant messaging.
Social media allows cheap targeted promotion and direct customer engagement.
Negative reviews and viral complaints can damage reputation rapidly.
Digital communication allows remote and flexible working, reducing premises costs.
Businesses must comply with data protection law when handling customer data.
Technology requires investment in equipment and staff training before benefits are realised.

weeks.unit: 3.2.2 Ethical and environmental considerations

lessons.title: Ethical considerations in business
objectives: I can explain what ethical business behaviour means
I can analyse the trade-off between ethics and profit
misconceptions: Assuming ethical behaviour always reduces profit
Confusing ethics with legality
Not weighing costs against reputational benefits

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Environmental considerations and sustainability
objectives: I can explain the environmental impacts of business activity
I can evaluate whether a business should invest in sustainability
misconceptions: Assuming environmental measures always increase costs with no return
Confusing sustainability with recycling only
Ignoring legal requirements on waste and emissions

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Business ethics are the moral principles that guide business decisions, beyond simply obeying the law.
Ethical issues include working conditions, supply chain labour, animal testing and honest advertising.
Fair trade guarantees producers in developing countries a minimum price for their goods.
Ethical behaviour can raise costs but also raises prices customers will pay and improves reputation.
Unethical behaviour risks boycotts, negative publicity and loss of long-term sales.
Corporate social responsibility means a business taking account of its impact on society.
Environmental impacts of business include traffic congestion, waste, noise and air pollution.
Sustainability means meeting present needs without preventing future generations from meeting theirs.
Businesses reduce environmental impact by recycling, using renewable energy and cutting packaging.
Reducing energy and material use often cuts costs as well as environmental impact.
Global warming and the depletion of scarce resources create pressure and regulation on business.
Environmental legislation makes some measures compulsory rather than optional.

weeks.unit: 3.2.3 The economic climate

lessons.title: Interest rates and their impact on business
objectives: I can explain how a change in interest rates affects business costs and demand
I can analyse the differing impact on borrowers and savers
misconceptions: Thinking higher interest rates only affect businesses with loans
Confusing the effect on savers with the effect on borrowers
Not linking interest rates to consumer demand

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Employment levels and consumer spending
objectives: I can explain how unemployment affects businesses
I can explain how consumer spending affects different types of business
misconceptions: Assuming a recession harms all businesses equally
Confusing income with disposable income
Not distinguishing luxury from essential goods

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement
commandWords: which business would be affected most

knowledgeComponents.statement: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing money or the reward for saving it.
The Bank of England sets the UK base rate.
Higher interest rates increase loan repayments, raising business costs.
Higher interest rates reduce consumer borrowing and spending, reducing demand.
Higher interest rates discourage business investment in new equipment and premises.
Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper and tend to increase spending and investment.
Businesses selling on credit, such as car dealers, are especially sensitive to interest rates.
Unemployment reduces total consumer spending in the economy.
High unemployment increases the supply of labour, making recruitment easier and cheaper.
Disposable income is income remaining after tax and essential spending.
Demand for luxury goods falls sharply in a recession; demand for essentials falls much less.
Some businesses, such as discount retailers, may see demand rise during a recession.
The economic cycle moves between boom, downturn, recession and recovery.

weeks.unit: 3.2.4 Globalisation

lessons.title: Globalisation and international competition
objectives: I can explain what globalisation means for UK businesses
I can analyse how UK businesses compete internationally on design, quality and price
misconceptions: Seeing globalisation only as a threat
Assuming price is the only basis of international competition
Confusing imports with exports

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Exchange rates and their impact
objectives: I can explain how exchange rates affect the price of imports and exports
I can calculate a price using a given exchange rate
misconceptions: Getting the direction of the effect the wrong way round
Dividing when multiplication is required in a conversion
Assuming a weak pound is always bad

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data
commandWords: work out the price in euros

knowledgeComponents.statement: Globalisation is the increasing integration of economies through trade, investment and communication.
Imports are goods bought from abroad; exports are goods sold abroad.
Globalisation gives UK businesses access to larger markets and cheaper suppliers.
Globalisation also exposes UK businesses to competition from lower-cost overseas producers.
UK businesses compete internationally on design, quality, branding and service as well as price.
A multinational operates in more than one country.
Tariffs are taxes on imports that raise the price of foreign goods.
An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another.
A strong pound makes UK exports more expensive abroad and imports cheaper.
A weak pound makes UK exports cheaper abroad and imports more expensive.
The mnemonic SPICED means Strong Pound, Imports Cheap, Exports Dear.
To convert pounds to another currency, multiply by the exchange rate.
A weak pound benefits UK exporters but raises costs for businesses importing raw materials.

weeks.unit: 3.2.5 Legislation

lessons.title: Employment law and health and safety law
objectives: I can explain the main requirements of employment and health and safety legislation
I can analyse the impact of legislation on business costs and operations
misconceptions: Confusing the National Minimum Wage with the National Living Wage
Thinking legislation only creates costs
Not linking legislation to specific business consequences

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Consumer law and its impact
objectives: I can explain the main protections consumer law provides
I can evaluate the impact of consumer law on a business
misconceptions: Thinking consumer law only applies to faulty goods
Assuming compliance is optional
Ignoring the reputational benefit of compliance

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Employment law covers pay, contracts, working hours, holiday entitlement and protection from discrimination.
The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage set legal minimum hourly pay rates by age.
Discrimination on grounds of age, sex, race, religion or disability is unlawful.
Employees are entitled to a written contract of employment.
Health and safety law requires businesses to provide a safe working environment, training and equipment.
A risk assessment identifies workplace hazards and the measures taken to control them.
Complying with legislation raises costs but reduces the risk of fines, compensation and lost reputation.
The Consumer Rights Act requires goods to be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and as described.
Consumers are entitled to a refund, repair or replacement for faulty goods.
Trading Standards enforces consumer protection law.
Consumer law also covers services, digital content and unfair contract terms.
Compliance builds customer trust, which supports repeat purchase and brand reputation.
Breaking consumer law risks fines, legal costs and lasting damage to reputation.

weeks.unit: 3.2.6 The competitive environment

lessons.title: Competition and its impact on businesses
objectives: I can explain how competition affects price, quality and customer service
I can explain how a business can compete effectively
misconceptions: Assuming competing only means lowering prices
Confusing a USP with a brand name
Not applying competitive strategy to the case study business

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Uncertainty and risk in business
objectives: I can identify the main risks businesses face
I can explain how businesses reduce uncertainty and manage risk
misconceptions: Confusing risk (measurable) with uncertainty (unpredictable)
Thinking risk can be eliminated
Not linking risk management to specific business actions

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Competition exists where several businesses sell similar products to the same customers.
Competition tends to lower prices, raise quality and improve customer service.
Competitive advantage is what makes a business better than its rivals in the eyes of customers.
A unique selling point (USP) is a feature that distinguishes a product from competitors.
Price competition attracts price-sensitive customers but reduces profit margins.
Non-price competition uses quality, branding, service, design and convenience.
Businesses in competitive markets must innovate continually to retain market share.
Risk is the chance of loss that can be estimated; uncertainty cannot be reliably predicted.
Business risks include falling demand, rising costs, new competitors, legal change and technology change.
Market research reduces risk by testing demand before committing resources.
Insurance transfers some risks, such as fire or theft, to an insurer for a premium.
Diversification spreads risk across several products or markets.
Holding cash reserves helps a business survive unexpected downturns.

weeks.unit: 3.2 Review and Autumn 2 assessment

lessons.title: Interrelating influences on business
objectives: I can explain how several external influences interact to affect a business
I can weigh which influence matters most to a given business
misconceptions: Treating each influence in isolation
Not prioritising when asked which is most important
Ignoring the type of business when weighing influences

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

lessons.title: Autumn 2 assessment: influences on business
objectives: I can answer a full range of question types on 3.2
I can produce a well-structured 9-mark justified answer
misconceptions: Producing balanced analysis but no judgement
Failing to apply to the case study
Poor time management across the paper

assessment.type: Timed assessment on 3.2

knowledgeComponents.statement: External influences on business are technology, ethics and environment, the economic climate, globalisation, legislation and competition.
External influences interact: for example a recession increases price competition.
The impact of an influence depends on the size, sector and market of the business.
A judgement should state which influence matters most and justify why in context.
Weighing influences requires considering both the size and the likelihood of the effect.
Topics 3.1 and 3.2 are examined on BOTH Paper 1 and Paper 2.
Nine-mark questions are marked on knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation.
A 9-mark answer should consider at least two developed points before reaching a judgement.
Analysis without evaluation caps a 9-mark answer below the top level.
Evaluation should be specific to the business rather than a general statement.
Section A multiple choice questions cover the whole specification content for that paper.
Time should be allocated at roughly one mark per minute plus reading time.

weeks.unit: 3.5.1 Identifying and understanding customers; 3.5.2 Segmentation

lessons.title: Identifying and satisfying customer needs
objectives: I can explain why identifying customer needs is essential to business success
I can explain the consequences of failing to meet customer needs
misconceptions: Assuming a good product sells itself
Confusing what the business wants to sell with what customers want to buy
Ignoring changing customer needs over time

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Market segmentation
objectives: I can explain segmentation by gender, age, location and income
I can explain the benefits of targeting a specific market segment
misconceptions: Confusing a segment with the whole market
Thinking segmentation is only about age
Assuming a niche market is always more profitable

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Identifying customer needs allows a business to design products people will actually buy.
Satisfied customers make repeat purchases and recommend the business to others.
Failing to meet customer needs leads to falling sales, poor reviews and lost market share.
A market-orientated business designs products around researched customer needs.
A product-orientated business focuses on the product first and then seeks customers.
Customer needs change over time, so businesses must research continuously.
Market segmentation divides a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics.
Common segmentation bases are gender, age, location and income.
Targeting a segment allows more focused product design, pricing and promotion.
A niche market is a small, specialised segment; a mass market is large and broad.
Niche markets face less competition but have fewer potential customers.
Segmentation can reduce wasted marketing spend by focusing on the most likely buyers.

weeks.unit: 3.5.3 Market research: purpose and methods

lessons.title: The purpose of market research
objectives: I can explain why businesses carry out market research
I can explain how research informs decisions about demand, competition and target market
misconceptions: Thinking research guarantees a correct decision
Confusing research purpose with research method
Ignoring the cost and time of research

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Primary and secondary research methods
objectives: I can describe primary methods including questionnaires, surveys, interviews and focus groups
I can describe secondary methods and compare the two
misconceptions: Confusing primary with secondary research
Assuming a larger sample is automatically better regardless of who is asked
Ignoring bias in questionnaire design

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Market research is the collection and analysis of information about customers, competitors and the market.
Research helps a business estimate demand before launching a product.
Research identifies competitors' prices, products and market share.
Research identifies the target market and its preferences.
Research reduces but does not eliminate the risk of a product failing.
Research findings inform decisions on price, product features, promotion and place.
Primary research is collected first-hand for a specific purpose.
Secondary research uses data already collected by someone else, such as government statistics or competitor websites.
Primary research is up to date and specific but costly and time-consuming.
Secondary research is cheap and quick but may be out of date or not specific to the business.
Quantitative data is numerical; qualitative data explores opinions and reasons.
Focus groups give detailed qualitative insight but from a small, possibly unrepresentative group.
A biased or leading question produces unreliable results.
A representative sample reflects the characteristics of the target market.

weeks.unit: 3.5.3 Using market research data; 3.5.4 Price

lessons.title: Interpreting and using market research data
objectives: I can interpret market research data presented in tables and charts
I can use research data to support a business recommendation
misconceptions: Drawing conclusions the data does not support
Ignoring sample size when judging reliability
Reading a chart without checking the axis scale

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data

lessons.title: Pricing methods
objectives: I can describe price skimming, penetration, competitive, loss leader and cost-plus pricing
I can recommend a pricing method for a given product
misconceptions: Confusing skimming (high initial price) with penetration (low initial price)
Thinking a loss leader means the whole business makes a loss
Applying cost-plus without knowing the unit cost

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Market research data must be interpreted with reference to sample size and how it was collected.
A trend is a general direction of change over time.
A larger, representative sample generally gives more reliable results.
Percentages allow fair comparison between groups of different sizes.
Data should support rather than replace a business judgement.
Price skimming sets a high initial price for a new, innovative product, then lowers it.
Penetration pricing sets a low initial price to gain market share, then raises it.
Competitive pricing sets price in line with rivals.
A loss leader is priced below cost to attract customers who buy other profitable items.
Cost-plus pricing adds a percentage mark-up to the unit cost.
Cost-plus price = unit cost x (1 + mark-up percentage).
Skimming suits technology products with few competitors; penetration suits crowded markets.
Pricing decisions depend on cost, competition, customer expectation and the product life cycle stage.

weeks.unit: 3.5.4 Product: development, design and differentiation

lessons.title: Product development and design
objectives: I can explain the process and importance of product development
I can explain how design influences customer appeal and cost
misconceptions: Thinking design is only about appearance
Assuming new products are always successful
Ignoring the cost of development

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Product differentiation: USP and brand image
objectives: I can explain how a business differentiates its product
I can analyse the value of a strong brand image
misconceptions: Confusing a brand with a logo
Assuming a USP must be a physical product feature
Not linking differentiation to the ability to charge a higher price

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Product development creates new products or improves existing ones.
Development typically moves from idea generation to research, prototype, testing and launch.
Design covers function, aesthetics and cost, and must balance all three.
Good design can reduce manufacturing cost as well as increase appeal.
Product development is expensive and risky, and many new products fail.
Continuous development is needed because customer needs and technology change.
Differentiation makes a product distinct from competitors' products.
A unique selling point is the specific feature that makes a product different.
A brand is a name, design or symbol that identifies a product and distinguishes it.
Brand image is how customers perceive the brand.
Strong brands allow premium pricing and encourage brand loyalty and repeat purchase.
Brand loyalty reduces the effect of competitors' price cuts.
Building a brand takes sustained investment in quality, promotion and consistency.

weeks.unit: 3.5.4 Product life cycle and extension strategies

lessons.title: The product life cycle
objectives: I can describe the stages of the product life cycle
I can explain how marketing changes at each stage
misconceptions: Reading the y-axis as profit rather than sales
Assuming every product passes through all stages at the same speed
Confusing maturity with decline

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Extension strategies
objectives: I can describe extension strategies and explain why they are used
I can recommend an extension strategy for a given product
misconceptions: Thinking extension strategies only mean price cuts
Recommending extension for a product in the growth stage
Not justifying the recommendation with case study evidence

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: The product life cycle has five stages: development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline.
During development there are no sales but high costs, so cash flow is negative.
During introduction sales are low and promotion spending is high.
During growth sales rise rapidly and the product may become profitable.
During maturity sales peak and competition is strongest; profits are usually highest.
During decline sales fall as customer tastes or technology change.
The product life cycle graph plots sales against time.
Products have very different life cycle lengths: fashion items short, staple foods very long.
Extension strategies aim to prolong the maturity stage and delay decline.
Extension strategies include new packaging, new variants, new markets, rebranding, price reductions and extra promotion.
Extension strategies are cheaper than developing a wholly new product.
Extension only delays decline; eventually a replacement product is needed.
The best extension strategy depends on why sales are falling.
