weeks.unit: 3.5.4 Product portfolio and Spring 1 assessment

lessons.title: The product portfolio and the Boston Matrix
objectives: I can explain what a product portfolio is and why businesses hold one
I can classify products using the Boston Matrix and explain the implications
misconceptions: Confusing the axes of market share and market growth
Assuming a cash cow should be discontinued
Thinking every dog should be dropped immediately

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Spring 1 assessment: marketing (part 1)
objectives: I can answer questions on customers, segmentation, research, price and product
I can use case study data in a justified recommendation
misconceptions: Recommending without weighing alternatives
Ignoring the data provided
Writing generic marketing theory

assessment.type: Timed assessment on 3.5 part 1

knowledgeComponents.statement: A product portfolio is the range of products a business sells.
A balanced portfolio spreads risk and provides income at different life cycle stages.
The Boston Matrix classifies products by market share and market growth.
A star has high market share in a high-growth market and needs investment.
A cash cow has high market share in a low-growth market and generates strong cash flow.
A question mark (problem child) has low share in a high-growth market and needs a decision.
A dog has low share in a low-growth market and may be discontinued.
Cash cows typically fund investment in stars and question marks.
A dog may still be retained if it completes a product range or covers its costs.
The Boston Matrix is a snapshot; products move between categories over time.
Justified recommendations must weigh at least two options using case study evidence.
Marketing questions frequently supply sales, price or market share data that must be used.

weeks.unit: 3.5.4 Promotion

lessons.title: Promotional methods: advertising, PR, sponsorship and sales promotion
objectives: I can describe the main promotional methods
I can explain the advantages and disadvantages of each
misconceptions: Confusing advertising (paid) with public relations (earned coverage)
Thinking sales promotion always increases profit
Not matching the method to the target market

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Digital and social media promotion
objectives: I can explain how businesses promote through social media and digital channels
I can recommend a promotional method for a given business and budget
misconceptions: Assuming social media promotion is free
Recommending an expensive method for a small business with no budget
Not considering the target market's media habits

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Promotion communicates with customers to inform and persuade them to buy.
Advertising is paid communication through media such as TV, radio, print and online.
Public relations builds a favourable image through unpaid coverage such as press releases and events.
Sponsorship associates a brand with an event, team or individual.
Sales promotion offers short-term incentives such as discounts, BOGOF offers and loyalty cards.
Sales promotion boosts short-term sales but can reduce profit margins and devalue a brand.
Point of sale promotion influences customers at the moment of purchase.
Social media promotion is low cost and allows precise targeting and two-way engagement.
Influencer marketing uses a trusted individual to promote a product to their followers.
Viral marketing relies on customers sharing content, giving large reach at low cost but is unpredictable.
Targeted digital advertising uses customer data to reach specific segments.
The promotional method chosen must suit the target market, the product and the budget.
Return on investment compares the additional profit generated with the cost of the promotion.

weeks.unit: 3.5.4 Place and distribution

lessons.title: Distribution channels: retailers, wholesalers and telesales
objectives: I can describe the main channels of distribution
I can explain the advantages of direct and indirect distribution
misconceptions: Confusing a wholesaler with a retailer
Thinking a shorter channel is always better
Ignoring the cost of holding stock

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: E-commerce and m-commerce as distribution
objectives: I can explain how e-commerce and m-commerce change distribution
I can analyse the impact of online selling on traditional retailers
misconceptions: Assuming online selling removes all distribution costs
Ignoring the cost and rate of returns
Not considering customers who prefer physical shopping

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A distribution channel is the route a product takes from producer to consumer.
A direct channel sells straight from producer to consumer.
An indirect channel uses intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers.
A wholesaler buys in bulk from producers and sells smaller quantities to retailers.
Using a wholesaler reduces the producer's storage, transport and admin costs.
Each intermediary takes a margin, reducing the producer's profit per unit.
Telesales sells by telephone, allowing direct contact but with high labour costs.
E-commerce allows direct national and global selling without physical stores.
M-commerce is selling through mobile apps and mobile-optimised websites.
Click and collect combines online ordering with in-store collection.
Omnichannel retailing integrates online, mobile and physical shopping.
Online selling incurs delivery and returns costs that physical retail does not.
Growth in e-commerce has reduced high street footfall and forced retailers to adapt.

weeks.unit: 3.5.4 The integrated marketing mix

lessons.title: Integrating the four Ps
objectives: I can explain how the four elements of the marketing mix must work together
I can identify inconsistencies in a business's marketing mix
misconceptions: Treating the four Ps as independent decisions
Recommending a premium price with budget promotion and distribution
Not linking the mix to the target market

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Adapting the marketing mix over time
objectives: I can explain how the marketing mix changes over the product life cycle
I can recommend changes to a business's marketing mix
misconceptions: Changing one element without considering the others
Recommending change without evidence from the case study
Ignoring cost when recommending changes

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement
commandWords: how should the business change its marketing mix

knowledgeComponents.statement: The marketing mix is the combination of price, product, promotion and place.
An integrated mix means all four elements send a consistent message to the target market.
A luxury product needs a premium price, high-quality design, exclusive distribution and aspirational promotion.
A budget product needs low price, functional design, wide distribution and value-focused promotion.
Inconsistency in the mix confuses customers and weakens brand positioning.
Positioning is where a product sits in customers' minds relative to competitors.
The mix must be built around the researched needs of the target segment.
During introduction, promotion is heavy and distribution may be limited.
During maturity, price competition intensifies and extension strategies are used.
Repositioning changes how a product is perceived, usually requiring changes across the whole mix.
Technology changes the mix, especially promotion and place.
Competitor actions may force a business to adjust price or promotion.
Any recommended change must be affordable and consistent with the rest of the mix.

weeks.unit: Marketing case studies and application practice

lessons.title: Applying the marketing mix to unfamiliar businesses
objectives: I can analyse the marketing mix of an unfamiliar business from a case study
I can use data from the stimulus to support my analysis
misconceptions: Describing marketing theory instead of applying it
Ignoring numerical data in the stimulus
Not naming the business or its products

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

lessons.title: Extended writing: justified marketing recommendations
objectives: I can structure a 9-mark justified marketing recommendation
I can weigh alternatives and reach a supported conclusion
misconceptions: Giving a recommendation with no consideration of alternatives
Concluding without giving reasons
Repeating analysis instead of evaluating

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Application means using specific facts, figures and context from the case study.
Numerical data in a stimulus is provided because it is expected to be used.
Analysis develops a point into its consequences for the specific business.
A generic answer that could apply to any business will not reach the top level.
Reading the whole case study before answering saves time overall.
A justified answer weighs at least two options against stated criteria.
Criteria for judging a marketing decision include cost, likely sales impact, risk and fit with the target market.
A conclusion should state the recommendation, the main reason, and a condition or limitation.
Evaluation considers how important a factor is, not just whether it exists.
The phrase 'it depends on' is useful only when followed by what it depends on and why.
Nine-mark answers benefit from a brief plan identifying two points and a conclusion.
Time allocation of about nine to eleven minutes suits a 9-mark question.

weeks.unit: Spring 2 assessment: marketing

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment: full marketing topic test
objectives: I can answer the full range of question types on 3.5
I can complete a marketing case study section under timed conditions
misconceptions: Poor time management across sections
Not using the stimulus material
Omitting judgements from extended answers

assessment.type: Timed assessment on 3.5

lessons.title: Assessment review and marketing consolidation
objectives: I can identify which marketing topics and skills I need to improve
I can rewrite a weak extended answer to a higher standard
misconceptions: Attributing lost marks to carelessness rather than technique
Rewriting without changing the structure of the answer
Not testing the improvement on a new question

assessment.type: Directed improvement

knowledgeComponents.statement: The marketing topic covers customers, segmentation, research and the four Ps.
Marketing content is examined on Paper 2 only, alongside finance.
Paper 2 also examines topics 3.1 and 3.2.
Calculation questions in marketing include market share, percentage change and cost-plus pricing.
Market share = (business sales / total market sales) x 100.
Time management should follow roughly one mark per minute.
Extended answers must end with an explicit judgement.
Level descriptors reward knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation in combination.
An answer can show strong knowledge and still score in the lower levels without application.
Redrafting one paragraph against the descriptor is the most efficient improvement task.
Improvement must be tested on a fresh question to confirm it has been learned.
Marking your own answer against the mark scheme reveals the gap between intention and effect.

weeks.unit: 3.6.1 Sources of finance

lessons.title: Internal and short-term sources of finance
objectives: I can describe internal sources of finance including retained profit and sale of assets
I can describe short-term external sources including overdraft and trade credit
misconceptions: Confusing an overdraft with a loan
Thinking retained profit is free money with no opportunity cost
Assuming trade credit is always available

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Long-term external sources of finance
objectives: I can describe loans, share capital, venture capital, crowdfunding and leasing
I can explain the advantages and disadvantages of each
misconceptions: Thinking share capital must be repaid like a loan
Confusing leasing with buying on hire purchase
Ignoring the loss of control when issuing shares

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Internal finance comes from within the business; external finance comes from outside it.
Retained profit is profit kept in the business rather than paid out to owners.
Retained profit is free of interest but is unavailable to new or loss-making businesses.
Sale of assets raises cash from items the business no longer needs.
An overdraft allows a business to spend more than it has in its account, up to a limit.
Overdrafts are flexible but have high interest rates and can be withdrawn at short notice.
Trade credit allows a business to buy now and pay a supplier later, typically in 30 to 90 days.
A bank loan is repaid in instalments with interest over an agreed period.
Share capital raises money by selling shares; it need not be repaid but dilutes ownership.
Venture capital provides investment plus expertise in return for a share of the business.
Crowdfunding raises small amounts from many people, often online.
Leasing rents an asset rather than buying it, spreading cost but costing more in total.
The best source depends on the amount needed, the time period, the cost and the risk to control.
Long-term assets should be funded by long-term finance, not an overdraft.

weeks.unit: 3.6.2 Cash flow

lessons.title: The importance of cash and the difference between cash and profit
objectives: I can explain why cash is essential to business survival
I can explain the difference between cash and profit
misconceptions: Believing a profitable business cannot run out of cash
Confusing cash flow with profit
Thinking a cash surplus means a profit

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Interpreting and completing cash flow forecasts
objectives: I can complete a cash flow forecast including net cash flow and closing balance
I can interpret a cash flow forecast and identify problem months
misconceptions: Adding rather than subtracting outflows
Failing to carry the closing balance forward as next month's opening balance
Confusing net cash flow with the closing balance

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data

knowledgeComponents.statement: Cash is the money a business has available to spend immediately.
Liquidity is the ability to pay debts as they fall due.
A business can be profitable and still fail if it runs out of cash.
Profit is revenue minus costs over a period; cash flow is money actually moving in and out.
Selling on credit records revenue before the cash is received.
Insolvency is being unable to pay debts when they are due.
Working capital is the cash available for day-to-day running of the business.
Net cash flow = total cash inflows - total cash outflows.
Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow.
The closing balance of one month becomes the opening balance of the next.
A negative closing balance means the business needs an overdraft or other finance.
A cash flow forecast predicts future inflows and outflows so problems can be anticipated.
Cash flow problems can be solved by delaying payments, chasing debtors, cutting costs or arranging finance.

weeks.unit: 3.6.3 Financial terms and calculations: revenue, costs and profit

lessons.title: Revenue, costs, gross profit and net profit
objectives: I can define and calculate revenue, gross profit and net profit
I can distinguish cost of sales from other expenses
misconceptions: Confusing gross profit with net profit
Including all costs in cost of sales
Forgetting to subtract expenses when calculating net profit

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data

lessons.title: Profit margins and interpreting profitability
objectives: I can calculate gross profit margin and net profit margin
I can interpret what a change in margin tells a business
misconceptions: Dividing by cost rather than revenue when calculating a margin
Confusing an increase in profit with an increase in margin
Interpreting a margin without comparing it to a previous year or a competitor

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data

knowledgeComponents.statement: Revenue = selling price x quantity sold.
Cost of sales is the direct cost of producing or buying the goods sold.
Gross profit = revenue - cost of sales.
Expenses are indirect costs such as rent, salaries, marketing and insurance.
Net profit = gross profit - expenses.
Gross profit measures how profitably a business buys and sells; net profit accounts for running costs too.
Gross profit margin = (gross profit / revenue) x 100.
Net profit margin = (net profit / revenue) x 100.
A margin shows how much of each pound of revenue is retained as profit.
A rising gross margin suggests better buying prices or higher selling prices.
A rising gross margin with a falling net margin suggests overheads have increased.
Margins should be compared over time and against competitors to be meaningful.
Margins should be given as a percentage to one or two decimal places as appropriate.

weeks.dates: Mon 3 May - Fri 7 May 2027 (bank holiday Mon 3 May)
weeks.unit: 3.6.3 Break-even analysis

lessons.title: Calculating and interpreting break-even
objectives: I can calculate the break-even level of output
I can calculate contribution per unit and margin of safety
misconceptions: Using total variable costs rather than variable cost per unit
Subtracting fixed costs from selling price
Confusing break-even output with break-even revenue

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data
commandWords: work out the margin of safety

lessons.title: Break-even charts and the limitations of break-even analysis
objectives: I can interpret a break-even chart and identify the break-even point
I can explain the limitations of break-even analysis
misconceptions: Reading the break-even point off the wrong axis
Assuming costs and prices stay constant at all output levels
Believing break-even analysis predicts actual sales

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Break-even is the level of output at which total revenue equals total costs and profit is zero.
Contribution per unit = selling price per unit - variable cost per unit.
Break-even output = fixed costs / contribution per unit.
Margin of safety = actual (or forecast) output - break-even output.
Margin of safety shows how far sales can fall before the business makes a loss.
Break-even revenue = break-even output x selling price.
Raising the selling price lowers the break-even output, if demand holds.
On a break-even chart, output is on the horizontal axis and costs and revenue on the vertical axis.
The break-even point is where the total revenue and total cost lines cross.
The area between the lines to the right of break-even is profit; to the left it is loss.
Break-even assumes all output is sold and that price and costs stay constant.
Break-even ignores bulk discounts, economies of scale and changing market conditions.
Break-even is a useful planning tool but not a prediction of actual sales.

weeks.unit: 3.6.3 Average rate of return and investment appraisal

lessons.title: Calculating average rate of return
objectives: I can calculate the average rate of return on an investment
I can interpret ARR when comparing two investment options
misconceptions: Forgetting to subtract the cost of the investment to find net return
Dividing by the number of years at the wrong stage
Comparing ARR without considering risk

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data
commandWords: calculate the average rate of return

lessons.title: Using ARR to make investment decisions
objectives: I can use ARR alongside qualitative factors to justify an investment decision
I can explain the limitations of ARR
misconceptions: Choosing the higher ARR without considering risk or timing
Ignoring non-financial factors
Not comparing ARR to the interest rate available on savings

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement
commandWords: which investment should the business choose

knowledgeComponents.statement: Average rate of return measures the annual profit from an investment as a percentage of its cost.
Total net return = total returns over the period - cost of the investment.
Average annual return = total net return / number of years.
ARR = (average annual return / cost of investment) x 100.
A higher ARR indicates a more profitable investment, all else being equal.
ARR should be compared to the interest rate available on a bank deposit.
ARR ignores the timing of returns: early returns are worth more than late ones.
ARR relies on forecasts, which may be inaccurate.
Qualitative factors include the business's objectives, staff impact, reputation and risk.
Opportunity cost is what the business gives up by choosing one investment over another.
A riskier investment may need a higher ARR to be worthwhile.
Investment decisions should combine financial calculation with business judgement.

weeks.unit: Quantitative skills consolidation

lessons.title: Consolidating business calculations
objectives: I can perform all the calculations required by the specification accurately
I can show working clearly and give answers with correct units
misconceptions: Omitting units or currency symbols
Rounding partway through a multi-step calculation
Not showing working and losing method marks

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data

lessons.title: Interpreting financial and marketing data
objectives: I can interpret tables, charts and graphs of business data
I can use data to support an analytical point
misconceptions: Describing data without interpreting what it means for the business
Misreading a chart axis or scale
Quoting data without linking it to the argument

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Required calculations include revenue, costs, profit, margins, break-even, margin of safety, ARR, cash flow and percentage change.
Method marks are available even when the final answer is wrong, provided working is shown.
Money answers should include the pound sign; percentage answers should include the percent sign.
Intermediate values should be kept unrounded until the final step.
Percentage change = (change / original) x 100.
A calculator is permitted in AQA GCSE Business exams.
Data interpretation means saying what a figure means for the business, not just restating it.
A trend should be quantified, for example 'sales rose by 12% between 2024 and 2025'.
Chart axes and scales must be checked before reading values.
Comparing data over time or against a competitor gives it meaning.
Using a figure from the stimulus is the quickest way to secure application marks.
An analytical point supported by data is stronger than an assertion.

weeks.unit: Summer 1 assessment: finance

lessons.title: Summer 1 assessment: finance topic test
objectives: I can answer the full range of finance questions accurately under timed conditions
I can complete calculations correctly under pressure
misconceptions: Calculation errors under time pressure
Not showing working
Omitting the judgement in extended answers

assessment.type: Timed assessment on 3.6

lessons.title: Finance review and error correction
objectives: I can identify and correct my recurring calculation errors
I can explain each formula rather than just recalling it
misconceptions: Memorising formulae without understanding what they measure
Repeating the same error type across questions
Not retesting after correction

assessment.type: Directed improvement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Finance content is examined on Paper 2 alongside marketing, 3.1 and 3.2.
Calculation questions typically carry 2 to 4 marks each.
Showing working protects method marks when an arithmetic slip occurs.
Extended finance questions require a judgement, not just a calculation.
A calculated figure should always be interpreted in the context of the business.
An error log records the specific type of error made, not just the question number.
Understanding what a formula measures makes it far easier to recall correctly.
Break-even, ARR and margin formulae are the most commonly confused at GCSE.
Retesting on a fresh question is the only reliable check that an error has been fixed.
Financial calculations should always be checked for plausibility against the data.
A negative net profit means the business made a loss.
Reading the units in a data table (thousands, millions) prevents order-of-magnitude errors.

weeks.unit: 3.6.4 Analysing financial performance

lessons.title: The purpose and components of financial statements
objectives: I can explain the purpose of an income statement and a statement of financial position
I can identify the main components of each
misconceptions: Confusing an income statement with a statement of financial position
Confusing assets with liabilities
Thinking financial statements only matter to accountants

assessment.type: Section B or C short answer from case study stimulus

lessons.title: Interpreting financial statements for decision making
objectives: I can interpret data from financial statements
I can explain how different stakeholders use financial statements
misconceptions: Interpreting a single year's figures without comparison
Assuming higher revenue always means better performance
Not linking the interpretation to the stakeholder's interest

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)

knowledgeComponents.statement: An income statement shows revenue, costs and profit over a period of time.
A statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and capital at a point in time.
An asset is something the business owns or is owed.
A liability is something the business owes.
Capital is the money invested in the business by its owners.
Financial statements allow performance to be measured and compared over time.
Published financial statements are a legal requirement for limited companies.
Shareholders use financial statements to judge returns and decide whether to invest.
Lenders use them to judge whether the business can repay a loan.
Employees use them to judge job security and the case for pay rises.
Suppliers use them to decide whether to offer trade credit.
A single year's figures mean little; comparison over time or with competitors is essential.
Rising revenue with falling profit indicates rising costs, not improving performance.

weeks.unit: Interrelationships between business functions

lessons.title: How marketing, finance, operations and HR interrelate
objectives: I can explain how business functions depend on one another
I can explain how objectives are broken into functional plans
misconceptions: Treating each function as separate
Not linking a marketing decision to its financial consequences
Ignoring the human resource implications of a decision

assessment.type: Analyse question (chain of reasoning from a case study)
commandWords: explain the impact on other areas

lessons.title: Whole-business decision making
objectives: I can make a recommendation that considers several functional areas
I can weigh short-term and long-term consequences
misconceptions: Recommending based on one function only
Ignoring the time horizon of the decision
Reaching a judgement with no supporting criteria

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Business functions are marketing, finance, operations (production) and human resources.
A marketing decision to cut prices affects revenue, profit margins and production volume.
A decision to expand production requires finance, recruitment and marketing support.
Business objectives are broken down into functional plans with linked targets.
Poor coordination between functions leads to stock shortages, wasted spending and missed targets.
Finance constrains what the other functions can do.
A holistic recommendation considers effects across several functions.
Short-term gains may come at long-term cost, such as cutting training to save money.
A judgement should state the criteria used, such as cost, risk and fit with objectives.
Trade-offs are unavoidable because resources are limited.
The right decision depends on the business's objectives and its circumstances.
Naming the specific consequence for the business is what earns evaluation marks.

weeks.unit: Exam technique: command words and answer structures

lessons.title: Command words and what each requires
objectives: I can identify what each command word requires
I can match answer structure to command word and tariff
misconceptions: Explaining when only stating is required
Analysing without evaluating on a justify question
Writing at length on a 1-mark question

assessment.type: Command word drill

lessons.title: Structuring analyse and justify answers
objectives: I can build a chain of reasoning in an analyse answer
I can structure a justify answer with two developed points and a conclusion
misconceptions: Producing lists rather than developed chains
Concluding without justification
Repeating analysis as the conclusion

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

knowledgeComponents.statement: 'State' or 'identify' requires a short factual answer with no explanation.
'Calculate' requires a numerical answer with working shown.
'Explain' requires a point plus a reason or consequence.
'Analyse' requires a developed chain of reasoning applied to the business.
'Justify' and 'recommend' require a supported judgement between options.
Answer length should be proportional to the mark tariff.
AO1 is knowledge, AO2 is application, AO3 is analysis, AO4 is evaluation.
A chain of reasoning links point, consequence, further consequence, impact on the business.
A 9-mark answer typically needs two developed points plus a conclusion.
A conclusion must add a judgement, not summarise what has already been said.
Useful conclusion openers state the recommendation and the main reason for it.
Adding a condition ('provided that...') strengthens a judgement.

weeks.unit: Case study practice: full Paper 2 sections

lessons.title: Timed case study practice: Section B
objectives: I can work through a full case study section under timed conditions
I can extract and use the relevant data from a stimulus
misconceptions: Reading the case study too quickly and missing key data
Answering from memory rather than from the stimulus
Running out of time on the final extended question

assessment.type: Full Paper 2 Section B

lessons.title: Timed case study practice: Section C
objectives: I can complete a second case study section without losing quality
I can maintain application throughout a full paper
misconceptions: Quality dropping in the second case study
Confusing details between the two case studies
Leaving the final 9-mark question unfinished

assessment.type: Full Paper 2 Section C

knowledgeComponents.statement: Paper 2 has three sections: A (20 marks), B (approximately 34 marks) and C (approximately 36 marks).
Each of Sections B and C is based on a separate case study with stimulus material.
Reading the whole case study before answering ensures data is not missed.
Underlining key figures in the stimulus makes them easy to retrieve while writing.
Every answer in Sections B and C should refer to the specific business.
Stimulus material often contains data specifically needed for a calculation later in the section.
Maintaining quality across two case studies requires deliberate pacing.
Details from the two case studies must not be mixed up.
The final 9-mark question in each section carries the most marks and must not be rushed.
Paper 2 lasts 1 hour 45 minutes for 90 marks.
Roughly one mark per minute leaves around 15 minutes for reading and checking.
Attempting every question is always better than perfecting some and omitting others.

weeks.unit: Revision: business in the real world and influences

lessons.title: Revision: 3.1 Business in the real world
objectives: I can recall and apply all of 3.1 confidently
I can answer 3.1 questions in both Paper 1 and Paper 2 style
misconceptions: Forgetting the detail of ownership types
Confusing economies with diseconomies of scale
Not applying to the case study

assessment.type: Justify / recommend extended response with a supported judgement

lessons.title: Revision: 3.2 Influences on business
objectives: I can recall and apply all of 3.2 confidently
I can weigh several external influences against each other
misconceptions: Getting the direction of exchange rate effects wrong
Treating influences in isolation
Not prioritising when asked which matters most

knowledgeComponents.statement: Topics 3.1 and 3.2 appear on BOTH Paper 1 and Paper 2, so they carry double weight.
Ownership types are sole trader, partnership, private limited company, public limited company and not-for-profit.
Unlimited liability applies to sole traders and ordinary partnerships; limited liability to companies.
Economies of scale reduce unit costs; diseconomies of scale increase them.
Growth can be internal (organic) or external (merger, takeover, franchising).
Location factors include market, materials, labour, competition, cost and infrastructure.
The six external influences are technology, ethics and environment, the economic climate, globalisation, legislation and competition.
SPICED: Strong Pound, Imports Cheap, Exports Dear.
Higher interest rates raise costs for borrowers and reduce consumer spending.
Influences interact and should be weighed against each other for a specific business.
Prioritising requires stating both how large and how likely each effect is.
Application to the case study is required in every answer worth more than one mark.

weeks.unit: Revision: marketing and finance

objectives: I can recall and apply the whole marketing topic confidently
I can answer questions on the integrated marketing mix
misconceptions: Confusing skimming with penetration pricing
Confusing the Boston Matrix axes
Treating the four Ps separately

objectives: I can perform every required financial calculation accurately
I can interpret financial data and make justified recommendations
misconceptions: Formula confusion under pressure
Interpreting a figure without comparison
Not showing working

assessment.type: Quantitative / calculation question from case study data

knowledgeComponents.statement: Marketing and finance are examined on Paper 2 only.
Price skimming starts high; penetration pricing starts low.
The Boston Matrix plots market share against market growth.
The product life cycle stages are development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline.
The marketing mix is price, product, promotion and place, and must be integrated.
Market share = (business sales / total market sales) x 100.
Break-even output = fixed costs / (selling price - variable cost per unit).
Margin of safety = actual output - break-even output.
Gross profit margin = (gross profit / revenue) x 100.
Net profit margin = (net profit / revenue) x 100.
ARR = (average annual return / cost of investment) x 100.
Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow.
Every calculated figure should be interpreted for the business, not left as a number.

weeks.unit: Year 10 end-of-year examination

lessons.title: Year 10 examination: full Paper 2 mock
objectives: I can complete a full AQA Paper 2 in 1 hour 45 minutes
I can demonstrate knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation across all sections
misconceptions: Poor time management across three sections
Calculation errors under pressure
Omitting judgements from 9-mark answers

assessment.type: Full Paper 2 mock examination

objectives: I can analyse my performance by assessment objective
I can plan priorities for Year 11, including the Paper 1 topics still to be taught

Assuming Paper 1 will be easier because it shares 3.1 and 3.2
Setting vague targets

Paper 2 examines 3.1, 3.2, 3.5 Marketing and 3.6 Finance.
Paper 1 examines 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 Business operations and 3.4 Human resources.

Because 3.1 and 3.2 appear on both papers, Year 11 revision of them serves both.
An AO profile shows whether marks are lost on knowledge, application, analysis or evaluation.
Most marks at GCSE Business are lost on application and evaluation, not knowledge.
Targets should name the skill and the action, such as 'end every 9-mark answer with a judgement'.
A calculator is allowed and should be used to check every calculation.

archivedSubjects.name: GCSE Design and Technology
archivedSubjects.notes: AQA GCSE Design and Technology 8552 - the specification named by the family. 8552 has NOT been reformed for 2028 exams; it remains the 2017 first-teaching specification. ASSESSMENT: one written paper (100 marks, 50%) and a non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%). The NEA weighting, mark distribution and 30-35 hour duration were verified on the AQA scheme-of-assessment page: Section A identifying and investigating design possibilities (10 marks), Section B producing a design brief and specification (10), Section C generating design ideas (20), Section D developing design ideas (20), Section E realising design ideas (20), Section F analysing and evaluating (20); a working prototype plus a concise portfolio of approximately 20 A3 pages. The written paper is 2 hours; its internal split into Section A core technical principles (20 marks), Section B specialist technical principles (30 marks) and Section C designing and making principles (50 marks) is from established practice and was NOT verified on a live page during this build. AQA's own page confirms the paper covers AO3 (10%) and AO4 (40%), and the NEA covers AO1 (20%), AO2 (30%) and AO3 (10%); at least 15% of the exam assesses mathematical skills and at least 10% assesses scientific knowledge. SPECIALIST MATERIAL AREA: 3.2 Specialist technical principles must be taught through at least ONE material category. This scheme uses TIMBERS - by far the most common school choice, the best supported by textbooks and revision material, and the most practical to resource in a home workshop or a shared workshop session. CRITICAL TIMING POINT: AQA releases the contextual challenges on 1 JUNE in the year before submission. For a summer 2028 examination that is 1 JUNE 2027 - the start of Summer 2 in Year 10. That is why this scheme deliberately front-loads all of 3.1, all of 3.2 and the designing side of 3.3 into Autumn through Summer 1, so that the NEA can begin the moment the contexts are published, at Week 34. CRITICAL WARNING FOR A HOME-EDUCATED CANDIDATE: the NEA is 50% of this qualification and must be completed under supervised conditions and marked by a registered exam centre with workshop facilities. Very few centres accept private candidates for D&T for exactly this reason. A centre MUST be secured before Year 10 begins, not during it - the centre must supervise the NEA from the June 2027 context release onwards, provide workshop access and equipment, authenticate the work, and mark it. If no centre can be found, the realistic alternatives are: (a) an online provider or FE college that runs D&T for external candidates with workshop days, or (b) switching to a 100%-examined design-related qualification. Do not defer this decision.
deferredToYear11: NEA Section E, realising design ideas (20 marks) - the entire manufacture of the prototype. Year 11 autumn and early spring. This is the conventional split because the contextual challenges are only released on 1 June of Year 10, so no more than the investigation, brief, specification, idea generation and early development can be completed before the summer holiday.

NEA Section F, analysing and evaluating (20 marks) - testing the prototype against the specification, third-party client and user evaluation, and suggested modifications. Year 11 spring, after manufacture.
Completion of NEA Section D, developing design ideas - final refinements arising from the making process. Year 11.

Specialist technical principles in a SECOND material category (e.g. polymers or metals) - optional enrichment only; the specification requires depth in one category, and Year 11 time is better spent on the NEA.
Full past-paper practice on the written paper under exam conditions - Year 11 spring, after NEA submission.
Advanced extended-response and evaluation technique for the 50-mark Section C - refined in Year 11.
Deeper study of a wider range of designers and companies from the AQA lists - Year 11 enrichment, once the NEA has established which are genuinely relevant.
Consolidation of the mathematical and scientific skill strands (15% and 10% of the paper) against past questions - Year 11.

weeks.unit: Course induction and 3.1.1 New and emerging technologies (part 1)

lessons.title: The shape of GCSE D&T: written paper, NEA and the iterative design process
objectives: I can explain how the qualification is assessed and weighted
I can describe the iterative design process
misconceptions: Thinking the NEA is coursework that can be redone indefinitely
Believing designing is linear rather than iterative
Underestimating that the written paper is 50% of the grade

assessment.type: Course overview and diagnostic

lessons.title: Industry and enterprise: how new technology changes manufacturing
objectives: I can explain how automation and CAD/CAM have changed industry
I can explain what enterprise means in a design and manufacturing context
misconceptions: Confusing CAD (design) with CAM (manufacture)
Assuming automation only reduces jobs
Confusing enterprise with entrepreneurship in general

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A (core technical principles) multiple choice / short answer

knowledgeComponents.statement: AQA GCSE D&T 8552 is assessed by one written paper (100 marks, 50%) and a non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%).
The written paper is 2 hours long.
The paper has three sections: A core technical principles, B specialist technical principles, C designing and making principles.
The NEA is a substantial design and make task of 30-35 hours producing a prototype and a portfolio of about 20 A3 pages.
AQA releases contextual challenges on 1 June in the year before submission.
The iterative design process cycles through explore, create and evaluate rather than running in a straight line.
At least 15% of the written paper assesses mathematical skills and at least 10% assesses scientific knowledge.
CAD is computer-aided design; CAM is computer-aided manufacture.
Automation uses machinery to perform tasks with little human intervention, raising consistency and speed.
Robotics allows repetitive or dangerous tasks to be performed accurately and continuously.
Automation reduces unskilled jobs but creates skilled roles in programming and maintenance.
Enterprise in design includes crowdfunding, virtual marketing and cooperative or fair trade business models.
Crowdfunding raises capital from many small investors, often before the product is manufactured.

weeks.unit: 3.1.1 New and emerging technologies (part 2)

lessons.title: Sustainability, people and the impact of technology on employment
objectives: I can explain how new technologies affect employment and communities
I can explain the sustainability implications of new technologies
misconceptions: Assuming technology change is always positive
Confusing sustainability with recycling alone
Ignoring the social cost of factory closure

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

lessons.title: Culture, society, environment and production techniques
objectives: I can explain how design must respond to different cultures and to inclusivity
I can describe modern production techniques including lean manufacturing and JIT
misconceptions: Thinking inclusive design means designing only for disabled users
Confusing lean manufacturing with cheap manufacturing
Not understanding the risk of just-in-time supply

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Planned obsolescence designs a limited life into a product, increasing waste.
Design for maintenance and repair extends product life and reduces environmental impact.
Automation and offshoring have reduced UK manufacturing employment and affected local communities.
Retraining allows workers to move into new roles created by technology.
Factory closures affect local suppliers, shops and services through a multiplier effect.
Building design and construction methods change as new materials and technologies emerge.
Inclusive design aims to make products usable by as many people as possible, regardless of age or ability.
Culture, religion and fashion all influence product form, colour, decoration and function.
Lean manufacturing minimises waste of material, time, movement and stock.
Just-in-time delivers materials only as needed, cutting storage costs but risking production stoppage.
Flexible manufacturing systems allow a production line to switch quickly between products.
Standardisation uses common components across products to reduce cost and simplify repair.
Critical evaluation of new technology weighs benefits against social, economic and environmental costs.

weeks.unit: 3.1.2 Energy generation and storage

lessons.title: Fossil fuels and nuclear power
objectives: I can explain how fossil fuels and nuclear power generate electricity
I can evaluate their advantages and disadvantages
misconceptions: Calling nuclear power renewable
Assuming nuclear power produces carbon dioxide during generation
Confusing fission with fusion

assessment.type: Scientific knowledge question within the written paper (at least 10% of the paper)

lessons.title: Renewable energy and energy storage
objectives: I can describe wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric and biomass generation
I can explain how batteries and other systems store energy
misconceptions: Thinking renewable means unlimited and free
Confusing solar thermal with photovoltaic
Assuming all batteries are rechargeable

assessment.type: Scientific knowledge question within the written paper (at least 10% of the paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas, formed over millions of years and therefore non-renewable.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, contributing to global warming.
Fossil fuel power stations heat water to drive steam turbines connected to generators.
Nuclear power uses fission of uranium to produce heat, with no carbon dioxide released during generation.
Nuclear power produces radioactive waste requiring storage for thousands of years.
Nuclear power stations have very high construction and decommissioning costs.
Wind turbines convert kinetic energy in moving air into electrical energy.
Photovoltaic cells convert light directly into electricity; solar thermal panels heat water.
Tidal and hydroelectric systems use moving water to turn turbines.
Biomass burns organic material and is considered close to carbon neutral if replanted.
Renewable sources have low running costs but are intermittent and need backup or storage.
Alkaline batteries are single-use; lithium-ion and nickel-metal hydride batteries are rechargeable.
Pumped storage uses surplus electricity to pump water uphill, releasing it to generate at peak demand.

weeks.unit: 3.1.3 Developments in new materials

lessons.title: Modern and smart materials
objectives: I can define modern materials and give examples with their uses
I can define smart materials and explain how they respond to a stimulus
misconceptions: Confusing modern materials with smart materials
Thinking smart materials change permanently rather than reversibly
Not knowing a specific application for each material

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A (core technical principles) multiple choice / short answer

lessons.title: Composite materials and technical textiles
objectives: I can explain how composite materials combine properties
I can describe technical textiles and their applications
misconceptions: Thinking a composite is simply a mixture
Confusing a technical textile with a smart material
Not linking the property of a composite to its application

assessment.type: Scientific knowledge question within the written paper (at least 10% of the paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Modern materials are developed through the invention of new or improved processes.
Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, extremely strong, light and electrically conductive.
Metal foams are light, strong and absorb impact energy, used in crash protection.
Titanium is strong, light and corrosion resistant, used in aerospace and medical implants.
Smart materials change one or more properties in response to an external stimulus and usually return to their original state.
Shape memory alloys such as nitinol return to a remembered shape when heated.
Thermochromic pigments change colour with temperature; photochromic pigments change with light.
A composite combines two or more materials to gain properties neither has alone.
Glass reinforced plastic (GRP) combines glass fibres with a polymer resin matrix.
Carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) is stronger and lighter than GRP but much more expensive.
Plywood is a composite of thin timber veneers glued with alternating grain direction.
Technical textiles are engineered for a specific function rather than for appearance.
Kevlar is used in body armour; Gore-Tex is breathable and waterproof; conductive fabrics carry current.

weeks.unit: 3.1.4 Systems approach to designing

lessons.title: Inputs, processes and outputs
objectives: I can describe a system in terms of input, process and output
I can identify input devices and the signals they produce
misconceptions: Confusing an input device with an output device
Drawing a system diagram without arrows showing flow
Thinking a process must be electronic

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A (core technical principles) multiple choice / short answer

lessons.title: Process and output devices, and feedback
objectives: I can describe process devices including microcontrollers and counters
I can identify output devices and explain the role of feedback
misconceptions: Confusing a microcontroller with a computer
Forgetting feedback in a closed-loop system
Mixing up a solenoid and a motor

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A (core technical principles) multiple choice / short answer

knowledgeComponents.statement: A system takes an input, applies a process, and produces an output.
Input devices detect a change and send a signal into the system.
A light dependent resistor (LDR) changes resistance with light level.
A thermistor changes resistance with temperature.
Switches, including push-to-make and toggle switches, are simple input devices.
A block diagram shows a system as labelled boxes joined by arrows showing signal flow.
A microcontroller is a programmable integrated circuit that carries out the process stage.
Counters and timers are process devices that respond to a number of events or a period of time.
Output devices convert the processed signal into a useful effect.
LEDs give light output, buzzers give sound, motors give rotary motion and solenoids give linear motion.
Feedback returns information about the output back to the input, allowing the system to self-correct.
A closed-loop system uses feedback; an open-loop system does not.
A thermostat is a closed-loop system: it senses temperature and adjusts heating accordingly.

weeks.unit: 3.1.5 Mechanical devices

lessons.title: Types of motion and mechanisms that change motion
objectives: I can identify linear, rotary, reciprocating and oscillating motion
I can describe mechanisms that convert one type of motion into another
misconceptions: Confusing reciprocating with oscillating motion
Not stating both the input and output motion of a mechanism
Assuming all cams produce the same follower movement

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A (core technical principles) multiple choice / short answer

lessons.title: Levers, linkages and gears: changing force and direction
objectives: I can identify first, second and third class levers and calculate mechanical advantage
I can calculate gear ratios and velocity ratios
misconceptions: Confusing the classes of lever
Inverting the gear ratio calculation
Forgetting that an idler gear changes direction but not ratio

assessment.type: Mathematical skills question within the written paper (at least 15% of the paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Linear motion moves in a straight line in one direction.
Rotary motion moves in a circle around a fixed point.
Reciprocating motion moves backwards and forwards in a straight line.
Oscillating motion swings backwards and forwards along a curved path.
A cam and follower converts rotary motion into reciprocating motion.
A crank and slider converts rotary motion into reciprocating motion, as in an engine.
A rack and pinion converts rotary motion into linear motion.
A pear cam gives a long dwell and short rise and fall; a snail cam rises gradually and falls suddenly.
In a first class lever the fulcrum is between the effort and the load, as in a pair of scissors.
In a second class lever the load is between the fulcrum and the effort, as in a wheelbarrow.
In a third class lever the effort is between the fulcrum and the load, as in tweezers.
Mechanical advantage = load / effort.
Moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot; a lever balances when clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal.
Gear ratio = number of teeth on the driven gear / number of teeth on the driver gear.
An idler gear reverses the direction of rotation without changing the gear ratio.

weeks.unit: 3.1.6.1 Material categories

lessons.title: Papers, boards, timbers and metals
objectives: I can name and describe common papers, boards and timbers
I can classify metals as ferrous, non-ferrous or alloys
misconceptions: Assuming hardwood is always harder than softwood
Thinking all metals containing iron are pure iron
Confusing MDF with plywood

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A (core technical principles) multiple choice / short answer

lessons.title: Polymers and textiles
objectives: I can distinguish thermoforming from thermosetting polymers
I can classify fibres as natural, synthetic or blended
misconceptions: Thinking thermosetting polymers can be remelted
Confusing a fibre with a fabric
Assuming all synthetic fibres are the same

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A (core technical principles) multiple choice / short answer

knowledgeComponents.statement: Cartridge paper is used for drawing; layout paper is thin and translucent for tracing.
Corrugated card is light and strong because of its fluted middle layer.
Foam board is light and rigid, used for modelling and display.
Hardwoods come from deciduous, broad-leaved trees and grow slowly; examples are oak, ash, beech and mahogany.
Softwoods come from coniferous trees and grow quickly; examples are pine, spruce and larch.
Balsa is a hardwood despite being very soft, showing the classification is botanical not physical.
Manufactured boards include MDF, plywood and chipboard, made from timber particles, fibres or veneers.
Ferrous metals contain iron and will rust; examples are mild steel, cast iron and high carbon steel.
Non-ferrous metals contain no iron; examples are aluminium, copper, zinc and tin.
Alloys are mixtures of metals, or metal and another element, such as brass, stainless steel and pewter.
Thermoforming polymers such as acrylic, HIPS and polypropylene can be reheated and reshaped.
Thermosetting polymers such as urea formaldehyde and epoxy resin set permanently and cannot be remelted.
Natural fibres include cotton, wool and silk; synthetic fibres include polyester, nylon and elastane.
Blended fibres combine properties, such as polycotton for strength and comfort.
Woven fabrics are made from interlaced yarns; non-woven fabrics are bonded or felted.

weeks.unit: 3.1.6.2 Material properties and Autumn 1 assessment

lessons.title: Physical and working properties of materials
objectives: I can define the physical properties of materials
I can define and apply the working properties of materials
misconceptions: Confusing strength with hardness
Confusing malleability (rolling/hammering) with ductility (drawing into wire)
Confusing toughness with brittleness

assessment.type: Scientific knowledge question within the written paper (at least 10% of the paper)

lessons.title: Autumn 1 assessment: core technical principles
objectives: I can answer Section A style questions across the whole of 3.1
I can select the right material property for a given application
misconceptions: Naming a property without justifying its suitability
Guessing on multiple choice without eliminating options
Not reading the context of the question

assessment.type: Timed Section A style assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: Absorbency is the ability of a material to soak up liquid.
Density is mass per unit volume, and determines how heavy a material feels for its size.
Fusibility is the ability of a material to be melted and joined.
Electrical conductivity is the ability to allow electricity to pass through.
Thermal conductivity is the ability to allow heat to pass through.
Strength is the ability to resist a force without breaking; it may be tensile, compressive or shear.
Hardness is the ability to resist scratching, abrasion and wear.
Toughness is the ability to absorb impact without fracturing.
Brittleness is the opposite of toughness: the material fractures without deforming.
Malleability is the ability to be permanently deformed by hammering or rolling without cracking.
Ductility is the ability to be drawn or stretched into a wire.
Elasticity is the ability to return to its original shape after a force is removed.
Material selection questions must justify the choice by naming a property and linking it to the application.

weeks.unit: 3.2.1 Selection of materials or components

lessons.title: Factors influencing material selection
objectives: I can explain how functionality, aesthetics and cost affect material choice
I can explain how availability and environmental factors affect selection
misconceptions: Selecting a material on cost alone
Confusing aesthetics with function
Ignoring the ethical source of a material

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

lessons.title: Ethical sourcing and material selection in practice
objectives: I can explain what ethical sourcing means for timber and other materials
I can justify a material choice for a given product
misconceptions: Assuming any timber is sustainable if it is replanted
Justifying without reference to the product's function or user
Not knowing what FSC certification guarantees

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Functionality means the material must perform the job the product requires.
Aesthetics covers appearance, texture, colour and form.
Cost includes the raw material price, processing cost and waste.
Availability affects lead times and whether a material can be sourced reliably at scale.
Environmental factors include the energy used in extraction, transport miles and end-of-life disposal.
Social and cultural factors influence colour, decoration and acceptable materials in different markets.
Material selection is always a compromise between competing factors.
Ethical sourcing ensures materials are obtained without exploiting workers or damaging communities.
FSC certification guarantees timber comes from responsibly managed forests.
Fair trade guarantees producers a minimum price and better working conditions.
Supply chain transparency allows a company to verify how its materials were produced.
A justified material choice names the material, names a property and links it to the product's requirement.

weeks.unit: 3.2.2 Forces and stresses

lessons.title: Tension, compression, bending, torsion and shear
objectives: I can identify the forces acting on a product
I can explain how each force affects a material
misconceptions: Confusing shear with tension
Thinking bending is a separate force rather than a combination
Not identifying where in a product the force acts

assessment.type: Scientific knowledge question within the written paper (at least 10% of the paper)

lessons.title: Reinforcing and stiffening materials
objectives: I can explain how lamination, bending, folding, webbing and interfacing strengthen materials
I can apply a reinforcement method to a design problem
misconceptions: Thinking reinforcement always means adding more material
Confusing lamination with veneering
Not explaining why a folded section is stiffer

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Tension is a pulling force that stretches a material.
Compression is a pushing force that squashes a material.
Bending combines tension on one face and compression on the other.
Torsion is a twisting force.
Shear is a sliding force acting in opposite directions across a material, as in a rivet or a pair of scissors.
Stress is force per unit area; a material fails when stress exceeds its strength.
Identifying where forces act determines where a product must be reinforced.
Lamination bonds thin layers together, often with grain in alternating directions, to increase strength and stiffness.
Bending or folding a flat sheet increases its stiffness by increasing the depth of the section.
Corrugation is repeated folding that dramatically stiffens a thin sheet.
Webbing adds a strong band of material to spread and carry a load.
Fabric interfacing is bonded to a textile to stiffen collars, cuffs and waistbands.
A gusset is a triangular reinforcement fitted into a corner to resist racking.

weeks.unit: 3.2.3 Ecological and social footprint

lessons.title: Ecological issues in the use of materials
objectives: I can explain the environmental impact of deforestation, mining, drilling and farming
I can explain product miles and carbon production
misconceptions: Thinking environmental impact begins only at manufacture
Ignoring transport and disposal in a life cycle assessment
Confusing carbon footprint with product miles

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

lessons.title: The six Rs and social issues in manufacture
objectives: I can apply the six Rs to a product
I can explain the social responsibilities of manufacturers
misconceptions: Listing the six Rs without applying them to a product
Confusing reuse with recycle
Assuming recycling is the best of the six Rs

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Deforestation destroys habitats, reduces carbon absorption and causes soil erosion.
Mining and drilling cause landscape damage, pollution and habitat destruction.
Product miles measure the distance materials and products travel from source to consumer.
A carbon footprint measures the total greenhouse gas emissions caused by a product.
A life cycle assessment considers extraction, processing, manufacture, distribution, use and disposal.
Intensive farming of natural fibres such as cotton uses large volumes of water and pesticides.
Reduce means using less material or energy in the first place.
Refuse means not using a material or product that is unnecessary or harmful.
Reuse means using a product again, either for the same or a different purpose.
Repair means fixing a product rather than replacing it.
Recycle means reprocessing a material into a new product, which uses energy.
Rethink means reconsidering the whole design approach to the problem.
Reduce and refuse are more effective than recycling because they prevent impact rather than mitigating it.
Social responsibility includes safe working conditions, fair pay and minimising pollution affecting communities.

weeks.unit: 3.2.4 Sources and origins: timbers

lessons.title: The source and conversion of timber
objectives: I can describe how timber is grown, felled, converted and seasoned
I can explain the difference between through-and-through and quarter sawing
misconceptions: Thinking timber is ready to use immediately after felling
Confusing conversion (sawing) with seasoning (drying)
Not knowing why quarter sawing reduces warping

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

lessons.title: Sources and origins of other material categories
objectives: I can outline the source and conversion of paper, metals, polymers and textiles
I can compare the environmental cost of different material sources
misconceptions: Thinking polymers come from plants rather than crude oil
Confusing an ore with a pure metal
Not knowing that paper is made from wood pulp

assessment.type: Scientific knowledge question within the written paper (at least 10% of the paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Timber is felled, converted into planks and then seasoned before use.
Conversion is the sawing of a log into usable boards.
Through-and-through (slab) sawing is quick and cheap but produces boards prone to warping.
Quarter sawing cuts radially, giving more stable boards and an attractive figure, but wastes more timber.
Seasoning reduces the moisture content of timber to prevent shrinkage and warping in use.
Air seasoning is slow and cheap; kiln seasoning is fast, controlled and kills insects but uses energy.
Unseasoned timber will shrink, twist, split and be difficult to finish.
Paper and board are made from wood pulp, which may be mechanical or chemical pulp.
Metals are extracted from ores by processes such as smelting in a blast furnace or electrolysis.
Polymers are made from crude oil, separated by fractional distillation and joined by polymerisation.
Natural textile fibres come from plants (cotton, linen) or animals (wool, silk).
Synthetic textile fibres such as polyester and nylon are polymers made from crude oil.
Extraction and primary processing usually account for the largest part of a material's environmental impact.

weeks.unit: 3.2.5 Using and working with materials: timbers (part 1)

lessons.title: Properties of timbers and their commercial applications
objectives: I can state the working properties of common hardwoods, softwoods and manufactured boards
I can justify a timber choice for a given product
misconceptions: Choosing a timber without reference to its properties
Assuming MDF is suitable for outdoor use
Not considering cost and availability

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

lessons.title: Modifying the properties of timber
objectives: I can explain how timber properties are modified by lamination, seasoning and treatment
I can explain the purpose of preservatives and stains
misconceptions: Confusing a preservative with a decorative finish
Thinking staining protects timber
Not understanding why laminated timber is stronger

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Oak is hard, tough, durable and attractive, used for furniture and flooring, but expensive and it corrodes steel fixings.
Ash is tough and flexible, used for tool handles and sports equipment.
Beech is hard, close-grained and takes a good finish, used for furniture and toys, but prone to warping.
Mahogany is durable, easy to work and attractive, but sustainability is a serious concern.
Pine is cheap, light, easy to work and widely available, but knotty and less durable.
MDF has a smooth uniform surface ideal for painting and machining, but is heavy and swells with moisture.
Plywood is strong in all directions because its veneer layers alternate grain direction.
Chipboard is cheap and stable but weak and easily damaged by moisture unless faced.
Lamination bonds thin layers of timber to create strong curved components.
Steam bending softens the timber fibres so a solid section can be bent around a former.
Preservatives such as tanalith are pressure-impregnated to resist rot and insect attack.
Stains change colour but give no protection; a varnish or oil is needed for protection.
Veneers are thin slices of attractive timber applied over a cheaper base such as MDF.

weeks.unit: 3.2.6 Stock forms, types and sizes; 3.2.7 Scales of production

lessons.title: Stock forms and standard components for timber
objectives: I can describe the standard stock forms and sizes timber is supplied in
I can identify standard components used with timber
misconceptions: Confusing nominal and finished sizes
Not knowing standard sheet sizes
Thinking standard components must be made rather than bought

assessment.type: Mathematical skills question within the written paper (at least 15% of the paper)

lessons.title: Scales of production
objectives: I can describe prototype, batch, mass and continuous production
I can select and justify a scale of production for a product
misconceptions: Confusing batch with mass production
Assuming mass production is always cheapest overall
Not linking scale of production to demand

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Timber stock forms include planks, boards, strips, dowels, mouldings and sheet materials.
Rough sawn timber is supplied at its nominal size straight from the saw.
PAR means planed all round; PSE means planed square edge.
Planing reduces timber below its nominal size, so a nominal 50 x 25 mm may finish at about 47 x 22 mm.
Standard sheet sizes for manufactured boards are commonly 2440 x 1220 mm.
Standard components are bought-in parts such as screws, nails, hinges, dowels and knock-down fittings.
Using standard components reduces cost, time and the need for specialist manufacture.
Prototype or one-off production makes a single item, is labour intensive and has a high unit cost.
Batch production makes a specific quantity, using jigs and templates to speed repetition.
Mass production makes large quantities on a production line, giving a low unit cost but high tooling cost.
Continuous production runs 24 hours a day for products in constant demand, such as glass or chemicals.
Higher volumes reduce unit cost because fixed tooling costs are spread over more units.
The scale of production must match forecast demand; over-production wastes materials and capital.

weeks.unit: 3.2.8 Specialist techniques and processes; Autumn 2 assessment

lessons.title: Production aids: jigs, templates, patterns and moulds
objectives: I can explain how jigs, templates and patterns speed production and improve accuracy
I can explain the use of tolerances and quality control
misconceptions: Confusing a jig with a template
Confusing quality control with quality assurance
Thinking tolerances mean inaccuracy

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

lessons.title: Autumn 2 assessment: specialist technical principles
objectives: I can answer Section B style questions on materials, forces, footprint and production
I can write an extended response justifying a design or manufacturing decision
misconceptions: Describing when justification is required
Not using technical vocabulary
Leaving extended questions unfinished

assessment.type: Timed Section B style assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: A jig holds a workpiece and guides a tool, ensuring repeatable accuracy.
A template is a shaped pattern drawn around or cut to, used to repeat a shape.
A former or mould shapes material into a required profile, as in laminating or vacuum forming.
Production aids reduce time, reduce skill required and improve consistency in batch production.
A tolerance is the permitted range of variation in a dimension, written as for example 50 mm +/- 0.5 mm.
Tolerances make manufacture possible because no process is perfectly accurate.
Quality control inspects products during and after manufacture to identify faults.
Quality assurance builds quality into the whole process so faults are prevented rather than detected.
A go/no-go gauge quickly checks whether a dimension falls within tolerance.
An extended response should name the technique, explain how it works and evaluate its benefit.
Technical vocabulary is explicitly credited in D&T extended responses.
Section B is worth 30 marks of the 100-mark written paper.

weeks.unit: 3.2.9 Surface treatments and finishes

lessons.title: Preparing and finishing timber
objectives: I can describe how to prepare a timber surface for finishing
I can select and justify a finish for a given product and environment
misconceptions: Applying a finish without preparing the surface
Using an interior finish on an exterior product
Confusing a stain with a protective finish

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

lessons.title: Finishes for other material categories
objectives: I can name appropriate finishes for metals, polymers and textiles
I can explain the functional and aesthetic purposes of a finish
misconceptions: Thinking polymers always need a finish
Confusing galvanising with painting
Not distinguishing functional from aesthetic purposes

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section B (specialist technical principles) short answer and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Timber must be sanded progressively through finer grits before finishing.
A lower grit number means a coarser abrasive.
Sanding sealer fills the grain and provides a smooth base for varnish or wax.
Varnish and polyurethane give a hard-wearing protective film; exterior grades resist UV and moisture.
Danish oil penetrates the timber, is easily repaired and gives a natural appearance.
Wax gives a soft sheen but little protection against moisture.
Paint requires a primer and undercoat and obscures the grain.
Finishes protect against moisture, wear, UV and insect attack as well as improving appearance.
Galvanising coats steel with zinc to prevent rusting.
Powder coating applies electrostatically charged powder that is then baked on, giving a tough coloured finish.
Anodising thickens the natural oxide layer on aluminium and allows it to be dyed.
Dip coating covers metal in a plastic layer for grip, insulation and corrosion resistance.
Most polymers are self-finishing and are coloured during manufacture.
Textiles are finished by dyeing, printing, and treatments such as waterproofing or flame retardancy.

weeks.unit: 3.3.1 Investigation, primary and secondary data

lessons.title: Investigating client and user needs
objectives: I can gather primary and secondary data about a client and user
I can identify a genuine problem or need from investigation
misconceptions: Inventing a client rather than working with a real one
Collecting data that is never used to inform the design
Confusing primary with secondary data

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Writing a design brief and a design and manufacturing specification
objectives: I can write a clear design brief from an investigation
I can write a measurable design specification with justified points
misconceptions: Writing vague specification points such as 'it must look nice'
Writing a specification with no justification for each point
Confusing the brief (the task) with the specification (the criteria)

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Primary data is collected first-hand: interviews, questionnaires, observation and product testing.
Secondary data is collected by others: existing product analysis, standards, books and websites.
A client commissions the design; the user is the person who uses the product.
The client and the user may be different people, and both may need investigating.
Anthropometrics is the study of human body measurements used to size products.
Ergonomics is the design of products for comfortable and efficient human use.
Investigation must lead to an identified problem or need that the design will solve.
A design brief is a short statement of what is to be designed, for whom and why.
A design specification lists the measurable criteria the product must meet.
Every specification point should be justified by reference to research evidence.
Measurable criteria can be tested; 'must be lightweight' becomes 'must weigh under 500 g'.
ACCESS FM (aesthetics, cost, customer, environment, size, safety, function, materials) is a useful specification framework.
A manufacturing specification adds the details a manufacturer needs: dimensions, tolerances, materials and processes.

weeks.unit: 3.3.2 Environmental, social and economic challenge; 3.3.3 The work of others

lessons.title: Designing for environmental, social and economic challenge
objectives: I can explain how sustainability influences design decisions
I can apply life cycle thinking to my own design work
misconceptions: Adding a sustainability paragraph without changing any design decision
Assuming a natural material is automatically sustainable
Ignoring the use and disposal phases

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section C (designing and making principles) short answer, design and extended response

lessons.title: The work of others: designers and companies
objectives: I can analyse the work of designers and companies from the AQA lists
I can use their work to inform my own designing
misconceptions: Copying a designer's product rather than learning from their approach
Writing a biography instead of analysing the design
Choosing a designer irrelevant to the project

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section C (designing and making principles) short answer, design and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Sustainable design considers the whole life cycle: materials, manufacture, use and disposal.
Design for disassembly allows a product to be taken apart for repair and recycling.
A circular economy keeps materials in use rather than discarding them after one life.
Choosing FSC-certified timber addresses deforestation within a design decision.
Reducing the number of different materials in a product makes recycling easier.
Fair trade addresses the social and economic conditions of the people producing materials.
Sustainability must change actual design decisions to be credited in the NEA.
AQA requires students to investigate at least two designers and two companies from its specified lists.
Analysing the work of others should identify the design approach, materials, form and user focus.
Design movements such as the Bauhaus, Art Deco and Memphis have recognisable characteristics.
Bauhaus design emphasised function, simple geometric form and the honest use of materials.
Learning from others means adopting a principle or technique, not copying a product.
Company analysis should consider brand identity, target market and manufacturing approach.

weeks.unit: 3.3.4 Design strategies
