lessons.title: Generating imaginative design ideas
objectives: I can use collaboration, user-centred design and systems thinking to generate ideas
I can avoid design fixation and generate genuinely different ideas
misconceptions: Producing several ideas that are all variations of the first
Selecting an idea before exploring alternatives
Not involving the user in generating ideas

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section C (designing and making principles) short answer, design and extended response

lessons.title: Exploring and developing ideas iteratively
objectives: I can develop an idea through repeated cycles of modelling and evaluation
I can record my design decisions and justify them
misconceptions: Presenting a single idea with no development
Making changes without recording why
Treating evaluation as a final step rather than a continuous one

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)
assessment.tariff: Section C: 20 marks; Section D: 20 marks

knowledgeComponents.statement: Design fixation is becoming stuck on one idea and failing to explore alternatives.
Strategies to avoid fixation include working collaboratively, using unrelated stimulus and deliberately changing constraints.
User-centred design keeps the user's needs at the centre of every decision, testing with them throughout.
Collaboration brings different perspectives and generates a wider range of ideas.
Systems thinking designs a product as a set of connected inputs, processes and outputs.
Ideas should be genuinely different in form, mechanism or approach, not just decoration.
Iteration means repeatedly exploring, creating and evaluating rather than working in a straight line.
Development improves an idea against the specification through modelling and testing.
Every design decision should be recorded with the reason for it.
Annotation on a sketch should explain materials, dimensions, function and the reason for a feature.
Evaluation happens continuously throughout the iterative process, not only at the end.
NEA Section C (generating ideas) and Section D (developing ideas) are worth 20 marks each.

weeks.unit: 3.3.5 Communication of design ideas: 2D and 3D drawing

lessons.title: Freehand sketching, isometric and perspective drawing
objectives: I can produce clear freehand sketches with correct proportion
I can draw in isometric and one- and two-point perspective
misconceptions: Drawing isometric with vertical lines sloping
Placing vanishing points inconsistently
Sketching without construction lines or crating

assessment.type: Design communication task (sketching, annotation, modelling)

lessons.title: Rendering, annotation and enhancing drawings
objectives: I can render a drawing to show material, form and texture
I can annotate a design to communicate materials, dimensions and function
misconceptions: Rendering without a consistent light source
Annotating with obvious statements rather than design reasoning
Rendering neatly but with poor underlying proportion

assessment.type: Design communication task (sketching, annotation, modelling)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Isometric drawing uses vertical lines and lines at 30 degrees to the horizontal.
Isometric drawings keep dimensions to scale along the three axes but look slightly distorted.
One-point perspective uses a single vanishing point on the horizon line.
Two-point perspective uses two vanishing points and gives a more realistic view.
Perspective drawings look realistic but cannot be measured from directly.
Crating sketches a simple box first and then develops the form within it.
Construction lines should be light and are kept, not erased, in design sketching.
Rendering uses tone, shadow and highlight to suggest three-dimensional form.
A single consistent light source must be assumed when rendering.
Texture is suggested by mark-making appropriate to the material, such as grain lines for timber.
Thick and thin line technique uses thicker outlines to make a drawing read clearly.
Good annotation explains materials, sizes, functions and reasons, not just names parts.
A drawing communicates a design only if another person could understand it without explanation.

weeks.unit: 3.3.5 Communication: technical drawing and digital tools; Spring 1 assessment

lessons.title: Orthographic projection, working drawings and exploded views
objectives: I can produce a third angle orthographic projection with correct conventions
I can draw an exploded view and a sectional view
misconceptions: Placing views in the wrong positions for third angle projection
Omitting dimensions, scale or the projection symbol
Using the wrong line type for hidden detail and centre lines

assessment.type: Mathematical skills question within the written paper (at least 15% of the paper)

lessons.title: Digital design tools and Spring 1 assessment
objectives: I can explain the advantages of CAD and digital modelling
I can produce a technical drawing to specification under timed conditions
misconceptions: Assuming CAD replaces the need for sketching
Omitting the scale from a technical drawing
Rushing and losing accuracy

assessment.type: Timed technical drawing and communication assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: Orthographic projection shows a product as separate 2D views: front elevation, plan and end elevation.
British Standards use third angle projection, indicated by its own symbol on the drawing.
In third angle projection the plan view is placed above the front elevation.
Hidden detail is shown as a dashed line.
Centre lines are drawn as long-short-long chain lines.
Dimension lines have arrowheads at each end and the dimension written above the line.
All dimensions on a drawing are given in millimetres, without units written each time.
A scale such as 1:2 means the drawing is half the size of the real object.
An exploded view shows how the parts of an assembly fit together.
A sectional view shows a cut-through, with the cut surface hatched at 45 degrees.
CAD allows fast modification, accurate dimensioning, testing and direct export to CAM.
Digital modelling can test a design virtually before any material is used.
Sketching remains faster than CAD for early idea generation.

weeks.unit: 3.3.6 Prototype development and modelling

lessons.title: Modelling to develop and test ideas
objectives: I can produce card, foam and sketch models to test a design
I can evaluate a model against the specification
misconceptions: Making a model that looks good but tests nothing
Not evaluating the model against the specification
Confusing a model with a finished prototype

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Evaluating fitness for purpose with client and user feedback
objectives: I can gather and act on user feedback during development
I can evaluate whether a prototype meets client wants and needs
misconceptions: Collecting feedback and then ignoring it
Asking leading questions that produce only positive feedback
Confusing your own opinion with user feedback

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A model is a physical representation used to test an aspect of a design.
A mock-up is a rough model testing size, proportion or ergonomics.
A prototype is a working version of the final product.
Card modelling is fast and cheap for testing form, proportion and assembly.
Foam modelling suits testing three-dimensional form and grip.
A scale model tests proportion when a full-size model is impractical.
Every model should be made to answer a specific question about the design.
Fitness for purpose means the product does the job it was designed to do for its intended user.
Third-party feedback from the client or user is required in the NEA and must be acted upon.
Objective testing measures against a criterion; subjective testing gathers opinion.
Leading questions produce unreliable feedback and should be avoided.
Evidence of acting on feedback is what earns marks, not the feedback itself.
NEA Section F, analysing and evaluating, is worth 20 marks.

weeks.unit: 3.3.7 Selection of materials and components; 3.3.8 Tolerances

lessons.title: Selecting materials and components for a prototype
objectives: I can select materials for my prototype based on functional need, cost and availability
I can justify each material and component choice
misconceptions: Selecting a material because it is available rather than suitable
Not costing the materials
Failing to justify each choice against the specification

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Working accurately using tolerances
objectives: I can apply appropriate tolerances to my own manufacturing
I can explain why tolerances are needed in industrial manufacture
misconceptions: Thinking a tolerance means an allowance for carelessness
Setting tolerances too tight to be achievable
Not considering how tolerances affect assembly

assessment.type: Mathematical skills question within the written paper (at least 15% of the paper)
commandWords: calculate the upper and lower limits

knowledgeComponents.statement: Material selection for a prototype must balance functional need, cost, availability and workability.
A cutting list records every component with its material, dimensions and quantity.
Costing the materials shows whether the product could be made economically.
Standard components should be used wherever possible to save time and cost.
Each material choice should be justified against a specification point.
Availability affects lead time and may force a design change.
A tolerance is the permitted variation from a nominal size.
A dimension of 40 mm +/- 0.5 mm has an upper limit of 40.5 mm and a lower limit of 39.5 mm.
Tolerances exist because no manufacturing process is perfectly accurate.
Tighter tolerances cost more because they need better equipment and more inspection.
Tolerances allow interchangeable parts, which is essential for mass production and repair.
Tolerances on a joint must allow the parts to fit together as intended.

weeks.unit: 3.3.9 Material management and 3.3.10 Specialist tools and equipment

lessons.title: Marking out, measuring and minimising waste
objectives: I can mark out accurately using appropriate tools and datum surfaces
I can plan a cutting list that minimises waste
misconceptions: Measuring from a different edge each time instead of a datum
Marking out with a pencil where a marking knife is needed
Not planning cuts to minimise offcuts

assessment.type: Mathematical skills question within the written paper (at least 15% of the paper)
commandWords: work out the percentage of waste

lessons.title: Selecting and using specialist tools and equipment safely
objectives: I can select the correct hand tools and machinery for a task
I can work safely, following risk assessments and using guards and PPE
misconceptions: Choosing a tool by familiarity rather than suitability
Assuming PPE alone makes a process safe
Not checking machine guards before use

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section C (designing and making principles) short answer, design and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: A datum is a fixed edge or surface from which all measurements are taken.
Using a single datum prevents cumulative measuring errors.
A try square marks and checks lines at 90 degrees to an edge.
A marking gauge scribes a line parallel to an edge.
A marking knife gives a finer, more accurate line than a pencil and severs the surface fibres.
A vernier caliper measures internal, external and depth dimensions to 0.1 mm or better.
Nesting arranges components on a sheet to minimise waste material.
Percentage waste = (waste area / total sheet area) x 100.
A tenon saw cuts straight lines in timber; a coping saw cuts curves.
A chisel pares and cuts waste from joints and must always be used with hands behind the cutting edge.
A pillar drill must have the workpiece clamped and the guard in place before use.
A laser cutter cuts and engraves accurately from a CAD file but cannot cut all materials safely.
A risk assessment identifies the hazard, who might be harmed and the control measure.
PPE is the last line of defence; safe working practice and guarding come first.

weeks.unit: 3.3.11 Specialist techniques and processes: timber joints and construction

lessons.title: Timber joints: selection and manufacture
objectives: I can identify and select appropriate timber joints
I can explain why a particular joint suits a particular application
misconceptions: Selecting a joint for appearance rather than for the forces acting on it
Thinking a butt joint is adequate for a load-bearing frame
Not considering the glue area of a joint

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section C (designing and making principles) short answer, design and extended response

lessons.title: Assembly, adhesives and knock-down fittings
objectives: I can select an appropriate adhesive for a material and situation
I can explain the use of knock-down fittings in flat-pack furniture
misconceptions: Using PVA where a waterproof adhesive is required
Not cramping a joint while the adhesive cures
Confusing a permanent fixing with a knock-down fitting

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section C (designing and making principles) short answer, design and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: A butt joint is the simplest and weakest joint, with a small gluing area.
A lap joint increases the gluing area and resists racking better than a butt joint.
A housing joint supports a shelf by seating it in a groove across a board.
A mortise and tenon joint is strong in a frame and resists twisting.
A dovetail joint resists being pulled apart in one direction and is used in drawer construction.
A dowel joint uses wooden pegs to locate and strengthen a butt joint.
A mitre joint gives a neat 45 degree corner with no end grain showing but is weak without reinforcement.
Joint strength depends largely on gluing area and on mechanical interlock.
PVA is a general purpose wood adhesive; exterior grades are water resistant.
Contact adhesive bonds on contact and is used for laminates and veneers.
Epoxy resin is a two-part adhesive that bonds dissimilar materials strongly.
Joints must be cramped while the adhesive cures to ensure full contact.
Knock-down fittings such as cam locks allow flat-pack furniture to be assembled and disassembled by the user.
Flat-pack construction reduces transport volume and cost.

weeks.unit: Focused practical tasks and Spring 2 assessment

lessons.title: Focused practical task: making a timber joint sample board
objectives: I can manufacture accurate timber joints to a tolerance
I can evaluate the accuracy and quality of my own work
misconceptions: Working quickly at the expense of accuracy
Not checking against the marking-out lines
Evaluating only the appearance and not the accuracy

assessment.type: Practical skills assessment

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment: designing and making principles
objectives: I can answer Section C style questions on designing and making
I can complete a design question with annotated sketches
misconceptions: Producing a sketch with no annotation
Not answering the design question against the given specification
Leaving the extended response unfinished

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section C (designing and making principles) short answer, design and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: Accuracy in practical work is judged against the marking-out lines and the stated tolerance.
Cutting on the waste side of a marked line leaves material to be trimmed to size.
A joint should be checked dry before glue is applied.
Quality of finish includes squareness, flushness of joints and surface preparation.
Honest self-evaluation identifies what would be done differently next time.
Practical skill directly affects NEA Section E, realising design ideas, worth 20 marks.
Paper 1 Section C is worth 50 marks, half the written paper.
Section C includes a design question requiring annotated sketches.
A design answer must respond to the specification given in the question.
Annotation on an exam design question carries a significant share of the marks.
Sketches in an exam should be quick, clear and proportioned, not highly rendered.
Extended responses in Section C should use technical vocabulary and reach a judgement.

weeks.unit: Mathematical skills in Design and Technology

lessons.title: Calculation of areas, volumes, materials and costs
objectives: I can calculate areas and volumes of components
I can calculate material quantities, waste and costs
lessons.specRef: AQA 8552 mathematical skills (at least 15% of the paper)
misconceptions: Mixing units within a calculation
Forgetting to convert mm to m before calculating cost per metre
Not showing working

assessment.type: Mathematical skills question within the written paper (at least 15% of the paper)

lessons.title: Ratio, proportion, scale and data handling
objectives: I can use scale and ratio in drawings and models
I can read and interpret data from charts and tables
misconceptions: Applying a scale factor to only one dimension
Misreading a graph axis
Confusing ratio with fraction

assessment.type: Mathematical skills question within the written paper (at least 15% of the paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Area of a rectangle = length x width.
Area of a circle = pi r squared.
Volume of a cuboid = length x width x height.
Volume of a cylinder = pi r squared x height.
Cost = quantity x unit price, with units matched before calculating.
Percentage waste = (waste / total material) x 100.
1 m = 1000 mm; 1 m squared = 1 000 000 mm squared.
A scale of 1:5 means the drawing is one fifth of the real size.
Applying a scale factor must be done to every dimension consistently.
A ratio compares quantities; a fraction expresses a part of a whole.
The mean of a data set is the total divided by the number of values.
The range is the highest value minus the lowest value.
Graph axes and units must be checked before values are read.
At least 15% of the D&T written paper assesses mathematical skills.

weeks.unit: Scientific knowledge in Design and Technology

lessons.title: Forces, motion and material behaviour
objectives: I can apply the science of forces and moments to a product
I can explain material behaviour in scientific terms
lessons.specRef: AQA 8552 scientific knowledge (at least 10% of the paper)
misconceptions: Confusing elastic with plastic deformation
Forgetting to use perpendicular distance when calculating a moment
Confusing stress with force

assessment.type: Scientific knowledge question within the written paper (at least 10% of the paper)

lessons.title: Electricity, energy and thermal behaviour
objectives: I can apply basic electrical principles to a designed system
I can explain thermal expansion, insulation and conduction in product design
misconceptions: Confusing series and parallel circuits
Rearranging Ohm's law incorrectly
Ignoring thermal expansion in a design

assessment.type: Scientific knowledge question within the written paper (at least 10% of the paper)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A moment is the turning effect of a force: moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot.
A body is in equilibrium when clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.
Stress = force / cross-sectional area.
Strain is the change in length divided by the original length.
Elastic deformation reverses when the force is removed; plastic deformation is permanent.
Fatigue is failure caused by repeated loading well below the material's ultimate strength.
Increasing the cross-sectional area of a member reduces the stress for the same force.
Ohm's law states V = I x R, where V is voltage, I is current and R is resistance.
In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere and voltages add.
In a parallel circuit the voltage is the same across branches and currents add.
Most materials expand when heated and contract when cooled.
Expansion gaps must be designed into structures to prevent buckling.
Good thermal insulators such as polymers and trapped air resist heat transfer.
At least 10% of the D&T written paper assesses scientific knowledge.

weeks.unit: Written paper technique

lessons.title: Section A and B technique: multiple choice and short answer
objectives: I can answer multiple choice questions efficiently
I can give concise, technically precise short answers
lessons.specRef: AQA 8552 Paper 1 Sections A and B
misconceptions: Writing a paragraph for a one-mark 'name' question
Using vague terms such as 'strong' without specifying the type of strength
Leaving multiple choice questions blank

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section A (core technical principles) multiple choice / short answer

lessons.title: Section C technique: design questions and extended responses
objectives: I can plan and answer an extended response with a judgement
I can produce an annotated design solution in exam conditions
misconceptions: Sketching without annotating
Describing rather than evaluating
Not meeting the specification points given in the question

assessment.type: Paper 1 Section C (designing and making principles) short answer, design and extended response

knowledgeComponents.statement: The written paper is 2 hours for 100 marks, so roughly one mark per minute plus checking time.
Section A is 20 marks of core technical principles.
Section B is 30 marks of specialist technical principles.
Section C is 50 marks of designing and making principles.
Multiple choice questions should always be attempted; there is no penalty for a wrong answer.
Eliminating obviously wrong options improves the odds on a multiple choice question.
Short answers should be precise: 'tensile strength' rather than 'strong'.
Answer length should match the mark tariff.
A design answer must address each specification point given in the question.
Annotation must explain materials, dimensions, construction and reasons.
Extended responses are marked in levels and require a supported judgement.
Technical vocabulary is explicitly rewarded in D&T mark schemes.

weeks.dates: Mon 3 May - Fri 7 May 2027 (bank holiday Mon 3 May)
weeks.unit: Design practice: responding to a design context

lessons.title: Analysing a context and writing a brief and specification
objectives: I can analyse an unfamiliar design context and identify user needs
I can write a brief and specification quickly and precisely
lessons.specRef: AQA 8552 3.3.1, NEA Sections A and B
misconceptions: Jumping to a product idea before analysing the context
Writing a specification that is a wish list rather than criteria
Not identifying a specific user

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)
assessment.tariff: Sections A and B: 10 marks each

lessons.title: Rapid idea generation against a context
objectives: I can generate a range of genuinely different ideas quickly
I can evaluate ideas against a specification and select one to develop
misconceptions: Generating variations rather than different ideas
Selecting an idea without justifying against the specification
Producing few ideas and developing none

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Context analysis should identify possible users, environments, problems and opportunities.
A specific user allows a far more focused and higher-scoring design response.
A brief states what will be designed, for whom, and why.
Specification criteria must be measurable and justified.
Constraints include cost, size, materials, skills and time available.
A design opportunity is an unmet need identified through investigation.
Divergent thinking generates many varied ideas; convergent thinking narrows to one.
An evaluation matrix scores each idea against each specification point.
Ideas should differ in function, form or mechanism, not just decoration.
Selection must be justified against the specification and the user's needs.
Recording rejected ideas and why they were rejected is evidence of decision making.
NEA Section C, generating design ideas, is worth 20 marks.

weeks.unit: Preparing for the NEA: what the assessment criteria reward

lessons.title: Understanding the six NEA assessment sections
objectives: I can describe what each NEA section requires and its mark allocation
I can plan how to evidence each section in my portfolio
lessons.specRef: AQA 8552 NEA assessment criteria Sections A-F
misconceptions: Producing a beautiful portfolio that does not address the criteria
Spending all the time on making and neglecting the portfolio
Producing more than the concise portfolio required

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Planning the NEA: time, resources and the portfolio
objectives: I can plan the NEA across the time available
I can plan a concise portfolio of about 20 A3 pages
misconceptions: Underestimating how long making takes
Producing 40 pages when 20 are required
Not securing workshop access and materials in advance

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: The NEA is worth 100 marks and 50% of the qualification.
Section A, identifying and investigating design possibilities, is worth 10 marks.
Section B, producing a design brief and specification, is worth 10 marks.
Section C, generating design ideas, is worth 20 marks.
Section D, developing design ideas, is worth 20 marks.
Section E, realising design ideas, is worth 20 marks.
Section F, analysing and evaluating, is worth 20 marks.
The NEA requires a working prototype AND a concise portfolio of approximately 20 A3 pages.
The NEA should take 30 to 35 hours in total.
A time plan with milestones prevents the making phase being squeezed at the end.
Marks are for meeting the criteria, not for portfolio presentation beyond clarity.
Workshop access, tools and materials must be secured before the making phase begins.
Sections C, D, E and F carry 80 of the 100 NEA marks between them.

weeks.unit: Portfolio and communication skills for the NEA

lessons.title: Producing clear, concise portfolio pages
objectives: I can lay out a portfolio page that communicates clearly
I can write concise, evidence-based commentary
misconceptions: Writing long descriptive passages instead of design reasoning
Including photographs with no explanation
Prioritising decoration over communication

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Photographing and documenting practical work
objectives: I can photograph work in progress to evidence making
I can annotate process photographs to show skill and decision making
misconceptions: Photographing only the finished product
Taking photographs without annotation
Not evidencing the more demanding processes used

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A portfolio page should communicate one clear stage of the design process.
Commentary should explain decisions and reasons, not describe what is visible.
Concise writing is explicitly required: the portfolio should be about 20 A3 pages.
Every photograph should carry a caption or annotation explaining what it shows and why it matters.
Clarity of communication matters more than decorative page design.
Digital and hand-drawn work can both be used in the portfolio.
Process photographs are the primary evidence for Section E, realising design ideas.
Photographs should show the more demanding processes and techniques used.
Photographing at each stage takes seconds and cannot be recreated later.
Evidence of accuracy, such as measurements taken, supports the quality judgement.
A finished-product photograph alone cannot evidence the skill used to make it.
Section E rewards the demand of the processes used and the quality achieved.

weeks.unit: Summer 1 assessment: full written paper practice

lessons.title: Summer 1 assessment: full written paper mock
objectives: I can complete a full 2-hour written paper
I can manage time across all three sections
misconceptions: Spending too long on Sections A and B
Rushing the 50-mark Section C
Not attempting the design question

assessment.type: Full written paper mock

lessons.title: Paper review and preparation for the NEA release
objectives: I can identify my weakest specification areas from the mock
I can prepare practically and organisationally for the NEA
misconceptions: Reviewing by mark rather than by specification area
Not preparing materials and workshop access before the NEA starts
Assuming the NEA context will suit a pre-planned idea

assessment.type: Review and NEA readiness check

knowledgeComponents.statement: The written paper is 100 marks in 2 hours and is 50% of the qualification.
Section C is worth 50 marks, so at least half the exam time should be reserved for it.
A design question in Section C can carry a large share of the marks and must be attempted.
Multiple choice and short answer questions in Section A should be answered quickly.
Sketching in an exam should be quick and clearly annotated, not highly finished.
Reviewing by specification reference identifies gaps more precisely than reviewing by mark.
AQA releases contextual challenges on 1 June in the year before submission.
For summer 2028 exams, the contextual challenges are released on 1 June 2027, at the end of Year 10.
The context cannot be predicted, so a pre-planned product idea is a risk.
Materials, tools and workshop time must be arranged before the NEA making phase.
The NEA must be the candidate's own work, completed under supervised conditions at a centre.
A realistic time plan across Year 10 Summer 2 and Year 11 Autumn is essential.

weeks.unit: NEA launch: the contextual challenges

lessons.title: Interpreting the AQA contextual challenges
objectives: I can analyse each contextual challenge released by AQA
I can identify possible users, problems and opportunities within a context
misconceptions: Choosing a context because it sounds easy rather than because it offers scope
Reading the context as a product specification
Narrowing to a product before exploring the context

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Selecting a context and beginning investigation
objectives: I can select a context and justify my choice
I can begin primary and secondary investigation of client and user needs
misconceptions: Selecting a context without checking the resources available
Beginning research with a product already decided
Collecting research that is never used

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: AQA releases three contextual challenges each year on 1 June.
Only one contextual challenge may be chosen for the NEA.
A context is a broad situation, not a product brief, and must be interpreted.
A good context offers scope for several possible users and problems.
Choosing a context should consider available materials, tools, skills and access to a real client.
Exploring the context before deciding on a product is what Section A rewards.
Section A requires identifying and investigating design possibilities within the chosen context.
Primary research for the NEA includes interviewing the client, observing users and testing existing products.
Existing product analysis examines materials, construction, cost, function and user response.
Research should be analysed, with conclusions drawn, not simply presented.
A real, identifiable client and user produce far stronger evidence than an invented one.
Section A is worth 10 marks and should be concise, typically two to three portfolio pages.

weeks.unit: NEA Section A: investigation

lessons.title: Investigating the client, user and existing products
objectives: I can carry out and analyse client and user research
I can analyse existing products against my emerging requirements
misconceptions: Presenting research without analysing it
Asking questions whose answers cannot influence the design
Ignoring anthropometric data when sizing a product

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Drawing conclusions from research
objectives: I can draw specific conclusions from each piece of research
I can use conclusions to justify specification points
lessons.specRef: AQA 8552 3.3.1, NEA Sections A and B
misconceptions: Ending research with a summary rather than conclusions
Writing conclusions that do not lead to design requirements
Not linking each specification point back to evidence

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Research is only credited when it is analysed and leads to a conclusion.
An interview with the client should produce specific, usable requirements.
Observation reveals needs users cannot articulate themselves.
Existing product analysis should identify what works, what does not, and why.
Anthropometric data gives the body measurements needed to size a product for a user group.
Percentile data (5th, 50th, 95th) is used to design for a range of users.
Ergonomics applies anthropometric data to make a product comfortable and efficient to use.
Each conclusion should state a requirement the product must meet.
A specification point without a research justification scores poorly.
Research should be selective: a small amount, well analysed, beats a large amount presented.
Standards and regulations relevant to the product are legitimate secondary research.
The chain from research, to conclusion, to specification point is what examiners look for.

weeks.unit: NEA Section B: design brief and specification

lessons.title: Writing the design brief
objectives: I can write a design brief that follows from my investigation
I can justify the brief against my research conclusions
misconceptions: Writing a brief that names a product before designing it
Writing a brief unconnected to the research
Making the brief so narrow that design freedom is lost

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Writing the design and manufacturing specification
objectives: I can write a measurable, justified design specification
I can distinguish design specification from manufacturing specification
misconceptions: Writing unmeasurable criteria
Writing a specification with no justification
Confusing the design specification with the manufacturing specification

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A design brief states what will be designed, for whom, why and within what constraints.
The brief should follow logically from the research conclusions.
A brief should describe the problem to be solved, not prescribe the solution.
Justifying the brief means showing which research led to each part of it.
A brief that is too narrow removes the design freedom needed to score well in Section C.
A design specification lists measurable criteria the product must meet.
Each criterion should state a target value, such as 'must support 15 kg'.
Each criterion needs a justification traced to research evidence.
A manufacturing specification adds dimensions, tolerances, materials, components and processes.
The manufacturing specification is written after design development, not before.
The specification is the standard against which the final product is evaluated in Section F.
Section B is worth 10 marks and should be concise and precise.

weeks.unit: NEA Section C: generating design ideas (part 1)

lessons.title: Generating a wide range of initial ideas
objectives: I can generate a range of genuinely different design ideas
I can use design strategies to avoid design fixation
misconceptions: Producing several near-identical ideas
Producing highly rendered ideas instead of many quick ones
Not annotating ideas with materials and construction

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Communicating ideas clearly through sketching and annotation
objectives: I can communicate ideas in 2D and 3D with clear annotation
I can seek and record client feedback on my ideas
misconceptions: Sketching without annotation
Collecting feedback that only praises the ideas
Not recording feedback in the portfolio

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Section C rewards a range of imaginative, workable and different ideas.
Design fixation is avoided by using varied stimulus, changing constraints and working with others.
Quick sketches communicate more ideas in the same time than rendered drawings.
Ideas must be annotated with materials, construction, dimensions and function.
Ideas should be different in concept, not just in surface decoration.
Innovation is rewarded, but ideas must remain workable within available resources.
Both 2D and 3D communication techniques should be evidenced.
Client and user feedback on initial ideas is required evidence in the NEA.
Feedback should be specific and critical to be useful.
Recorded feedback must be shown to have influenced the next iteration.
Section C is worth 20 marks, twice the weight of Sections A and B.
Ideas should be evaluated against the specification before one is selected.

weeks.unit: NEA Section C: generating design ideas (part 2)

lessons.title: Modelling initial ideas to test them
objectives: I can produce quick models to test the form and function of ideas
I can evaluate models against the specification
misconceptions: Making models that test nothing
Modelling only the final idea
Not photographing models for the portfolio

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Evaluating and selecting an idea to develop
objectives: I can evaluate ideas against every specification point
I can justify the selection of one idea to take forward
misconceptions: Selecting a favourite idea without evaluation
Evaluating against only some specification points
Not involving the client in the selection

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Modelling at the idea stage tests form, size, proportion and basic function cheaply.
Card and foam models are quick, cheap and adequate for testing early ideas.
Every model should be photographed and annotated with what it tested and what was learned.
Modelling more than one idea produces better evidence than modelling only the chosen one.
Testing against the specification produces objective evidence for selection.
An evaluation matrix scores each idea against each specification criterion.
Selection must be justified with reference to the specification and to client feedback.
The selected idea may combine strengths from several initial ideas.
Recording why other ideas were rejected is evidence of design decision making.
The client should be consulted at the point of selection.
Selection is the transition from Section C to Section D.
The selected idea must be achievable within the time, skills and resources available.

weeks.unit: NEA Section D: beginning to develop design ideas

lessons.title: Developing the chosen idea through iteration
objectives: I can develop my chosen idea through repeated modelling, testing and refinement
I can record and justify each development decision
misconceptions: Presenting a single development stage
Making changes without recording the reason
Developing appearance only and not function

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Resolving materials, construction and components
objectives: I can resolve the materials, joints and components for my design
I can justify each technical decision
misconceptions: Choosing materials without justification
Selecting joints that cannot be made with available tools
Not producing a cutting list or costing

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Development is the iterative refinement of one idea, not the generation of new ones.
Each development iteration should be driven by a test result or piece of feedback.
Development must address function, ergonomics, materials and construction, not just appearance.
Every development decision must be recorded with its justification.
Models at the development stage should be more accurate than at the idea stage.
Development should continue until the design is fully resolved and ready to manufacture.
Material choices must be justified against properties, cost, availability and the specification.
Joints must be chosen for the forces acting on them and for the tools available.
Standard components reduce making time and improve reliability.
A cutting list records every component with material, dimensions and quantity.
Costing the materials demonstrates commercial awareness.
Section D ends with a resolved design and a manufacturing specification.

weeks.unit: NEA Section D: manufacturing specification, planning and Year 11 handover

lessons.title: Producing a manufacturing specification and working drawings
objectives: I can produce a fully dimensioned working drawing of my design
I can write a manufacturing specification with tolerances
misconceptions: Producing a drawing without dimensions or scale
Omitting tolerances
Producing a drawing another person could not manufacture from

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

lessons.title: Production plan and Year 11 handover
objectives: I can produce a production plan with stages, tools, timings and quality checks
I can plan my Year 11 NEA and revision schedule
lessons.specRef: AQA 8552 3.3.9, 3.3.10, NEA Sections D and E
misconceptions: Writing a production plan with no quality control points
Underestimating manufacturing time
Leaving the whole making phase to the final term

assessment.type: Non-exam assessment (100 marks, 50%)

knowledgeComponents.statement: A working drawing must be fully dimensioned, to scale and in third angle projection.
A working drawing should allow another person to manufacture the product without further explanation.
An exploded view clarifies assembly on a working drawing.
Tolerances must be specified for critical dimensions.
A manufacturing specification lists materials, components, dimensions, tolerances, processes and finishes.
All dimensions are in millimetres and the scale is stated on the drawing.
A production plan sequences every manufacturing stage with tools, equipment and timings.
Quality control points should be built into the production plan at each critical stage.
A risk assessment should accompany the production plan.
Making almost always takes longer than planned, so contingency time is essential.
Section E, realising design ideas, is completed in Year 11 and is worth 20 marks.
Section F, analysing and evaluating, is completed in Year 11 and is worth 20 marks.
The NEA must be submitted in the spring of Year 11 for a summer 2028 examination.
